News.title: ‘Mini-tsunamis’ strike Brit holiday hotspot as sunbathers left fleeing waves and waterfront restaurants flooded
News.content:
A POPULAR beach resort has been hit by a series of mini-tsunamis, forcing holidaymakers to flee the waves.

A sudden change in the sea level led to water flooding Platja de s’Arenal beach and the promenade in Ibiza this morning.



San Antonio waterfront was left covered by seawater which swept away containers, coolers and bars installed for a concert.

A stage prepared for a tribute concert celebrating the music of a famous Spanish rock band was also surrounded by seawater.



San Antonio Town Hall reacted by announcing the cancellation of the 10pm event “for security reasons.”

Weather chiefs had warned of mini-tsunamis, or rissagues as they are known locally, in parts of the Balearic Islands today.



What is a meteotsunami? A meteotsunami is a large, tsunami-like wave driven by extreme weather. It can also be caused by fast-moving atmospheric disturbances, like air pressure. This differs from standard tsunamis which are triggered by underwater earthquakes. Most mini-tsunami waves are under two feet tall but in some rare cases can reach 10-20 feet. They often present similar warning signs such as a receding coast line or a roaring sound from the sea.

In Majorca they affected the ports of Alcudia, Andratx and Soller as well as Port Adriano in the municipality of Calvia which includes resorts like Magaluf.

In Puerto Alcudia the sea swept onto part of the beachfront promenade this afternoon and left holidaymakers having to wade through the water.

It also surprised tourists enjoying drinks at a terrace bar at the back of the beach.



Ciutadella in Menorca was also put on standby with warnings of oscillations in the sea level of up to four feet (1.2 metres) which will remain in place until midnight.

The first mini-tsunami hit the area at just before 8am, with the change in sea level recorded at 86 centimetres or 2.8 feet.

There were no immediate reports of any injuries.

The extreme weather phenomena known in the Balearics as rissagues are caused by sudden atmospheric pressure changes rather than earthquakes or seismic activities and are not new to the islands.

Harbours are the main risk areas.



In July 2018 mini-tsunamis reaching up to five feet flooded coastal roads, beach bars, and restaurant terraces in areas like Alcudia, Andratx, and Porto Cristo as well as snapping boat moorings and dragging vessels out to sea.

Tourists were seen running to avoid getting soaked and potentially knocked over by the strong currents.

News.title: Mum, 31, & daughter, 2, die after being struck by lightning as heartbroken husband says ‘I’ve just lost my best friend’
News.content:
STORM TRAGEDY Mum, 31, & daughter, 2, die after being struck by lightning as heartbroken husband says ‘I’ve just lost my best friend’

A MUM and one of her toddler twins have died after being struck by lightning during a Florida thunderstorm.

Kenya Glasgow, 31, and her daughter Kennedi, 2, were found with burn marks and smoke emanating from their bodies in Margate, close to Fort Lauderdale.



An unnamed male who made the grim discovery called 911 and said that Kenya had two “holes” in her chest.

Heartbroken husband Kam Glasgow paid a moving tribute to his wife and daughter, and said his other toddler, Kensli, now has to grow up without her identical twin.



He said: “I just lost my best friend. My daughter just lost her best friend”.

The horror unfolded shortly before 2.30pm, when a bystander alerted emergency services to the mother and daughter.

He told local news station NBC6: “I told one of the family members we need to slip her over to perform CPR, but she had two holes in her chest.

“The ambulance was coming down the street. I said, ‘They’re here, they’re here,’ and I directed him to the baby, and they took the baby right away and a second ambulance came for the mother.”

Paramedics immediately began attempting CPR, but their efforts were unsuccessful.

Kenya and Kennedi were then rushed to nearby trauma centres.



Police said: “Tragically, despite the life-saving efforts of first responders and medical personnel, both victims were pronounced deceased shortly after arriving at the hospitals.”

Kam lamented the catastrophic “1 in 1.2 million” misfortune of his loved ones being struck by lightning, saying: “S*** can’t be real.”

Reflecting on the tragedy, he said: “After I lost my father a few years ago, I learned a very valuable lesson and that’s to never question God.



“My babies didn’t suffer. I’m hurt we are hurt but if you gotten the chance to feel that beautiful light my wife and daughter brought into your life cherish it.

“It’s there for a reason. It gives us all the blueprint to just love others and always remember it doesn’t take much to be kind.”

Margate police expressed its “deepest condolences to the victims’ family and loved ones during this incredibly difficult time.”

Residents told NBC6 that the fatal Sunday storm began like any other, until lightning struck so close to their homes that it shook their furniture.

After another lightning strike nearby, paramedics rushed a child to a trauma centre.



While thunderstorms frequently hit southern Florida during the summer rainy season from June to September, lightning rarely claims lives.

The odds of being struck are extremely rare, and almost 90 per cent of victims survive.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Until the two deaths this weekend, there had been nine fatal lightning strikes in the US so far this year, according to the National Weather Service.

An investigation into Sunday’s tragedy continues.

News.title: Moment driver smashes into two cars after speeding down wrong side of the road as ‘number of people’ rushed to hospital
News.content:
THIS is the moment a driver smashes into two cars after speeding down the wrong side of the road leaving a number of people in hospital.

Cops scrambled to the collision in Benfleet, Essex, in the early hours of Friday morning.



Shocking dashcam footage shows the heart-stopping moment the vehicles collided on Hart Road just before 1.30am.

A car can be seen travelling down the quiet street as it approaches a bend before the horror unfolded.



Out of nowhere, another motor screeches round the corner as the occupants of the car behind watch on in shock.

The speeding car smashes into the other vehicle head-on and with such force that both cars are briefly thrown into the air.



Both drivers are seen trying to swerve out of the way at the last minute.

An explosion of debris, including one of the car’s tyres, is sent flying across the road on impact as the car that was hit was launched onto the pavement.



The car behind, recording the crash, was also hit by the wreckage and forced to pull over.

Meanwhile, the speeding car skids further down the road with another clip showing severe damage to the front and rear of the vehicle.

The footage circulated online claimed the car hit by the speeding driver was a family travelling home from Southend Airport.

Essex Police say they were called to the incident just before 1.30am on August 21.

The force said a number of people, including drivers and passengers in the vehicles, were injured and received medical treatment.



The extent of their injuries remains unclear.

A spokesperson said: “Essex Police are investigating following a collision in Benfleet in the early hours of Friday morning (21 August).

“Officers were called to the collision involving three vehicles in Hart Road at just before 1.30am.

“A number of people, including drivers and passengers in the vehicles, were injured and received medical treatment.

“Our enquiries are ongoing to understand the circumstances leading up to the collision and we want to hear from anyone who has information or footage which has yet to be shared with us.”



Any witnesses or anyone with information is urged to get in touch with the police quoting incident 0091 of August 21.

News.title: Woman ‘sexually assaulted’ in city centre car park as cops share CCTV of man they want to speak to

News.title: Owners of ‘neglected’ country house used as Wayne Manor in Batman Begins face losing home… because bats moved in
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

BAT CAVE Owners of ‘neglected’ country house used as Wayne Manor in Batman Begins face losing home… because bats moved in

THE owner of a sprawling country house featured in Batman Begins faces losing the iconic home as it becomes overrun by bats.

The Grade I-listed house in Buckinghamshire was used as Wayne Manor in the popular Christopher Nolan superhero film.



Mentmore Towers, Buckinghamshire, has been served a formal listed-building repairs notice following a deterioration it’s condition.

Built between 1852 and 1854, the country house has hosted a number of affluent families, including the Rothschild family.



It is also the only major surviving work of Sir Joseph Paxton – the architect behind the Crystal Palace.

But Mentmore Towers, used in Batman Begins, could face a compulsory purchase order if a licensed bat ecologist is not appointed.



Buckinghamshire Council said the work is “reasonably necessary for the proper preservation” of the building which has faced accusations it has been left to fall into disrepair.

The property has deteriorating roofs, chimneys, rooflights, roof lanterns and leadwork with Historic England describing the condition as “very bad”.



Site photographs on the notice show cracks in walls, broken windows, and ivy clad walls and when the property was visited, bat droppings were found.

In the notice, Bucks Council have said the owners must demonstrate that it is appointing a contractor with a experience of repairing listed buildings.

If no action is taken, the council could seek government approval to acquire the mansion and further legal action.

Three bat-emergence surveys must be completed by August 2027, alongside any necessary Natural England licence and recommendations.

Once work begins, council and Historic England officers must be allowed to inspect it weekly.



Henrietta Billings, director of SAVE Britain’s Heritage, says: “We welcome this action taken by Buckinghamshire Council requiring the current owner to carry out urgent and overdue repairs to this great house.

“We urge the owners, who have owned the building for over 25 years, to step up and undertake immediate repairs.

“This exceptional landmark has been neglected for too long.”

News.title: Fears UK defence chiefs could be targeted by assassination plots as Putin rages over Storm Shadow arsenal on doorstep
News.content:
RAGING Vladimir Putin could target Britain’s defence chiefs after the UK agreed to hand Storm Shadow missile blueprints to Ukraine.

Kremlin mouthpiece Dmitry Peskov blasted Britain for “adding fuel to the fire” before Prime Minister Andy Burnham hit back and said: “Who started the fire? That’s the question, isn’t it?”



Ahead of his first overseas trip since entering No10, Burnham pledged to give Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky information on the British components on Storm Shadow missiles so that Kyiv can manufacture the weapon itself.

Peskov reacted with fury – accusing Britain of “participating” in the war.



It comes days after Russia warned the UK there would be “consequences” over supplying weapons to Ukraine.

Outlining how Putin could retaliate, Brit ex-Army commander Hamish de Bretton-Gordon warned that Russia’s secret service could set its sights on EU defence bosses – including those in the UK.



Pointing to the poisoning of Alexander Litvinenko in 2006 and Sergei Skripal in 2018, Hamish told The Sun: “We have been in a hybrid war with Russia for some time.

“We’ve heard of numerous cyber attacks in the UK and across Europe, a number of sabotage and bombings that have been directly associated to the Russian secret service.

“It seems clear Russian proxies or Russian secret service have been trying to target some key European defence leaders.

“One assumes that might also be the case in the UK. I expect these leaders are well protected… at times of war, people in key positions – their security is absolutely paramount.”



“We know a lot about the Russians, we know how they act, we know that they use their secret service for espionage and assassinations and other subterfuge.

“Those key executives will know that they are potentially targets. I’m sure each individual country will make sure they can do all they can to protect them.

“I expect, although they’ll be concerned, there will also be confidence that these people can be kept safe.”



European defence CEOs supplying weapons to Kyiv have found themselves in the crosshairs of Russian spooks since Putin’s illegal invasion of Ukraine.

Earlier this year, German police foiled an assassination plot targeting Stefan Thumann, the CEO of German drone manufacturer Donaustahl.

They were tipped off by a foreign intelligence service and arrested two suspected attackers who were caught filming his home and company headquarters.

The case was reminiscent of a similar plot against Armin Papperger, the CEO of the German defence giant Rheinmetall, two years ago.

Russia appeared to be targeting him for Rheinmetall’s role in supporting Ukraine’s war effort.



Of the plot, Papperger told DPA news agency: “The jobs have to get done, and anyone who cracks doesn’t belong in a job like this.”

Papperger has had bodyguards ever since and Thumann is now believed to be under police protection.

Germany has been plagued by these threats this month, from a drone laden with explosives being found near a fleet of Ukrainian cargo planes to a stash of Russian-linked weapons being discovered in a Berlin forest.



Britain’s defence chiefs could now find themselves looking over their shoulders as revenge for supplying the Storm Shadow missile blueprints.

Hamish said: “The British Secret Service, MI6 and MI5, and also the police counter-terror organisation will no doubt also be looking at this very, very carefully and very closely.

“And the capabilities of the British Secret Service seem to be rather more effective than the Russians.

“I don’t think anybody will be blasé about this. I’m sure that those leaders of those key companies will make sure that they are protected as best they can be.”

Despite the threats, Hamish said sharing information on Storm Shadows is a “really important step forward” for Ukraine to start building the missiles.



He said: “Because these weapons will be manufactured in Ukraine, they’re much closer to the frontline.

“It will be a really big boost for the Ukrainians, and for the Russians who will understand that they will be under a more direct attack from these highly effective cruise missiles.

“It certainly gives it a significant advantage… they have a very powerful warhead that can penetrate deep underground to destroy ammunition dumps.



“They are a significant addition to the Ukrainians’ military capability – not least because the Russians know that they have great difficulty knocking them down.

“These weapons are the sort of things that hopefully will mean that the Russians will have to stop fighting sooner rather than later.”

It comes amid mounting pressure on Putin’s war machine.

Ukrainian forces have repeatedly pummelled the nation’s equivalent of Amazon and are systemically blasting apart their fuel hubs.

For a third night in a row, Ukrainian drones have blitzed Ozon, Russia’s second-biggest online retailer, in an attempt to bleed Putin‘s war chest dry.



Russia provoking Britain is just ‘tip of the iceberg’ By Jerome Starkey RUSSIA provokes Britain every single day, warns Defence Secretary Wes Streeting. But the goading goes mostly unseen by the public. Hinting at the secret briefings he receives in his new job, Streeting said what is in the public domain is “only the tip of the iceberg”. Speaking to The Sun on a visit to Ukraine, Streeting said: “Incidents like buzzingairspacee or the shooting in the Channel are performative, irresponsible and designed to provoke. “It does at least provide the ­British with a visible manifestation of the day-to-day provocations that we see from Russia every day.” Streeting insisted the only response was to stand up to Russian aggression. Reflecting on Ukraine’s experience, he said: “With tyrants like Putin — if you compromise, they come back for more.” Read more here.

Hamish said; “As Ukraine is attacking Russian factories where they’re making missiles and munitions, one has to assume that Russia will try and do the same.”

Kremlin foreign minister Sergei Lavrov said that Russia would target and “destroy” facilities producing the Storm Shadow missile in Ukraine while accusing the UK of participating in the war.

In a speech in front of St Sofia cathedral in Kyiv, Burnham vowed: “Despite Russia’s outrageous threats to my country, we will continue our support for Ukraine.

“This is the moment to keep up the pressure on Russia, the moment to squeeze their ability to fund this illegal war. The sheer strength of the Ukrainian people is truly awesome.



“The Ukrainian people deserve not just our continued support but our gratitude and respect.”

Speaking alongside Burnham, Zelensky said Ukraine would “not submit” to Russia.

He added: “Ukrainians will not be cobblestones under the feet of tsars and rulers.”

The united front will no doubt be putting Putin and his cronies increasingly under the cosh as they struggle to fund the war.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Hamish said: “I think it’s pretty clear that Putin is in the most difficult position he’s been in his 25 years as president of Russia.



“The hope [is that] issues like Storm Shadow being built in Ukraine will be enough to make Putin see that it is futile to continue this war.”

News.title: Two huge superyachts worth £410MILLION both belonging to US billionaire appear at UK harbour
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

SHIP AHOY Two huge superyachts worth £410MILLION both belonging to US billionaire appear at UK harbour

TWO major superyachts worth a combined £410m have moored up in a popular south coast harbour.

The fleet, which belongs to billionaire American video game developer Gabe Newell, is turning heads in Poole Harbour.



Leviathan and Draak are the latest superyachts to visit the Dorset harbour, renowned for hosting some of the world’s most expensive private boats.

Leviathan, which is 364ft long, was commissioned by Mr Newell and worked on by Dutch boat builders.



Work on the lavish boat began in 2020 and was completed last year.

On board there are 11 suites for up to 26 guests as well as accommodation for its 37 crew.

There is also a communal dining area for up to 54 people on the main deck.

Leisure facilities include a gaming lounge with 15 stations, two racing simulators, a gym, spa, sauna and jacuzzi and a basketball court.



There are also conference facilities on board.

The 5,000 tonne yacht, estimated to be worth a staggering £300million, is powered by a hybrid diesel-electric engine and has a maximum speed of 17 knots.

It is accompanied by Draak, also built by Oceanco, which is 300ft long and has an Oriental themed interior with bamboo, wenge and gold leaf.



The yacht’s facilities include a beach club, spa, gym, sauna, Turkish bath and a 20 square metre swimming pool with jets.

Mr Newell acquired it in 2023 and it is said to be worth £110million.

Poole has deep-water berths, top security and is relatively close to London.

It has also been awarded five gold anchors, the prestigious global marina accreditation scheme managed by The Yacht Harbour Association (TYHA).

Marinas are rated across categories such as ambience, customer service, on-water and onshore facilities and infrastructure.



The Poole Harbour Commissioners hope it will become the UK’s number one marine leisure location.

Earlier this month, the £220million new superyacht Milky Way, which has a 50 sqm swimming pool on board, moored in the harbour.

Poole Harbour is next to the millionaires‘ playground of Sandbanks.

News.title: Organised crime arrests as police investigate A66 crash that killed two officers
News.content:
Twelve people have been arrested as part of the investigation into the A66 crash that killed seven people, including two police officers.

Nine men and three women, aged between 19 and 61, have been arrested across Teesside on suspicion of a range of offences including possession of a firearm and being part of an organised crime group.

In the early hours of Saturday, a Volkswagen Passat that had been pursued by police travelled the wrong way down the A66 near Middlesbrough and crashed into an oncoming police car - two PCs and all five Passat occupants died.

Cleveland Police said it was investigating "serious criminal activity that resulted in this fatal incident".

PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died in the crash, as did Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and 17-year-old Cole Robert Worthy.

Earlier, Cleveland Police released more details of its investigation into the lead-up to the crash and information about the 12 people it had arrested.

The force said:

It received several reports of two vehicles "being driven dangerously" on Saturday morning

The first vehicle, believed to be a Volvo XC60, was seen "ramming properties" in the Middlesbrough area

The second vehicle, a Passat, is believed to have been associated with this activity

Both vehicles were operating with cloned number plates but were picked up by automated number plate recognition technology

The Volvo has been recovered in Middlesbrough

Four of the five people in the Passat had previous convictions

Assistant Chief Constable Wayne Fox said the investigation had been "fast moving and complex".

He said: "The events of that tragic night will have a lasting and profound impact on the Cleveland area and the communities we seek to protect.

"We have a duty to respond to, and thoroughly investigate, the serious criminal activity that resulted in this fatal incident and to bring all those responsible to justice."

News.title: How the deadly A66 crash unfolded leaving seven dead
News.content:
Two police officers and five people within a Volkswagen Passat travelling the wrong way down the A66 motorway were killed after the car collided with a marked police car around 03:30 BST on Saturday.

Using doorbell footage, pictures of the scene and police reports, we can now piece together exactly how this fatal incident unfolded.

We also know that four of the five people in the car had previous convictions. One of them, Makai Saddington, 18, previously pleaded guilty to assaulting a police officer.

PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough were the two police officers who died in the crash.

The BBC's UK correspondent Daniel Sandford explains what we know so far.

More on this story.

News.title: Is UK's Storm Shadow missile a game changer for Ukraine?
News.content:
The UK has handed secret blueprints to Ukraine that will allow the country to build its own long-range cruise missiles.

The announcement came during Andy Burnham's first visit to Kyiv as prime minster, where he met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

But faced with an almost daily barrage of Russian ballistic missiles, correspondent Joe Inwood explains why the offer may not be enough to win the war.

News.title: Charity? Acting? The Cotswolds? What will Harry and Meghan's UK life look like?
News.content:
Within the next few days, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex and their two children will have departed California and become residents of the UK.

Since news broke of the move, there has been some confusion as to what British life for Harry and Meghan will look like - but a picture is emerging of the family's priorities.

Over the weekend, there was a deluge of stories about Meghan's return to acting with speculation she would have a role in the next series of The Gentlemen on Netflix, created by British director Guy Ritchie.

Talks are still said to be in the early stages and we understand filming for the third series of the show is imminent - but Netflix has made no comment on who will star, leaving the way open for a former working member of the royal family with an acting background to be cast.

The comedy is about a duke turned drug baron and is mostly filmed in the Cotswolds.

What is clear is that a return to acting more broadly is very much on the agenda for Meghan. It would be financially lucrative for the family in a world of expensive homes, school fees and international travel.

News.title: World's oceans hit highest temperature on record as El Niño grows
News.content:
The world's oceans are hotter than ever recorded, new data suggests, as they suffer from human-caused climate change and the growing El NiÃ±o weather phenomenon.

The average surface temperature of the planet's seas outside the polar regions hit 21.1C (70F) on Saturday, according to figures from the European Copernicus climate change service.

That edges past the 21.09C recorded on three separate days in March 2024, and is far above average for the time of year.

Warmer oceans can have wide-reaching consequences, including supercharging extreme weather, raising sea levels and harming marine life.

"This record is another clear signal of an ocean under growing stress," said Dr Samantha Burgess, deputy director of Copernicus.

"El NiÃ±o is adding heat to the system, but it is doing so on top of decades of human-driven warming," she added.

News.title: Briton fighting for Russia killed in Ukraine
News.content:
A British national has been killed in Ukraine while fighting for Russia.

Bradley Townsend is said to have died following an attack by a remote-controlled FPV drone in Ukraine's eastern Donetsk region. His death, on 10 June, is believed to be the first of a British citizen fighting for Russia in the conflict.

The 33-year-old left his home in Barnsley, South Yorkshire, earlier this year after telling his family he was going to Romania, according to the Yorkshire Post, external.

The Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) confirmed it was aware of reports a British national had died in Ukraine, adding it was in contact with his family.

The news emerged as Andy Burnham arrived in Kyiv for his first foreign trip as UK prime minister.

The visit coincides with the 35th anniversary of the country's independence from the Soviet Union.

The government has agreed to hand over blueprints for British-made components for the Scalp missile, a French version of the UK's Storm Shadow cruise missile - allowing Ukraine to produce the weapon domestically.

News.title: Police pass Mohamed Al Fayed case file to prosecutors
News.content:
The Metropolitan Police have sent a file of evidence to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) relating to a man in his 80s as part of its investigation into claims of sexual assault against Mohamed Al Fayed.

A man and a woman, both in their 80s, were interviewed under caution last month on suspicion of aiding and abetting rape and sexual assault, and assisting the commission of sexual offences.

The CPS will now decide whether a charge can be made.

Earlier this year, three women, aged in their 40s, 50s and 60s, and one man in his 60s were also questioned. The former Harrods owner died three years ago aged 94 having never faced any charges.

Al Fayed was accused by more than 20 women of sexual assault in a BBC document and podcast that aired in September 2024.

Since those allegations more than 400 alleged victims or witnesses have come forward to lawyers.

A Met Police spokesperson said "detectives submitted a full evidential file" to the CPS for a "charging decision".

"The file relates to one suspect, a man in his 80s, and relates to two indecent assaults on two women in London. Officers will continue to work closely with CPS prosecutors as the case progresses.

"To date, seven suspects have been interviewed under caution on suspicion of offences including aiding and abetting rape and sexual assault, assisting in the commission of sexual offences, and human trafficking for the purposes of sexual exploitation."

Co-chairs of the Justice for Fayed and Harrods Survivors, Jen Mills and Lindsay Mason, welcomed the latest development.

"The submission of a full evidential file to the CPS is a significant step, and it matters most of all for the two women whose allegations are at the centre of it," the statement said.

"Both are members of Justice for Fayed and Harrods Survivors and, as with all those impacted by this scandal, we stand alongside them with love and empathy."

A spokesperson from another Fayed survivor group, No One Above, said: "We call on the Met to confirm it is securing evidence on all perpetrators and co-conspirators - including the financial and documentary evidence of how victims were recruited, screened, moved, harboured and silenced."

Harrods - which was sold by Al Fayed in 2010 - previously told the BBC it was in the process of settling more than 250 claims for compensation.

News.title: Snooker champion Graeme Dott guilty of child sex abuse
News.content:
Former world snooker champion Graeme Dott has been found guilty of child sexual abuse.

The 49-year-old denied two charges of lewd and libidinous behaviour towards a girl and a boy between 1993 and 2010.

During a trial, the High Court in Glasgow heard that Dott had exposed himself and inappropriately touched a primary school girl in the 1990s and attacked a young boy between 2006 and 2010.

Lord Harrower told Dott, who won the World Snooker Championship in 2006, he would be sentenced at a separate hearing in Edinburgh on 29 September.

Dott covered his face with his hands and shook his head while the verdict was delivered by jurors following a five-day trial.

He previously called the allegations made against him "disgusting".

News.title: Prince Harry steps down from African wildlife charity board
News.content:
The Duke of Sussex has stepped down from the board of an African wildlife charity whose rangers had been found to have committed human rights abuses against indigenous people.

A spokesman for Prince Harry confirmed he was stepping down after being president for the charity, African Parks, for six years before becoming a member of its board of directors in 2023, but said he remains a "supporter of its mission".

Last year the organisation admitted human rights abuses were committed by its rangers in Congo-Brazzaville.

Prince Harry's resignation comes shortly after it was announced he was relocating with the Duchess of Sussex, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet from California to the UK.

Prince Harry's spokesman said "the Duke is proud of his 10 years with African Parks and fully supports the ongoing strengthening of its board.

"His commitment to conservation in Africa continues, and he remains a supporter of African Parks' mission."

African Parks manages around 20 national parks and protected areas across 12 countries.

It was subject to an independent human rights investigation into allegations guards managed and paid by the charity had beaten, raped and tortured indigenous people in the Odzala-Kokoua National Park.

The charity said in 2025 it had improved its safeguarding processes both in the Odzala-Kokoua National Park and institutionally.

Announcing a "governance refresh of its board of directors", the charity thanked Prince Harry for his association, saying he had "brought global attention to the urgent need for biodiversity protection for the benefit of people and wildlife, and has contributed greatly to promoting philanthropy for the cause of conservation in Africa".

It added: "The duke remains deeply committed to this cause, and remains a strong supporter of African Parks' work."

The charity's website says Prince Harry served as part of the expert team that helped implement the first phase of the 500 Elephants project, which was "one of the largest and most significant elephant translocations in conservation history".

It saw wildlife experts move elephants from a park in Malawi to help increase population in areas where they have been heavily poached.

Prince Harry has said helping move elephants to safer homes was an "amazing" experience.

The Sussexes are back in the spotlight after the revelation last week they were returning to the UK this month after enrolling their children to start at a British school in September.

No change is expected to the official status of Prince Harry and Meghan and they will remain as private individuals.

Their pending return to the UK has raised questions on their security arrangements.

Last year, Prince Harry lost a legal challenge over the levels of security he and his family are entitled to while in the UK.

It is unclear what provisions will be made for their security once they return to the UK.

The couple's plans while they are in the UK are also unclear.

The BBC learned the Duchess of Sussex was in talks to return to acting with a role in Netflix series The Gentlemen, which would be her first significant acting role since her marriage to Prince Harry.

In early 2020, the Sussexes left the UK and stepped back from their royal duties before settling in California in March that year.

News.title: Victims describe 'house of terror' abuse by mother, grandmother and stepfather
News.content:
A mother, grandmother and stepfather who subjected three children to years of abuse in a "house of terror" have avoided jail.

Shirley Freeman, Julia Stephen and David McColl's victims were beaten, starved and psychologically tormented between 2003 and 2012.

Freeman, 51, and Stephen, 69, were earlier found guilty of cruel and unnatural treatment. McColl, 50, admitted the crimes.

At Aberdeen Sheriff Court, Sheriff Craig Findlater said no sentence could "repair the awful childhoods" of the trio's victims.

Warning: This article contains descriptions of child abuse

Freeman was sentenced to 18 months probation, 240 hours of unpaid work, and a 12-month restriction of liberty order, as a direct alternative to custody.

Stephen was ordered to carry out 150 hours of unpaid work and given 18 months probation.

And McColl was sentenced to 220 hours of unpaid work, 18 months probation, and an 11-month restriction of liberty order.

News.title: Race Across the World star dies year after son
News.content:
A former Race Across the World contestant has died, a year after her son and co-star's death in a car crash.

Jo Gardiner, 61, died "following a long and courageous battle with cancer", her family said.

Gardiner, a physiotherapist from Manchester, travelled across South America with her son Sam in the second series of the BBC show, which aired in 2020.

Her family said she was "one of a kind" who "lived fully, fiercely and never did anything by halves".

News.title: Boy died after leaping from window, inquest finds
News.content:
A coroner has concluded that a five-year-old boy died after he leapt from the 15th floor of a tower in the belief he could fly, owing to his autism and inability to assess risk.

Aalim Ahmed died instantly when he fell from a kitchen window, which could tilt and turn, at a residential block in Plaistow, east London, on 16 May 2024.

Contrasting accounts about the condition of the windows were heard at the inquest into the boy's death.

Delivering a narrative conclusion, assistant coroner Ian Wade said that while the window was "compromised", there was "no compelling reason why a landlord should've considered that placing this little boy on the 15th floor was inappropriate".

The inquest had heard that an engineer sent by Newham Council in December 2023 to carry out an inspection and look at overhauling the windows and handles, found they were functioning when he saw them.

In contrast, the boy's mother, Sahra Osman, had a list of complaints spanning several months that included her fears the windows were opening too wide and she did not have a key, the court was told.

She previously said she was "horrified" when Newham Council put them in the top-floor flat, which needed repairs, and said the authority "could have prevented this tragic thing from happening".

The council was exonerated from culpability by the inquest.

In a statement, councillor John Gray from Newham Council said: "This was a tragic accident which resulted in the heartbreaking death of a young five-year-old child.

"Our thoughts continue to be with Aalim's family and friends during this incredibly difficult time.

"We are grateful to the coroner Ian Wade KC for his thorough and fair hearing of the facts of this case, which have at times been very difficult to hear and revisit.''

News.title: Rail companies sued for £5m over oil spill caused by derailment
News.content:
Network Rail is suing two rail companies for more than Â£5m after a fuel spill caused by a train derailment threatened an "environmental disaster" at a designated site for protection.

The body filed a legal claim earlier this month against DB Cargo UK and Touax Rail over the derailment near Llangennech, Carmarthenshire, in August 2020.

The incident saw 10 wagons of the 25-wagon train derail, causing 446,000 litres of fuel to spill, and about 300 people had to leave the area due to the blaze.

In High Court documents, Network Rail claimed that the derailment occurred because the wagon had "not been maintained with reasonable care" and is seeking damages for negligence.

No one was injured, but 116,000 litres of fuel ignited while 330,000 litres drained into surrounding wetlands, which form part of a Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) and a Special Area of Conservation.

The Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB) concluded in January 2022 that the derailment was caused by a set of wheels on one of the wagons locking, likely the result of a brake defect after "inadequate maintenance practices" were found in the investigation.

Network Rail, which owns, operates, maintains and develops Britain's railways, claimed that the derailment occurred because the wagon had "not been maintained with reasonable care" by Touax.

News.title: Teen pleads guilty over Channel boat with 165 migrants
News.content:
A teenager who piloted a dinghy carrying a then-record 165 migrants across the English Channel to the UK has pleaded guilty to endangering others during a sea crossing.

Chan Mathok Atak, 19, originally from South Sudan, admitted the offence at Canterbury Crown Court in relation to a crossing on 23 July.

Rescuers said they were astonished and alarmed to see the number of people packed onto the dinghy.

It was said to have been about the same length as a bus before it began deflating in the world's busiest shipping lane.

News.title: Graduate job vacancies drop by almost 50% in a year, survey suggests
News.content:
The number of graduate jobs has fallen almost in half in the past year, according to new figures, as employers cut entry-level roles in favour of AI and battle rising costs.

Jobs website Adzuna said it had just 8,383 graduate vacancies listed in July, down from 15,397 at the same point last year.

Adzuna also found competition among job seekers across all levels is rising, with an average of 2.14 job seekers per vacancy in July, up from 1.93 a year earlier.

However, some have said the data might not be reflective of the whole graduate job market and may instead suggest a shift in the way the roles are advertised.

Businesses have said employer national insurance and minimum wage hikes have made hiring more expensive, particularly for junior staff.

The number of graduate vacancies listed hit its lowest level since Adzuna started recording such data in 2016. The firm pointed to a peak for graduate roles in 2017, when it had more than 55,800 listed on its website. That is more than six times the number of roles listed on the site in July.

Andrew Hunter, the co-founder of Adzuna, said the figures show "employers still haven't found a reason to open up hiring" for recent graduates.

But graduate jobs expert Charlie Ball said the numbers might not be as bad for graduates as they first appear.

He said they could instead suggest that firms are advertising fewer roles specifically for graduates, even if the roles themselves still exist and end up being filled by graduates.

From his experience in the sector, Ball said the graduate market has "not collapsed" but added: "We know the graduate jobs market is weak. We know it's not in great shape."

Official figures show the UK's youth unemployment rate - which covers 16-to-24-year-olds - was 16.2% in the three months to March 2026. The number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) is now over one million.

Young people have told BBC News previously they have applied for hundreds of jobs before even receiving a response.

They also expressed frustration at the growing number of employers using AI to screen applications.

Former government minister Alan Milburn is leading a major review of the youth unemployment crisis. He has previously said the number of entry-level jobs is shrinking, as is the number of part-time jobs traditionally filled by teenagers and students.

The Adzuna data also showed vacancies for jobs in travel, teaching and construction rose in recent weeks.

But sectors including healthcare, nursing, hospitality and logistics posted fewer vacancies.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently changed the rules for public contracts so that companies bidding for them have to show how they will create jobs and training opportunities.

A government spokesperson said on Monday: "The latest figures show there are 253,000 more people in work than this time last year with unemployment continuing to fall.

"We are determined to go further to restore opportunity for young people through our Â£2.5bn youth employment package which will deliver almost one million opportunities to earn or learn."

News.title: Sharing dangerous driving videos is 'truly reprehensible', PM says
News.content:
The government has urged social media companies to remove posts celebrating dangerous driving, as Prime Minister Andy Burnham branded sharing them "truly reprehensible".

Earlier Defence Minister Luke Pollard told BBC Breakfast that "social media companies could take the content down easily and adjust their algorithms to stop it being distributed".

Two police officers died when a car going the wrong way down a dual carriageway crashed into their vehicle near Middlesbrough on Saturday. Five passengers in the other car were also killed.

A TikTok account believed to belong to one of the five passengers, 18-year-old Makai Saddington, previously shared videos appearing to show dangerous driving, which have since been removed.

But Cleveland Police said "there is no evidence to indicate that filming of the activities that took place on Friday night and Saturday morning has taken place for the purposes of TikTok".

Prime minister Andy Burnham has hit out at President Vladimir Putin during his first state visit to Kyiv, amid mounting tensions between Russia and the UK.

The British leader chaired his first meeting of the so-called Coalition of the Willing to emphasise Britain’s continued support for Ukraine through the provision of long-range missile blueprints.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said that the move would add “fuel to the fire” and “prevent any progress in the peace process”.

“Who started the fire? That’s the question isn’t it?” Burnham hit back in an address to Ukraine’s European allies on Monday.

“Putin is now hoping he can win through a campaign of terror using ballistic missiles against Ukrainian civilians.

“This can never be the route to victory, and we need to be clear in sending that message. It means doing everything we can all do, and working with our allies as well, beyond this coalition, to dig into our own stocks of air defence... to protect Ukraine from the missiles that are falling now.”

open image in gallery Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky, right, greets British Prime Minister Andy Burnham during a ceremony to mark Independence Day in Kyiv ( AP )

Both Zelensky and Burnham delivered speeches outside Kyiv’s St Sofia cathedral on the anniversary of the country’s 35th year of independence.

“Despite Russia’s outrageous threats to my country, we will continue our support for Ukraine,” he said.

The prime minister compared Ukraine’s battle with Russia to the British fight against Nazi Germany, saying: “My nation kept the flame of European freedom alive in the 20th century, you hold that flame in the 21st.”

It marked his first foray on the international stage, heading the coalition of the willing group of 34 countries, that was set up by his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer in support of Ukraine.

Tensions between London and Moscow have been mounting for weeks with it emerging over the weekend that Russia had withdrawn its ambassador to the UK, Andrei Kelin, last month after seven years in the diplomatic post.

The lower-ranking charge d’affaires has taken the lead in his absence, according to an embassy spokesperson who spoke to The Times.

open image in gallery President Zelensky has warned his country faces a tough winter without further support from allies ( Reuters )

The latest announcement of support by Burnham means that the British government has agreed to allow defence firm MBDA to release classified information and blueprints on UK components for the long-range Scalp missile. The weapons are the equivalent of the French-produced version of the UK’s storm shadow.

Last Tuesday it was reported that British-made drones had been used in Ukraine prompting Moscow to threaten “consequences” for the support. It said ominously that the deeper the assistance that Britain provided “the higher price it will pay”.

At the time, Burnham doubled down saying: “This is the UK doing what it has long said it would do, which is to support Ukraine 100 per cent against this illegal war led by Vladimir Putin.”

The European Commission, meanwhile, has approved a further €6.1 billion ($7.12 billion) in financial aid for Ukraine for the purchase of defence systems, such as air defence, missiles, ammunition and radars.

open image in gallery Russia has warned that the UK will suffer ‘consequences’ for supporting Ukraine ( Reuters )

The latest aid package came on top of €16 billion of previously approved procurement plans, of which €8.35 billion had already been disbursed, according to the EU.

"As Russia intensifies its attacks, we are stepping up to help Ukraine protect its people and defend its skies. Europe stands with Ukraine and we will deliver what it needs, when it needs it," president Ursula von der Leyen said in a statement.

In other developments in the ongoing war, Russian attacks killed three people near Kharkiv overnight, according to the region’s governor, while Moscow claimed debris from a Ukrainian drone killed two children in Russia’s Krasnodar on Sunday.

Sandra Bullock has said she feared developing “a little bit of a mental issue” if she continued acting while caring for her late partner Bryan Randall.

Randall, Bullock’s partner of eight years, died in 2023 after being diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis in 2020, an incurable nervous system disease in which the brain gradually loses its connection with the muscles.

Speaking about his death on Monday’s episode of the SmartLess podcast, Bullock admitted that she was concerned for her mental health while juggling filming the 2022 action movie The Lost City with caring for Randall and looking after her two children, Louis, 16, and Laila, 12.

“When Bryan got sick, after Lost City, I was like, ‘I can't.’ I thought I was going to have a little bit of a mental issue. I was like, ‘I can't, I can't, I can't,’” she said.

The actor explained that when she returned to the movie set in the Dominican Republic for reshoots, she was exhausted from her caregiving responsibilities.

open image in gallery Bryan Randall and Sandra Bullock were together for eight years before his death in 2023 ( Getty )

open image in gallery Sandra Bullock has said she feared developing ‘a little bit of a mental issue’ if she continued acting while caring for her late partner Bryan Randall ( Getty )

“I came for the reshoot on a couple of hours' sleep and I remember walking in and everyone went, ‘What, what, did you not sleep?!’” she recalled.

“I looked so bad, and when I say so bad, like my face, it was horrific. I could maybe manage four hours of the reshoot and they were like, ‘Can you just give us [another take]?’ I was like, ‘I can't, I can't, I've got to go home.’ And I went home.”

The star continued: “The amount of money they had to spend to fix my face to match the rest of the film digitally. It was a horror show.”

The 62-year-old said she then decided to take a break from acting, adding: “So I did that and then I just pulled the plug. I said I can't anymore. I have nothing to give right now. Nothing. Zero.”

Randall, a model-turned-photographer, met Bullock in 2015 after she hired him to photograph her son Louis’ fifth birthday party. They were together for eight years.

Bullock revealed that Randall had requested she keep his diagnosis private, but she found it isolating not to talk to anyone about it apart from telling her sister, Gesine Bullock-Prado.

Bullock said she told herself, “Oh, I can handle that. I can be quiet.” But caring for Randall while raising her two young children during the pandemic ultimately became “a trifecta that was pretty dark,” she said.

“I started grieving Bryan four years before he passed. Something in me said, ‘Start grieving now’ because I knew I would be the caregiver,” the Practical Magic 2 star continued.

open image in gallery Sandra Bullock was filming the 2022 movie ‘The Lost City’ while caring for her partner Bryan Randall ( AFP/Getty )

“I could see that the bright eyes that I knew – there was something that had shifted. It was a traumatic diagnosis.

“My person left a lot earlier than the body left. I don’t think I ever dealt with that until after he passed, because you’re just on this treadmill,” she said.

Bullock gave further insight into the care that Bryan received, sharing that she hired four male nurses to provide round-the-clock help for him, and hired a children’s therapist specializing in dealing with terminal illness and grief to work with her kids.

“The guys, they were like four big brothers in my kitchen and we became students at the same time,” she said, explaining that she separated part of her house for Randall to receive his care, and that she required all visitors to take multiple Covid-19 tests.

“I found four men who were strong enough – Bryan was 6ft 2in,” she explained of the nurses, adding that finding the right people while keeping Randall’s diagnosis a secret was “the most covert CIA operation known to man.”

“The understanding that I now have of caregiving… those who are in the caregiving position, I was left alone. I didn’t know what to do; I didn’t know who to call. I am so grateful to them,” she said.

Disney’s latest collaboration with the NFL has officially been released and football fans are less than thrilled.

Announced in July, the Disney and Champion NFL Collection pairs all 32 NFL teams with characters from Disney, Star Wars, Marvel and Pixar.

The first eight pairings were revealed with the initial collaboration announcement at Fanatics Fest NYC and included the Buffalo Bills and the Beast from Beauty and the Beast, the Dallas Cowboys and Woody from Toy Story, and the Las Vegas Raiders and Star Wars’ Darth Vader.

The merchandise collection became available for purchase online Monday, with the full slate of pairings released to the disappointment of NFL fans hoping for a different happy ending.

“@Disney and @packers did anyone even try with our shirts? Atrocious. Everyone gets cool slogans and designs and I get Chewbacca (not even classic Pixar/disney) with packers at bottom. HORRIBLE!!!!!!!!!!!” one fan wrote on X while another said, “With so many possibilities is this the best they came up with? NFL and Disney really dropped the ball here.”

open image in gallery Disney's latest collaboration with the NFL has been released ( Disney Consumer Products )

“Kinda disappointed. I was so looking forward to this collab but felt that the ones you showcased to present the collab got the best representation then just half-assed it the rest of the way,” another fan wrote as someone agreed, “Whoever was in charge of assigning the Disney characters to the NFL teams must be fired because wtf is this s***?”

“The Seahawks getting the seagulls from Nemo is laughable. Literally Super Bowl champs and didn’t even get a character that says more than 1 word,” someone else added while another wrote, “Pretty underwhelming tbh… some teams got incredible selections while others got the short end of the stick.”

Other fans voiced disappointment over pricing and sizes, with one writing on X, “Hey @NFL @Disney how about offering plus sizes above a 2x/3x :))) Most of your players can't even fit in these sizes friends. Sincerely, a disappointed, plus size football and Disney fan.”

Another agreed, writing, “Hey @NFL and @Disney, we didn’t think to put the new NFL Disney collab on toddler and infant sizes? You missed out big! A lot of parents and grandparents would have spent big. If I’m missing something please inform me where I can get! I See nothing but youth sizes.”

“@NFL @Disney wtf is this robbery? 65 dollars for 3 pair of socks? So 70+ with tax for socks. That's just outrageous and scummy. #nfl #disney,” someone else wrote.

open image in gallery C. J. Mosley (left), Wayne Chrebet, Buzz Lightyear and NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell spoke onstage during the Disney Fan Draft at Fanatics Fest NYC 2026 ( Getty )

The Independent has contacted Disney, the NFL, and Champion for comment.

When the collaboration was announced, Bret Healey, Disney’s Director of Graphic Design at Disney Consumer Products, said in a statement, “Today’s consumers view fandom as an extension of personal style, and this collection was designed with that mindset from the start.

“Each piece transforms team affiliation into something expressive, collectible and culturally relevant.”

The release comes just weeks ahead of the September 9 start of the 2026-2027 NFL season when the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks will host the New England Patriots.

On the 35th anniversary of Ukraine’s independence from the Soviet Union (ie Russia), one distinguished guest in Kyiv was the British prime minister, Andy Burnham. He follows a long line of British politicians travelling to meet Volodymyr Zelensky and restate the UK’s loyalty to their cause.

But this was more than a purely symbolic gesture – and it tells us much about the emerging style and substance of Mr Burnham’s foreign policy.

The ostensible reasons for visiting the Ukrainian capital are perfectly in order. There is a meeting of the “coalition of the willing” to attend, as co-chair with France, of this ad hoc Western alliance.

This national birthday is a significant one, given the circumstances, and it would be hard to say “no” to any invite from the embattled Ukrainians. But Kyiv is also “not Washington”.

It is telling that Burnham did not choose to make a visit to DC his first foreign trip as prime minister, which has always tended to be the aim of most incoming premiers, at least where practicable.

It doesn’t take much diplomatic nous to see the logic for giving the Americans a miss. Burnham isn’t a natural soulmate of Donald Trump, and he will be conscious of the ultimate fate of Sir Keir Starmer’s initially successful bid to be the “Trump whisperer”.

Burnham is also more sensitive to the climate of opinion about the Trump administration, both within the Labour Party and across Britain more generally, which is increasingly hostile, if not appalled. There is no significant diplomatic, economic or political benefit for Mr Burnham or the UK in paying immediate obeisance to President Trump, especially while he is wrecking the world economy and waging a vicious trade war against Canada.

The downside of the prime minister being humiliated, Zelensky-style, in some ambush in the Oval Office is also all-too obvious. One stray remark about immigration and it would be curtains for what little is left of the special relationship. A gift to Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage, an encounter with Mr Trump is not without risk.

Mr Burnham is also keen to demonstrate continuity of policy on the Ukraine war – he is the fifth British leader Mr Zelensky has had to deal with since the full-scale invasion in 2022. If anything, Mr Burnham is perhaps even more actively pro-Ukraine than his predecessor.

The significant news from the multinational talks in Ukraine is that Britain, with France, is to take a step forward in arming Ukraine and helping the war effort. So Mr Burnham has agreed that the defence firm MBDA can release classified information on UK componentry for the long-range missile, SCALP, as Ukraine looks to establish local assembly lines.

MBDA is a joint defence manufacturer controlled by Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Spain; and SCALP is the alternative name for the Storm Shadow long-range ballistic missile, a weapon that Ukraine has used to great effect with strikes against Russian industrial, defence and infrastructure targets deep into enemy territory.

The UK will also continue its joint leadership with France of the “coalition of the willing” and Britain’s “100-Year Partnership” with Ukraine. The coalition is committing £25bn in funding, including £16bn in military assistance, and £5.6bn in non-military support. Mr Burnham also wants to find alternatives to the US Patriot missiles to counter Russian bombardments. UK-made drones have also just seen action in Russia.

Nonetheless, British “war aims” do seem to have gradually changed since the early unconditional support offered by Boris Johnson. The “maximalist” expression of British ambitions on behalf of Ukraine probably reached a zenith during Liz Truss’s brief premiership when she declared, in October 2022: “Ukraine can win, Ukraine must win, and Ukraine will win.”

Since then, the war has dragged on and Mr Trump has returned to the White House – and that stance has quietly evolved into one which has had to accommodate attempts at agreeing a ceasefire and peace talks, albeit fruitlessly. So British support remains staunch, but no longer explicitly pinned on Ukrainian victory in the sense of regaining all the territory lost since 2022 or the first invasion in 2014. As Mr Burnham puts it: “Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve. We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace.” That is not the same as winning the war.

The signs are that Mr Burnham is in no rush to meet Mr Trump, and he may limit his foreign exposure to events and issues where he has to be present and exert leadership. He seems much more focused on the domestic agenda than his predecessor, and in Ed Miliband he has a foreign secretary with ample political experience and ability.

Mr Miliband has made it his business to build a relationship with the sanest man in the administration (a small field), the secretary of state Marco Rubio, also a plausible successor to Mr Trump. Mr Miliband, who has also been organising international resistance to illegal Israeli settlement in the occupied West Bank, will be pushing the climate change agenda and taking on Britain’s challenging post-Brexit quest for a role. Mr Burnham will concentrate on the economy, public services and migration.

After “never here Keir”, welcome to “always around Andy”.

Taiwanese prosecutors charged nine people Monday, including one from Nvidia and two from Super Micro, for illegally exporting “high-end AI servers” to mainland China, adding another wave of turbulence in the AI ​​rivalry between China and the United States.

AI infrastructure, including advanced semiconductors mostly made in Taiwan, has become a key point of competition between the U.S. and China. Washington began imposing restrictions on Nvidia’s exports of advanced chips to China in 2022 and tightened them in subsequent years. In April 2025, the U.S. required licenses for exports of Nvidia’s H20 chips to China, before allowing some sales to resume later that year.

Under export controls, any sale by Nvidia of high-end AI servers — the computer infrastructure that houses the chips needed to power AI systems — requires a strict review process, according to a document from Keelung District Prosecutors' office in Taiwan. The document also said purchases of more than eight high-end AI servers require company staff to conduct on-site checks to the clients.

Prosecutors said the servers involved were graphics processing units known as “B300,” which have been banned from sale to China.

“We will work with the Taiwan authorities to help them resolve the allegations as quickly as possible,” Nvidia spokesperson Patrick Rutherford said in a written statement.

Super Micro said in a written statement that the arrests of two of its former employees were due to its cooperation with the Taiwanese authorities and the company will continue to work to “enhance its robust export compliance program to protect American innovation."

Seventy-four servers arrived in China successfully, according to the prosecutors. Of those, 50 were sent through Indonesia, 16 delivered directly to China and eight sent to Japan first, then Hong Kong, before they landed in mainland China.

Another attempt involving 56 servers failed, and the servers remain in Taiwan, said the prosecutor's office.

Prosecutors are seeking the maximum five-year sentences for four of the nine defendants, including Chang, an Nvidia manager identified just by his family name. Chang was the “key figure” responsible for “authorizing the release of the B300 GPUs” in this case but “demonstrated a clearly poor attitude following the offense,” the document said.

Some of the defendants set up a company in Japan, which helped successfully transfer eight of the servers, prosecutors said. Some allegedly created fake websites and falsified information to evade export restrictions.

News.title: How the No. 2 pencil became a staple of American schools
News.content:
Your support helps us to tell the story Read more Support Now From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. The Independent is trusted by Americans across the entire political spectrum. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it. Your support makes all the difference. Read more

For generations of Americans, the sharpened No. 2 pencil has long symbolized youth and growing up. Still a staple of back-to-school shopping lists, it helps children trace their initial letters, erase their mistakes and doodle in the margins during moments of daydreaming.

For decades, clammy hands clutched the ridged yellow wood on exam day. "Bring two sharp No. 2 pencils," generations of Americans were instructed, as they readied themselves to fill in answer bubbles on the SATs and additional standardized tests that could shape their futures. Whether Scantron devices genuinely required No. 2 markings remains open to debate, but those were nonetheless the set rules.

The writing instrument was not invented in the United States, yet American industry and innovation made it iconic.

For decades, clammy hands clutched the ridged yellow wood on exam day ( AP Photo/Dario Lopez-Mills )

“The idea of painting a pencil yellow and putting an eraser on top is specifically American,” says Caroline Weaver, a pencil historian and author of “The Pencil Perfect: The Untold Story of a Cultural Icon.” Until the mid-1800s, pencils in America had no eraser, and the eraserless pencil is still standard in the rest of the world.

One of America's early pencilmakers was John Thoreau, father of Henry David Thoreau. The writer worked for his dad’s Massachusetts pencil company in the mid-1800s before moving to a cabin in the woods and composing “Walden.”

The young Thoreau is credited with pioneering the concept of grading pencils on a scale of 1 to 4, with No. 2 striking a balance of graphite and clay that is dark enough, yet not too smudgy for writing. (“Pencils have never contained lead. This is a myth!” says Weaver.)

The rest of the world uses a similar scale to grade pencils, known as “HB,” measuring hardness and blackness.

The other end of the pencil contains another American invention. The ferrule is a metal piece that has held the eraser for more than a century — except during World War II, when rationing forced a shift to plastic and even cardboard.

In an increasingly digital world, pencils are less commonplace. Most school testing has moved online. Students use laptops and touch screens as early as kindergarten.

But all this tech has produced a backlash. In the age of AI, many schools and colleges are requiring handwritten exams and paper tests to safeguard against cheating — or just to give kids a break from screens.

And so many will pick up a No. 2 — like generations before. In that way, Weaver says, the pencil represents democracy itself. No matter who you are or where you live, you have written with a No. 2, sharpened its point or possibly, in moments of stress or boredom, chewed on one.

News.title: This summer’s wildfire epidemic is one of the worst in decades – so why are deaths so low?
News.content:
Wildfires in Britain and Europe this year are among the worst in decades, yet direct deaths are at some of the lowest levels, according to a Telegraph analysis.

As of early August, 505,683 hectares of land have burned across Europe, forcing the evacuation of more than 360,000 people as uncontrollable flames reach major cities, towns, and villages.

The problem is global – in the US, Nevada declared a state of emergency over the weekend after a wildfire caused more than 42,000 people to evacuate their homes.

But what sets 2026 apart isn’t just the vast areas of land burned, but how few deaths have been caused by the fires.

This summer, just 14 people are reported to have died in European wildfires, the vast majority in a single blaze in Almería, southern Spain.

By comparison, more than 130 people were killed in the summer of 2017 – a toll driven largely by the Pedrógão Grande disaster in Portugal, where more than 60 people died on a single stretch of road.

In 2018, at least 100 others died in a single afternoon in the Mati disaster near Athens, despite total hectares burned that year being roughly a third of current levels.

Since the modern phenomenon of summer wildfires exploded in Europe a decade ago, the direct death toll has broadly trended downward, as the chart below shows.

News.title: Swine flu outbreak in Delhi swamps clinics and hospitals
News.content:
India is battling a surge in H1N1 flu infections, prompting the federal health ministry to step up surveillance and hospital preparedness.

The national capital New Delhi has recorded 1,777 cases this year, almost eight times the number (229) reported during the same period in 2025.

Dr Randeep Guleria, a senior pulmonologist and director of Medanta Medical School, Gurugram, says the H1N1 cases are much higher than reported.

“It’s quite likely that the reported numbers are an underestimate because they depend on how many people are tested,” Guleria said. “If you speak to patients admitted to hospital who test positive for H1N1, you often find that other members of their family have similar symptoms, although they have not been tested.”

“There is a surge and we are seeing a lot of patients. We are testing only those who come to hospital and are more seriously ill,” Guleria said.

H1N1, commonly known as swine flu, is a subtype of influenza A. It is a contagious respiratory infection that can cause fever and cough and in severe cases it can lead to pneumonia and respiratory failure.

Officials at the Indian Council of Medical Research said the rise did not mean the emergence of a new strain of the virus.

The surge comes during India’s rainy season, when seasonal influenza and other respiratory infections typically increase.

Doctors in Delhi say they are seeing more patients with high fevers, persistent coughs and flu-like symptoms, although most cases remain mild.

The H1N1 cases have been reported beyond New Delhi. The metro cities like Mumbai, Chennai and Bangaluru have reported a high number of cases, although the pattern is not uniform across the country.

Doctors in Bangaluru have reported more influenza A infections among children, with some developing pneumonia and respiratory distress.

India’s health minister JP Nadda said there was a need for continued vigilance and robust surveillance. He has asked officials to monitor unusual increases and clusters of cases and ensure hospitals could respond quickly.

“Swine flu (H1N1) can show up through symptoms such as fever, cough, sore throat, headache, runny nose, body aches and fatigue… If you experience these symptoms, seek medical advice at your nearest healthcare centre,” the health ministry said on X.

Delhi’s health minister, Pankaj Kumar Singh, said the capital had enough beds, doctors, medicines and medical equipment to manage the increase. “Delhi is fully prepared to deal with the present health situation,” Singh said.

India has had several waves of H1N1 since the virus emerged globally in 2009.

The infection, commonly called swine flu, became a recurring seasonal respiratory illness after the 2009 pandemic rather than disappearing from circulation.

India recorded 3,320 H1N1 cases and 14 deaths in 2025, according to Ministry of Health data.
