12m ago 14.53 EDT Four of the big summer signings start tonight: Gonzalo Garcia and Cesar Palacios for Fulham, Morgan Rogers and Maxence Lacroix for Chelsea. Share

19m ago 14.47 EDT Billy Munday After a season of struggle and regression, with two head coaches and two spells under a caretaker, there is cautious optimism that this campaign will bring something like stability. Much of that optimism centres around the appointment of Xabi Alonso, an elite manager with something to prove. There is also an expectation that the young players brought in as part of BlueCo’s £1.8bn splurge in recent years are beginning to come into their best years. There is no European football to complicate the schedule and a return to the Champions League by finishing in the top four or five would suffice for now. More importance will be placed on the domestic cups after a season without trophies. Alonso’s squad is more rounded than what Enzo Maresca or Liam Rosenior had at their disposal. Maxence Lacroix and Morgan Rogers bring quality to positions where Chelsea were lacking it – at centre-back and out wide. Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson – the “uncs” as Tosin Adarabioyo has called them – will contribute as much off the pitch as on it. The signing of Marco Palestra, a specialist wing-back, suggests Alonso wants to be tactically flexible. He has used a back four and a back three in pre-season. Premier League 2026-27 preview No 6: Chelsea Read more Share

19m ago 14.46 EDT John Brewin Marco Silva cutting the cord after five years by the river came as little surprise. If his time at Craven Cottage was successful in re-establishing Fulham as a Premier League club, he rarely concealed his ambitions to manage in European competition. He was frequently explicit in his disappointment that the club’s ownership did not meet him halfway by funding a stronger squad. Silva’s powers of rebadging and replenishing talent will be missed now that he has decamped to Benfica. Under him, Fulham played entertaining football, a collection of ugly ducklings showing their renewed worth for a club that, despite falling short of European qualification, looked upwards rather than downwards at the relegation battle. They were often a pleasure to watch, and ornery opposition for all-comers. Álvaro Arbeloa is a very different type of appointment, with far less experience than his predecessor in frontline coaching terms, even if he arrives with Real Madrid on his CV. His arrival, though, has opened up a working relationship with the Spanish aristos, Gonzalo García and César Palacios arriving to work with a coach who helped them through the ranks in Madrid. By little coincidence, all three share the same agency as their representatives. There have been links with Endrick and Thiago Pitarch, two further young Real jewels, leading to a sense of Fulham becoming some form of Madrileño nursery, a Santiago Bernabéu on Thames. Should that play out, it would represent another sea change. Premier League 2026-27 preview No 10: Fulham Read more Share

1h ago 14.04 EDT Team news Fulham (4-2-3-1) Leno; Castagne, Bassey, Cuenca, Robinson; Iwobi, Berge; Bobb, King, Palacios; Garcia. Subs: Lecomte, Tete, Reed, Rodrigo Muniz, Kevin, Charles, Sessegnon, Smith Rowe, De Fougerolles. Chelsea (3-4-2-1) Sanchez; Acheampong, Lacroix, Colwill; Gusto, James, Lavia, Hato; Palmer, Rogers; Joao Pedro. Subs: Penders, Barco, Pedro Neto, Fernandez, Bynoe-Gittens, Welbeck, Quendal, Chavarria, Estevao. Referee John Brooks. Share Updated at 14.57 EDT

1h ago 14.03 EDT Jacob Steinberg It is a necessary reset. Although it would be pushing it to say that Chelsea have switched from development centre to retirement home, even after the signings of Jordan Henderson and Danny Welbeck, there has been a clear shift in strategy this summer. Some grownups are in the room at last and, for Xabi Alonso, the hope is that bringing in more experience will help a squad still packed with youngsters show more composure when adversity strikes. Discipline was a problem for Chelsea last season: they had 11 red cards in all competitions and a lot of the wounds were self-inflicted. Chelsea were impetuous, on the receiving end of too many bookings for dissent and prone to collapsing at the first sign of trouble. No wonder Alonso, who was the epitome of calm during his playing career, has focused on maintaining “emotional control” before opening his tenure as manager with Monday’s trip to Fulham. It will be a test of Chelsea’s mentality. Craven Cottage has been the setting for some spectacular implosions during the BlueCo era, the path to two 2-1 victories for Fulham over their neighbours smoothed by João Félix earning a red card on his Chelsea debut in 2023 and by Marc Cucurella getting himself sent off after 22 minutes last season. Chelsea change course with Alonso primed to banish the chaos of youth Read more Share

Sports.title: ‘Enough is enough’: players pile pressure on under-fire Gianni Infantino to resign
Sports.content:
A group of influential current and former footballers have added to the pressure on Gianni Infantino by calling for change at the top of Fifa, saying “enough is enough” in a statement shared widely across social media.

The intervention is particularly significant given some of those behind its circulation have undertaken ambassadorial activities for Fifa as part of its “Fifa Legends” programme. Among them is the former Manchester United and Arsenal defender Mikaël Silvestre, who also sits on the governing body’s 16-strong players’ voice panel designed to assist with anti-racism initiatives.

Others to have shared the statement include the England defender Lucy Bronze, the former England keeper David James and the France 1998 World Cup winner Emmanuel Petit. More signatories are expected to follow in a concerted reaction to Infantino’s ill-fated attempt to sell stakes in the World Cup.

“We share the exact same concerns as the millions of fans around the world,” part of the statement read. “Like them, we have watched the game we love drift away from its core values under Fifa’s current leadership. For too long, we’ve seen major decisions taken without players being consulted or considered, and without any regard for the fans who sustain the sport.

“Change is necessary. Power has blurred the current leadership’s ability to distinguish between its own interests and what is best for football. Recent events have made silence impossible. Enough is enough.”

The group called for efforts to “reshape the future of our sport”, continuing: “There are good people within Fifa who want to rebuild trust, but a new era requires a structured change: a real, direct say for players and fans in how football is run. Those who step onto the pitch and those who sit in the stands deserve a genuine voice to help reshape football’s future together.”

Infantino has resisted calls to resign and spent Saturday at a youth tournament in the Dominican Republic, attempting to smooth relations with some of the smaller Caribbean member associations on whose support his fate may hinge.

One ex-player with a different perspective on Infantino is the former Real Madrid, Barcelona and Chelsea striker Samuel Eto’o, who is president of the Cameroonian football federation. In an interview with CNN, Eto’o said Infantino had not committed any missteps and called for the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) scheme to be put back on the table if Infantino is re-elected next March. He said the money from FFE would “reset the balance of power” in football and ensure African countries avoided losing top players to other national teams.

“I don’t think that [Infantino] has done anything wrong,” he said. “All of this has happened because there’s an election coming out, that’s all there is.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“I want to see all of my colleagues, all of the presidents, re-reading the project. After president Infantino is re-elected, we will have the strength to ask for this project to be put back on the table for discussion. I remain convinced that, if there is a democratic vote, this project will be adopted because it’s good for the majority.”

Sports.title: San Francisco 49ers owner Jed York pleads no contest after arrest at Ohio trailer park
Sports.content:
The San Francisco 49ers owner Jed York has pleaded no contest to two criminal charges after being arrested at an Ohio trailer park over the weekend.

KRON4 News in San Francisco reported that York was initially arrested on suspicion of engaging in prostitution but that count was amended to a charge of disorderly conduct. He was also charged with possessing criminal tools.

A no contest plea is not an admission of guilt but the defendant in question does accept the punishment for the alleged crimes in question. York was sentenced to a day in jail for each count to be served concurrently and was released on Monday morning. He was also fined a total of $1,150 and ordered to complete an online course. The arrest report does not specify what the criminal tools were in York’s case.

According to the New York Post, court documents say York responded to an advert on a website and “arranged to have sexual activity with [a] female in exchange for $140.” York was arrested later arrested at a trailer park in East Palestine, Ohio in the early hours of Sunday morning. The East Palestine Police Department and the Mahoning Valley Human Trafficking Task Force were involved in the arrest. York, 46, was born and raised in Youngstown, a 30-minute drive from East Palestine and still has a home in the area.

York is the nephew of former 49ers majority owner Edward J DeBartolo Jr. York took day to day control of the 49ers in 2008 when he became the team’s CEO. After acquiring his mother’s shares, he became the team’s principal owner in 2024.

Since York took over as CEO, the 49ers have reached three Super Bowls but lost each time.

He also owns stakes in the Premier League’s Leeds United and Scotland’s Rangers through 49ers Enterprises.

Sports.title: Julián Álvarez walks alone at Atlético in transfer saga with no end – and no winners | Sid Lowe
Sports.content:
Julián Álvarez entered a long, dark tunnel on his own. “We’re stronger together,” Giuliano Simeone said but that wasn’t the way it went. At the end of their first home game of the season, a 2-2 draw with Villarreal, all of Atlético Madrid’s players gathered by the centre circle, shook hands with their opponents and each other, then headed towards the south end of the Metropolitano. Almost all of them did, anyway: one was left behind. Somebody in a suit had a quiet word then the press officer came, pointing in the other direction. So, while his teammates turned to the supporters who had turned on him, the man wearing No 19 went west, to the exit.

Álvarez walked alone. Head down in silence, as he had been all afternoon and beyond, he set off slowly across the pitch accompanied only by his thoughts and the whistles that followed him. Not offered a hand to shake or a nod of acknowledgment, he stepped past the Atlético badge on the touchline where the mouth of the tunnel opens. Either side, supporters hung over the void, whistling and shouting. Way off to his left, Atlético’s other players paused, seemingly waiting for him to slip out of sight before approaching the stand, but none turned back. A scarf was thrown, landing at Álvarez’s feet and left lying there. And then he disappeared into the dark, a portrait of the place he is in.

No one was waiting for him on the other side. Álvarez went up the stairs, past a couple of security guards and turned left to an empty dressing room, not lifting his gaze and not invited to either. Four minutes would pass before his teammates came up the stairs together. But at least it was quiet now, for a little while. The noise had been loud; no one could recall supporters turning on their own player quite like this. Atlético’s fans, still his fans, had whistled him when his name was read out, whistled him when he had warmed up, whistled him when he came on wearing red and white there for the first time since April and since he declared it his “dream” to leave, and they had whistled him out of there too, for good.

Good? “Unhappily, this situation isn’t comfortable for anyone,” Jan Oblak said, and amid the damage done, the mutual accusations, the hurt pride and spited faces, nor is it easy to see a solution. The situation, in short, is this: Julián Álvarez wants to leave for Barcelona. Barcelona want to sign him. But he has a contract until June 2030, a €500m buyout clause, and Atlético won’t sell him. And definitely not to them. And so, here they are. Stuck.

View image in fullscreen Julián Álvarez trudges off the pitch alone as his Atlético Madrid teammates applaud the fans. Photograph: Manu Reino/DeFodi Images/Shutterstock

The first time Álvarez hinted he may not continue was after facing Tottenham in the Champions League last March. The timing seemed odd then: it hadn’t been an easy season, the feeling that something was wrong growing and about to be confirmed, but he had just scored twice and Atlético had won 5-2. It seemed odder still when he chose the moments after Argentina beat Austria at the World Cup to announce he wanted to go. “It’s not the time to talk about this but nor can I hide,” he said. “I spoke with the people I needed to [at Atlético] and the best thing for everyone is a transfer. I want to fulfil my dream.”

There had been a “bid” that wasn’t really a bid at all from Real Madrid but the dream was Barcelona and they were the ones who had been speaking to Álvarez, planning how to make it happen. Which was one of the reasons why Atlético were so determined it wouldn’t, deciding to take a stand instead, make this a cause. This was not about him wanting to go, or not only, but about the way it had been done.

From New York, Joan Laporta claimed that Barcelona had made an “important” offer. “If Atlético are prepared to accept, fantastic,” he said, but they weren’t and they didn’t think much of the offer either. Atlético’s chief executive, Miguel Ángel Gil Marín, insisted they would not sell at any price: they had told Álvarez, his agent and Barcelona that. “I know Joan: he’s always acting up for the media, fans, his own personal circus,” Gil Marín said. “I told him: ‘Leave it, please. We don’t want to sell and won’t sell, stop insisting’. He loves to play the part but he knows perfectly well that Julián won’t play for Barcelona next season.”

Barcelona insisted that they had approached a potential transfer the right way, with “respect”, but Atlético reported them to the RFEF (Spanish Football Federation) and refused to budge, a statement made, territory defended. This had become a point of principle, examples to be made of them. The noise though refused to go away. When Álvarez arrived for pre-season, still wanting out, he cut an isolated figure. If every silence and furrowed brow was analysed to death, it was true that there was an absence about him. This weekend Jorge Valdano took a line from Julio Cortázar to explain it: “When someone says they’re going, they’re already gone.”

Even if they’re not going. While Atlético quietly investigated other options, Gil Marín gave a statement again insisting that Álvarez was staying. “We can’t allow other clubs and media to dictate our policy and disrespect us,” he said. “We have values.” He attacked Álvarez’s agent too, saying that Alvarez had been poorly advised. To which Fernando Hidalgo – whose version has Atlético promising that if Álvarez publicly said he wanted to go, taking responsibility, they would allow him to – replied with a post: “Never ask a liar to explain why he lied; he would only have to lie again.”

As for the head coach, watching his superiors take the lead, he was ready to put Álvarez back in the team. “You can’t be clearer than the club’s been. It’s like when the judge says: ‘Denied!’” Diego Simeone said. As if it was that simple, the case so easily dismissed. While Atlético said they would “look after” him, while accusing Barcelona and Hidalgo lifted some blame from his shoulders, Álvarez’s return instead underlined that coming back from this might be even harder than anticipated, redemption more of a reach than imagined.

View image in fullscreen Diego Simeone left Julián Álvarez (bottom right) on the bench to start with. Photograph: Sheng Cheng/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

Sunday did not suggest a solution, a moment for the healing to start. Instead, it felt unsustainable, the case eclipsing all else, pressure building to find a proper conclusion. This was a fun match, but it was all about one man, the bad guy, and the verdict against him – and that affects everyone, maybe no winners any more. After the game there was a moment when, hands raised in front of him, the press officer asked journalists if there were any more questions, pausing to add … about the game … and the hands went down again. Before it, every photographer gathered in front of the bench as Álvarez took up his place to the left of Juan Musso and José María Gimenez, staring at the floor, the only movement his clenching jaw, while 60,000 people whistled his name. That, it turned out, was just the beginning.

Quick Guide La Liga results Show Rayo Vallecano 1-1 Alavés, Real Betis 1-0 Real Sociedad, Espanyol 1-2 Real Madrid, Valencia 0-0 Celta Vigo, Athletic Club 1-3 Sevilla, Elche 0-5 Barcelona, Getafe 1-0 Racing de Santander, Atlético Madrid 2-2 Villarreal Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

When he went to warm up on 51 minutes, they whistled again. From the south end, there were chants of “Fuck Barcelona! Fuck Catalonia!” They sang: “We are Atlético”. And “Atlético yes, mercenaries no!” Another one ran: “Tell him to go, once and for fucking all!” (To which Álvarez might have thought: yeah, that’s what I’m trying to do). As Atlético’s players came to the touchline after their first goal, the fitness coach said Álvarez was about to go on. “Careful, eh,” Marc Pubill replied. The noise when he did was deafening and didn’t relent. There weren’t many touches but with every one the angry volume rose, the rejection not receding all the way to the final whistle, which was not the final whistle at all: that too was for Álvarez. With eight days left in the window, it could still have been a good riddance, but … if it’s not?

“Julián is with us in the team and for as long as he is, we’re going to support him,” Oblak said. “All I know is that if Atlético want to win titles we have to be together, we need strikers and we need important strikers,” Simeone noted, admitting he had apologised to Ademola Lookman for making him play there in the absence of Álvarez and the injured Alex Sørloth. They do have strikers, the coach said the second time he turned to that line, but they would have to “take care” of them, the coach confirming that the club had told him it was their decision that he shouldn’t greet the fans, not Julián’s.

Yet if it had been designed to protect Álvarez and if this statement had too, absolving him of having chosen to turn his back on them, it also exposed him. Leaving first without the others, none joining him, served as an expression of his isolation, his othering, of how broken the situation had become. “Together we’re stronger, that’s always characterised us, made Atlético Madrid different. He is our player so we will die for him on the pitch,” Giuliano Simeone said, but when the time came, Álvarez went alone.

Sports.title: Rennes push PSG all the way to show they are the best of the rest in Ligue 1
Sports.content:
On the scale of expressions of prowess and power, Paris Saint-Germain bringing almost €150m worth of attacking talent off the bench – including the man who scored the winning goal in the World Cup final last month – ranks only a couple of rungs below the level of the extravagant aggression of a military parade. Imposing, dominating, reasserting, this wasn’t about expression but necessity as the reigning European champions initially floundered against a Rennes team that lived up to their billing as the best of the rest in Ligue 1.

PSG were forced into rolling out their new attacking arsenal early. For 45 minutes, Rennes’ incessant pressing and fluidity in transition had Luis Enrique’s side under duress. Sebastien Szymanski opened the scoring with a sliced effort from outside the box that clipped in off the inside of a post.

PSG had territorial dominance but could not equalise. Two former Rennes players – Désiré Doué and Ousmane Dembélé – had the best chances, the latter particularly wasteful with a skied first-time effort from inside the box. Esteban Lepaul, the top scorer in Ligue 1 last season, picked up where he left off, beating Matvey Safonov with a first-time effort towards the near post to double Rennes’ lead.

A reaction was needed, and it drew a very strong one from Luis Enrique. Off came perhaps the two most talented players in the league, Dembélé and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia. On came Ferran Torres and Mika Godts, signed for a combined fee of nearly €100m, at half-time. The former hauled PSG back into the game.

In the meantime, the €50m signing Maghnes Akliouche had come on for his Ligue 1 debut for the champions, as had Fabián Ruiz and it was the Spanish connection that ensured a point for PSG. Ruiz teed up both of Torres’ goals, the first after an exquisitely timed run in behind from the former Barcelona forward and the second a close-range header. Willian Pacho was called upon in the dying moments, making a goalline clearance to secure the draw.

“If you think about what you’ve won, you won’t win anything else. You have to show every day that you are ready,” said Luis Enrique when asked about his decision to replace Dembélé and Kvaratskhelia. He added that there had been a “a big difference in rhythm” between Rennes and PSG.

View image in fullscreen Ferran Torres scored twice for PSG in their 2-2 draw against Lens. Photograph: Stéphane Mahé/Reuters

PSG’s lethargy is no surprise; it was only the nature of their opponents – Nantes and Angers – that prevented them from slipping up at the start of last season, once again after limited preparation time. “We have to be more ready,” said Luis Enrique. The same applies to the groundstaff at the Parc des Princes. The state of PSG’s pitch meant this game moved last minute to Roazhon Park; it suited Rennes, especially if, as they argue should be the case, the second game is also played at their home ground.

There is a burgeoning positivity around Roazhon Park. While the prospects of other challengers have dwindled, Rennes’ have multiplied. The wealth of the Breton club’s owners, the Pinault family, has bought them a form of immunity to the financial crisis that has now struck down Marseille and Monaco; other challengers: Lille, Lyon, Strasbourg and Lens are consigned to stagnation, for now.

Rennes approached the season looking second-best on paper, and after Sunday night, that perception now aligns with reality. Rennes fended off competition from the Premier League to sign the England youth international Charlie Cresswell from Toulouse. One of the best defenders in Ligue 1 last season, he was excellent against PSG; in Adrien Thomasson, Rennes also acquired the most valuable piece of Lens’ success last season, arguably the best midfielder in the division, and on a free, no less. And in Lepaul, they have a prolific striker who is very much in contention to be in Zinedine Zidane’s first France squad next month.

They have a strong spine and a brilliant manager. Franck Haise began his managerial career as a youth coach at Rennes, and they were only too happy to bring him back in February after things turned sour at Nice. There has always been the perception that there has been a missing piece in the puzzle at Rennes. Despite their means, their talented squad, their renowned academy, they had reached a ceiling. Questionable managerial appointments played their part. Haise may well be the right man, the missing part.

“There is more positive than negative,” he said after the 2-2 draw. The negative is the way the two points were ceded, a laxness creeping in, particularly from Abdelhamid Aït-Boudlal, who is nonetheless another exciting prospect. The positive is that Rennes did not look second-best on the night, but they could be come the end of the season, and for all clubs in Ligue 1, that has to be the aspiration. PSG flexed their muscles, but only because Rennes made them.

Quick Guide Ligue 1 results Show Ligue 1 results Angers 0-2 Lille Le Havre 0-1 Monaco Rennes 2-2 PSG Lens 5-2 Auxerre Le Mans 2-2 Brest Nice 0-0 Lorient Toulouse 0-2 Lyon Troyes 0-0 Paris FC Marseille 4-0 Strasbourg Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Talking points

Strasbourg should be worried after their 4-0 defeat to Marseille. They had to replace Gary O’Neil in the summer when he moved to Ipswich but there are doubts about Hugo Oliveira. This is not a vintage Marseille side, but they looked it as they put four past goalkeeper Filip Jörgensen, who is on loan from Chelsea. Strasbourg’s cause was not aided by a petulant Samir El Mourabet kick on Pierre-Emile Højbjerg, which rightly earned the Morocco international a red card on the hour mark. Conceding 21 goals in seven friendlies can be dismissed as “just pre-season”, but when that form carries into the campaign, there may be a problem for a club with European ambitions.

Despite losing Pierre Sage and the spine of their side, Lens did not look any weaker as they swept aside Auxerre on Will Still’s return to the Beaujoire, winning 5-2. The former Lens manager, who is back in Ligue 1 after a failed stint at Southampton, saw his side comprehensively beaten thanks in part to an inspired Florian Thauvin. Now wearing the captain’s armband, he scored twice and set up another as Dino Toppmöller got off to a roaring start as Lens manager. European football will provide a fresh challenge once it arrives in September, but this emphatic win eases fears that last season was a flash in the pan.

The matches in Marseille, Le Mans and Nice were preceded by tributes to Éric Roy, who was still in his post as Brest manager when he died from pancreatic cancer in June. Roy led Brest in the club’s first ever European campaign in the 2024-25 season. “We have him in our thoughts,” said Julien Lachuer, an internal appointment at the club over the summer. The new era at Brest began with a draw against Le Mans on Saturday.

Sports.title: Liverpool are still haunted by the mess of last summer | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
The good news for Liverpool is that, Arsenal aside, every other team with vague title aspirations who played over the weekend looked undercooked, and that Andoni Iraola’s men did, in the end, come away from Newcastle with a point. But the vulnerability to the counter that undermined them so often last season has not gone away, and nor have they suddenly found a new creativity under Iraola.

The main theme of the first three days of the new season was the value of stability. Manchester City under a new manager were poor and fortunate to overcome Bournemouth. Aston Villa, after big changes of players and backroom staff, were hammered at Brighton. Tottenham, midway through yet another overhaul, were dismal in losing at Brentford. Manchester United at least provided a degree of stability by looking very much like the United of the past decade in their defeat to Hull.

Liverpool, for much of the first 96 minutes of their fixture at St James’ Park, looked like joining the list of challengers struggling to emerge from a summer of churn. Arne Slot spent much of last season complaining about how opponents always scored with their first chance and about Liverpool’s inability to deal with direct attacks, and as Anthony Elanga put Newcastle ahead, it seemed that not much had changed. Joe Willock’s goal to restore the Newcastle lead was much the same: opponents running at pace through vacant space.

What is odd is how pressing the need for a replacement for Fabinho has been since the defensive midfielder left in 2023. Even as Liverpool won the league under Slot in 2024-25, the discussion was of how the squad needed of an overhaul, and how a dedicated holding player to operate alongside Ryan Gravenberch was a priority. Which was what made the spending spree of last summer so surprising: it wasn’t so much who came in as who didn’t.

Without a holding midfielder, the flaws of the centre of defence, where Virgil van Dijk’s lack of pace on the turn is becoming increasingly obvious, are magnified. Liverpool could perhaps get away with it were he prepared to operate 10 yards higher in possession but the 35-year-old, aware of his ageing legs and worried about balls played in behind him, instinctively drops deeper, giving opponents just the sort of opportunities that Yoane Wissa kept exploiting on Sunday.

Iraola insisted it wasn’t “just about personnel” – which itself seemed an implicit acknowledgment that it is in part about personnel. Had he scored, Iraola said, everybody would have praised Gravenberch, who had advanced to the edge of the Newcastle box in the attack that led to the first Liverpool concession. “I don’t want us to take that from his game but we have to adapt as a team to these situations,” said Iraola. “We have to know these situations can happen.”

Of Newcastle’s second goal, he said: “It wasn’t like they caught us by surprise. We should compete for the first ball and probably make a foul – be a bit more aggressive against the ball carrier. There were different reasons for both the goals which happened in transition. We have been preparing in the week for these transitions but there’s a reason why Newcastle are so good at them. It’s not just because one person is playing there. It’s something we have to correct between a lot of players.”

But conceding on the break isn’t the only familiar issue for Liverpool. Their full-backs, Jeremie Frimpong and Milos Kerkez, were unconvincing. Alexander Isak, booed throughout by the home fans, rarely looked dangerous in the first full 90 minutes he has completed since his British record transfer from Newcastle last summer. Florian Wirtz produced a characteristic performance full of neat touches and little incision.

Iraola’s career suggests it often takes him time to instil his ideas at clubs. There is no reason for panic. Liverpool at least had the resilience to come back and pinch the draw. It’s not like any side other than Arsenal has looked particularly impressive. But perhaps there does need to be a reconsideration of what has gone before.

The familiar narrative is that Slot drove the car that Jürgen Klopp had put together to a league title and was then found wanting. But while the Dutchman cannot escape blame for last season, an equally valid interpretation might be that Slot coaxed an ageing team to an unexpected league title. Then, with an overhaul badly needed – Jamie Carragher wasn’t alone in speaking towards the end of that season of Liverpool needing half a dozen new players – he was let down by those charged with recruitment.

Michael Edwards left his role as chief executive for football at Fenway Sports Group, which owns Liverpool, in July, but the mess caused by last summer’s spree endures. Of the six most expensive signings of last summer for a combined fee of around £410m (about $560m), the only one who has looked remotely impressive, Hugo Ekitike, is still out for months with a ruptured achilles. Rarely has so much been spent in football to such destructive effect.

Sports.title: Women’s Super League 2026-27 preview No 3: Birmingham City
Sports.content:
Guardian writers’ predicted position: 12th (NB: this is not necessarily Tom Garry’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)

Last season’s position: 1st (WSL2)

Prospects

Founding members of the Women’s Super League when it launched in 2011, Birmingham are back in the top flight after four years in the second tier, having won promotion as WSL2 champions on the final day of last season. After a decent summer transfer window, Birmingham look to have a fighting chance of staying up, and perhaps even surprising a few teams, while off the pitch they are the best-equipped of the three promoted sides to cement themselves in the top division.

Forwards Lily Crosthwaite and Wilma Leidhammar and defender Neve Herron, are all 23-years-old and likely to continue improving. Birmingham have also added players with WSL experience, such as the former Brighton goalkeeper Sophie Baggaley and the centre-back Millie Turner.

Inconsistency was nearly their downfall last season; they won the most games in WSL2, but also lost six times. They delivered under pressure, boosted by the performances of Leidhammar after her club-record arrival in January, ensuring they avoided a repeat of the heartbreak of 12 months earlier when they missed out on promotion on the final day. Nonetheless, Birmingham are still a long way off from the days when they were runners-up in the top tier and their first two away fixtures are against Manchester City and Chelsea. They also host fellow promoted sides Crystal Palace and Charlton relatively early in the campaign and those home fixtures could be key to building confidence.

Off-field picture

Birmingham’s women’s team were sold to the club’s ownership group in February, with Shelby Companies Limited – an affiliate of Knighthead Capital Management – owning 97%. The remaining 3% was purchased by investors including the former England midfielder Karen Carney and the four-time grand slam tennis champion Kim Clijsters. The club appear to be in a relatively healthy position with ambitious owners determined to reestablish the 2012 FA Cup winners as a regular, competitive presence in the WSL. They train at the recently renovated Knighthead Performance Centre, on the same site as the men’s team’s former Wast Hills training base, with a new gym among other extensive refurbishments.

The manager

Amy Merricks has been in charge since April 2024 She holds a Uefa Pro Licence and was 30 years old when she was appointed by Birmingham. She has previously coached within the England youth setup as well as at Gillingham, Millwall and Brighton, where was stepped up to be interim manager three times.

Star signing

View image in fullscreen Lisa Naalsund arrives from Manchester United to boost Birmingham’s midfield. Photograph: DeFodi Images/Getty Images

Birmingham have recruited players with international experience, including the Canada defender Marie Levasseur from Montpellier, but their two most eyebrow-raising additions are Turner and Lisa Naalsund from Manchester United. They were starting members of United’s FA Cup-winning side of 2024 and played in a Women’s Champions League quarter-final as recently as April. Naalsund will be an influential force in the midfield – she has won 39 caps and was part of Norway’s squad at last year’s Euros.

Stat attack

Birmingham topped WSL2 last season despite not scoring the most goals or conceding the fewest. One stat they led was big chances, Opta’s metric for opportunities where it is reasonable to expect the attacker to score. While their tally will be much harder to repeat in the top flight, their attacking process looks in good order.

Set for a breakthrough

There is plenty of excitement at Birmingham about another of their new signings, the 19-year-old France youth forward Chancelle Effa Effa, who arrived from Le Havre for a fee understood to be about €120,000 (£100,000) this month. She broke into Le Havre’s first team at the age of 15 and scored 17 times in 28 games for France’s Under-17 and Under-19 teams, having helped France win 2023’s Under-17 Euros.

What they say …

“We know it’s going to be a massive challenge, but it’s a challenge that, as players, you thrive upon. As long as we can take that togetherness, that relentlessness, into the games, I’m sure we’re going to be just fine” – Chelsea Cornet.

Where are they playing their home games?

Birmingham play their home fixtures at St Andrew’s, which has been the women’s team’s home since 2021. They set a club record attendance for a women’s game there on the final day of the 2024-25 season – 8,749. Long-term, the club have announced plans to build a new women’s team stadium as part of the ‘Sports Quarter’, which also includes the proposed 62,000-seater men’s team Powerhouse Stadium as well as an indoor arena, training ground facilities and a new railway station.

Sports.title: Amorim’s Milan live up to billing as teenage star Cissè upstages signings | Nicky Bandini
Sports.content:
“I love Cissè. I love Cissè.” Ruben Amorim had not yet taken charge of his first competitive game as Milan head coach but already he was furnishing journalists with soundbites and supporters with memes, clippable moments that you just knew we were destined to revisit.

Alphadjo Cissè is a 19-year-old attacking midfielder who signed for Milan from Verona in February but only joined up with them this summer, after completing the season-long loan he had already begun at Catanzaro in Serie B. He scored six goals in 22 games there, missing the second half of the campaign with a thigh injury. Previously he had played a combined 14 minutes for Verona across three substitute appearances in the top flight.

Yet Amorim spoke of Cissè like a man who knew something that the rest of the world doesn’t. More than his words, it was the body language: hands rubbing together in anticipation, lip curled at one corner into an emoji-like version of a smirk.

Cissè would start away to Torino the following evening. Within 75 seconds of kick-off, he had taken the first shot of the game: racing forward to hook a Ruben Loftus-Cheek cross into the side netting from an acute angle beyond the far post.

For an Italian teenager to make Milan’s first XI on the opening weekend was already a significant detail. The scarce opportunities afforded to young domestic talent in Serie A has been a national talking point ever since the Azzurri failed to qualify for a third consecutive men’s World Cup.

Data compiled by Football Benchmark found that Italians who qualified for the under-21 category accounted for only 3.9% of minutes played last season, while foreign players in that age group took 8.2%: “In other words, young foreign players receive more than twice as many opportunities as their Italian counterparts.”

There were signs of a possible shift this weekend. The season began with 21-year-old Pio Esposito delivering a man-of-the-match performance for the champions, Inter, in their 4-1 win over Monza, but he was the exception who stood apart already last year.

More surprising were the new faces popping up elsewhere. Cissè, born in Treviso to Guinean parents, was one of three Italian teenagers on the pitch at the Olympic stadium in Turin, with Diego Mascardi and Alessio Cacciamani, both 19, lining up at goalkeeper and left wing-back for the Granata.

View image in fullscreen Ruben Amorim won his first Serie A match in charge against Ignazio Abate’s Torino. Photograph: Daniele Mascolo/Reuters

The 18-year-olds Matteo Palma (an Italian-German dual national) and Simone Lontani started for Udinese and Parma respectively, and the 19-year-old Mathis Mout for Monza. Even Como, whose project has been criticised for relying almost exclusively on foreign talent, gave Mattia Liberali, 19, some minutes off the bench. It is far too soon to draw conclusions, but certainly a trend worth tracking.

In any case, putting your faith in untested young talent can feel like a greater gamble for a club with Milan’s expectations. After a disappointing fifth-place finish last season under Massimiliano Allegri, the Rossoneri have spent big – appointing Amorim and then dropping a club-record €74m to sign Gonçalo Ramos from Paris Saint-Germain, as well as another €50m on the midfielder Diego Moreira from Strasbourg and €30m on the defender Mario Gila from Lazio.

Amorim has not shied away from ambition, saying his goal is to win the Scudetto, even while acknowledging it may take time to bridge the gap to Inter. More than that, he has won over fans with the promise of a front-footed team who will seek to set the tempo and dictate how games are played – a welcome change from the caution and reactivity of Allegri.

There were promising performances in pre-season – not least the 4-2 win over Amorim’s last club, Manchester United, with Cissè on the scoresheet. But friendlies are not the real thing. Sunday’s visit to a Torino side undergoing a renewal of their own under a new head coach, and former Milan player, Ignazio Abate, was always going to be a fascinating first challenge.

Ramos and Gila started, at centre-forward and on the right of defence. Moreira, who only completed his move on 19 August, stayed on the bench. Cissè was the other truly new face, playing to the left of Ramos in a 3-4-2-1, though Yunus Musah and the right wing-back Samuel Chukwueze were also returning after spending last season out on loan.

Amorim’s approach lived up to billing. From the start, Milan dominated the ball and the pitch – claiming more than 70% of first-half possession while outshooting their opponents by 11 to one. And yet, they struggled to break Torino down in the final third. Aside from one solo effort by Chukwueze, who dribbled in from the right and forced a save from Mascardi, they had rarely looked like scoring.

Quick Guide Serie A results Show Parma 0-1 Cagliari, Genoa 0-2 Napoli, Udinese 1-1 Como, Inter 4-1 Monza, Torino 1-2 Milan, Atalanta 2-1 Sassuolo, Venezia 0-2 Lecce, Frosinone 0-1 Juventus Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Cissè thought he had earned Milan a penalty after the interval, when his cross struck the arm of Nikola Vlasic. That the VAR booth did not call the referee, Luca Zufferli, to take a second look may be an early indicator – together with incidents from other games – of a shift in approach under the new refereeing designator, Daniele Orsato. He has stated a desire to “put referees back at the centre of the match” and return to the idea that technology should only be used for those elusive “clear and obvious” mistakes.

Torino were growing into the game. But that might also have been their undoing. In the 64th minute, Musah turned his man in midfield, surging into space left open by the home team’s press. He fed Adrien Rabiot, a second-half substitute, on the right. The Frenchman crossed to Cissè, who brought the ball down with his waist and curled a half volley into the far corner. The teenager slid to his knees as he celebrated in front of the away fans.

Within moments it was 2-0, Rabiot himself converting a Chukwueze delivery. Torino kept battling, and Scotland’s Ché Adams scored the best goal of the game in injury time, an outrageously nonchalant right-foot volley over his own left shoulder. But the three points went to Milan.

Cissè laughed when the interviewer from Dazn asked him at full time what he thought about Amorim’s professions of love. “It makes me happy,” he said. “But I didn’t hear the press conference. All my friends told me about it instead.”

View image in fullscreen Alphadjo Cissè’s half volley gives Milan the lead in Turin. Photograph: Valerio Pennicino/Getty Images

He was still recovering from injury when he first joined up with Milan this summer. Cissè said he had tried to watch training as closely as possible, getting to know what the head coach wanted. Still, he acknowledged, it was “beyond a dream” to get to start, and score, in the season opener.

The numbers say he is the youngest Italian to score for Milan since Patrick Cutrone in 2017, as well as the first Italian to score for them on a debut Serie A start since Daniel Maldini in 2021. Those names should remind everyone not to get ahead of themselves. Cutrone, now 28, was a substitute for Monza this weekend and has only reached double figures for goals once in a top-flight season. Maldini, 24, has played for seven clubs since 2022, and begins this campaign with Cagliari.

But Amorim clearly thinks highly of Cissè, who has represented Italy at various age categories up to under-21, saying he looked at times in the first-half like the most experienced player on the pitch.

The head coach, conducting his interviews mostly in English, said Milan have “a lot to improve”, acknowledging both their struggles to break Torino down early on and the way they faded at the end. “[But] the first thing is also win. That is the most important thing. We talk about ways of playing, but there is one goal in calcio. Vincere.”

Sports.title: Journey to Wembley: After a fortnight of fretting over floodlights on the fritz, Nelson's FA Cup journey ends at Witton Albion - where home fans toasted victory with pina coladas!
Sports.content:
It’s the annual pina colada festival in the Witton area of Cheshire – the song about the drink, which topped the US charts in the late 1970s, was written by someone local to the place and they’ve spotted the commercial opportunity – so there are people walking around dressed as pineapples and wearing big yellow glasses on Saturday lunchtime. But life has not exactly been a cocktail party for Nelson, an East Lancashire ninth tier club, just lately.

They breeze through one of the challenges which faces them after arriving to face opponents one step above them in the pyramid. Their new yellow away kits for the season haven’t arrived and last season’s issue, which they’re still using, don’t have a No 18 jersey – needed today because you’re allowed seven subs in the FA Cup. Someone finds a white marker pen and inks the number on to a plain yellow away shirt. Wearing numbers on your back is mandatory in the tournament.

This is a minor obstacle compared with the floodlight problems which have been testing Nelson minds since we left them celebrating extra preliminary round victory at their ‘Little Wembley’ ground two weeks ago. That was the first part of our journey to Wembley told in 13 instalments, following a club as far as they go and then picking up with the team who knock them out, all the way to the final.

They’d signed off on a £30,000 contract, helped by FA grants, to replace the system of lights which had started to fail during evening games, only to find that the new ones still didn’t work.

The approved contractors didn’t seem to have mentioned that the cables and wiring supplying the lights also needed ripping out, and yet were sending the club legal letters demanding payment, as Nelson’s directors sought advice from the FA about the black hole they risked disappearing into.

Inside the home dressing room at the Bedspace Trust Community Stadium

Nelson captain Bill Priestley receives some treatment ahead of kick-off

A home steward - proudly sporting Witton Albion's colours - tucks into a pie at half-time

When we caught up with Nelson at their league away game at Charnock Richard in Lancashire, last Tuesday night, the floodlights were the prime topic of conversation as the players arrived in the car park. There had even been talk of a temporary ground move, which did not exactly delight the North West Counties League. Nelson’s proactive club sponsor Monks Contractors had offered supplying temporary structures.

In the end, they just went to work again. Volunteers helped dig two 100m trenches to lay the new cabling to the new lights and on Wednesday, they flicked the switch once more. ‘Let there be light?’ The look on Nelson director Rob Doherty’s face as the visiting contingent are welcomed into Witton’s snug little boardroom suggests so. ‘As of three days ago, they were working,’ he relates. The FA provided emergency funding.

Both these teams badly want to win this FA Cup Preliminary Round game. In his extremely modestly proportioned office Witton manager Benny Harrison, whose day job is a teacher at a special educational school, reflects at 2pm on the profound effects Marine experienced after playing Tottenham in the Third Round in 2021. The windfall helped win them two promotions in three years.

But as the rival teams’ executives gather in that boardroom, there’s a sense of mutual empathy about the existential threats which can be just around the corner for any non-league club.

‘There’s what goes on out on the pitch, and the fans and all that the lovely stuff,’ says Witton director Paul Sanderson, when Nelson relate their floodlight troubles. ‘And then there’s survivability stuff that fans don't know about. Trying to navigate things that can threaten your existence if you’re not prepared for anything.’

Nelson were on a precipice before new co-owners Stewart Fort and Chris Price arrived three years ago, invested and built up the team of volunteers who are their lifeblood. But Witton’s excellent little club museum, charting a 139-year history and signposted ‘probably the best non-League football museum in the world’, shows that they’ve also ridden football’s rollercoaster.

The museum chronicles the club’s journey to the 1992 FA Trophy final at Wembley, where they lost to Colchester. That period, which included a brief stay in the Conference, saw them splashing the surplus earned after selling their old ground to Sainsburys and building a new one, on players. The rewards were painful temporary. Witton struggled when the money ran out and the new stadium required major repair sooner than anticipated.

The sun’s out, though, and the FA Cup is blowing everyone’s troubles away. ‘Welcome to the best football competition in the world by a long chalk,’ states the stadium announcer. The appropriately named Witton groundsman James Spruce is reversing his mower out onto the excellent playing surface, his partner Katy Hulse is nursing a pina colada and her friend Barbara Bazley is watching the warm-up.

Groundsman James Spruce applies the finishing touches to the playing surface

Katy Hulse (left) enjoys a pina colada with her friend Barbara Bazley

Albion statistician Phil Chadwick has helped to curate one of the best club museum's in non-League

Nelson's 87-year-old superfan Harry Manning’s immaculate handwritten notes will be converted into a match report for the local Nelson Leader

‘When you make s*** decisions, it goes pear-shaped, so if someone makes a s*** decision, back them up and help sort it out,’ shouts assistant coach Liam Lishman, as he puts the squad through their paces. Thursday’s training session focussed on not allowing Freddie Garbutt, Witton’s towering 22-year-old striker, the chance to control and shoot.

At Charnock Richard, Nelson won 2-0, led by their own dangerous target man Sefton Gonzalez, who scored and hurled himself through his trademark somersault. Today, goalkeeper Chris Thompson is back after a bout of sciatica. There’s optimism in the air.

Against the backdrop of the chemical plants in salt-mining territory, Nelson discover what they’re up against in Garbutt and Witton’s attacking pace.

Nelson wing-back Darren Holden, outstanding in the previous round and at Charnock in midweek, is operating in his own half far more, protecting Nelson territory, yet removing one of the Lancashire team's attacking dimensions.

Jamie Edwards, Nelson’s force field, draws a sharp save and Gonzales has just headed a great opportunity into the ground when Witton’s Garbutt leaps to meet a corner and send his team ahead.

He’s one of only two players Witton have signed up to a contract, protecting his match fee if he’s injured and protecting the club if someone else tries to sign him, Witton chairman Graham Wood relates, back in the boardroom at half-time.

The winners today will collect £1,444 in prize money and that would be just as precious to Witton, a fan-owned club with 400 registered shareholders, none of them hugely wealthy, who are currently trying to make a community football facility.

Nelson players warm up at the side of the pitch before kick-off

Witton Albion play in the Northern Premier League Division One West, one division higher than Nelson

Visiting goalkeeper Chris Thompson keeps a Witton player at bay

Freddy Garbutt's first-half goal settled the game and sent Witton through to the next round of the FA Cup

Home boss Ben Harrison addresses his players at full time

‘That will bring us an income to put back into the club,’ says Wood, who has helped bring a commercial sponsorship deal with a locally based homelessness charity.

Nelson dominate a second half in which Holden is pushed forward more, encouraged by his wife Amy, who is live tweeting the match for the club’s website with another volunteer, Abi Lawson, and taking photographs for next week’s match programme and the website.

In the main stand, 87-year-old superfan Harry Manning’s immaculate handwritten notes, which will be converted into a match report for the local Nelson Leader, reflect the growing frustration. The ‘18’ inked onto sub James Hooper’s jersey is impressive. But it’s raining in Nelson hearts when the whistle blows and they tumble out of the competition.

Manager Arron Ripley stands in the sun-dappled centre circle ten minutes later and reflects on the way his ambitious side are evolving. ‘Last year we’d have kept launching it in a situation like that but we’re looking after the ball. We look like we’re enjoying it. We just weren’t clinical enough.’

Nelson can return fortified to their league campaign, confident, in so many ways, that the lights will stay on.

Sports.title: Man City reach £34m agreement on Allan Elias as Newcastle edge closer to signing Nico Gonzalez and Coventry agree £6m deal for Ethan Pinnock: WINDOW WATCH
Sports.content:
It's that time of the year again – the transfer window is now open until September 1 and it's sure to be a busy period as clubs look to make big signings ahead of the new season. Here are today's latest developments from Simon Jones and the Daily Mail Sport team... City hope Allan holds key as they agree deal Manchester City have reached an agreement with Palmeiras over the signing of Allan Elias. The deal for the winger is worth up to £34million. City are paying £32m plus £2m in add-ons. Allan is a left-footed winger who predominantly plays off the right like Savinho, who is heading to Spurs for £75m plus £10m in add-ons. Coventry pinning hopes on Pinnock Coventry have agreed a £6m deal to sign Ethan Pinnock from Brentford. Earlier today Daily Mail Sport reported that the clubs were in talks over a move. The Jamaica international has been on the periphery of Keith Andrews' first team but has been attracting enquiries from a number of clubs including West Ham. However, Coventry manager Frank Lampard has recognised that the 33-year-old Pinnock's Premier League experience could benefit his side during what will be a testing season. Pinnock could sign in the next 24 hours. Ethan Pinnock is set for a move to promoted Coventry Gonzalez edges closer to Toon move Newcastle United are continuing to edge closer to agreement with Manchester City over a deal for Nico Gonzalez. Gonzalez is valued around £50million. The 24-year-old was an unused substitute in City’s win over Bournemouth on Sunday with Marc Guehi playing in midfield and it is clear that a move away may now be in his best interests. Nico Gonzalez is closing in on a move to Newcastle after falling out of favour at Man City Matthias Jaissle wants to add a midfielder with Premier League experience before the window closes. City agreed an £86m deal with Lille for midfielder Ayyoub Bouaddi yesterday and want another before the window closes. Newcastle also admire Tottenham's Archie Gray though he has captained the side in pre-season and at the weekend in their 3-0 defeat to Brentford. Newcastle back in for Pardo Newcastle have rekindled talks over Lille forward Matias-Fernandez Pardo. The clubs have been discussing an offer worth around £40million for the Belgium international who can play across the front line. Daily Mail Sport has previously reported Newcastle's interest in the 21-year-old while Red Bull Leipzig and Atletico Madrid have made proposals recently too. Pardo was on Liverpool's watchlist previously and played for Belgium at the World Cup. Tigers target towering forward Hull are in talks for towering Union Berlin forward Ilyas Ansah. The Germany Under-21 international was considered for selection by Ghana ahead of the World Cup and Hull are offering £19m, including add-ons. The 21-year old is 6ft 6in tall and was a target for Besiktas earlier this year. He scored five goals and registered two assists in 26 games for Union Berlin last season. Hull had a £7m offer for Stoke City winger Sorba Thomas knocked back last week and are continuing to work on other options. Imps land Wheatley Manchester United striker Ethan Wheatley has joined Championship side Lincoln City. The 20-year-old agreed the move on Friday after seeing Everton pull out of a deal to sign him permanently earlier last week. Wheatley, who had a spell at Bradford last season, joins on loan for the rest of this campaign.

Sports.title: Revealed: Brydon Carse WAS arrested on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly during nightclub visit with Ben Stokes - with police now RE-OPENING investigation into England bowler
Sports.content:
Brydon Carse was briefly arrested on suspicion of being ‘drunk and disorderly’ in Derby on Saturday night, before being de-arrested, it has emerged.

Carse was dropped earlier today from England’s squad for Thursday’s second Test against Pakistan at Lord’s while the Cricket Regulator investigates the events that led to police handcuffing him outside a nightclub.

He was then de-arrested - meaning the arrest was cancelled before he was taken into custody. But Daily Mail Sport understands the matter is now back in the hands of the police, who are looking into the precise sequence of events.

A statement by Derbyshire police read: ‘A man in his 30s was arrested on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly in Derby city centre on Saturday night. However the man was de-arrested shortly afterwards having agreed to leave the area.’

Brydon Carse was handcuffed by police outside the nightclub in Derby

Ben Stokes (in background) was also in attendance after Durham's big win over Derbyshire

Carse has been replaced in the 16-man squad by Hampshire fast bowler Sonny Baker

It is understood the man in question is 31-year-old Carse, who has been replaced in the 16-man squad by Hampshire fast bowler Sonny Baker.

A social-media video showed the moment Carse was handcuffed, with four policemen in attendance, and Durham team-mates Ben Stokes and Matthew Potts both featuring briefly on camera.

And while Carse, who has not played a Test since last winter's Ashes, was not on England duty, he has an ECB central contract.

After a year in which Harry Brook, Ben Duckett and Stokes have been involved in separate alcohol-related incidents, the sight of another England cricketer making headlines for the wrong reasons has not gone down well at Lord’s.

An ECB statement said: ‘Brydon Carse will no longer be available for selection for the Second Men’s Rothesay Test Match while this investigation is ongoing and the full facts are obtained.’

The Cricket Regulator has at is disposal a range of options, including no further action, caution or bringing a charge for a breach of the regulations – among them, bringing the game into disrepute.

Sports.title: Michael Carrick must make his mark as capitulation in dismal defeat by Hull raises fresh concerns over this Man United squad's ability to build on his achievements, writes CHRIS WHEELER
Sports.content:
When Michael Carrick celebrated his return to Old Trafford in January with back-to-back wins against Manchester City and Arsenal, the message from the head coach was calm and consistent. 'Nobody is getting carried away,' was Carrick's mantra at the time.

So he was never likely to have a public meltdown at the MKM Stadium on Saturday after Manchester United suffered a shocking defeat at Hull City, losing to a newly-promoted team on the opening weekend for the first time in the club's history.

As bad as the result and United's performance were, Carrick's approach remained the same as it was seven months ago. Calm down, it's just one game.

He is right, of course, but Carrick has also been around United long enough to know that you are only ever one game from a crisis.

Lose to Ipswich in United's first home game of the season on Sunday, and Carrick's softly softly approach will be drowned out by the alarm bells ringing around Old Trafford.

The 45-year-old's placid exterior has always masked his real emotions, first as a player and now as a coach. At United, his calm demeanour and measured approach have been a welcome antidote to the emotional incontinence and public self-flagellation of his emotional predecessor Ruben Amorim.

Michael Carrick exuded calmness despite seeing Manchester United lose 2-0 at Hull City

The 45-year-old hides his emotions a lot better than his United predecessor Ruben Amorim

Nobody who knows Carrick would doubt the competitive edge and hunger to win that was seared into the heart of all Sir Alex Ferguson's teams - and which he must imbue into the squad that surrendered so tamely on Humberside.

The players certainly got the message after Carrick suffered his first defeat in charge at Newcastle in March, but the manner of their capitulation to Hull has raised fresh concerns over the ability of this group to build on what he achieved in the second half of last season after replacing Amorim.

Managers react differently to defeat. Erik ten Hag took his players on a 13.8km run the day after United lost their first away game of the season 4-0 at Brentford in 2022 to make up for the overall distance they had lagged behind their opponents - a result just as shocking as this defeat at Hull. Amorim damaged a TV during a dressing-room rant after his team lost at home to Brighton in January last year.

The challenge for Carrick this week is to strike the right balance. He is the last man to press the panic button - certainly after one game - but he also has to make it abundantly clear to the players and supporters that Manchester United losing to Hull City is not acceptable.

At the MKM Stadium, he was asked if the cool-headed approach that has served him so well thus far might actually be viewed negatively by fans expecting a few choice words from their head coach.

'I know there's a lot goes on outside of our football club, yeah,' Carrick said with a smile. 'I understand. I understand the responsibility I've got, but it doesn't make me do things differently just because of that.

'I'm talking to you quite calmly, but I'm not exactly calm inside and enjoying the day, you know? So there's a big difference. I played here for a long time. You don't get to play here for a long time without just going day by day, the results, the ups and downs, but you just carry on as normal. It's 100 per cent not that, trust me.

'It just doesn't mean that we all have to shout and scream and create some chaos just because of it. Inside we're hurting. The boys know, and we need to get better. But the calmness doesn't mean that there's no emotion in it, for sure.

'It's not a nice feeling at all. It doesn't mean it's going to change the direction of how we're going as a team or as a football club. It's one game and results can happen in football, we all understand that. It's not nice when they do, but it does happen. We can be better, and we will be better.'

Reflecting post-match, Carrick insisted that his side know they have to be better after losing

Youri Tielemans was worryingly ineffective in midfield for Manchester United on his debut

United couldn't be much worse, in fairness, but at least Carrick will have a stronger squad available against Ipswich.

Carlos Baleba won't be available once his £70million move from Brighton goes through due to an ankle injury, but Kobbie Mainoo will have benefitted from another appearance off the bench at Hull, and Mason Mount could be fit again after impressing in pre-season until he was injured in the friendly against Paris Saint-Germain.

The two midfielders United have already bought for a total of £85m so far this summer, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans, were worryingly ineffective at Hull.

The minor nature of the injury Amad Diallo suffered in training late last week suggests he could return on the right flank, potentially releasing Bryan Mbeumo to play through the middle again after Matheus Cunha struggled there on Saturday. Benjamin Sesko is another option after making his first appearance of the summer off the bench due to a shin problem.

Lisandro Martinez and Diogo Dalot could also return to the line-up after another week of training following their late return from the World Cup, in place of Ayden Heaven - who struggled against Hull's combative striker Oli McBurnie - and Noussair Mazraoui.

Carrick has no shortage of options. He just has to get the balance right on and off the pitch.

Sports.title: Manchester City agree £81.4m deal to sign Morocco's teenage World Cup star Ayyoub Bouaddi, 18, after new boss Enzo Maresca insisted club urgently need a Rodri replacement
Sports.content:
Manchester City agree £81.4m deal to sign Morocco's teenage World Cup star Ayyoub Bouaddi, 18, after new boss Enzo Maresca insisted club urgently need a Rodri replacement

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Manchester City are set to complete the signing of Moroccan teenager Ayyoub Bouaddi for an initial £81.4million.

A breakthrough in protracted talks with Lille came in the hours before City’s Premier League season kicked off against Bournemouth, with City paying an initial £81m and an additional £4.3m in bonuses.

The Morocco international has been pulled out of their game with Angers today and is due to travel for his medical.

It provides a major boost for Enzo Maresca, whose side have looked light in midfield after the sale of Rodri to Barcelona and Bernardo Silva’s free transfer to Real Madrid.

City have now spent around £200m this summer and are expected to have a busy final week of the transfer window as they look to add more quality.

Maresca had suggested on Friday that he is looking for around 20 senior outfield players. Given that Omar Marmoush is heading to Tottenham and Newcastle United remain in discussions over Nico Gonzalez, there is an acute need for more bodies.

Ayyoub Bouaddi has been targeted by Man City to replace the gap left by Rodri's departure

Despite being only 18, Bouaddi has played almost a century of professional games and lit up the World Cup over the summer.

Lille had wanted to keep the midfielder for the campaign but City pushed for a deal that saw him join straight away. City are also closing on the £35m signing of Palmeiras winger Allan Elias.

Sports.title: 'I want to put a rocket up him!': Gary Neville hits out at Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak, claiming £240m Liverpool duo are 'too nice' as he warns 'enough is enough' after another poor display
Sports.content:
'I want to put a rocket up him!': Gary Neville hits out at Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak, claiming £240m Liverpool duo are 'too nice' as he warns 'enough is enough' after another poor display

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Gary Neville has warned Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak they need to improve and become more tenacious if they are to succeed as Liverpool players.

The pair are the most expensive signings in the club's history with Wirtz's £116million price-tag only bettered by Isak's £125m transfer as a Premier League record signing.

The pair endured underwhelming debut seasons at Liverpool last season as the club finished fifth, relinquishing their Premier League crown to Arsenal.

Both started in Sunday's 2-2 draw at Newcastle United - in what was the Reds' opening fixture of this campaign.

However, both failed to shine with Wirtz hooked after 63 minutes, while Isak failed to perform against a backdrop of vitriol in his first appearance back at St James' Park since his acrimonious exit last year.

And reflecting on their output, Neville believes the pair are 'too nice' and need a nastier side to their game.

Florian Wirtz (left) and Alexander Isak (right) have come under-fire from Gary Neville

Neville believes both are 'too nice' and has warned them they need to improve due to their fees

'The big thing for Liverpool is they've got a quarter-of-a-billion-pound front-two, Isak and Wirtz, and bloody hell we've been kind to them,' the Manchester United legend said on his Gary Neville Podcast.

'They are going to have to start playing soon or else to be fair they're going to get a lot of criticism. They're going to have to start delivering.

'For a start they're too nice and if you're going to be nice, you better be incredible at football.

'I don't see a tenacity in Wirtz in particular - Isak maybe a bit more - but in Wirtz I just see a nice player moving around the pitch, not really ever looking like he's busting a gut to do anything.'

Expanding further about Wirtz, Neville wants the playmaker to sharpen up - insisting he wants to put a 'rocket up him' at times due to his languid style on the pitch, adding that he needs to redefine his role to start producing goals and assists.

'You have players that are more graceful that just flow around the pitch - like [Mesut] Ozil and [Kai] Havertz - but I want to put a rocket up him,' he continued.

'There's ability and talent there and an understanding of his position. Sometimes I think he moves too much and isn't close enough to his striker. Sometimes I don't think he understands where the game is going to be won and lost.

'I don't see him combining with Isak. So for me, and I've said this for 12 months, he drifts too much. I just feel like Wirtz has got to think about being involved in the build-up less, he's got to think about being a second striker rather than a third midfield player, and has got to think about his output and what he needs to do, which is feed Isak with little passes and down the side of centre backs.

Speaking about Wirtz, Neville said he would like to put a 'rocket' up the £116million signing

'They've got to improve. I'm laying it on them now as I've watched them for 12 months but I have faith in them. I think Isak is an exceptional player - I never saw anyone give Gabriel and Saliba, or Van Dijk and Konate, a tougher time than he did when he was at Newcastle - so I've seen him be devastating.

'Liverpool's team-mates and coaches need to see that because it's £125m, and Wirtz needs to sort himself out. Enough is enough now. He's young and come into a different country and I can see a real player there, but we can't keep watching this stuff. He's been subbed after an hour and they need a goal. That's not right. The biggest disappointment for me is those two.'

Wirtz and Isak can let their feet do the talking on Saturday when Liverpool host Nottingham Forest in the 12.30pm kick-off.

Sports.title: Christian Horner's accuser mysteriously leaves her next role in motor racing after departure from Red Bull - moments before she was due to fly to a race
Sports.content:
Little more than a year on from Christian Horner leaving his £12million-a-season job as team principal of Red Bull, his accuser of coercive behaviour has been mysteriously released from her latest role in motor racing.

Daily Mail Sport can reveal that the woman executive involved, whose identity cannot be disclosed for legal reasons, parted company from her employers ahead of the Hungarian Grand Prix last month.

A source has told Daily Mail Sport that she was informed her services were no longer required moments before her scheduled flight to Budapest, a race won by McLaren’s British world champion Lando Norris.

Her then employers, who can also not be named, said: ‘We do not comment on personnel matters.’

It is understood that her latest position was terminated after her new boss, with whom she worked closely, lost confidence in her ‘for a lack of discretion’.

Daily Mail Sport has tried to contact the woman in question for a response to the suggested reasons for the parting, which followed a period during which she did not attend races.

Christian Horner with wife Geri Halliwell last year shortly before his departure from Red Bull

Horner oversaw eight drivers' titles at Red Bull, including four in a row with Max Verstappen

In one of Formula One’s most high-profile controversies, Horner – the husband of former Spice Girl Geri Halliwell – was accused of controlling behaviour over the employee.

He has always denied the claims and was twice cleared of any impropriety in internal investigations at Red Bull, despite a tranche of supposedly intimate text exchanges between the pair being made public in an explosive email sent to F1 figures ahead of the 2024 Bahrain Grand Prix.

Halliwell has resolutely and publicly stood by Horner throughout the turmoil, and they continue to split their time between their north London and Oxfordshire homes, along with their children Bluebell, Olivia and Montague.

Horner lost his job following last year’s British Grand Prix in a power struggle within the Austrian-based team he led to eight drivers’ and six constructors’ titles in two phases over 20 years through Sebastian Vettel and Max Verstappen.

Horner received an £80m package on leaving. The woman who made her accusations remained at Red Bull for several months as the saga unfolded before receiving a payout of some £3m.

She returned to motor racing in July last year in her then new position.

Horner, who has been courted by Ferrari and Aston Martin, and linked to Alpine, is considering how he might get back on the grid wall in a position that best suits him, ideally, as a team owner rather than as an employee.

FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem, speaking on the day of the British Grand Prix in July, vouched that Horner would ‘definitely’ return to F1.

Sports.title: Man City make shock Cody Gakpo approach to leave Liverpool and Tottenham with transfer dilemma
Sports.content:
Man City make shock Cody Gakpo approach to leave Liverpool and Tottenham with transfer dilemma

Manchester City have had a relatively quiet window in Enzo Maresca’s first summer at the helm but that could all change this week with moves for Cody Gakpo and Ayyoub Bouaddi

View 2 Images Cody Gakpo is being eyed by both Spurs and Man City (Image: Getty Images)

Manchester City have entered the race for Liverpool forward Cody Gakpo as they attempt to beat rivals Tottenham to his services. Gakpo, 27, has been linked with a move away from Anfield this summer.

‌



Spurs had emerged as potential suitors over recent days, having already had a bid turned down for his services. The Dutchman has already agreed terms on a move to North London.

‌



But it appears that they are facing competition for Gakpo’s signature, from Enzo Maresca’s Manchester City. According to reports, City have made their first move to sign the Dutchman and indeed beat Spurs to a deal.

‌



It remains to be seen how much Liverpool would sell the 27-year-old for, albeit it has previously been suggested it would take over £70m to agree a deal. Gakpo was signed from Dutch side PSV Eindhoven in 2023 and has gone on to score 51 goals in 181 appearances for the Reds - including one in the opening day draw with Newcastle at St James’ Park.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

He remains under contract with Liverpool until 2030, while Andoni Iraola has underlined his admiration of the forward.

‌



Speaking ahead of the trip to the North East, the Spanish coach said: "Cody is performing really well. I think he has been training very well from the first day and understanding everything we need from his position.

"When you talk to him, you can feel that he understands the game and he is very smart. He has been one of our best players in the friendlies and performing very well. I cannot tell you the starting XI, the players don't know it, but he is definitely in a great spot."

Should Man City get a deal over the line, Gakpo could become the third big-money arrival at the Etihad late in the window. City are also on the verge of completing a lucrative move for Lille and Monaco star Ayyoub Bouaddi, while a deal has also been agreed with Palmeiras for Allan Elias.

‌



View 2 Images Man City are close to selling Savinho and Omar Marmoush to Spurs (Image: Getty Images)

Their interest in Gakpo is also an intriguing development, given they are about to do business with Spurs in the final week of the window. Savinho and Omar Marmoush are thought to be close to a double deal worth around £140m.

Speaking about the pair, City boss Enzo Maresca said: "Omar is still here, still with us, it's a different situation to Savio and we see. Savio, since day one, asked to leave, and Omar didn't ask to leave since day one, not yet.

‌



"It's always complicated when someone leaves, and one has to arrive. We'll see if Omar stays or what happens."

He added: "It's quite clear that when players want to leave for any reason, it is complicated to convince them to stay and to change. It happened with Rodri, the same is happening with Savinho.

"Since day one, he has been clear that he wants to leave. Now we are waiting. It's complicated when players are clear they want a new challenge, or they want to go to Spain or play more minutes, it becomes complicated to convince them to stay."
