World.title: Air Chief Decries Misinformation, Hostile Narratives About Military Operations
World.content:
* Says they undermine public confidence

Linus Aleke in Abuja

The Chief of the Air Staff (CAS), Air Marshal Sunday Kelvin Aneke, has decried the menace of misinformation, disinformation and hostile narratives surrounding military operations, insisting that these digital vices undermine public confidence.

Air Marshal Aneke made the condemnation on Monday while declaring open the 2026 Directorate of Public Relations and Information (DOPRI) Annual Media Workshop and Meeting with information officers at the Headquarters of the Nigerian Air Force, Abuja.

The CAS, who was represented by the Chief of Policy and Plans (COPP), Nigerian Air Force, Air Vice Marshal Abubakar Yaro Abdullahi, said: “Today’s information environment is increasingly complex, dynamic and highly contested. News travels at unprecedented speed, while misinformation, disinformation and hostile narratives continue to challenge military operations and public confidence.

“In such an environment, effective public communication is no longer merely supportive; it is an operational necessity that contributes directly to mission success.

“As information officers, you represent the voice and image of the Nigerian Air Force. Your responsibilities extend beyond issuing press releases and organising media engagements. You are strategic communicators entrusted with shaping public understanding of our operations, projecting the professionalism of our personnel, preserving institutional credibility and strengthening public trust in the service. Every communication, every engagement and every response to a crisis must therefore reflect accuracy, professionalism, integrity and timeliness.”

The special guest of honour said the service must remain proactive in communicating its activities with credibility, transparency and strategic intent while confronting evolving security challenges.

“We must continually improve our ability to engage stakeholders, counter misinformation, manage crises effectively and reinforce public confidence in the service. Together, we can build a public relations and information system that reflects the professionalism, discipline and operational excellence for which the Nigerian Air Force is renowned,” he said.

In a paper titled ‘Building and Maintaining Strategic Media Relationships: Best Practices for NAF Public Relations and Information Officers’, the Director-General of Voice of Nigeria (VOA), Mallam Jibrin Baba Ndace, said the Nigerian Air Force operates in an increasingly complex security environment where narratives can be weapons and information vacuums can become strategic vulnerabilities.

“At the same time, credible communication can be a force multiplier: it strengthens public confidence, protects institutional reputation and supports the overall mission of the service,” he said.

Earlier, in his welcome address, the Director of Public Relations and Information (DOPRI), Nigerian Air Force, Air Commodore Ehimen Ejodame, said military operations were no longer contested only on the battlefield but were also fiercely contested in the information environment.

He stressed that what people believe, see, hear and share can greatly influence the outcome of an operation, almost as significantly as what happens on the battlefield, adding: “This is why we consider strategic communication an operational capability.

“A photograph can inspire confidence. A video can demonstrate professionalism. A well-written report can correct a false narrative. But a single careless communication can undermine years of institutional credibility.”

The workshop was themed ‘Enhancing Strategic Media Operations of Nigerian Air Force Public Relations and Information Personnel Through Capacity Building in Crisis Management Skills.’

World.title: The Next Level: Making Nollywood Films That Travel
World.content:
Femi Odugbemi

I recently had the privilege of presenting a masterclass to members of the Directors Guild of Nigeria (DGN) during the Guild’s National Awards Week. The subject was one I believe has become increasingly urgent for Nigerian cinema: What is the next level for Nollywood? For more than three decades, we have achieved something remarkable. We built an industry. We learned to produce quickly, economically, and under immense pressure. We created stars, filled cinemas, fed television schedules, and increasingly supplied streaming platforms. We found ways to tell stories that resonated with audiences, often against formidable odds. These are significant achievements.

The original Nollywood model was built on efficiency: modest budgets, rapid production, and fast distribution. It emerged from necessity, but necessity became innovation. We created an industry where, arguably, none previously existed. But industries must evolve. Today, Nollywood has bigger budgets, better cameras, more sophisticated infrastructure, premium locations, celebrity talent, drones, visual effects, 4K workflows, Dolby sound, and every other tool of contemporary filmmaking. Yet one critical question remains: Are our films becoming more artistically distinctive simply because they are becoming more expensive?

Unfortunately, the answer is no.

A N50 million film can still feel ordinary, while a N10 million film can possess extraordinary visual and emotional power. Budgets do not make films memorable. Creative decisions do.

That is the challenge of Nollywood’s next revolution.

From Access to Expression

The first Nollywood revolution was about access: access to cameras, stories, audiences, distribution, and an industry that had once seemed inaccessible. We mastered volume, speed, efficiency, and market reach.

The next revolution must be about something deeper: Vision. Aesthetics. Craft. Authorship.

A director’s job is no longer simply to get a film made. The director must shape what the film means, how it feels, and what it looks like.

That requires a fundamental shift—from seeing the director as a coordinator of production to understanding the director as the author of a cinematic experience.

Every major creative decision should begin with a question: Why this story? Why now? Why me? Why this crew? Why this frame? Why this colour? Why this location? Why this actor? Why this sound? Why this cut? Why this silence?

The answer cannot always be, “Because that’s how we’ve always done it.”

Nor can it simply be, “Because that’s what the producer, investor, or distributor wants.”

Filmmaking is collaborative and commercial. Directors must work within budgets and negotiate competing interests. But within those realities, there must still be a distinctive creative point of view.

That is authorship.

What Does It Mean For A Film To Travel?

The title of my masterclass was “The Next Level: Making Films That Travel.”

Travel has two meanings.

The first is literal: a film moves beyond its original market into festivals, cinemas, television networks, streaming platforms, airlines, universities, cultural institutions, and diaspora communities.

The second is more important: the idea travels. A character becomes unforgettable. A scene lingers. A Nigerian experience enters a global conversation. A filmmaker in Lagos tells a story that resonates in Johannesburg, London, Toronto, Nairobi, New York, or São Paulo.

This is why film is more than entertainment. It is soft power. Our films tell the world who we are, how we see ourselves, and how we want to be seen.

So what makes a film travel?

I believe it requires three things: A local truth — something culturally specific and rooted in place. A human truth — something emotionally universal. A cinematic language — a storytelling approach that transcends borders.

A story about a Nigerian father and son may be deeply Nigerian. But love, ambition, disappointment, grief, reconciliation, and shame are universal. The more honestly we tell our local stories, the more likely they are to find global audiences.

Devt is The Missing Revolution

One area where we must improve dramatically is development. Too often, development is treated as the period between receiving a script and beginning production.

In reality, development is where the film is discovered. It should include research, rewriting, table reads, character exploration, visual references, location studies, production design concepts, casting explorations, the director’s treatment, lookbooks, sound concepts, and even editing approaches.

A film should be designed before it is shot.

This does not make filmmaking rigid. In fact, preparation creates freedom. The better we understand the world of the story, the more room we have for meaningful creative discoveries on set.

Aesthetics is Not Decoration

Aesthetics is often mistaken for beauty. It is actually storytelling. Space tells us where we are. Light tells us how a world feels. Composition directs attention. Movement shapes emotion. Colour builds atmosphere.

When these choices are intentional, a film develops a visual language.

For instance, Nigeria possesses a rich sonic identity: Lagos traffic, owambe celebrations, generators, market sounds, highlife music, mosque calls, church services, danfo conductors, rainfall on zinc roofs, distant conversations, and sudden silence. These are not background noises. They are part of our cinematic identity. We should record them deliberately, design them carefully, and use them emotionally. We must also embrace silence. A look can function as dialogue. A silent room can provide exposition. An off-screen sound can be more powerful than showing an event directly.

One of our most persistent habits is the “coverage mentality”: Wide shot. Medium shot. Close-up. Reverse shot. Insert. Repeat.

That is coverage. It is not necessarily cinema.

Directors must ask: Whose perspective are we seeing? What should the audience feel before they understand? Why this angle? Why this movement? What story beat does this shot serve?

A camera should have a personality.

A handheld image can create intimacy or instability. A static frame can suggest observation or isolation. A long lens may create distance; a wide lens may create immersion. A slow push-in can reveal psychology.

The principle is simple: Do not move the camera because you can. Move it because the story requires it.

A director’s aesthetic is not only visual; it is behavioural. We need to rethink our definition of strong performances. Not every emotion requires shouting. Not every pain requires tears. Not every conflict requires dramatic gestures or lengthy speeches. Subtlety is not the absence of emotion. It is controlled emotion.

The camera often reveals what a character chooses not to say. That is where performance and cinematic language intersect. The director’s responsibility is to create the conditions for those moments to emerge.

Every serious director should be able to present a visual bible before production: What are the references? What is the colour palette? How will the film be framed? How will the camera move? What lenses are appropriate? What is the lighting strategy? What language will guide production design, costume, sound, performance, and editing?

If you cannot show what your film feels like before you shoot it, you may not yet know what your film feels like.

Nigeria is Our Greatest Visual Asset

Nigeria itself is one of our greatest cinematic resources. Its villages, rivers, beaches, forests, mountains, festivals, durbars, craft communities, historic sites, traditional architecture, and energetic cities offer extraordinary visual possibilities. Yet too many films feel as though they were shot nowhere in particular.

A location should do more than provide a backdrop. It should reveal character, history, culture, and relationships. Production design allows us to place meaning within the frame, enriching the story beyond dialogue.

We need to travel across Nigeria, rediscover its landscapes, and learn to see familiar places with fresh eyes. Few countries offer such diverse cinematic possibilities.

Post-Production is Where The Film Becomes A Film

Editing should involve more than asking whether the story is understandable.

We must also ask: Does the scene breathe? What should be withheld? When should we leave? When should we stay longer? Pacing and rhythm are not technical concerns alone. They are storytelling tools. Editors do more than assemble footage. They help discover the film itself. In many ways, the film continues to be written in the edit.

Colour should always be intentional.

Perhaps childhood is warm while adulthood is cooler. Perhaps memory is desaturated. Perhaps danger is green, and desire is red. Or perhaps the film rejects conventional colour symbolism altogether. The point is not which choice is made but rather that a choice is made. Intentionality matters

If we want Nigerian films to travel, we must rethink subtitles. Subtitling is not an administrative task. It carries rhythm, humour, meaning, context, and culture. Poor subtitles can undermine great performances. Excellent subtitles invite audiences into our world.

In many ways, subtitles are our passport to global audiences. They should be treated as part of production quality, not an afterthought.

We must make films for the second watch. The first viewing asks: What happens?

The second asks: How did they do that?

The third asks: What does it mean?

Great films reward repeated viewing.

We need to create films that audiences discover rather than merely consume. Discovery endures. Consumption is fleeting.

Films achieve longevity when they contain layers—visual, emotional, thematic, sonic, and narrative. That is the cinema that builds legacy.

The Director Needs A Creative Tribe

None of this means the director should become a one-person army. Quite the opposite. Every director needs a creative tribe: researchers, writers, script editors, production designers, location scouts, sound designers, composers, editors, colourists, VFX supervisors, acting coaches, festival strategists, and distributors. The director’s role is increasingly to lead a creative ecosystem.

The best directors are not those who can do every job themselves, but those who can assemble talented collaborators and communicate a vision clearly enough for everyone to contribute their best work.

Festival Strategy Begins Before Production

Another common mistake is waiting until a film is complete before thinking about festivals.

Festival strategy should begin during development. What kind of film are we making? Who is the audience? Which festivals programme this type of work? Does premiere status matter? Which territories are important? Do we need a sales agent? The same applies to distribution.

A film designed to travel must be conceived with its journey in mind. This is not about making films to satisfy festivals. It is about understanding the ecosystem in which cinema operates.

A NEW DEFINITION OF SUCCESS

For years, our primary measure of success has been simple: How much money did the film make? That question remains important. Film is both art and business.

But we should also ask: Did the film travel? Did it expand our cinematic language? Did it say something meaningful? Did it inspire future filmmakers? Did it represent Nigeria honestly? Did it discover new talent? Did it achieve artistic recognition?

These are not alternatives to commercial success. They are complementary measures of cultural and artistic impact.

If Nollywood is to become one of the world’s great cinemas, it needs both.

The Next Nollywood Revolution

The next level for Nollywood is not simply more money, bigger sets, more celebrity actors, or more expensive technology. The next level is intentionality.

It is the courage to develop stories properly. The discipline to create a visual language. The confidence to trust our sonic identity. The sophistication to embrace silence. The patience to allow performances to breathe. The understanding that editing is storytelling. The imagination to see Nigeria anew. The wisdom to build creative tribes. And the foresight to think about distribution from the beginning.

Above all, it is the willingness of directors to move from being efficient filmmakers to becoming authors. Nollywood has already proven that Nigerians can build an industry, cultivate audiences, and create economic value through storytelling.

Now we must prove something more: That our cinema can develop a distinctive artistic voice, one that travels across borders without losing the cultural truth from which it emerges.

The world does not need Nigerian filmmakers to imitate films from elsewhere. It needs films that could only have come from us, yet speak to something deeply human in everyone.

That is the next level.

*Femi Odugbemi is an award-winning filmmaker, film scholar and storyteller. He writes from Lagos.

World.title: The Biggest Threat to Africa’s Data Centre Race Is the Grid
World.content:
Oluwaseyi Ayodeji

Ever so often, another headline declares a winner in Africa’s data centre race. South Africa is pulling ahead. Kenya just landed a billion-dollar deal. Nigeria is falling behind. Read enough of these, and you start to believe this is a contest between three countries, decided by whoever signs the biggest cheque or announces the most facilities.

It isn’t. The real contest is each of these countries against its own electricity grid, and the country that wins will not be the one with the most press releases. It will be the one that keeps the lights on.

On paper, South Africa is way ahead. It has 56 data centres (~350 megawatts), more than any other African market, and is widely reported to account for roughly 70% of the continent’s data centre capacity. That lead was built over more than a decade of investment from global cloud and data-centre operators, including Amazon, Microsoft and Google.

Nigeria, by contrast, is still building out its capacity market by market, with Lagos alone currently running around 78.6 megawatts of installed data-centre capacity and a pipeline projected to push past 218 megawatts by 2030. That is genuine, meaningful growth and nothing to be sneezed at. But set against South Africa’s existing base, the gap looks like a straightforward story of one country executing and another catching up.

It is not that simple, and the reason why is the entire point of this piece.

The capital flows tell you where investors currently believe the race is being won. South Africa recently secured a $438 million Equinix investment plan that includes a further 160 megawatts of data-centre capacity, while Kenya has drawn ambitious mega-project commitments, including the Microsoft-G42 initiative centred on a geothermal-powered facility with an initial target of 100 megawatts and an eventual ambition to scale towards 1 gigawatt.

Set against those numbers, Nigeria’s pipeline can look like it’s playing catch-up in a game it is already losing. Investment committees read headlines like these and draw conclusions quickly: the capital is voting with its feet, and it is voting for South Africa and Kenya over Nigeria.

I spent years managing large-scale cloud infrastructure programmes, the kind where a single facility’s timeline depends on dozens of workstreams landing in the right order: land acquisition, power interconnection studies, equipment procurement, construction, commissioning and testing, often running in parallel across multiple continents and vendors. If there is one lesson that experience taught me, it is this: a capital commitment is not a completed facility, and a signed deal is not delivered power.

The gap between an announcement and an operating asset is where infrastructure projects actually live or die, and it is the gap the headlines rarely cover, because a press release is easy to write and a commissioned facility takes years of unglamorous execution.

In 2024, Microsoft and the UAE-based firm G42 announced a $1 billion digital investment initiative in Kenya, centred on a geothermal-powered data centre in Olkaria, near Naivasha. The first phase was planned at around 100 megawatts, with the potential to scale towards 1 gigawatt. The broader initiative also included a new East Africa cloud region, local-language AI development, connectivity investments and digital-skills programmes.

The data-centre project has since stalled. Reporting in 2026 indicates that disagreements over the amount of power capacity the Kenyan government could commit to the project contributed to the breakdown in negotiations, with the original May 2026 launch target no longer achievable. The project has not simply disappeared, but the original timetable and scope are clearly no longer proceeding as initially announced.

This is not a story about Kenya’s failure. It is a story about what happens when even a well-funded, well-intentioned, geothermal-powered project runs into a hard physical and institutional constraint that money alone cannot remove. Kenya has a relatively diversified electricity mix and substantial geothermal resources, and it still found itself having to reconsider how much power could realistically be committed to a single digital infrastructure project.

That should tell every policymaker in this region something important about what actually determines who wins this race. It should also temper how confidently anyone declares a winner based on deal announcements alone.

Nigeria’s problem is not that it has no generation capacity. It is that the amount of power actually available to the grid is dramatically lower than the country’s installed capacity. Nigeria has roughly 13 – 14 gigawatts of installed generation capacity, but available generation is typically in the 4 – 6 gigawatt range, depending on gas supply, plant availability, transmission constraints and outages. South Africa, by comparison, has an electricity system with roughly 48 gigawatts of installed Eskom capacity, although its reliably available output is substantially lower than that figure.

That is not primarily a technology gap or a capital gap. It is a power-security gap, and it is a major reason South Africa’s data-centre lead has proved so durable.

A hyperscale AI facility needs enormous, continuous, reliable electricity, the kind of load that a fragile or frequently disrupted grid simply cannot guarantee, no matter how much capital or ambition sits behind the project. South Africa’s data-centre ecosystem did not emerge because South Africa wanted data centres more than Nigeria did, or because its founders and operators were somehow more capable. It emerged in an environment where the underlying power and infrastructure systems gave global operators greater confidence to make decade-long investment decisions.

This is precisely the constraint I watched shape infrastructure decisions from the inside for years: site selection for large compute facilities almost always comes down to power availability before it comes down to almost anything else, including tax incentives, land cost or even connectivity. A country can offer every other advantage on paper and still lose the deal the moment a serious operator runs the power feasibility studies.

It would be a mistake to treat this purely as a technology competitiveness story. Every gigabyte of data processed abroad, in a facility Nigeria does not host and does not control, represents a small transfer of digital leverage to whichever country does. As African economies build more of their financial systems, government services and AI products on top of cloud infrastructure, the question of where that infrastructure physically sits stops being merely a business decision and becomes a question of national standing and strategic autonomy.

Nigeria’s own financial regulator is already treating it this way. In June 2026, the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) issued a circular requiring financial institutions and participants facilitating payments within Nigeria to ensure that payment transaction data generated within Nigeria is stored and managed within Nigeria, with compliance effective from January 1, 2027. The circular explicitly identifies the localisation of critical payment data as part of its effort to strengthen the resilience and oversight of the Nigerian payments system.

That is more than a compliance measure. It is an acknowledgement that critical digital infrastructure cannot be separated from national control. The CBN is telling financial institutions that if Nigerian payment data is important enough to regulate, it is important enough to keep within the country’s jurisdiction. And once that data must remain in Nigeria, the physical infrastructure required to store, process and protect it becomes a national infrastructure issue as well.

A country that cannot reliably power its own data centres will, over time, find itself renting critical digital capacity from foreign providers on terms it did not set. That is not a hypothetical. It is the direction all three countries in this race are confronting, at different speeds, for the same underlying reason.

Closing this gap will not come from another facility announcement or foreign investment press release. Nigeria has spent decades announcing power-sector reforms, generation projects and transmission investments while businesses and households continue to contend with an electricity system that cannot reliably deliver power across the country. The problem is no longer a lack of understanding of what needs to be built; it is the country’s chronic inability to execute, maintain and scale what it already knows it needs.

For the data-centre economy, that means treating reliable electricity as digital infrastructure in its own right. Nigeria needs sustained investment in transmission capacity, enough generation to provide genuine reserve capacity, and a grid with sufficient redundancy to withstand failures without repeatedly taking large parts of the country offline. Generation cannot be the only measure of progress. Power that exists on paper but cannot be transmitted consistently to where it is needed is not useful capacity, and megawatts that disappear every time the grid trips do not give a hyperscale operator the certainty required to commit billions of dollars.

Most importantly, Nigeria needs to stop treating persistent power outages as an unavoidable feature of economic life. A hyperscale data centre cannot be built around the assumption that the national grid will fail and a diesel generator will take over. Nor can an AI economy serving hundreds of millions of people be powered indefinitely through thousands of individual captive-generation arrangements. Those solutions may work at the facility level, and in many cases they are necessary, but they do not solve the national infrastructure problem.

The country does, however, have the ingredients for a different outcome. Nigeria has a large domestic gas resource base that remains significantly underutilised for power generation, alongside growing private-sector interest in embedded generation specifically designed to serve data-centre and industrial demand. The raw materials for a different outcome exist, both in the ground and in the willingness of private operators to invest around a clearly defined need.

What has been missing is the same sustained execution focus that data-centre operators are already applying to their own captive power projects, but applied at national grid scale rather than at the fence line of a single facility. If a private operator can commission a dedicated 100-megawatt gas plant to guarantee power for one facility, the underlying capability to solve this problem clearly exists inside the country. The challenge is applying that same urgency, discipline and coordination to the national system, and sustaining it long enough for businesses to stop planning around the assumption that the grid will fail.

Nigeria does not need to reinvent the technology or wait for some future breakthrough to solve this problem. It needs to make reliable power a national infrastructure priority, execute consistently across generation and transmission, and create enough confidence in the system that data-centre operators can build for the next decade rather than simply insure themselves against the next outage.

So the next time you see a headline declaring that Nigeria is losing the data-centre race to Kenya or South Africa, ask the more useful question instead: losing to whom exactly, and on what terms?

South Africa’s lead is real, but it is largely a product of infrastructure and market development built over decades, not evidence of a technology gap Nigeria cannot close. Kenya’s experience shows that even a hugely ambitious, well-funded project cannot simply wish away the infrastructure and institutional constraints around power capacity. That should reshape how confidently anyone ranks these three countries against each other based on investment announcements alone.

The country that ultimately leads Africa’s AI infrastructure future will not be the one that announces the most gigawatts. It will be the one that delivers them, reliably, at scale, year after year.

That is a power-sector achievement before it is ever a technology one, and it is the metric this region should actually be tracking, far more closely than it tracks facility counts or investment announcements.

What would it take for Nigeria to make grid reliability its top digital economy priority? I’d like to hear where you land.

* Ayodeji is a senior programme leader in AI/Cloud Infrastructure with two decades in the tech industry

World.title: Olu’s 5th Anniversary: Olori Atuwatse III Unveils Bold Vision for Women, Culture, Human Capital Development
World.content:
Sylvester Idowu in Warri

Olori Atuwatse III, Queen Consort Warri Kingdom, has said the last five years of her tenure alongside her husband, His Royal Majesty Ogiame Atuwatse III, the Olu of Warri, have been devoted to building human capacity, empowering women, preserving Itsekiri culture and creating stronger connections among Itsekiris at home and in the diaspora.

The Olori, who spoke to journalists at her residence in Warri weekend, as part of activities marking the Olu’s fifth coronation anniversary, said the progress recorded in the kingdom’s women empowerment programmes had become one of the most gratifying aspects of her royal responsibilities.

According to her, the elevation of women within the Warri Kingdom has become increasingly visible, with women, particularly wives of chiefs, becoming more confident, recognised and willing to take ownership of their voices and responsibilities.

“Seeing how the women in the kingdom have become more naturally elevated, I always give the stories of how the chiefs’ wives have now become more esteemed in many ways and more recognised,” she said.

She stated that women were increasingly moving beyond seeking permission to participate in community affairs to becoming active owners of their voices and initiatives.

“I really love the esteem of women in the kingdom, and I’m really thankful for that,” she said, adding that: “Leadership has taught me to enlarge my heart.”

Reflecting on the challenges and lessons of her five-year journey as Olori, Queen Ashley said she would rather describe the experience as a period of learning than as a series of challenges.

She identified understanding human nature, managing differences and learning to appreciate the strengths of different people as some of the most important lessons she had acquired.

“I think it would be what I used to learn leadership. It is understanding the dynamics of human nature and the differences in different people and just learning how to enlarge my heart to love every person and pick out the strengths from people and discard the weaknesses,” she said.

The Olori, a lawyer, author and founder of ‘Women-focused initiatives’, explained that her royal position had provided her with a platform to convert privilege into service, particularly through initiatives targeted at women, education, skills development and access to opportunities.

She said she regarded herself primarily as a mother serving the people entrusted to her care rather than simply as a queen.

“I’m a mother more than any queen,” she declared, explaining that her approach to service was built around two key principles, agency and access.

According to her, the first objective was to help people, especially women regain control over their lives and overcome what she described as a “learned sense of helplessness”.

The second was to provide access to skills, networks, finance and other resources required to transform aspirations into sustainable livelihoods.

She said the philosophy underpins programmes such as ‘Women Aligning Women’, operated under ‘Elevate Africa’, and ‘Establish Her’, operated under the ‘Royal Iwere Foundation’.

The Olori disclosed that findings from their engagement with women in the community had shown that women constituted a significant proportion of household breadwinners, particularly among women aged between 18 and 35.

She said about eight out of 10 women engaged through the initiative were breadwinners supporting several dependants.

“That meant we had to begin to see how we can establish our women by working with the whole woman, not just giving her skills or access to finance, but actually looking to raise the whole woman,” she explained.

She said the programme therefore begins with developing the mindset of participants, helping them understand leadership, identify their leadership styles and build confidence before introducing business and entrepreneurship components.

The Olori also placed strong emphasis on the preservation of Itsekiri language and culture, describing the Itsekiri people as a “micro minority” whose cultural heritage must be deliberately protected against the pressures of modernisation and globalisation.

“We Itsekiris, we’re a micro minority. So inside the minority, we are a minority. And so it’s important to preserve our culture, to preserve our language,” she said.

According to her, the rapid erosion of indigenous languages across communities, including among larger ethnic groups, makes the preservation of Itsekiri language an urgent responsibility.

She disclosed that a language competition was introduced around the period of the Olu’s coronation anniversary to encourage children from communities across the kingdom and those in the diaspora to learn and speak Itsekiri.

On her relationship with the Olu and how they manage the demands of royal duties, public expectations and family life, Queen Ashley said the strength of their family remains the foundation of everything they do.

She stressed that before their identities as king and queen, they were husband and wife and regarded their relationship as a partnership that required deliberate nurturing.

“That is our foundation, the strong family unit behind the closed door is our primary foundation. We are first husband and wife. We are first a strong unit together, and we take those duties very seriously. We take our bond and our connection very seriously,” she said.

She said their relationship and responsibilities were also firmly anchored in their faith, adding: “Everything is embedded under God. God is our third cord, and then we take it from ther.”

The Olori also spoke about her fashion choices, particularly her blend of contemporary elegance with traditional Itsekiri and wider African attire.

She said her intention was not merely to make a fashion statement but to demonstrate that African culture could be celebrated with confidence, sophistication and contemporary relevance.

Looking ahead after five years in the royal household, the Olori expressed gratitude for the journey but said she regarded the period as the beginning rather than the culmination of their work.

“I’m really thankful for the last five years. It’s been like five years that has felt like 50 years, but at the same time felt like five months,” she said.

World.title: FG Unveils ​‌⁠⁠​‍⁠⁠‌‌⁠‌​​‌‌New Reforms to Tackle Almajiri, Out-of-School Children
World.content:
The Federal Government has unveiled new reforms aimed at ensuring every Nigerian child returns to school and acquires relevant knowledge and skills.

Dr Balarabe Kakale, The Special Adviser to the Minister of Education on Almajiri and Out of School Children, Dr Balarabe Kakale, disclosed this in Kaduna on Monday while speaking at a National Education Sector Renewal Initiative (NESRI) advocacy and stakeholders engagement on Almajiri and out-of-school children.

He said the Federal Ministry of Education has introduced transformative policies to address challenges confronting Almajiri, out-of-school and other non-formal education systems.

According to him, the reforms are designed to strengthen coordination between federal and state agencies working in the education and out-of-school subsectors.

He said the policies were anchored on five pillars, including foundational literacy, numeracy, vocational and technical education, digital education and civic education.

Kakale said proper implementation of the policies by states would ensure that no Nigerian child was left without access to education.

He urged states to domesticate the National Commission for Almajiri and Out-of-School Children Education Act according to their peculiar educational challenges.

He also called for domestication of policies on Almajiri education, non-state schools, alternative pathways and Accelerated Basic Education Programme.

Kakale commended the Kaduna Government for implementing several reforms through the Reaching Out-of-School Children (ROSK) project.

He described Kaduna as a model that could provide lessons for national scale-up of interventions addressing out-of-school children.

The special adviser said the Federal Government was promoting data sovereignty through the Nigerian Education Data Infrastructure and other digital education management systems.

He said the initiative would ensure that every child, school, teacher and infrastructure gap was properly captured for effective policy interventions.

Kakale said Nigeria currently had no final figure for out-of-school children, stressing that reliable and verifiable data remained critical to solving the challenge.

He said the Federal Government would no longer depend on third-party estimates, but would track children from enrolment through retention and academic progress.

The special adviser urged North-west states to embrace federal education policies and digital data initiatives to accelerate efforts to return children to school.

He expressed optimism that coordinated implementation would help Nigeria achieve its goal of becoming a leading nation in Africa.

Representing the Executive Secretary of the National Commission for Almajiri and Out-of-School Children Education, Malam Halliru Musa Halliru, said the commission was committed to transforming Almajiri education.

Halliru said the commission had developed a 10-year strategic plan for 2025–2035 to provide coordinated and sustainable interventions in Almajiri and out-of-school education.

He said the National Policy on Enhancement of Almajiri Education sought to strengthen traditional education through literacy, numeracy, vocational training and quality assurance.

According to him, the policy seeks to build bridges between traditional and modern education without discarding the religious and cultural values of the Almajiri system.

Halliru said about 200 Almajiri learners at the Tinubu Legacy Skills Training Institute in Kaduna had received Arabic, English, vocational and practical skills training.

He said the learners had also excelled in examinations conducted by the National Board for Arabic and Islamic Studies.

The commission’s representative said 119 learning centres had been established nationwide to support Almajiri learners and out-of-school children.

He added that the commission had mapped more than 700,000 out-of-school children to support targeted interventions and enrolment.

Halliru said the commission was also collecting comprehensive data on Tsangaya centres to improve planning, support, coordination and quality assurance.

He said the commission had established offices in all states and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) to strengthen collaboration and monitoring.

Kaduna State Commissioner for Education, Prof. Abubakar Sambo, said the challenge of Almajiri and out-of-school children required coordinated action by governments and stakeholders.

Sambo said poverty remained a major factor forcing children out of school, particularly in rural and peri-urban communities.

He said some parents also sent very young children to Almajirai, describing the practice as a growing challenge in northern states.

The commissioner urged participants to carefully study the federal policies and develop strategies for implementing them across states and local governments.

He identified accurate data on out-of-school children as critical to successful planning and intervention.

Sambo said Kaduna State had fully embraced the Federal Government’s policies and remained committed to addressing the out-of-school children challenge.

Coordinator of the Kaduna ROOSC project, Mr Ezra Angai, said the state had adopted a holistic approach to returning children to learning.

Angai said the project was designed to return 100,000 out-of-school children to education through formal schools and alternative learning pathways.

He said Kaduna had mapped 187,912 out of school children across its 23 local government areas.

According to him, the project had established alternative learning systems, including Accelerated Basic Education Centres and interventions within Tsangaya schools.

Angai said the state had signed memoranda of understanding with 25 Tsangayas, reaching 6,326 learners, while plans were underway to engage 50 more.

He said the project would also provide interventions for Tsangayas, recognising them as important learning centres within communities.

The coordinator said 272 schools, comprising new and renovated facilities, were planned under the project, including 102 new schools.

He said six Tsangayas would benefit from the first phase of infrastructure intervention, while 27 others were proposed for the second phase.

Angai said more than 25,000 children had already been returned to learning through the ROOSC project.

He said over 40,000 teaching and learning materials had been distributed, alongside uniforms, textbooks and psychosocial support.

According to him, more than 2,000 children with disabilities had received assistive devices across nine local government areas.

Angai said the project had received support from development partners, including the Islamic Development Bank, Kuwait Fund, UNICEF and Save the Children International.

He said the project also collaborated with Education Above All and the Global Partnership for Education.

He urged stakeholders to sustain collaboration with the Federal Government to strengthen implementation of policies addressing education exclusion.

The engagement brought together government agencies, traditional rulers, Islamic scholars, Alarammas, Tsangaya proprietors, civil society organisations and development partners.

Participants also called for stronger collaboration, improved data collection and community mobilisation to ensure vulnerable children returned to learning.

The stakeholders pledged continued support for reforms aimed at integrating Almajiri education with broader educational opportunities and reducing the number of out-of-school children.

They also stressed the need to move beyond data collection and policies towards practical interventions capable of improving children’s access, retention and learning outcomes.(NAN)

World.title: Breaking: NNPC, Shell, Esso, Agip Sign PSC, DSA Addenda on $21bn Bonga South-West Aparo Project
World.content:
*Asset inches towards FID, to become Nigeria’s largest deepwater devt

*To unlock 175000bpd of oil, 140mmscfd of gas

Peter Uzoho

The Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPCL) and its Contractor Parties — Shell Nigeria Exploration and Production Company Limited (SNEPCo), Esso Exploration and Production Nigeria (Deepwater) Limited, and Nigerian Agip Exploration Limited (NAE) on Monday executed the Addendum to the Oil Mining Lease (OML 118) Production Sharing Contract (PSC) and the Addendum to the Dispute Settlement Agreement (DSA).

The development marked a major milestone in the advancement of the deepwater Bonga Southwest/Aparo project (BWSAp) towards Final Investment Decision (FID).

NNPCL announced the deals in a statement signed by its Chief Corporate Communications Officer, Mr. Andy Odey.

The execution gives effect to the fiscal and commercial terms approved by the federal government to support the development of BSWAp and it reinforces Nigeria’s commitment to creating a competitive, stable and attractive environment for large-scale deepwater investment.

The milestone follows the approval of the Deep Offshore Oil and Gas Projects Incentives (Tax Remission) Order, 2026, by President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, an important component of the government’s ongoing reforms to enhance the competitiveness of Nigeria’s deepwater sector and unlock new investment.

NNPCL said the BSWA PSC and DSA Addenda demonstrate the practical impact of these reforms in translating policy into investment and project development.

The company added that BSWAp was expected to be one of Nigeria’s largest deepwater developments, with the potential to attract $15 billion to $21 billion in investment over the life of the project and achieve peak production of about 175 kbopd of oil and 140 mmscfd of gas.

The development is expected to contribute significantly to Nigeria’s economy through increased oil and gas production, government revenues, foreign exchange earnings, local content development, employment and expanded opportunities for Nigerian businesses.

Speaking on the milestone, the Group Chief Executive Officer of NNPCL, Bayo Ojulari, said: “The execution of the BSWAp PSC and DSA Addenda demonstrates the effectiveness of President Tinubu’s reforms in translating policy into investment. This is about unlocking a major deepwater project and demonstrating that Nigeria has a competitive fiscal framework and a clear pathway for sustainable investment in its energy sector.

“NNPC Ltd will continue to work closely with the Federal Government, our partners and other stakeholders to ensure that this project delivers maximum value for the Federation and the Nigerian people.”

The Contractor Parties also announced the successful completion of the project’s Pre-Front End Engineering Design (Pre-FEED) phase, marking an important milestone in maturing the technical and commercial scope of the development and positioning the project to progress into the Front End Engineering Design (FEED) phase, subject to applicable partner, assurance and governance requirements.

Following a competitive selection process, a bidder has been identified as the preferred Floating Production Storage and Offloading (FPSO) contractor for the BSWA project, subject to completion of applicable partner, regulatory, assurance and governance processes, the statement said.

The national oil firm further said the selection provides a basis for progressing the FPSO concept into FEED and for undertaking the further engineering and commercial work required to mature the project towards FID.

It added that any eventual award of the FPSO Engineering, Procurement, Construction and Installation (EPCI) contract remains subject to the completion of all applicable approvals and requirements.

“Once operational, BSWAp is expected to become one of Nigeria’s most significant new deepwater production hubs, contributing materially to national oil production and supporting the country’s ambition to sustainably grow oil and gas output over the coming years.

“The project is expected to deliver substantial benefits to Nigeria through billions of dollars of investment, increased participation by Nigerian contractors and suppliers, and significant direct and indirect employment opportunities across engineering, fabrication, offshore construction, logistics and operations.

“BSWAp is also expected to strengthen Nigerian content through increased contracting opportunities for indigenous companies, enhance local fabrication, marine and engineering capabilities, facilitate technology transfer and skills development, and create lasting value across the wider Nigerian economy”, the statement said.

It said the milestone reflects the strong collaboration among NNPC Ltd, the Federal Government, relevant regulatory agencies and the OML 118 Contractor Parties , and reinforces Nigeria’s position as a competitive destination for deepwater investment.

NNPCL reaffirmed its commitment to working with all stakeholders to advance the BSWA project safely, competitively and responsibly, while maximising value for Nigeria and the Nigerian people.

World.title: Oil Prices Fall Ahead of US, Iran Sanctions
World.content:
Oil prices fell more than one dollar on Monday as investors took profits and awaited expected new U.S. sanctions on Iran.

Brent crude futures fell $1.16, or 1.23 per cent, to $93.23 a barrel at 11:31 a.m. GMT.

U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude declined $1.55, or 1.78 per cent, to $85.51 a barrel.

Both contracts recorded a second consecutive weekly gain last week, rising more than five per cent.

The gains followed stalled U.S.-Iran peace negotiations, which have constrained oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.

The waterway previously carried about one-fifth of global oil supplies and remains a major route for energy shipments.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is expected to announce new measures against Iran during a press conference later Monday.

Bessent has threatened to impose what he described as “the toughest sanctions in history” on Iran.

U.S. President Donald Trump has also threatened sanctions against countries trading with Iran.

PVM analyst Tamas Varga said an embargo could reduce regional oil supplies and prompt tighter restrictions on Iranian oil exports.

He added that Iran could retaliate with fresh attacks against oil installations across the Middle East.

Iran has condemned the planned U.S. sanctions, while President Masoud Pezeshkian has called for a diplomatic solution.

Pakistan’s army chief was visiting Tehran on Monday for mediation talks ahead of the expected U.S. announcement.

Shipping data showed fewer than 20 commodity vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz during the weekend amid restrictions affecting energy shipments.

Iran, however, allowed some Iraqi oil tankers to pass through the strait following repeated requests from Baghdad, Iranian state news agency IRNA reported.

Traders said Iraq’s SOMO and QatarEnergy had also offered crude for loading inside the strait.

SEB analyst Bjarne Schieldrop said current Brent prices suggested that sufficient oil was still flowing through the Strait of Hormuz.

He said a major turning point could occur if Iran decided to completely close the waterway using rockets and drones.

Brent crude has risen to about $92 a barrel from $71 in June, driven by declining inventories and concerns over prolonged Middle East disruptions.

Morgan Stanley analysts said they had raised their Brent price forecasts, projecting prices could peak at $100 a barrel in the fourth quarter.

Meanwhile, the International Energy Agency is not currently considering another release of oil from strategic reserves, its chief Fatih Birol said. (Reuters/NAN)

World.title: Tunji-Ojo Calls for Stronger Partnerships to Secure Borders
World.content:
The Minister of Interior, Dr Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo, has called for stronger collaborations among universities, security agencies, regional institutions and development partners to strengthen border security, migration management and regional integration.

Tunji-Ojo made the call at the opening ceremony of the African Borderlines Research Network (ABORNE) 2026 conference on Monday in Lagos.

The minister was represented by a Senior Special Assistant to the minister on Policy, Dr Kareem Olajoku.

The four-day conference was with the theme: ‘Connected Borderlands, Socio-Cultural Integration, and the Centrality of Policy, Research, and Security.’

He posited that the country must increasingly adopt evidence-based approaches to border management while ensuring that research remains responsive to practical realities.

The conference brought together scholars, policymakers, practitioners and development partners to examine issues surrounding Africa’s security, integration and development.

The partnership is particularly relevant as Nigeria continues to modernise its approach to migration and border management, through improvements in biometric identity systems, passport administration, automated border control and technology enabling border security.

He buttressed that the developments reflect the country ‘s determination to build a border management system that protects national security while facilitating legitimate travel and regional mobility.

He commended Lagos State University (LASU) and ABORNE for co-hosting the conference, describing the partnership as an example of how academic research and practical experience, when brought together could address contemporary security challenges.

According to him, the collaboration between the academia and practitioners is particularly important, as Nigeria continues to modernise approaches to migration and border management.

He highlighted ongoing improvements in biometric identity systems, passport administration, automated border control and technology-enabled border security as efforts to drive modernisation.

He noted that the developments demonstrate Nigeria’s determination to build a border management system capable of protecting national security while facilitating legitimate travel and regional mobility.

Tunji-Ojo further stressed the strategic importance of Lagos as the host location for the conference, describing the state as a major gateway for the movement of people and goods through its land connections, seaports and international airports.

He said Lagos provided an appropriate setting for discussions on the relationship between security, mobility, trade, community interaction and regional integration.

The minister called for greater attention to border communities, noting that they are often the first to experience the effects of insecurity and irregular migration.

He, however, said such communities should not be viewed merely as populations requiring protection, but as important partners capable of contributing to early warning, conflict prevention and effective border management.

“Building a resilient borderline therefore requires us to see border communities not merely as populations to be secured but as partners in security, peace and development.” he said.

Tunji-Ojo equally stressed that research should help governments anticipate emerging challenges rather than merely explain past developments.

He described ABORNE 2026 as more than an academic conference, saying it offered an opportunity to strengthen the relationship between knowledge and action, communities and institutions, as well as national security and regional cooperation.

According to him, the conference provides Nigeria with an important platform to contribute to the development of secure, integrated and resilient borders across West Africa and the wider African continent.

The minister urged participants to move beyond identifying challenges and focus on developing practical, collaborative and sustainable solutions.

He also expressed hope that the partnerships established during the conference would continue beyond the event and that knowledge generated through the gathering would contribute to policymaking and practice across Africa.

On her part, the Vice-Chancellor of LASU, Prof. Ibiyemi Olatunji-Bello, said that for the university, the gathering was much more than the hosting of an international academic conference.

Olatunji-Bello said that it was an affirmation of the university’s commitment to producing knowledge that responds to the country’s realities and continent and its development.

She noted that Africa needed a new generation of scholars and professionals who understand that borders are not mere communities.

According to her, they are also communities of people, livelihoods, identity, security, development and human mobility.

“The university must therefore do more than observe these realities. It’s more the help to understand them, interrogate them and contribute to shaping policies and practices that govern them,” she said. (NAN)

World.title: Born and bred in SA : Meet Tharina Botes, Miss Universe Thailand
World.content:
South African-born model Tharina Botes has won Miss Universe Thailand. Images via IG

South African-born model and former Miss SA finalist, Tharina Botes, has been crowned Miss Universe Thailand.

The beauty queen and businesswoman was born in Randburg to a South African father and Thai mother.

Tharina moved abroad in 2019 at the age of 22.



THARINA BOTES CROWNED MISS UNIVERSE THAILAND

Over the weekend, Tharina Botes added another pageant title to her name – Miss Universe Thailand

Tharina, representing Bangkok, was awarded a diamond crown, a cash prize, sponsorship deals and the opportunity to represent Thailand at the Miss Universe pageant on 24 November in Puerto Rico.

“Dreams really come true”, the 29-year-old model and businesswoman shared in an Instagram post.

In another, Tharina added that convinced that hearing a Tyla song during the competition was a “sign”.



WHO IS THE SOUTH AFRICAN-BORN STUNNER?

Tharina Bortes was born and raised in Roodepoort to a South African father and Thai mother.

She attended Monument High School in Krugersdorp and became involved in modelling and pageantry as a teenager. She studied a BCom at Damelin College and later pursued economics through UNISA.

In her early days, she won Miss Teen Gauteng and Miss Rand Show, and represented South Africa at Miss International in Tokyo

In 2018, she entered the Miss South Africa pageant at the age of 21. The pageant, which included finalists like Bryoni Govender and Margo Fargo, was won by Tamaryn Green.

After the pageant, Tharina Botes moved to Thailand, where she continued pageantry.

Tharin won Miss Grand Phuket and Miss Thailand World in 2019 and 2023, respectively.

Before winning the title of Miss Unirsee Thailand, she was named first runner-up in 2021.

World.title: Orlando Pirates superstar moves overseas
World.content:
Patrick Maswanganyi celebrates scoring for Orlando Pirates in the MTN8. Image: Official PSL

Orlando Pirates confirmed that an agreement had been reached with the Bahraini club. The club revealed Maswanganyi expressed his desire to continue his career abroad.

His departure brings an end to a spell in which he established himself as a popular figure among the Orlando Pirates supporters.

PATRICK MASWANGANYI GETS ORLANDO PIRATES FAREWELL

Maswanganyi remained an important part of the technical team’s plans for the new season. However, discussions between the player, his representatives and the club ultimately led to Orlando Pirates agreeing to allow him to pursue the opportunity overseas.



The club confirmed that the 28-year-old Maswanganyi’s decision was respected despite his importance to the squad.

“In recognition of his service to the Club and his ambitions for the next chapter of his career, Orlando Pirates agreed not to stand in his way,” the club said.

A transfer was subsequently concluded with Alkhaldiya Sports Club, allowing Maswanganyi to begin a new chapter in Bahrain.

“Tito” leaves Orlando Pirates as a league champion and a firm favourite among the Ghost. His performances in the famous black and white jersey earned him a special place among the supporters.

The club also highlighted his commitment to representing Orlando Pirates with pride throughout his time in Soweto.

Also read: Latest report: SAFA make decision on Pitso Mosimane



THE BUCCANEERS THANK TITO

Maswanganyi departs having made a lasting impression both on and off the field. His personality and performances made him a popular member of the Buccaneers squad.

“From his first appearance in the famous black and white jersey, he gave the Ghost countless moments to celebrate and represented this club with pride,” Orlando Pirates said.

His exit will now leave the technical team with another important squad decision as the club continues its campaign across domestic competitions.

Orlando Pirates thanked the playmaker for his dedicated service and wished him success in the next chapter of his career.

The club added: “He departs as a league champion, a firm favourite among the supporters and a player who understood the responsibility of representing Orlando Pirates Football Club.”

Maswanganyi will now look to make his mark in the Bahrain Premier League after closing the door on his Orlando Pirates chapter.

World.title: SA passport holders can travel to these 101 countries without a visa
World.content:
SA passport holders can travel to 101 destinations without obtaining a visa in advance, according to the latest Henley Passport Index. Image: Allianz Travel Insurance

Holders of a South African passport can travel to 101 destinations without obtaining a visa in advance, according to the latest edition of the Henley Passport Index compiled by Henley & Partners.

The updated ranking places South Africa 96th out of 199 passports globally, with a visa-free score of 101.

The index evaluates passports based on the number of countries their holders can enter without needing to obtain a visa before departure.



It covers 199 passports and 227 travel destinations, making it one of the most widely cited indicators of global mobility.

Where does South Africa rank?

With a visa-free score of 101, South Africa’s passport ranks behind Qatar, which offers access to 112 destinations, and is one ahead of Belize in the global standings.

The ranking means South African travellers can visit 101 destinations with relative ease, although visas or advance authorisations are still required for many countries worldwide.

World’s Most Powerful Passports

According to the index, Asian and European countries continue to dominate global travel access.

Singapore holds the most powerful passport , with visa-free access to 192 destinations .

, with visa-free access to . Japan, South Korea and United Arab Emirates follow closely, each offering access to 188 destinations .

. Sweden ranks fifth, with a score of 187.

At the other end of the spectrum, Afghanistan remains the lowest-ranked passport, with access to only 22 destinations without a prior visa.

Measuring Global Mobility

The Henley Passport Index is widely used as a benchmark for global mobility.



The rankings reflect a range of factors including diplomatic relations, international agreements, and security considerations, all of which influence visa policies between countries.

Three Types of Visa Access

The 101 destinations available to South African passport holders fall into three main travel categories:

Visa-Free Access: Travellers can enter the destination simply by presenting their passport at immigration, with no advance application required.

Travellers can enter the destination simply by presenting their passport at immigration, with no advance application required. Visa on Arrival: Visitors can obtain a visa at the airport or border entry point, often after paying a fee.

Visitors can obtain a visa at the airport or border entry point, often after paying a fee. Electronic Travel Authorisation (ETA): Travellers must complete a short online application before departure but do not need to visit an embassy or consulate.

While the 2026 ranking highlights moderate global mobility for South Africans, it also underscores the gap between South Africa’s travel access and that enjoyed by holders of the world’s most powerful passports.

World.title: The only Western Cape town where you can buy land for R100 000
World.content:
The average house price in the Western Cape is R1.82 million.

A handful of suburbs and towns offer land for R150 000 or more. But one small town bucks this trend, with land listing at R100 000.

Western Cape Town with R100 000 Land

Klawer along the N7 is the only Western Cape town where it’s possible to buy land for R100 000.



This small inland town in the Matzikamma region is 20.5 kilometres from Vredendal.

Those who know the area know the wine farms or its proximity to the Olifants River.

The small town also made headlines in 2022 because of a series of tragic events.



Those exploring the Namaqualand flower bloom will likely have passed the small town en route to other towns along the West Coast, the Northern Cape or Namibia, fueling up at the Engen 1 Stop within its boundaries.

But the area is undergoing some renewal.

In 2025, the Department of Sport, Arts and Culture (DSAC) opened the town’s upgraded sports ground.



The Western Cape Department of Infrastructure (WCDOI) also handed over the keys to a housing project in the area.

According to 2022 census data, 14 277 people reside in Klawer, more than double the 6 234 residents in 2011.

The town is finding some appeal among young buyers.



Young buyers, those between 18 and 49, make up 62.9% of the most recent transactions, according to available data.

These sales have also pushed up property prices.

As of August 2026, the average home price is R725 000, the highest it’s been in the last 9 years.



Could this be the opportunity for the Western Cape’s hopeful buyers to get on the property ladder?

Does it make sense to buy land in Klawer?

While Klawer is cost-effective, buyers have to consider the cost of moving to a small town kilometres from an established centre of commerce.

There are two primary schools in Klawer.

But the nearest high school is in Vredendal.

It may make sense as an affordable location for those who already have work in the area or don’t need to go into the office.



The town’s revival could also make it appealing for investors.

But its remote location and affordable housing may mean it becomes a retirement destination for those who enjoy the platteland.

The town has its own clinic and police station.

The nearest beach is a 50-minute drive.

Being close to Vredendal also puts other amenities like hospitals and larger retailers within driving distance.

World.title: ‘Give us a full mandate’ :  Morero’s pitch for the Joburg mayor position:
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The ANC's Dada Morero believes he is still the man for the job.

Morero was speaking to eNCA on Monday and stated his case as to why Johannesburg residents should give him and his party another chance.

It comes two days after the ANC unveiled potential candidates for the 2026 local government elections set for November as it opted not to name its final mayoral candidates.

Morero’s name was enlisted alongside his deputy Loyiso Masuku and party veteran Reverend Frank Chikane.

READ | ‘ANC cannot be trusted to fix what it has broken’ - DA

He said they have worked hard to revive the City of Johannesburg.

“The work that we've done in Johannesburg, considering what has happened between 2016 and 2022, is an indication that since we took over power in 2023.”

Much of what he told eNCA mirrors his State of the City Address back in May 2026, where he acknowledged the City’s mounting infrastructure and financial challenges but defended his record under the banner: We are a City at work.

As he did then, Morero once again painted a picture of a city that is functioning and growing despite decay and service delivery failures.

“There's been serious interventions that we're doing to reclaim the city, to ensure that we bring back the city to where it was, by law enforcement, dealing with financial sustainability of the city, and dealing with issues around service delivery,” he told eNCA.

But Morero’s hopeful picture of the city of gold comes at the back of critics who claim that it has lost its shine.

For residents living through water shortages, roads ridden by potholes, crime at its peak, and decaying infrastructure, seeing the glimmer of hope in Morero’s future almost feels impossible.

READ | Power outage leaves these Joburg areas with dry taps

Morero has put voters to the test: “Give the ANC a mandate to lead once more.”

This mandate, according to him, will act as a guide to delivering.

World.title: 'They're desperate': Pupils turn to fire hydrant for drinking water
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Pupils at Reiger Park Secondary School in Gauteng are reportedly being forced to endure shocking conditions just to get through the school day.

With more than 2,000 pupils and only a handful of functioning toilets, the school is also allegedly without access to drinking water.

The situation has become so desperate that pupils are reportedly turning to fire hydrants to quench their thirst.

READ | Water woes, broken toilets plague Reiger Park school

This is according to a source who asked not to be identified.

"They're really desperate for water...They can't get water from the toilets because they're quite disgusting... The cleaners are refusing to clean, and we've had this problem for a while now," the source told eNCA.

Continuing to paint a grim picture of the situation, the source said they often have to wait for a long time to use the bathroom given the limited number of toilets available.

The situation is reportedly worse during break time.

"The only taps that are running are the ones in the staff room and we can't get water from those taps and when we try to get water from those taps, they tell us to go to the taps in the bathrooms," he said.

School Governing Body (SGB) claims it was not aware of the extent of the conditions faced by pupils.

Chairperson Charona Louw said the matter has now been escalated to the district office.

This loss of power also disrupted water supply.

According to a statement by Joburg Water, due to the power outage which impacted the bulk supplier, the Randburg and Roodepoort System have declined to low and critically low water levels.

This has resulted in poor pressure to no water in various supply zones.

Some of the systems affected include:

Honeydew Reservoir and Tower

Boschkop Reservoir

Linden 1 Reservoir

Waterval and Quellerina Towers

Helderkruin Reservoir

Florida North and Horizon Towers

Constantia Tower

Witpoortjie Reservoir

"Despite the restoration of pumping to full capacity, customers will experience a delayed impact on water supply due to the period which there was no pumping from the Eikenhof Pump station," the statement read.

Meanwhile, City Power has confirmed that it has made progress in restoring supply following the Fordsburg Substation fire.

READ | Dry taps, leaking pipes: Lenasia residents demand answers

According to the power utility's spokesperson, Isaac Mangena, Bree Substation remains the only substation without power, affecting customers in the inner city of Johannesburg, Newtown, Hillbrow and surrounding areas.

World.title: Are you affected ? Throttling expected in these parts of Joburg
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Daily throttling is expected to start at 6pm in Orange Farm, Lenasia, Lenasia Hospital and President Park, with the level of restriction varying between areas.

The throttling will continue until 5am on Tuesday.

READ | Dry taps, leaking pipes: Lenasia residents demand answers

At the same time, Johannesburg Water will once again close Sandton meters from 8pm tonight until 4am tomorrow as part of its water demand management.

Areas including Illovo, Bryanston and Morningside could be affected, with residents warned that supplies may take several hours to fully recover.

World.title: Stuart to spend a week behind bars
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Stuart Scharnick will remain in custody until his next court appearance next week Tuesday.

He made a brief appearance at the Randburg Magistrate's Court on Monday.

READ | 'Let's take it outside': journalist speaks out after Scharnick altercation

The controversial Scharnick was charged with contravening the Firearms Control Act.

He was arrested on Friday on the sidelines of Fadiel Adams' testimony at the Madlanga Commission, following a confrontation with a Sowetan journalist.

World.title: 'It was not yet Zolani's time' | Boxing world mourns Tete
World.content:
MDANTSANE - The death of former two-time boxing world champion Zolani Tete has been described as a huge loss, not only to the boxing fraternity but to the Eastern Cape at large.

Former boxer-turned-pastor Masibulele “Hawk” Makepula says the whole continent is devastated.

"People across the world are mourning Zolani's passing. Words cannot describe how we feel.

"No one came and said this was the will of God. No one can say Zolani ran his race and completed it, and no one can say his time came," Makepula said.

"It was not yet Zolani's time. His life was taken prematurely, and brutally so. Zolani died before his time."

July marked the end of Tete’s four-year ban following a doping scandal, which he denied. Makepula says Tete was ready to return to doing what he loved most.

"He kept himself fit and ready the whole time during the ban so that when the time came, he would be ready to get back in the ring.

"He was not selfish with his time and talent. He was training other boxers. It was only a matter of time before he became a world champion again. He was going to fight one or two fights and move on to a title fight because he was destined for greatness."

Boxing promoter Ayanda Matiti says what makes Tete’s death even more difficult to come to terms with is the way he was killed.

"It was a brutal assassination. No assassination can ever be accepted. Zolani was like a sheep; he did not deserve this.

"His body was full of bullets. Logic tells us that if it was a robbery, then they would have taken something. They did that to an unarmed man."

Matiti thanked authorities for acting swiftly but said this would be a difficult loss to overcome.

"We are all very sad. We are all mourning, not just his family or the boxing fraternity, but the whole province. In fact, the whole country," he said.

Tete was killed on Friday night while waiting for his gate to open. He was with a 27-year-old woman who was wounded and taken to hospital.

On Saturday, two people were taken in for questioning. One suspect, aged 30, was later released, but police spokesperson Brigadier Nobuntu Gantana said he remains a potential suspect.

The remaining 22-year-old suspect is appearing in the Mdantsane Magistrate’s Court. He has been charged with murder and attempted murder.

Two additional suspects, both aged 27, were arrested in Scenery Park on Sunday. They are expected to appear in court on Tuesday.

World.title: Springboks change half-backs for second All Blacks Test
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The Springboks have changed their half-backs for the second Test against New Zealand on Saturday in Cape Town, promoting experienced duo Handre Pollard and Cobus Reinach.

Fly-half Pollard and scrum-half Reinach replace Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu, now on the bench, and Grant Williams, who is unavailable due to a "niggle".

The changes were predictable as Feinberg-Mngomezulu, playing only his second match after injury, and Williams performed poorly in a 33-16 first Test loss last Saturday.

A third alteration to the team that fell in Johannesburg is Ethan Hooker coming in on the left wing in place of Kurt-Lee Arendse.

Arendse, who went off concussed early in the match at Ellis Park, moves to the right wing in place of Cheslin Kolbe, another "niggle" casualty.

There could yet be a fourth change to the starting line-up. If flanker Siya Kolisi is passed fit after a hamstring injury, he will replace Paul de Villiers.

"Handre has delivered for us under extreme pressure, and we feel that is what he and Cobus have the potential to bring at the beginning of the game," said head coach Rassie Erasmus.

"Then we have Morne (van den Berg) and Sacha coming on later with their different styles of play that will be good for us this weekend.

"Cheslin and Grant suffered niggles last weekend, which ruled them out of contention for selection.

"We have bracketed Siya alongside Paul to allow us time to monitor how Siya comes through training this week."

Loose forward Pieter-Steph du Toit will continue as captain and is set to win his 100th cap on Saturday, one week after centre Damian de Allende reached the milestone.

Ox Nche, widely regarded as the best loosehead prop in the world, will make his 50th appearance for the Springboks.

The bench has been reshuffled with only two survivors from the first Test -- 'hybrid' player Andre Esterhuizen, a centre who can play as a loose forward, and prop Gerhard Steenekamp.

Among those promoted is Deon Fourie, who will celebrate his 40th birthday in September. He can operate as a hooker or flanker.

Should he take the field, Fourie will become the oldest Springbok to play in a Test, surpassing Victor Matfield and Schalk Brits, who were 38 years old in their final Tests.

South Africa (15-1)

Damian Willemse; Kurt-Lee Arendse, Jesse Kriel, Damian de Allende, Ethan Hooker; Handre Pollard, Cobus Reinach; Jasper Wiese, Pieter-Steph du Toit (capt), Siya Kolisi or Paul de Villiers; Ruan Nortje, Eben Etzebeth; Wilco Louw, Malcolm Marx, Ox Nche

Replacements: Deon Fourie, Gerhard Steenekamp, Thomas du Toit, Lood de Jager, Andre Esterhuizen, Cameron Hanekom, Morne van den Berg, Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu

Coach: Rassie Erasmus

World.title: Relief for schools as government releases Sh18.5b capitation
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Education CS Julius Ogamba. [File, Standard]

The government has released Sh18.5 billion in capitation to support operations in public basic education institutions during the third term of 2026, as schools reopened across the country on Monday.

Education Cabinet Secretary Julius Ogamba said the funds have already been released and will support learners in pre-primary, primary, junior and senior schools.

The allocation is intended to facilitate smooth school operations and ensure learning activities continue without disruption.

The Sh18.5 billion has been distributed across three major capitation programmes, with Free Day Secondary Education (FDSE) allocated Sh10.963 billion, accounting for the biggest portion of the Term Three capitation.

The money will support operations in public day and secondary schools and comes as institutions prepare learners for a busy academic term.

Free Day Junior School Education has received Sh6.1 billion, to support learners in the second tier of basic education and help institutions meet operational requirements as the Competency-Based Education system continues to expand.

Meanwhile, Free Primary Education has been allocated Sh1.4 billion to support learning in public primary schools.

The funds come as a relief to school heads who had raised concerns on the insufficient funds disbursed to schools this year.

However, Ogamba said the disbursement demonstrates the Government's commitment to ensuring that learners have access to free and compulsory basic education as provided for under Article 53(1)(b) of the Constitution.

“The Government affirms its commitment to fulfil its duty to learners and educational institutions,” said the CS.
