World.title: The Jewish-Mexican food traditions hiding in plain sight
World.content:
My friend Jorge Fitz once told me a story about his childhood visits to the town where his grandfather grew up, Juliantla, just outside of Taxco, Mexico. He remembers many particular things about the way the town celebrated festivities and holidays, but one thing that stuck out in his memory was a special braided bread they made called pan de Juliantla.

As an adult, Jorge said he started making Jewish friends, and when he saw pan de Juliantla on their tables, he wondered how they knew about it.

“Jorge, that’s challah bread,” they would respond.

He later learned that Juliantla is believed to be the first Jewish settlement in the Americas, complete with a spiritual cleansing bath known as a mikveh that dates back to the 16th century.

As far as Jorge could tell, a majority of the townspeople didn’t realize where many of their customs and food came from. He and his parents definitely didn’t know about their Jewish ancestry until much later.

Hearing this story illuminated just how deeply rooted Jewish food is in Mexican culture, so much so that even when origins have been forgotten, they remain an integral part of community life.

Waves of migration and a culinary legacy

The first Jews to grace Mexican shores sailed in on the ships of Spanish conquistadors during the 1500s and 1600s. They were fleeing the Catholic Inquisition of the Iberian Peninsula, but found little solace in the New World as the Inquisition migrated across the ocean.

Many of these early Jews “converted” to Catholicism while continuing to practice their own religion in secret. In Spanish, they are called “conversos,” or the converted. In English, we often refer to them as Crypto Jews.

With these Sephardim came cinnamon, grapes, figs, dates, almonds, cherries, apricots, olives and olive oil, nutmeg, ginger, cardamom and mustard, as well as black pepper, thyme, basil, clove, fennel, oregano, cumin and other Mediterranean spices.

They also had a strong tradition of pickling what they brought to the New World. In northern Mexico, cabrito, slow-roasted baby goat, is a traditional dish among the Sephardic Jews of the Iberian Peninsula. Similarly, the region’s dessert bread known as pan de cemita and la capirotada, a kind of bread pudding, are also attributed to those early Iberian Jewish immigrants.

The second wave of Jewish immigrants to Mexico arrived at the end of the 1800s from the failing Ottoman Empire. Jews who were part of the diaspora from Spain and Portugal, now living in the countries of the Levant, came because of economic opportunities in Mexico. They arrived from what is today Lebanon, Syria and Turkey, and because they were not fleeing persecution, their culture, religion and food were much more visible.

Preserving culture in the neighborhood oven

A third wave of Jewish immigrants came to Mexico during and between the two world wars. Some had plans of continuing on to the United States but were turned away at Ellis Island because of the Immigration Act of 1924, which severely limited the numbers of Southern and European immigrants allowed into the country.

These immigrants brought the Ashkenazi dishes of Eastern European countries like Poland, Ukraine and Germany — hearty soups and stews made with root vegetables like borscht, matza ball soup, gefilte fish, schmaltz (rendered chicken fat), tzimmes, gribenes and braised meats like brisket.

Food is paramount for any immigrant community trying to preserve their identity. The Jewish community was no different.

When Syrian Jews moved into Colonia Roma at the beginning of the 20th century, they not only built one of the city’s oldest synagogues but also opened a community oven down the street where special traditional breads were baked and sold to worshipers coming from services. At the local market were kosher butchers, while elderly folks sat in neighborhood cafes sipping thick, Turkish-style coffee and eating the sweets of home.

Unlike some of the immigrant groups I have researched, the diverse Mexican-Jewish community not only preserved the traditional dishes of their culture, but also, over the generations, adapted and innovated with local ingredients and cooking methods, creating a distinct Judeo-Mexican cuisine.

The fusion kitchen and home recipes

“Sabor Judío,” published in 2024, is a recipe collection by two authors whose Jewish grandmothers passed down handwritten recipe books. They gathered together a comprehensive archive of recipes from kitchens across the Mexican-Jewish community. Among the book’s pages are traces of many cuisines — Mexican mestizo, Spanish, Sephardic-Iberian, Sephardic-Middle Eastern and Ashkenazi.

Yiddish blintzes with huitlacoche (Mexican corn smut considered a local delicacy), matza chilaquiles, a variation of shakshuka with poblano peppers and Mexican oregano, and brisket tacos with three-chile salsa are all included in the collection. Irma Appel’s stuffed poblano peppers with guacamole include a smattering of gribenes (often referred to as Jewish bacon), and Pati Jinich, of PBS’s “Pati’s Kitchen,” provided her recipe for jalapeño-mushroom matza ball soup.

Then there are traditional Mexican recipes that the Mexican-Jewish community has adopted as their own, cooking them for high holidays and other festivities. That includes nopal and tomato salad made in advance to eat cold during Shabbat, or ceviche with prepared horseradish on top, supposedly invented during a Passover Seder.

Not everything is kosher, but the community’s many identities are on full display.

Scanning through the menus of Jewish restaurants in Mexico City, however, it’s hard to find the fusion dishes represented in “Sabor Judío.” For whatever reason, these dishes hold sway in family kitchens, but haven’t yet made it to commercial dining rooms.

Where to find Jewish food in Mexico City

Maybe the world isn’t ready for spicy gefilte fish?

That’s not to say that you can’t get glimpses of them — the salami chilaquiles at Klein’s in Polanco is a delicious example. You’ll also find chiles making guest appearances in the Israeli dishes at Merkava, and kosher cafe Guacho Grill has al pastor tacos made with fish and chicken, as opposed to the traditional pork.

So maybe fusion is yet to take off in restaurants, but at places like Klein’s or Niddo, which once described itself in an interview as Jewish-Mexican-Canadian, diners will at least find Jewish and Mexican dishes coexisting on the table.

Plenty of other expressions of Jewish food can be encountered throughout the city — Mendl, for instance, has incredible U.S.-style deli sandwiches and bagels with lox. And at Pat Patz, chef Mijeal Seidel has a labneh recipe that he adds dill to as a shout-out to his Eastern European side, along with tons of other dishes worth exploring.

You may have to make some fusion dishes at home, but a taste of Jewish-Mexican heritage is definitely available across Mexico City.

Lydia Carey is a freelance writer and translator based in Mexico City. She has published extensively both online and in print, sharing her insights about Mexico for over a decade. She lives a double life as a local tour guide and is the author of “Mexico City Streets: La Roma.” Follow her urban adventures on Instagram and see more of her work at mexicocitystreets.com.

World.title: How the Middle East has shaped Mexico for almost 2,000 years
World.content:
I’m sitting in the courtyard of Guanajuato’s Museo Iconográfico del Quijote, admiring the stone arches and columns, waiting for a chamber music concert to begin. I probably walk through at least one courtyard a day in Guanajuato because they’re everywhere in town – not just in museums, but in restaurants, universities, government buildings and parks. Even the classic Mexican colonial home has a courtyard with a fountain in the center, surrounded by rooms.

Mexican courtyards reflect the influence of the Moors, the North African Islamic group that ruled Spain for 800 years and whose ornate tilework, intricate geometric patterns and decorative calligraphy influenced the art and architecture of Spain. After the fall of the Moors in 1492, Spain continued to use Islamic patterns in its designs, creating a unique style that blended Islamic and Christian elements known as mudéjar, which later made its way to Mexico.

But it’s not just courtyards that bear the mark of the Moors. From architecture and folk medicine to crafts and textiles, here’s a quick roundup of the Islamic group’s lasting impact on Mexican culture.

Alhambrismo

This is an architectural style in Spain and Latin America inspired by the decorative Islamic arts of the Alhambra, a palace and fortress complex in Granada, Spain, with Moorish elements such as horseshoe arches, intricate stucco and colorful tilework.

A well-known example of this is the Kiosk of Santa Maria la Ríbera, an ornate octagonal pavilion made of wrought iron with a glass cupola dome on the top, in Mexico City’s Alameda Park.

Churches

In many colonial Mexican churches, you can see echoes of the mudéjar architectural style, including azulejos, blue-glazed tiles that adorn domes, bell towers and facades; intricate geometric carved-wood ceilings resembling inverted ship hulls; and arches and doorways.

Oaxaca’s famous Templo de Santo Domingo de Guzmán, for example, displays these design elements in the intricate geometric arabesque patterns on the ceiling and the genealogical tree of the temple’s namesake saint.

Inward-facing living

I remember when my husband and I first saw the house we bought in Guanajuato. Although one of its assets was a close-up view of the dome atop one of the city’s signature churches, San Francisco, we could barely see it from the tiny window in one of the bedrooms.

Unlike in the U.S. and Canada, traditional Mexican houses face inward, revealing their Moorish and Andalusian roots, with walled enclosures and internal gathering spaces.

Urban layouts

While Spanish colonial urban planning in the Americas officially ordered a strict grid system, some historic Mexican towns like Guanajuato and Taxco have narrow, winding streets, reflecting the medieval and southern Andalusian urban layouts shaped by centuries of Moorish influence.

Tiles, pottery and ceramics

Moorish craftsmen influenced Iberian ceramic styles, including tin-glazed pottery, by integrating geometric patterns and calligraphic bands into their work. When the craft was established in Puebla during the colonial period, artisans carried over these traditional Iberian-Islamic design elements, including abstract script borders and traditional brushstroke motifs.

Puebla’s famous Talavera pottery also blends Indigenous styles with Spanish and Moorish glazed-tile traditions.

Crafts and textiles

Mudéjar geometric inlaid woodworking and carpentry techniques influenced traditional lacquerware and furniture crafts in regions like Michoacán and Guerrero. Precise interlaced framing merged with Indigenous wood-carving and pre-Hispanic lacquering, creating colonial furniture like desks with repetitive geometric paneling and floral touches.

As for weaving, the traditional Mexican sarape displays complex linear, diamond and star-centered layouts that show cross-cultural parallels to Middle Eastern flat-weave blanket traditions.

Curanderismo (folk medicine)

Moorish and Islamic medical practices influenced curanderismo, the herbal medicine still widely practiced in Mexico. Ritual cleansing, petitionary prayers and talismanic magic elements arrived via Spanish traditions that had absorbed Moorish folk customs.

For example, the belief that the “mal de ojo,” or “evil eye,” can cause physical discomfort like fever, crying and restlessness was brought to the New World via Spanish and Moorish folk magic.

Middle Eastern influences beyond the Moors

Influential as the Moors were, they are not the only Middle Eastern influence in modern Mexico.

Following the fall of the Moors, many Sephardic Jews fled from the Middle East to colonial Mexico to escape the Inquisition. Later waves of Sephardic Jews arrived from the crumbling Ottoman Empire in the early 20th century. These communities established synagogues, cultural institutions and social networks, primarily in Mexico City.

While Mexico has seen periods of antisemitism throughout its history, modern Mexico hosts one of the largest and most vibrant Jewish communities in Latin America, mostly in Mexico City.

Meanwhile, the Lebanese diaspora in Mexico — currently standing at more than 500,000 descendants — has shaped the nation’s culture, cuisine and commerce since the late 19th century.

In the 1890s, they left to escape political oppression, heavy taxes, religious conflict and military conscription. At the same time, Mexico’s then-president, Porfirio Díaz, encouraged foreign immigration and trade, offering a welcoming environment and growing business opportunities.

During the period between the 1890s and 1930s, more than 100,000 mostly Lebanese immigrants arrived from Arabic-speaking nations, settling predominantly in the Yucatán, but also in Veracruz, Puebla and Mexico City.

In the early 20th century, the Lebanese community contributed around 50% of the total immigrant input to Mexico’s economy, and it remains one of Mexico’s most successful immigrant groups.

I’ve known for years that words like ¡ojalá!, albañil, and azotea are Arabic in origin, but I had no idea about other enduring Middle Eastern influences. The next time I use the Talavera dish I bought in Puebla, I’ll appreciate its ancient Moorish history, going back almost 2,000 years.

Louisa Rogers and her husband Barry Evans divide their lives between Guanajuato and Eureka, on California’s North Coast. Louisa writes articles and essays about expat life, Mexico, travel, physical and psychological health, retirement and spirituality. Her recent articles are available on her website, authory.com/LouisaRogers.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Fugitive swaps, a strawberry spat and a stronger peso
World.content:
Mexico and the United States spent the week of Aug. 17 trading shows of security cooperation, from fugitive handovers to a new drone-technology pact, culminating Wednesday in a federal operation in Michoacán that saw nine alleged members of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel arrested and set off narco-blockades at more than 20 points across the state.

That cooperation ran alongside friction on other fronts. Mexico is contesting a proposed U.S. antidumping tariff on strawberry exports and objecting to Washington’s decision to deport some Mexicans to Central America rather than home, as trade uncertainty lingers more than a month after the U.S. declined to renew the USMCA free trade deal in its current form. Domestically, the fallout from the U.S. visa revocation of former president López Obrador’s son continued to shadow the government’s messaging on fuel-smuggling enforcement. Against that backdrop, the peso’s push below 17 to the dollar stood out as a rare point of good economic news, as the central bank held its interest rate steady on lingering inflation concerns.

The week also brought a new Mexico-made electric vehicle, a national debate over kids and social media, and a presidential sick day. Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Fugitive returns and a new drone pact mark security cooperation

Mexico and the United States kept up a steady drumbeat of security announcements this week. Ambassador Ronald Johnson said U.S. authorities returned three wanted fugitives to Mexico in a single day — one linked to the CJNG, one wanted for murder in Zacatecas and one for fraud — while separately handing over six more fugitives wanted for crimes including murder and firearms offenses. Jalisco police also captured Antoni Covarrubias, wanted for second-degree murder in California, in Puerto Vallarta, which Johnson called the ninth high-profile U.S.-targeted arrest in the state in recent weeks. At the same time, the U.S. and Mexico conducted a joint security exercise along the El Paso-Ciudad Juárez border, and the two countries signed a declaration of intent on drone technology that will let Mexico’s Defense Ministry access the U.S. Army’s marketplace for unmanned aircraft systems, though no models, quantities or purchases have been agreed.

Security Minister Omar García Harfuch drew public praise from DEA Administrator Terry Cole at the 40th International Drug Enforcement Conference in Buenos Aires, where García Harfuch said U.S. agencies are processing 155 arrest warrants tied to Mexican investigations and reported that Mexico’s Financial Intelligence Unit has frozen more than 8.6 billion pesos in assets. He also cited a more than 50% drop in daily homicides, from 86 to 42, over the past two years, a figure attributed to his ministry’s own count of arrests and seizures.

The Michoacán operation capped the week’s security news: Soldiers and National Guard troops arrested nine people, including two women identified as relatives of CJNG plaza boss Heraclio “Tío Lako” Guerrero Martínez, who evaded capture as the operation set off blockades that were largely cleared by Wednesday afternoon.

That flow of cooperation announcements ran alongside a separate dispute over fuel smuggling and politics. Sheinbaum said at Tuesday’s mañanera that fuel smuggling, or huachicol fiscal, is “practically over” in Mexico thanks to customs interventions and arrests — a claim she offered in the context of defending her government against opposition criticism. That criticism stems partly from the U.S. revocation of the visa of Andrés Manuel López Beltrán, son of former President López Obrador, which Sheinbaum has called a political matter, saying he “was not” ever on authorities’ radar for criminal involvement. The fuel-trafficking case itself advanced this week when Rear Admiral Fernando Farías Laguna, accused of leading a Pemex-linked smuggling ring, was extradited from Argentina and jailed at the Altiplano maximum security prison. The case has damaged the Navy’s reputation and drawn indirect allegations, which Sheinbaum has rejected, involving López Beltrán.

Strawberries, Vietnam imports and a Canada call test trade ties

Mexico is contesting a U.S. Commerce Department finding that could impose antidumping tariffs on Mexican strawberries, which supplies 98% of U.S. strawberry imports. Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard called the U.S. criteria “arbitrarily applied” and inconsistent with USMCA provisions; a final ITC ruling isn’t expected until early 2027, and the case could affect roughly 5,000 Mexican producers and 151,000 jobs if it proceeds. Sheinbaum has warned the case could set a precedent for challenging other Mexican agricultural exports.

Separately, Mexico’s imports from Vietnam more than doubled in the first half of 2026 to $18.4 billion, a jump that has raised suspicions — flagged in a recent White House report naming Mexico a “Tier 1” transshipment risk — that Chinese goods are being routed through Vietnam to dodge Mexico’s tariffs on non-free-trade-agreement countries. Mexico has denied being a transshipment hub for Chinese goods bound for the U.S.

Against that backdrop, President Sheinbaum and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney discussed North American trade by phone on Thursday. Carney’s office said the two underscored the importance of renewing the USMCA pact soon, and separately thanked Mexico for deploying more than 400 firefighters to help combat wildfires in British Columbia. The call came as Trump-imposed tariffs on Canadian goods, delayed this week, loomed for Saturday absent a deal. (The U.S. tariffs on Canada ultimately went into effect after trade talks collapsed late Friday night.)

Peso strength collides with a cautious Banxico

The peso dropped below 17 to the U.S. dollar this week, dropping below 16.9 on Friday, largely on dollar weakness following a U.S. Treasury bond buyback announcement. The currency has appreciated nearly 6% in 2026, a gain Banxico credits with helping cool inflation.

Even so, the central bank held its benchmark rate at 6.5% earlier this month. In meeting minutes released this week, four of five board members cited persistent services inflation as a driver of that decision. Headline inflation slowed to 3.12% in July, but Banxico now doesn’t expect it to reach its 3% target until the fourth quarter of 2027. The bank also flagged Middle East tensions as an upside risk to oil prices. Separately, INEGI’s preliminary July data showed the economy growing 2.7% annually, which Rodríguez called “another piece of good news” following 2.1% growth in the second quarter.

Other business and finance news this week:

Mañanera themes: EVs, phone lines and a presidential sick day

On Monday, Sheinbaum said she opposes a social-media ban for minors like Australia’s, calling the idea “very problematic” and noting enforcement challenges, while Education Minister Mario Delgado announced a nationwide teacher consultation on classroom device rules ahead of the Aug. 31 school year.

At Thursday’s press conference, Sheinbaum unveiled a prototype of Olinia Carga, the government’s second domestically developed electric vehicle, a light-cargo EV that can carry 650 kilograms and will sell for around 150,000 pesos starting in late 2027. The same day brought a new arrest in the 2024 kidnapping case of Sinaloa Cartel figure “El Mayo” Zambada.

On Friday, Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez, standing in for an ill Sheinbaum, told U.S. Ambassador Johnson that Mexico disagrees with Washington’s decision to deport some Mexicans to Guatemala, Honduras and Costa Rica rather than to Mexico.

Elsewhere, millions of Mexican cell phone lines were suspended after an Aug. 15 mandatory registration deadline passed, though regulators say most affected users can still recover service. Mexico also abstained from an OAS vote, which passed 29-1, to convene an emergency session on Nicaragua’s move to bar opposition candidates, with representative Alejandro Encinas citing Mexico’s non-intervention principle. Friday’s mañanera, run by Rodríguez after Sheinbaum announced she had the flu, also touched on new archaeological finds in a Chiapas cave tied to Zoque ritual traditions.

Regional news roundup:

And some good news to close out the week:

Looking ahead

Several threads left open this week are likely to develop further: Security cooperation with the U.S. continues to strengthen, while trade friction between the two countries shows no sign of easing. On a practical note, cell phone users facing the next registration deadlines — Aug. 31 for numbers ending in “1” — should act before their lines are suspended.

The Benefit Concert and Its Success

The Voices for Life concert raised 11.193 billion pesos (about US$3.7 million) for families hit by the 10 August earthquake in Colombia. This figure comes from Infobae, Minuto60, and La Meganation, all reporting on 24 August 2026.

The show took place on 23 August 2026 at the Vive Claro Distrito Cultural stadium in Bogotá. More than 30 national and international artists performed, including Maluma, Sebastián Yatra, and Karol G remotely.

Organizer Megalive partnered with Canal RCN, RCN Radio, and La República, who donated production services. The event drew over 43,000 individual transactions, according to Infobae’s breakdown.

Ticket sales through Ticketmaster generated 4.961 billion pesos, while artist contributions added 4.203 billion pesos. Corporate donors contributed 1.375 billion pesos, and QR-code donations brought in 653 million pesos.

Disputed Final Amount Raises Questions

While Colombian outlets report the 11.193 billion pesos total, UA.News claimed on 24 August 2026 that the final amount was not published. This contradiction highlights uncertainty about the official verification process.

Before the concert, campaigns had already raised over 3.5 billion pesos, per UA.News and Semana. Infobae noted more than 4.5 billion pesos came from over 21,000 donations before the event.

The discrepancy may stem from pending disbursements of artist pledges, which Infobae says are confirmed but not yet paid. Organizers have not publicly addressed the conflicting reports.

Despite the confusion, the Voices for Life concert remains a major fundraising effort for earthquake relief. The final verified total may depend on future audits by Presentes Corporación.

How the Funds Will Be Used

Presentes Corporación, an organization with 43 years of emergency management experience, receives 100 percent of the funds raised. The money will finance reconstruction of the most affected zones, per Infobae reports.

Semana specified that funds target rebuilding homes that were completely destroyed by the 7.4-magnitude earthquake. The organization awaits further assessment to determine investment priorities.

A committee of execution and monitoring will distribute resources alongside Presentes Corporación. This ensures transparency in how the Voices for Life concert money is spent.

The earthquake struck western and central Colombia on 10 August 2026, leaving many families without shelter. Reconstruction efforts will take time, and the concert funds provide initial relief.

Isagen’s Solar Acquisition Plan

Separately, Colombian power firm Isagen requested permission to buy 100 percent of Sol de la Ciénaga, owner of the Caracolí solar project. La República reported this on 24 August 2026, citing the Superintendencia de Industria y Comercio (SIC).

The SIC, Colombia’s competition regulator, said the transaction poses no substantial risks to free competition. It assessed the deal in the context of the electricity generation market.

The Caracolí I solar park has a generation capacity of 56 megawatts and is located in Malambo, Atlántico department. Halcones y Palomas reported on 21 August 2026 that Isagen bought the company from Recurrent Energy, part of Canadian Solar.

Isagen operates 27 generation plants totaling about 3,210 megawatts, according to La República. The acquisition would expand its solar portfolio, but the exact closing date is not disclosed.

The SIC has not issued a formal approval decision yet, as the exact date remains unpublished. La República quoted the regulator saying the deal is competitive, but final sign-off is pending.

Isagen’s purchase of Sol de la Ciénaga was reported as completed in Bogotá, but legal details remain unclear. No source specifies the signing date of the share purchase agreement.

For the Isagen deal, the SIC’s formal approval is expected soon, though no date is set. The transaction’s completion depends on this regulatory clearance.

Key Facts — What happened President Abelardo de la Espriella ordered deportations of criminal migrants, El País reported on 24 August 2026.

— The offensive The government is stepping up operations against criminal groups as part of the same security agenda.

— The catch No published document ties deportations and the criminal offensive into one order naming specific groups.

— Energy stakes ANLA may raise the Hidroituango reservoir to 420 meters, adding 390 million cubic meters of storage.

— The deadline The licensing agency has five working days to explain its criteria ahead of a possible El Niño.

— What comes next A decision on Hidroituango’s reservoir level is due before the rains, between October and November.

President orders migrant crackdown as security operations expand, while a watchdog demands clearer dam rules.

President Abelardo de la Espriella ordered operations against irregular migration, El País reported on 24 August 2026. Migrants who commit crimes or lack regular status face deportation first. He also reported intensified offensive actions against Colombia criminal groups, with 1,574 captures and 10 extraditions so far.

Bogotá’s Plaza de Bolívar. The government has ordered deportations of foreign criminals and new security operations.

President Orders Migrant Crackdown and Deportations

The president directed the operations at a security meeting in Atlántico, El País reported on 24 August 2026. The intervention will start with immigrants committing crimes, then those without regular status, and authorities will deport them after procedures.

‘I will not accept illegal immigrants who are committing criminal activities; they leave and are deported,’ he said in Barranquilla. He called it a political decision and said he assumes it.

The policy targets individual criminal conduct and migration status, not membership in specific armed groups. El País clarifies that deportations target those breaking the law or lacking documents, not named criminal groups.

Separately, a leader of the group ‘La Inmaculada’ was deported from Panama to Colombia, El País reported on 22 August 2026. This confirms a deportation involving a criminal group, but it was Panama sending the individual to Colombia.

Security Balance Shows Strong Numbers

The president cited 1,574 captures, 10 extraditions and 23,642 kilos of drugs seized since he took office. This includes 12,296 kilos of cocaine, according to El País’s report on 24 August 2026.

These numbers reflect intensified actions against Colombia criminal groups since he took office on 7 August 2026. NTN24 noted on 20 August that in just 13 days, the military destroyed about three cocaine laboratories.

The destroyed labs were located in the departments of Putumayo and Norte de Santander, according to NTN24. This shows a broad offensive against criminal structures across the country.

In Barranquilla he ratified what he called a categorical, non-negotiable order. Criminals will be fought ‘as what they are: terrorists,’ he said, without special treatment by the state.

Specific Operations Target Named Groups

El País reported specific captures in operations against Colombia criminal groups on 24 August 2026. Eleven members of the 53rd front of Segunda Marquetalia were captured, and two Clan del Golfo members were caught in flagrante.

These captures occurred in Fundación, Magdalena, for the Clan del Golfo members, and other operations took place in Puerto Gaitán, Meta. A laboratory for processing coca paste was destroyed in La Macarena.

The laboratory destruction included inputs and crops used by these criminal structures, according to the president’s statement. This shows a direct effort to dismantle drug production infrastructure.

These operations are part of a broader strategy to combat organized crime, not just a single deportation campaign. The government frames them as decisive blows against criminal networks.

Watchdog Presses for Hidroituango Rules

The Procuraduría, Colombia’s inspector general, pressed licensing agency ANLA for a decision on Hidroituango on 24 August 2026. This follows a formal request from 24 June 2026, after Hidroituango filed a proposal on 12 June.

The proposal seeks to temporarily modify Resolution No. 2306 of 2019 due to the forecast El Niño phenomenon. The Procuraduría demands updated information on the process and planned measures from ANLA.

ANLA has five working days to report the evaluation’s status and explain its technical and legal criteria. This includes contingency measures, environmental management, and monitoring plans.

The plan involves managing outflow flows, ensuring the Cauca River’s ecological flow, and monitoring the dam and rock mass stability daily. The Procuraduría wants a clear timeline given the imminent El Niño.

El Niño Risks Threaten Energy Security

The strict application of Resolution 2306 of 2019 could limit the reservoir’s storage capacity during low water periods, the Procuraduría noted. This creates risks for the reservoir’s operation, water management, and national energy security.

The plan would raise the reservoir to 420 meters between October and November 2026, El Tiempo reported. This must be analyzed against climate forecasts and environmental restrictions.

ANLA issued Resolution 002230 on 20 August 2026, authorizing Hidroituango to apply transitory changes to its operating rule. This allows adaptive management under low hydrology conditions to maintain system reliability, according to Caracol Radio.

The authorization permits operating under Resolution 1891 of 2009 rules, without the condition added by Resolution 2306 of 2019. This is a preventive measure against the forecast El Niño 2026–2027, reported El Heraldo on 21 August.

Hidroituango Can Store More Water

ANLA’s authorization allows Hidroituango to raise the reservoir from elevation 408 to 420, storing additional water from the Cauca River. Infobae reported on 22 August 2026 that this could store 390 million cubic meters more.

This extra reserve, according to EPM, equals the energy that Medellín consumes in about 15 days. This quantifies the energy security stakes in a potential ‘Super Niño’ scenario.

Ideam projects a 69% probability that El Niño will reach ‘very strong’ intensity between October and December 2026. Conditions could persist until the first quarter of 2027, according to Infobae.

The authorization has conditions, including a maximum duration until 31 July 2027 and ecological flow minima for the Cauca River. It terminates once Ideam declares El Niño over or the river recovers for at least 30 days.

Procuraduría Seeks Clear Justification

Despite ANLA’s resolution, the Procuraduría still demands detailed criteria, contingency plans, and monitoring obligations from the agency. This suggests the oversight body wants clear, formally documented rules beyond the existence of the resolution.

The Procuraduría’s statement on 24 August 2026 asks ANLA to explain the technical, legal, and environmental grounds for its decision. It also requires a timeline for adopting a final decision, considering the imminent El Niño.

This includes specific measures for managing outflow flows, maintaining the Cauca River’s ecological flow, and controlling the speed and volume of impoundment. Monitoring must be permanent, daily, and real-time for the dam and rock mass.

The watchdog’s pressure reflects the high stakes of balancing energy security with environmental protection during a climate event. Clear rules are essential to manage risks associated with reduced water inflows.

Deportations and Offensive Remain Separate

No single published document bundles the deportations and the offensive against Colombia criminal groups into one ‘deportation offensive’ targeting named organizations. El País frames deportations in terms of criminal activity and migration status, not organizational membership.

The security operations and migration operations are related strands of the same president’s policy but are reported separately. The government presents them as broader security and migration measures.

The deportation orders focus on immigrants committing crimes or lacking regular status. They do not name members of specific armed groups, a key distinction for the policy’s scope.

The offensive against criminal groups is distinct from the deportation order. Both sit inside the president’s security agenda, but deportations do not target named organizations.

President Abelardo de la Espriella ordered operations against illegal migration, focusing first on immigrants committing crimes and then those without regular status. Authorities will deport these individuals after completing procedures. How many captures were reported in the security balance? The government reported 1,574 captures, 10 extraditions, and 23,642 kilos of drugs seized, including 12,296 kilos of cocaine. These numbers cover the start of the president’s administration, which began on 7 August 2026. What is the Procuraduría asking ANLA to do about Hidroituango? The Procuraduría asked ANLA to explain its technical, legal, and environmental criteria for a decision on Hidroituango’s operating rule. It gave the agency five working days to report on the status and measures. Why is Hidroituango’s reservoir level important during El Niño? Raising the reservoir to 420 meters stores 390 million extra cubic meters, enough for Medellín’s energy for about 15 days. This helps maintain system reliability during low water inflows from El Niño. Do deportations target specific criminal groups? No, deportations target individuals committing crimes or lacking regular status, not members of named groups like Segunda Marquetalia. The offensive against criminal groups is a separate security operation.

World.title: Ecuador and Singapore Sign Cooperation Pact in Historic Visit
World.content:

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Ecuador · DIPLOMACY

Key Facts — What happened Ecuador and Singapore signed a cooperation memorandum on 24 August 2026 in Singapore.

— How big The pact covers six areas—education, governance, digitalisation, sustainability, public health, and trade.

— Who signs Singapore’s Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan and Ecuador’s Foreign Minister Roberto Carlos Kury Pesantes signed.

— The catch A memorandum is a framework, not money—no funded projects or budgets were announced.

— What comes next Both governments will likely set up working groups to turn the framework into concrete actions.

The memorandum sets a framework for cooperation in six areas, but no money or projects were attached.

Ecuador and Singapore signed a cooperation memorandum on 24 August 2026 in Singapore, during President Daniel Noboa’s state visit. Foreign ministers Vivian Balakrishnan and Roberto Carlos Kury Pesantes signed the document, witnessed by both presidents.

Supporters of President Daniel Noboa in Ecuador. Noboa signed a cooperation memorandum during a historic visit to Singapore.

A Historic First State Visit

President Daniel Noboa made the first state visit by an Ecuadorian leader to Singapore, arriving on 24 August 2026. His trip aimed to strengthen ties with one of Asia’s most dynamic economies.

Singapore’s President Tharman Shanmugaratnam received Noboa, highlighting the importance of the visit. The leaders oversaw the signing of a cooperation memorandum between the two nations.

The memorandum establishes a formal framework for collaboration across multiple sectors. It reflects a shared interest in learning from each other’s strengths and building long-term partnerships.

For Ecuador, the visit opens doors to Singaporean expertise in technology and governance. For Singapore, it expands its network of partners in Latin America.

What the Memorandum Covers

The Ecuador Singapore agreement names six main areas of cooperation: education, leadership and governance, digitalisation, sustainability, public health, and trade and economy. Each area is a broad field where both countries see potential for joint work.

Education and leadership may involve student exchanges and training programs for officials. Digitalisation could focus on smart government services and e-governance, areas where Singapore excels.

Sustainability and public health are global priorities, and the memorandum acknowledges shared goals. Trade and economy remain central, given Ecuador’s exports and Singapore’s role as a trade hub.

The memorandum does not specify budgets or timelines for these areas. It serves as a starting point for future negotiations and project development.

Signing Ceremony Details

The signing took place in Singapore on 24 August 2026, during Noboa’s official program. Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan signed for Singapore, while Roberto Carlos Kury Pesantes signed for Ecuador.

Both presidents were present as witnesses, signaling high-level political backing. The ceremony was also attended by other officials from both governments.

The document is described as a memorandum of understanding, a common tool in international diplomacy. Such documents outline intentions but do not carry binding financial commitments.

This is the first such agreement between the two countries, according to reports from El Universo and The Straits Times. It marks a new chapter in bilateral relations.

Why Singapore Matters to Ecuador

Singapore is a global hub for finance, technology, and trade, making it an attractive partner for Ecuador. Its small size but high economic output offers lessons in efficient governance.

Ecuador seeks to diversify its economy beyond oil and agriculture, and Singapore’s expertise could help. The memorandum creates a channel for knowledge exchange and technical assistance.

Singapore, in turn, sees Latin America as a growing market and a source of natural resources. This agreement could open doors for Singaporean companies in Ecuador.

Trade between the two countries has been modest but has room to grow, and the memorandum supports that goal.

No Money, No Funded Projects

Despite the enthusiasm, the memorandum is not a funding deal. No budgets, loans, or grants were announced as part of the signing.

The document is a framework that guides future cooperation, not a commitment to specific projects. This is the key detail that observers should keep in mind.

Both governments will need to negotiate separate agreements for any concrete initiatives. The memorandum simply lays the groundwork for such discussions.

It is common for such documents to be followed by working groups or joint committees. These would then identify and propose specific projects.

Leadership and Governance Focus

One of the six areas is leadership and governance, which could involve training for public officials. Singapore is known for its clean and efficient civil service, and Ecuador may seek to learn from that model.

Exchange programs for mid-career professionals and joint seminars are likely outcomes. These would be low-cost but high-value activities.

The memorandum mentions ‘human development’ in some reporting, suggesting a focus on people. The Straits Times headline referred to cooperation in human development.

Such initiatives could improve public administration and policy-making in Ecuador over time.

Digitalisation and Sustainability

Digitalisation is a priority for both countries, and the memorandum includes it as a key area. Singapore is a leader in e-government and smart city solutions.

Ecuador could adopt similar technologies to improve services and transparency. The agreement may lead to technical cooperation in this field.

Sustainability is another shared interest, with both nations facing environmental challenges. Singapore invests in green infrastructure, while Ecuador has vast biodiversity to protect.

Joint research or pilot projects in sustainability could emerge from this framework.

Public Health and Trade Potential

Public health cooperation could involve sharing best practices in healthcare delivery and pandemic response. Singapore’s strong health system is a model for many countries.

Ecuador may benefit from training and knowledge transfer in this sector. The memorandum does not specify details, but it opens the door for future collaboration.

Trade and economy remain the core of the agreement, with both sides eager to boost commerce. Ecuador exports bananas, shrimp, and flowers, while Singapore is a major re-export hub.

The memorandum may lead to trade facilitation measures, but no concrete steps have been announced yet.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Ecuador and Singapore sign on 24 August 2026? They signed a memorandum of understanding on cooperation, covering education, governance, digitalisation, sustainability, health, and trade. The document was signed by the foreign ministers of both countries. Who signed the Ecuador Singapore agreement? Singapore’s Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan and Ecuador’s Foreign Minister Roberto Carlos Kury Pesantes signed on behalf of their governments. Presidents Tharman Shanmugaratnam and Daniel Noboa witnessed the signing. Does the memorandum include any money or funded projects? No, it is a framework without funding commitments. No budgets or projects were announced at the signing. What are the six areas of cooperation? The areas are education, leadership and governance, digitalisation, sustainability, public health, and trade and economy. These were named in the reporting. What happens next after the memorandum? Both governments are likely to set up working groups to develop specific projects. No timeline has been announced.
