A group of Polish civil society organisations has urged a former government minister to withdraw his candidacy to become a Constitutional Tribunal (TK) judge, saying his close ties to the prime minister could undermine confidence in the court’s independence. In a joint statement, the nine organisations say that restoring the legitimacy of the court, which has been in crisis since 2015 following illegitimate judicial appointments made by the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, requires not only addressing legal irregularities but also rebuilding public trust. “The existence of the Constitutional Tribunal as an organ of judicial power only makes sense if it is an independent arbiter,” they say. 🔴Wspólnie z innymi organizacjami apelujemy do dr. M. Berka o rezygnację z kandydowania do TK, a do Sejmu o wybór osoby niezależnej politycznie. Droga do praworządności to nie „odbijanie” Trybunału, ale odbudowa jego autorytetu. Przeczytajcie nasz apel, link w komentarzu ⬇️ pic.twitter.com/LPlbk39lNr — Helsińska Fundacja Praw Człowieka (@hfhrpl) August 20, 2026 The appeal follows Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s announcement that Maciej Berek, who until recently served as a government minister and whom Tusk has described as his “right-hand man”, would be put forward as a candidate for the Constitutional Tribunal. The choice has drawn particular attention because Tusk came to power promising to “depoliticise” the court after the previous PiS government appointed former politicians as judges. “Regardless of the extent to which the tribunal has become politicised, the way to reform this institution cannot be for it to be ‘recaptured’ or ‘taken over’ by another ruling majority,” the NGOs write in the statement. The organisations, including the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights, the Institute of Public Affairs and the Stefan Batory Foundation, say Berek’s close ties to the current political leadership could cause his appointment to be perceived as political, regardless of his legal qualifications or personal integrity. “Not only must courts and tribunals operate independently and impartially, but citizens must also recognise and have confidence in that independence and impartiality. This is not possible when judges are appointed whose links to the government are immediately apparent,” the organisations add. “We therefore call on Dr Maciej Berek to withdraw his candidacy in the interests of the independence of the constitutional judiciary.” The proportion of Poles who negatively assess the justice system has increased under the current government, despite its promises to restore the rule of law. State pollster @CBOS_Info found 61% now hold a negative view, up from 55% in 2022 and 51% in 2017 https://t.co/P3fbTTbS5C — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026 The organisations also argue that Berek’s nomination goes against a principle that the current ruling coalition sought to introduce: that anyone who has held political office within the previous four years should be barred from appointment to the tribunal. Berek was a government minister until last week. The coalition’s proposal was included in a bill approved by parliament in 2024. However, the Constitutional Tribunal itself later ruled the provision unconstitutional after former President Andrzej Duda, an ally of PiS, referred the legislation for review. “Although this law has not come into force, it would be reasonable for the Sejm to adhere to the standard it has adopted,” they said, referring to the lower chamber of the parliament, which is responsible for nominating new TK judges. Poland’s constitutional court has rejected two government bills seeking to overhaul the court itself, with the aim of reversing the politicisation that took place under the former administration. It found that the measures "violate judicial independence" https://t.co/uBJr1bXFv4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 30, 2025 However, the selection of Berek, whose candidacy was put forward by MPs from Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO), has exposed divisions within the ruling coalition, which ranges from centre-right to left. “We were supposed to be different from PiS; we were supposed to do things differently, not exactly the same way,” Anna Maria Żukowska, the head of The Left’s (Lewica) parliamentary caucus, told Polsat News. Paweł Śliz, leader of the centre-right Poland 2050’s (Polska 2050) caucus, said Berek would make an excellent Constitutional Tribunal judge were it not for his recent role as a government minister. “I consider him an excellent, outstanding professional; I value his experience and expertise. However, my position on this matter is unequivocal. I will not compromise my principles,” he told the Polish Press Agency (PAP). The chief justice of the constitutional court has refused to accept four new judges appointed by parliament but whom the opposition-aligned president has refused to swear in. The decision deepens an unprecedented standoff over Poland's top court https://t.co/B02DKA3uBL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 9, 2026 Given that the government has a majority of just nine in the 460-seat Sejm, it would only require a small number of MPs from Tusk’s coalition opposing Berek’s nomination for him to lose the vote. Last week, Tusk said that he “understands” concerns from some coalition partners but that he would “try to convince those who have doubts”. However, even if Berek is approved by the Sejm, the law states that new TK judges must swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki has used this requirement to refuse to swear in four of the judges chosen by the Sejm this year. He has, however, sworn in three others. It remains unclear what the president would do in the case of Berek. Presidential spokesman Rafał Leśkiewicz told PAP on Thursday that “there are serious doubts” about Berek’s formal qualifications to become a Constitutional Tribunal judge. Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 Since Tusk’s government came to power in December 2023, it has ignored all TK rulings because three of the tribunal’s judges were appointed illegitimately under the former PiS government. The new ruling coalition also criticised the fact that some TK judges were former PiS politicians. Two of them, for example, were appointed in 2019 shortly after stepping down as PiS MPs. Another, the current TK chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, previously served as a deputy justice minister in the PiS government (though he was never a member of the PiS party). ​ Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland summons Israeli ambassador over discontinued investigation into killing of Gaza aid workers
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has summoned Israel’s ambassador to express its “great disappointment” that the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) have discontinued an investigation into the strikes on an aid convoy in Gaza in 2024 that killed seven humanitarian workers, including a Pole, Damian Soból. “Partnership requires mutual respect,” declared foreign minister Radosław Sikorski. “The humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza, as well as the failure of accountability for [the] IDF’s excessive use of force[,] are undermining public support in even pro-Israel nations.” Partnership requires mutual respect. The humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza, as well as the failure of accountability for IDF’s excessive use of force are undermining public support in even pro-Israel nations. https://t.co/9H0nhiDE4H — Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) August 20, 2026 The incident in question took place in April 2024, when Israeli drones struck a convoy delivering humanitarian aid from World Central Kitchen (WCK), a major international food relief NGO. The attack killed seven aid workers, including Soból. The incident caused outrage in Poland, whose government demanded that Israel fully explain the circumstances. The IDF expressed “sincere sorrow” over the deaths and pledged to carry out a “thorough and transparent” investigation. On Wednesday this week, the IDF announced that it had closed the case after determining “no reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct that would justify the opening of a criminal investigation or the taking of additional measures against any of those involved in the incident”. The IDF said that its troops had identified a gunman on one of the trucks in the convoy. It also claimed that WCK had hired an armed security force to protect the convoy without coordinating that with IDF authorities and that the convoy deviated from the route previously agreed with the IDF. However, the IDF also acknowledged that it had mistakenly identified several individuals as being armed. It added that attempts to contact WCK representatives over a half-hour period while the convoy was on the move were unsuccessful. The IDF noted that, after the incident, two military officers were removed from their positions while three others were reprimanded. But it found that there was no basis for any further action. ⚖️ IDF prosecution rules on five FFAM cases: The IDF says its General Staff Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism has completed reviews of approximately 150 exceptional wartime incidents since the beginning of the war and transferred them to the Military Prosecution. Decisions… pic.twitter.com/H5g4qOu5e2 — Israel Realtime (@IsraelRealtime) August 19, 2026 On Thursday, Poland’s foreign ministry issued a statement saying that it was “greatly disappointed to receive the information provided about the discontinuation of the proceedings by the Israeli military authorities”. It announced that it had summoned the Israeli ambassador in order to “communicate a critical assessment of the actions taken to date to clarify the causes and course of the tragedy”. It also noted that Polish prosecutors are still conducting their own investigation and that the foreign ministry had informed the Israeli ambassador that they “expect the Israeli side will provide the relevant Polish authorities with all necessary explanations and materials requested”. “The circumstances of the tragedy should be fully investigated and [we] do not accept that the perpetrators are avoiding legal and moral responsibility,” concluded the ministry, adding that “the families deserve adequate compensation”. We strongly condemn the Israeli military prosecutor’s account of the deaths of our seven colleagues on April 1, 2024. And we fundamentally disagree with their decision about criminal investigations into the IDF airstrikes that killed our team. Read our full statement here:… — World Central Kitchen (@WCKitchen) August 19, 2026 The IDF’s findings were also condemned by WCK itself, which called them “inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive”. It added that, “at the time of the lethal attacks, the IDF knew that our team in Gaza was unarmed and posing a threat to nobody”. The NGO repeated its demand for an independent investigation into the incident, “because the IDF cannot credibly investigate its own conduct”. On Friday, the UK, Canada and Australia, whose citizens were also killed in the strike, issued a joint statement calling the IDF’s decision to drop the investigation “shameful” and another example of the lack of accountability for incidents in Gaza. Joint statement from the foreign ministries of Australia, Canada and the United Kingdom on Israel closing the investigation into strikes on the World Central Kitchen convoy in Gaza on 1 April 2024 ⬇️ pic.twitter.com/V3CZe286tN — Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (@FCDOGovUK) August 21, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Main image credit: World Central Kitchen

World.title: New official tasked with promoting Poland criticised over error-strewn, potentially AI-generated report
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A government official appointed last month to promote Poland abroad has been hit by a wave of criticism after it emerged that she authored a report containing errors and which shows signs of being generated by artificial intelligence. The document mislocated major Polish cities and included bizarre language mixing Polish and English. It was marked as being part of a project financed by the sport and tourism ministry, though the ministry itself has denied that claim. The opposition has called on prosecutors to investigate potential misuse of public funds. ⁉️ Czy “Markę Polska” ma nam wygenerować sztuczna inteligencja? ⁉️ Czy Ministerstwo Sportu i Turystyki zapłaciło 200 000 złotych w ramach zadania publicznego za raport wygenerowany przez AI? ⁉️ Czy mogę prosić Panią Minister prof. @b_mroz_gorgon o odniesienie się do tych pytań… pic.twitter.com/lM2AY88oAh — Sebastian Meitz (@MeitzPL) August 20, 2026 The official in question, Barbara Mróz-Gorgoń, is a professor at Wrocław University of Economics who was appointed three weeks ago as the government’s plenipotentiary for the promotion of Poland’s brand, a newly created position. She was presented at a press conference by Prime Minister Donald Tusk. However, this week, journalists and commentators began highlighting cases of bizarre errors from a report, titled A Self-Portrait of the Poles (Polaków Portret Własny), published last year with Mróz-Gorgoń named as the author, in her position as president of a think tank called Marka Polska (Brand Poland). The report contained some glaring errors, such as describing the city of Katowice as being in “north central” Poland (whereas in fact it is in the south) and Wrocław as being in the “northwest” (when it is actually in the southwest). Geografia – czyli gdzie leżą Katowice A propos miast jest też ciekawy chochlik lub też, jakby to powiedział ktoś złośliwy, klasyczna halucynacja AI. Przy opisie badań FGI miasta opisane są w następujący sposób (zdjęcie poniżej): 👉 Olsztyn – północny wschód 👉 Szczecin -… pic.twitter.com/SF6XBRfhWS — Sebastian Meitz (@MeitzPL) August 20, 2026 Other parts contain strange analysis, such as noting that “after World War Two, Germany did not build its brand on the Holocaust”. The text also features unusual language, including random use of words in English, some of which have been turned into Polish ones. It is also regularly features words written in capital letters. One sentence, for example, refers to “INSTABILNOŚĆ” and “REZILIENCE”, presumably meaning “instability” and “resilience”, but neither of which is a Polish word. Another section claims that 95% of Poles born after 1990 are “polilingwalni” (an invented Polonised version of “polylingual”) who speak “angielski fluent”, a strange linguistic mix that means they speak English fluently. As well as the unusual language, the very claim that 95% of young Poles speak fluent English, as well as that many additionally speak Mandarin, has been questioned by many commentators. The report also contains bizarre errors in footnotes, which are numbered randomly (on one page, three consecutive footnotes are numbered “41, 517, 6”) and some of which are completely empty. A number of expert commentators have suggested that the text contains clear indications that it was generated by AI, a claim supported by evidence from programmes that check texts for AI-generated content. AI czy nie AI, oto jest pytanie Czytając ten raport kilkukrotnie, trudno mi było pozbyć się wrażenia, że nikt poważny, a szczególnie naukowiec z tytułem doktora habilitowanego, nie wygenerowałby dużych części raportu, za który zapłacili podatnicy, w jakimś LLM. No bo przecież… pic.twitter.com/jyTexgmeXS — Sebastian Meitz (@MeitzPL) August 20, 2026 As well as bearing Mróz-Gorgoń’s name as author, the report also features on its front cover the logo of the sport and tourism ministry. The first page then includes a note saying that the project was carried out under an initiative co-financed by the ministry. After the issue began to draw attention and criticism on Thursday, the ministry issued a statement saying that the report was not ordered by them, was not part of any agreement to which the ministry was a party, and that no request to use the ministry’s logo was submitted. However, a social media post last November by deputy sport and tourism minister Piotr Borys shows him attending an event to present the report. He thanked Mróz-Gorgoń for coordinating the project and inviting him to the presentation. 📚W Akademii Leona Koźmińskiego odbyła się prezentacja raportu „Polaków Portret Własny”, przygotowanego Think Tank Marka Polska. To wyjątkowe wydarzenie poświęcone premierze badań dotyczących DNA Marki Polska. 🧬To pierwsze tak kompleksowe badanie, które pokazuje, kim jesteśmy… pic.twitter.com/jb7KdCJTPM — Piotr Borys (@piotr_borys) November 26, 2025 On Thursday evening, Mróz-Gorgoń herself addressed the controversy in an interview with Polsat News. She said that the report was actually a “work in progress” that “should never have appeared in the public space”. However, she still defended the work, saying that “the research was conducted reliably” and “the conclusions stand up to scrutiny”. But she also admitted that the writing of the report had been “aided by artificial intelligence”. In separate remarks to the Polish Press Agency (PAP), she said that “we used AI tools solely for transcription, summarising and text editing; they did not design research content or draw conclusions…We worked according to social science methodology, diligently and without cutting corners”. Meanwhile, on the Marka Polska think tank’s website, where the report had been published, it was initially changed on Thursday to being marked as a “draft version” before later being deleted entirely. Od raportu i deklaracji, że “praca badawcza [została] przeprowadzona zgodnie z zasadami nauk społecznych, rzetelnie i merytorycznie, w oparciu o opisaną metodologię”, przez “work in progress”, aż do “Oops! That page can’t be found”. Myślę, że to słowo “Oops!” jest najlepszym… pic.twitter.com/OaSTxkwKwa — Sebastian Meitz (@MeitzPL) August 20, 2026 On Thursday evening, the main opposition party, Law and Justice (PiS), announced that it was submitting requests to both prosecutors and the Central Anti-Corruption Bureau (ABW) to investigate the use of around 200,000 zloty (€46,380) in state funds for the project that the report was allegedly part of. PiS has also called on Mróz-Gorgoń to resign or to be fired. On Friday, a deputy digital affairs minister, Dariusz Standerski, told the Wirtualna Polska news website that “all the circumstances surrounding the creation of this report will be clarified”. The controversy around Mróz-Gorgoń comes just days after the sport and tourism ministry was involved in the launch of a new advertising campaign designed to encourage tourism to Poland, but which many commentators have argued was poorly conceived and executed. Poland has launched a new advertising campaign to attract tourists from Europe and the US. The first video, under the slogan "Poland. More than you expected", features footballer Robert Lewandowski, Hollywood star Jesse Eisenberg and supermodel Anja Rubik https://t.co/3jtqyUWQyy — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 19, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Partial Lunar Eclipse to Be Visible From Prague at Dawn on August 28
World.content:
Prague residents willing to get up early on Friday, August 28, will have a chance to witness a partial lunar eclipse, with almost the entire Moon passing into Earth’s shadow shortly before it sets.

The eclipse will reach its maximum at 6:12 a.m. CEST. By then, only a narrow section along the Moon’s northern edge will remain illuminated.

In Prague, the Moon is expected to set at approximately 6:17 a.m., leaving only a few minutes to observe the eclipse at its peak.



The partial phase will begin at 4:33 a.m. As the event progresses, Earth’s shadow will gradually cover the lunar surface, reducing the bright portion of the Moon until only a thin illuminated crescent remains visible.

Astronomers at the Silesian University in Opava say observers will need an unobstructed view towards the southwest, as the Moon will be low above the horizon throughout the most important part of the event.

The eclipse follows another major astronomical event visible from the Czech Republic earlier this month, giving skywatchers a second opportunity to observe a rare celestial phenomenon within a short period.

Unlike a solar eclipse, observing the Moon does not require protective eyewear. The eclipse can be seen with the naked eye, while binoculars or a camera may provide a closer view.

For the best chance of seeing the maximum phase, observers should choose a location with a clear southwestern horizon and arrive before dawn. Weather conditions will also play a decisive role in whether the eclipse is visible.

World.title: September 19: Prague Hosts Indian Festival of Music, Food, and Community
World.content:
Prague will host its annual celebration of Indian culture, Ganeshotsav, on Saturday, September 19, at Kulturní dům Ládví.

Ganeshotsav, the festival honoring Lord Ganesha, is more than a celebration of Indian culture—it’s a way to bring people together.

Since 2021, the festival has grown into a space where Indian and Czech communities can meet, connect, and enjoy shared traditions.

The event is organised by Maharashtra Mandal, Czech Republic, a registered non-profit dedicated to promoting friendship and understanding between Indian and Czech residents.

The festival features traditional Indian rituals, music, dance, and food, and welcomes everyone to join in the fun. This year, the festival also adds a charitable aspect: part of the registration fees will go to support non-profits in India (Matrubhoomi) and the Czech Republic (Karmabhoomi).

“With this initiative, we want to contribute to the development of communities both in our country of origin and in the country that is now our home,” says the organizers to Prague Morning.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Maharashtra Mandal Czech Republic (@maharashtramandalczechrepublic)

By partnering with like-minded organisations, the festival encourages intercultural dialogue, mutual respect, and connections between diverse communities living in the Czech Republic.

Like last year, organizers will support small entrepreneurs from the Indian community who will present the diversity of Indian cuisine.

The project is called “The Taste of Every Indian Household”, and will offer visitors a diverse selection of traditional dishes from different corners of India.

The cultural program, featuring music, dance, and traditional rituals, will run from 5:00 PM to 7:30 PM.

Link for registration: https://forms.gle/kJe9RJ7qvjGrS4TB8

World.title: A Multi-Brand K-Beauty Pop-Up Is Coming to Prague This September
World.content:
A Korean beauty pop-up will bring eight K-beauty brands and K-pop entertainment to Prague’s Vltava River this September.

The HARUNARU K-Beauty Pop-up will take place aboard KVASOUL, a self-brewing boat restaurant, from September 4 to 8.



An industry preview for beauty professionals and influencers will be held on September 3.

Visitors will be able to discover, test and buy products from eight Korean brands, including GASH, ranked No. 1 at Olive Young, South Korea’s leading beauty retailer, and ilso, known for its pore-care products.

The event will also feature K-pop performances, a Random Dance Challenge, an idol-style makeup show and a dedicated selection of K-pop albums and merchandise.

The pop-up is aimed at introducing emerging Korean beauty brands to consumers and industry professionals in the Czech Republic and across Central and Eastern Europe.

Entry is free, although visitors are encouraged to register online in advance.

The event is organized by Bramasole Prague s.r.o., which operates several Korean restaurant brands in Prague.

World.title: Dancing House Marks 30 Years With a Free Weekend of Dance in Prague
World.content:
Prague’s Dancing House will celebrate its 30th anniversary with a free two-day program of dance classes, performances and workshops on August 29 and 30.

Jiráskovo náměstí, next to the landmark on the Vltava embankment, will host a temporary stage and dance floor throughout the weekend.



The program will run from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. on both Saturday and Sunday.

Visitors can join professional instructors for classes in bachata, street dance and Latin American dance. There will also be sessions for children, dance demonstrations and opportunities to meet and talk with instructors.

The event is open to all levels, with participants able to watch performances or take part in the classes.

Weekend program

The schedule is the same on both days until the evening finale.

11:00 a.m. – Opening

11:05 a.m. – Children’s dance class

11:50 a.m. – Talk with the instructor

12:00 p.m. – Bachata demonstration

12:05 p.m. – Bachata class

12:50 p.m. – Talk with bachata instructors

1:00 p.m. – Street dance demonstration

1:05 p.m. – Street dance class

1:50 p.m. – Talk with the street dance instructor

2:00 p.m. – Latin American dance demonstration

2:05 p.m. – Latin American dance class

2:50 p.m. – Talk with instructors

3:00 p.m. – Hat Jazz performance

3:05 p.m. – Children’s dance class

3:50 p.m. – Talk with the instructor

4:00 p.m. – Bachata demonstration

4:05 p.m. – Bachata class

4:50 p.m. – Talk with bachata instructors

5:00 p.m. – Street dance demonstration

5:05 p.m. – Street dance class

5:50 p.m. – Talk with the street dance instructor

6:05 p.m. – Latin American dance class

7:05 p.m. – Hula Hoops performance

The closing acrobatic performance will differ each day. Saturday will feature a handstand performance, while Sunday will bring Duo ReAct.

Admission is free. Organizers will also provide light refreshments.

Completed in 1996, the Dancing House is one of Prague’s best-known examples of modern architecture. It stands at the corner of Rašínovo nábřeží and Jiráskovo náměstí, overlooking the Vltava.

The building was designed by Croatian-Czech architect Vlado Milunić in collaboration with Canadian-American architect Frank Gehry. Its curved forms and leaning towers give the impression of a dancing couple, which inspired its Czech name, Tančící dům.

The building is also known by the nickname “Ginger and Fred,” referring to American dancers Ginger Rogers and Fred Astaire.

World.title: Bolt Launches App-Free Ride Kiosks in the Czech Republic
World.content:
Bolt has introduced self-service kiosks in the Czech Republic that allow customers to order a ride without a smartphone, mobile data or the Bolt app.

The first kiosk is now operating at Westfield Chodov in Prague. A second will open at Westfield Černý Most on September 1. The company says it plans to consider other high-traffic locations in the future.



The kiosks use TapBox technology and provide access to the same Bolt driver network, pricing and safety standards available through the app.

Customers can place an order directly at the screen, making the service available to people who do not use smartphones or cannot access their phones at the time.

Both shopping centres have also introduced dedicated parking spaces for Bolt drivers collecting passengers. Customers are directed to these designated areas rather than having to meet drivers at potentially unsafe stopping points such as bus stops.

How Bolt kiosks work

Ordering a ride takes several steps. Customers enter their destination, select a ride category and provide their phone number. The available categories are Standard, Comfort, Premium and XL.

Payment is made by card. Once the booking is completed, the kiosk prints a confirmation and sends an SMS containing the vehicle details, estimated arrival time and instructions for finding the driver.

The kiosks operate around the clock and support Czech, English, German, French and Ukrainian.

Each ride booked through a kiosk carries an additional CZK 25 fee.

Bolt says the system could also benefit drivers by connecting them with customers who might otherwise be unable to use the app. The company expects the kiosks to reduce waiting times between rides at busy shopping centres and create additional opportunities for drivers.

The Czech launch follows the introduction of similar kiosks in Slovakia earlier this summer, including at airports.

World.title: Prague Adds 18 Kilometers of Cycle Routes but Cycling Numbers Barely Rise
World.content:
Prague is continuing to expand its cycling infrastructure, but the number of recorded bicycle journeys across the city has remained largely unchanged.

Automatic counters installed on major cycling routes recorded about 5.6 million passages in 2025, roughly 1 percent fewer than the previous year.

After adjusting for counter failures and temporary route closures, however, the Technical Road Administration (TSK) calculated a 0.4 percent increase in cycling traffic.



Prague Adds 18 Kilometers of Routes Away From Traffic

The city added 18 kilometers of two-way cycle paths and other cycling routes separated from motor traffic during the year. The total length of marked cycling routes increased by one kilometer to approximately 550 kilometers.

Routes separated from car traffic now account for 263 kilometers of the network, an increase of seven kilometers compared with the previous year.

TSK operates automatic counters at 31 locations on Prague’s main cycling routes. The devices use induction loops or radar to record cyclists and can determine their direction of travel.

The largest increase in two-way cycling routes came over the past year. Their combined length grew from 63 to 81 kilometers. These routes allow cyclists to travel in both directions on streets that are otherwise one-way for motor vehicles.

New two-way routes were added mainly in Prague 7 around Letná, in Prague 5 in Barrandov, and in Prague 6 around Na Petynce, Rozdělovská and Podbaba.

Modřany Remains Prague’s Busiest Cycling Route

The highest number of cyclists was recorded in Modřany, at the intersection of Vltavanů and U Kino streets. The counter registered 578,016 passages during the year.

Another 540,656 cycling journeys were recorded on Povltavská Street south of Troja Castle.

The largest year-on-year increase was recorded on the Barrandov Bridge, where cycling traffic rose following the completion of its more than two-year reconstruction.

World.title: “Upcycling” Prague: Old Offices and Industrial Sites Find New Life as Apartments
World.content:
Former offices, commercial properties and industrial sites in Prague are being converted into apartments rather than demolished, giving developers another option in a city struggling to build enough new homes.

The approach is sometimes described as “upcycling” — adapting ageing buildings for a new purpose while making use of structures and land that are already developed.

One recent example is in Pankrác, near Vyšehrad, where an office building has been converted into the Mo-cha HOME residential complex.



Developed by Cimex, the project opened this spring with 91 fully equipped apartments, most of them in the Czech 2+kk layout, consisting of a living room with a kitchenette and one separate bedroom.

Existing buildings offer valuable locations

Owners of older properties increasingly have to decide whether to renovate them, change their use or demolish them. Many were built for different needs and standards than those expected from buildings today.

Their locations, however, can be a major advantage. Older properties are often close to public transport, shops and other services, making them attractive for residential conversion.

Transforming an existing building can also be faster to prepare than developing a completely new project on a brownfield, although each property must be assessed individually.

The approach can preserve existing structures, reduce demolition and make better use of land that is already developed.

More former offices are becoming homes

Pankrác is not the only part of Prague where old buildings are being converted into housing.

In Holešovice, the former Tesla complex, once used for light-bulb production, has been transformed into a residential project with 149 apartments. The building had stood unused for years, but its main structure remained in relatively good condition.

In Prague 7, another former administrative building near Urania has also been adapted for residential use.

In Prague 3, PSN is preparing the reconstruction of a former telecommunications exchange on Fibichova Street. Built in 1926 and designed by architect Bohumír Kozák, the building is expected to become a rental housing project with 116 units.

One of the largest transformations is planned in Žižkov, where the functionalist former General Pension Institute will be converted into an apartment building with smaller units. The project received a building permit last year.

Not every older building is suitable for conversion. Technical condition, layout, location, project costs and future use all determine whether redevelopment makes economic and practical sense.

World.title: More Czech Companies Test Four-Day Work Weeks Despite Political Resistance
World.content:
A growing number of companies in the Czech Republic are experimenting with a four-day working week, with some reporting higher productivity and greater employee satisfaction.

But politicians remain reluctant to make the arrangement a standard option across the country.

Under the model, employees work four days instead of five while keeping their full salaries. Companies that have introduced the system say workers can maintain their output while having more time to rest.



At Trinity Group, the arrangement has been in place for five years. Jan Hanulík, the company’s product and marketing director, said productivity had risen despite employees working one day less each week.

“Although we have one working day less, productivity has increased,” Hanulík said, adding that the company’s results have roughly doubled since the system was introduced.

A survey cited in the report found that around 70 percent of employees in the Czech Republic would welcome a four-day working week.

Politicians remain cautious

The idea has already been adopted in different forms elsewhere in Europe. In Belgium, for example, employees can request to work their weekly hours over four days rather than five. The system therefore does not necessarily mean fewer working hours.

Czech politicians, however, argue that a single system would not work across all sectors.

Labor and Social Affairs Minister Aleš Juchelka of ANO said a legally mandated four-day week could create problems in areas already facing staff shortages, including social services and health care.

SPD lawmaker Lucie Šafránková also said the working week should reflect the conditions of individual professions and employers rather than follow one nationwide rule.

Czech companies are already experimenting

Several companies have introduced or tested four-day schedules, including SAB Finance, Phonexia, Sherpas, Digiskills and Café Eternity.

Not every experiment has lasted. The Cognito agency eventually returned to a traditional five-day working week after testing the shorter schedule.

World.title: Hungarian Gripen crash: Swedish Saab offers support as investigation begins
World.content:
The fighter jet that crashed near Szolnok on Monday was a single-seat Gripen C, not the latest E/F model. Saab says it will assist the Hungarian investigation, while the crash has also briefly affected the Swedish defence company’s share price.

Saab has confirmed that the Hungarian Gripen fighter jet that crashed near Szolnok on Monday was a single-seat Gripen C. The Hungarian pilot ejected from the aircraft and survived the crash. Hungarian authorities are responsible for investigating what caused the accident, while Saab says it will provide technical assistance to the investigation.

“Of course, Saab will assist in the investigation,” Mattias Rådström, the company’s press manager, told Swedish news agency Direkt.

Gripen developed a fault during a training flight

The aircraft was flying alongside another Gripen during a training exercise when a warning indicating a malfunction appeared in the cockpit. The training mission was aborted, and the two aircraft headed towards Szolnok, as the damaged fighter could reportedly no longer reach Kecskemét.

However, another incident occurred during the final stage of the landing. The pilot decided to eject, after which the aircraft left the runway area and caught fire.

The pilot survived the ejection and is currently reported to be in a stable condition.

Hungary’s air force has suspended Gripen training flights until the investigation is completed. The aircraft assigned to alert and operational duties continue to perform their missions. Investigators have already begun examining the crash site, while data from the fighter’s flight recorder – commonly known as its black box – could prove crucial in determining exactly what happened.

Could Hungary ground its Gripen fleet?

Saab has not announced a general flight ban for the Gripen following the accident. Asked whether the aircraft could potentially be grounded while the investigation is under way, Rådström said the company would have to return to the question if such a decision became necessary.

The crash leaves Hungary with 17 Gripen aircraft in service.

Saab said in June that it had completed deliveries under an additional agreement signed by Sweden’s Defence Materiel Administration (FMV) and Hungary’s Ministry of Defence in January 2024. Hungary had subsequently operated a total of 18 Gripen C/D aircraft: 16 single-seat Gripen C fighters and two two-seat Gripen D aircraft. Hungary has not purchased the newer Gripen E/F variant.

The Gripen is a single-engine, supersonic multirole fighter designed for missions including air combat, ground attack and reconnaissance.

Saab shares briefly fall after the crash

The accident also had a short-term impact on Saab’s shares on the Stockholm Stock Exchange, according to Világgazdaság. The stock initially reversed an earlier gain of around 0.8% and briefly fell by approximately 0.6% following reports of the Hungarian crash.

The shares subsequently recovered much of the lost ground. By around noon, Saab stock was up approximately 0.1% for the day.

World.title: The Guardian: Hungary is ‘de-Orbánising’ at record speed
World.content:
Péter Magyar’s government has launched Hungary’s most dramatic transformation since the fall of communism, according to a Guardian editorial – but concerns remain over constitutional moves targeting Fidesz politicians and the fate of more than EUR 10 billion in EU funds.

Hungary is undergoing its most far-reaching political transformation since the fall of communism in 1989, according to The Guardian, which says Péter Magyar’s government is dismantling Viktor Orbán’s 16-year political legacy at an “extraordinary pace”.

In an editorial published on Sunday, the British newspaper assessed Magyar’s first three months as prime minister, describing the changes as a “peaceful political revolution”.

The Guardian portrays Orbán’s former system as a “soft autocracy” that flourished on corruption and extended its influence across much of Hungarian society, from religion and culture to the media. Now, it argues, that system is being dismantled at remarkable speed.

New president and a shake-up of state media

One of the most significant developments highlighted by the newspaper is the appointment of András Baka as Hungary’s new president. Baka, a former president of Hungary’s Supreme Court, was removed from his judicial position during Orbán’s rule in a case that was later found to have violated his rights by the European Court of Human Rights.

His appointment stands in stark contrast to the departure of his predecessor, Tamás Sulyok. Magyar had accused Sulyok of effectively rubber-stamping the erosion of the rule of law, while a constitutional amendment brought his presidential term to an early end.

The Guardian also points to the return of news bulletins to Hungary’s main state television channel on 20 August, after a six-week suspension. The newspaper describes ending what Magyar has portrayed as overt political bias in state media as one of his key campaign promises. Magyar won April’s election despite an electoral system that the Guardian says was weighted in Orbán’s favour.

Hungary goes after the legacy of corruption

The government’s efforts to dismantle corruption networks established during the previous administration have also been moving quickly, according to the editorial. The Guardian says well over EUR 100 billion in public funds, including billions in EU money, is believed to have been siphoned off during Orbán’s years in power.

Investigators have been given new powers to pursue allegedly misappropriated assets through Hungary’s newly established National Asset Recovery and Protection Office. Magyar has also confirmed Hungary’s participation in the European Public Prosecutor’s Office, a move intended to strengthen the protection of EU funds and the investigation of financial crimes.

The next major test could come as soon as this autumn. Brussels has given Hungary until the end of August to demonstrate that sufficient measures have been taken to tackle corruption. More than EUR 10 billion in frozen EU funding is at stake.

The Guardian considers it likely that the vast majority of the money will eventually be released, arguing that this would further cement the rapprochement between Hungary and the European Union after years of conflict.

Concerns over Fidesz and ‘revenge’

Despite its broadly positive assessment of the new government’s direction, The Guardian also raises concerns about some of Magyar’s methods. The newspaper points to constitutional manoeuvring aimed at preventing a number of Fidesz MPs from standing in future elections.

President Baka has himself warned against creating the impression that the new government is seeking revenge against Orbán’s supporters. The Guardian nevertheless argues that a root-and-branch effort to dismantle the former system was necessary, and notes that Magyar’s approach continues to receive strong public backing in opinion polls.

At the same time, the newspaper cautions that rebuilding Hungary as a “normal pluralist European democracy” will take time.

For now, it describes Magyar as a “one-man political whirlwind” at the head of what is effectively a national unity government, supported by voters from across the political spectrum.

From symbolic gestures to a political revolution

The Guardian also highlights the symbolic changes introduced by Magyar. In May, the new prime minister moved his office out of the Carmelite Monastery, the heavily guarded building used by Orbán during his premiership. The building has since been opened to the public.

“I was not elected simply to change the government, but to change the regime,” Magyar said shortly after taking office, the newspaper recalls.

Three months later, The Guardian argues, that symbolic break with the past has been accompanied by much more substantial changes.

World.title: Hungary begins EUR 275 school-starting support payments to families
World.content:
The first HUF 50,000 instalment of Hungary’s new school-starting allowance has begun reaching eligible families, with the government saying the scheme will support the families of more than 400,000 children.

Hungary has begun paying the first instalment of a new HUF 100,000 (roughly EUR 275) school-starting allowance to eligible families, Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced on Monday.

“Today we began the payment of the first instalment of the HUF 100,000 school-starting support to the families of 400,000 children,” Magyar said in a Facebook post, adding: “We promised it, and we delivered it.”

The first payment amounts to HUF 50,000 (EUR 138) and is being distributed ahead of the new school year to help families cover the costs associated with starting school.

Second HUF 50,000 payment coming in November

The remaining HUF 50,000 will be paid by the end of November in the form of a voucher that can be used for the child’s schooling needs. According to the government, the support is intended to help with significant back-to-school expenses, including school supplies, clothing and other essential items.

The first instalment is being paid by the Hungarian State Treasury in the same way as the family allowance. Families who receive their family allowance into a bank account will receive the school-starting support in the same account, while those who receive it in cash will receive the money through the post.

The school-starting allowance is paid separately from the family allowance. The State Treasury is also bringing forward the payment of September’s family allowance, as well as several other family support benefits, including GYES, GYED, CSED and GYET.

Who is eligible for the HUF 100,000 support?

The new benefit is targeted at families considered to be in greater need of financial assistance. Eligibility depends on several conditions. According to a statement by the Hungarian government, the child must meet at least one of the following criteria:

be eligible for regular child protection benefits;

have a long-term illness or severe disability and therefore qualify for a higher family allowance;

have special educational needs;

participate in the Dobbantó programme or workshop-school training;

be raised by a single parent;

live in the child protection care system; or

receive an orphan’s benefit.

In addition, family allowance must be paid for the child for August, with at least one of the above conditions already applying at that time. The child must also attend a public education or vocational training institution, or be starting their first year of school in September.

No application is required

Eligible families do not need to submit an application for the payment. The government says the payments will be arranged automatically using existing official registers, meaning parents do not need to register, submit a separate request or complete any forms.

The HUF 100,000 benefit is also tax-free and cannot be subject to enforcement proceedings, meaning the full amount is intended to remain available for the child’s needs.

With the first HUF 50,000 now being distributed and the second instalment due by 30 November, the government says the scheme will provide direct financial help to the families of more than 400,000 children as the new school year begins.

World.title: Hungarian spa to close in bid to save millions as town struggles with budget
World.content:
A spa in the Hungarian town of Szerencs will temporarily close from 1 September as the municipality looks to cut costs and save almost HUF 25 million (around EUR 69,000) by the end of the year.

The Szerencsi Fürdő & Wellnessház will remain closed to visitors until at least 17 December, according to an announcement by Szerencsi Hírek and Mayor Attila Kiss. The decision comes as the town seeks to reduce spending across its municipal operations.

Low visitor numbers make spa costly to operate

Szerencs operates two water facilities: the Szerencsi Fürdő & Wellnessház and a municipal swimming pool. While the swimming pool benefits from state support and energy-efficiency improvements, the spa has to be financed from the town’s own resources.

Visitor numbers at the spa have remained relatively low despite efforts to attract more guests, including free entry vouchers provided by the municipality.

The town had previously ordered the Szerencsi Városüzemeltető Nonprofit Kft., which operates the spa, to cut its costs by around 10 per cent because of the municipality’s financial situation. After examining the available options, the company concluded that temporarily closing the spa would deliver the largest savings.

Nearly HUF 25 million in savings expected

Mayor Attila Kiss said the closure between 1 September and 17 December could generate substantial savings across several areas.

The municipality expects to save approximately:

HUF 9.8 million on wages and related contributions

on wages and related contributions HUF 5.2 million on natural gas

on natural gas HUF 6.8 million on electricity

on electricity HUF 2.2 million on water and sewage charges

on water and sewage charges HUF 570,000 on water testing and monitoring

on water testing and monitoring HUF 340,000 on chemicals

Together, these measures could save the town close to HUF 25 million by the end of the year.

The closure will not mean that the entire building becomes unused. Tenants operating businesses there will continue to have access to their premises, while a smaller and more economical heating system will be introduced to heat the necessary parts of the building. Staff working at the spa will, where possible, be reassigned to other duties.

If you missed it: Hungary’s famous Miskolctapolca Cave Bath finally reopens after almost two years

Spa could reopen around Christmas

The municipality says it does not want residents to be left without access to swimming facilities for an extended period. The town’s swimming pool is normally scheduled to close temporarily after 19 December for maintenance and a water change. If Szerencs’ financial position improves and the planned savings are achieved, the municipality may therefore reopen the spa from 18 December until around mid-January.

The aim is to ensure that one of the town’s two water facilities remains available to residents whenever possible. Residents who still have free vouchers for the spa can use them until 31 August. After the temporary closure begins, unused vouchers will be accepted at the municipal swimming pool instead.

The Szerencsi Fürdő & Wellnessház was previously closed in autumn 2022 due to soaring electricity and gas prices and did not reopen until June 2023, according to Borsod24.

World.title: Baby taken from German hospital found on Hungarian motorway
World.content:
A sick baby who was taken from a German hospital without permission has been found safe in Hungary after police tracked the vehicle carrying the child and intercepted it on the M43 motorway.

German authorities issued a wanted notice after the infant was removed from the hospital. Hungarian police were alerted to the case and immediately passed the information to officers on patrol in Csongrád-Csanád County.

Police tracked the vehicle to the M43

According to the Csongrád-Csanád County Police Headquarters, officers were able to determine the vehicle’s expected route by monitoring its movements.

The information enabled police to organise a rapid and coordinated intervention. Officers eventually stopped the vehicle at a rest area on the M43 motorway in southern Hungary. The circumstances surrounding why the baby was taken from the German hospital have not been disclosed.

Baby taken to hospital in stable condition

Police said the infant was found in a stable condition. With the assistance of Hungary’s National Ambulance Service, the baby was taken to hospital to receive the necessary medical treatment. The officers involved in the operation are set to receive official recognition from the deputy national police chief responsible for policing.

The Hungarian police described the operation as a race against time to protect a vulnerable child. Thanks to the swift intervention, the baby was brought to safety.

World.title: Looking beyond price per square metre: how Budapest, Warsaw and Bucharest’s new-build home markets differ
World.content:
Lower new-build property prices in Bucharest and Poland’s major cities may catch the attention of Hungarian buyers, but the success of a property investment abroad is determined by much more than the purchase price and achievable rental income. An analysis by Cordia comparing the Hungarian, Polish and Romanian markets, while also looking at Spain, examines the differences, costs and yields investors should consider when thinking about entering a new-build market in the region or buying a newly built home in a popular holiday destination.

By the end of the first quarter of this year, the average price per square metre of new-build homes in Budapest had risen above HUF 1.9 million, 8% higher than in March 2025. Against this backdrop, Bucharest may look particularly attractive: even using the average exchange rates recorded during the first quarter, the gross average price remained below HUF 1.3 million per square metre despite annual price growth of more than 10%.

Among Poland’s major property markets – Warsaw, Kraków, the Tricity area (Sopot, Gdańsk and Gdynia), Wrocław, Poznań and Łódź – the capital is the most expensive. By the end of March, the average price per square metre of new-build homes in Warsaw, calculated in forints and referring to properties in shell-and-core condition, approached HUF 1.7 million. In Poznań, meanwhile, the average remained below HUF 1.2 million. These figures are among the findings of a regional market comparison prepared by Cordia, one of Hungary’s leading residential property developers.

“These potentially significant price differences may also spark the interest of Hungarian investors. For our projects abroad, we naturally assist buyers who are considering purchasing a new-build apartment either in regional markets or even on the Spanish Riviera,” said Áron Görög, Sales Director at Cordia.

“On the Costa del Sol, where we are now developing our second project, we are seeing significant appreciation. The average price of €7,220 per square metre recorded in March this year – equivalent to around HUF 2.6 million – was almost 9% higher than a year earlier. It is also important to note that developers there traditionally advertise net prices, to which 10% VAT is then added.”

If you missed it: Good news for homebuyers and students: vast student city and residential district could rise on Budapest’s derelict waterfront

What about rental prices?

For a property investment, achievable rental income and the characteristics of the local rental market are also crucial.

In Poland, for example, lower prices per square metre come with unit rental prices comparable to or higher than the Budapest average. As a result, gross rental yields calculated in euros range between 4.5% and 6%, even after taking into account the additional costs required to bring a property to a fully finished, move-in-ready condition.

It is also worth looking at the differences between individual Polish cities. Poznań, for instance, is a major industrial and logistics hub, with low unemployment and more moderate new-build property prices. In Warsaw, on the other hand, investors can expect relatively high property prices but also stable rental demand, as the capital is the country’s main business centre.

In Bucharest, relatively low new-build prices compared with other regional markets offer an attractive entry point. However, gross rental yields are also broadly in line with the Polish average, at around 5–6%.

“Sales have recently begun at Cordia’s latest Bucharest project, the 274-apartment Centropolitan development. We are seeing significant interest in the project from buyers in Hungary as well,” the expert said.

Double land costs and shell-and-core apartments in Warsaw

It is also worth examining what lies behind the significant differences in property prices across the region.

When interpreting Warsaw’s prices, it is important to bear in mind that, unlike in Hungary and Romania, developers traditionally offer apartments in shell-and-core rather than fully finished condition. This means buyers face substantial additional costs beyond the purchase price before they can move in.

At the same time, construction costs for an average Warsaw or Bucharest development are 25–33% lower than in Budapest. Land prices, however, tell a different story. In Warsaw, land represents a cost more than twice as high in the per-square-metre price of a property compared with the Hungarian or Romanian capital.

Differences in tax systems must also be taken into account. In Hungary, the standard VAT rate for new-build homes is currently 5%, and VAT can also be reclaimed in the case of homes in designated brownfield regeneration zones. In Poland, an 8% VAT rate applies to residential properties smaller than 150 square metres, while the portion above that threshold is subject to a 23% rate. In Romania, following a temporary period with a lower tax burden, the standard VAT rate returned to 21% in August this year.

“Alongside differences on the cost side, prices are also strongly influenced by the complexity of administration, the varying strength of demand and the range of government measures available to support buyers,” Görög emphasised.

Air conditioning is now a basic requirement in Bucharest and Budapest

“The technology used in the buildings we develop is fundamentally similar. There is also no difference in the fact that we build apartments with terraces everywhere, although this is less important to Polish buyers. Efficient floor plans are expected across all markets, but environmental awareness and energy efficiency are less prominent considerations in Poland and Romania.

“As summers become increasingly hot, buyers in both Budapest and Bucharest are placing greater emphasis on effective cooling systems, whereas this is not as common in Poland, particularly in the northern parts of the country,” the expert said.

Interestingly, Poland is introducing energy-efficiency ratings for multi-apartment buildings only this year, making it the last EU member state to do so. Experts believe this could encourage investors to sell older, energy-inefficient apartments and instead seek out newly built, energy-efficient properties.

According to Cordia’s experience, however, there is one common trend across all markets: buyers everywhere are increasingly demanding higher quality, better-equipped homes and additional services, such as communal spaces and facilities, co-working areas, lounges and gastro bars.

Here, the company can draw particularly strongly on its experience in the more developed Spanish market. This gives Cordia a competitive advantage in markets such as Romania, where such extras are still relatively uncommon in projects developed by other companies.

World.title: Two light aircraft collide and crash in Austria, killing both pilots
World.content:
Two light aircraft collided and crashed near Krems Airport in Lower Austria on Monday morning, killing both pilots, according to local police.

Two aircraft caught fire after collision

The accident happened near Krems Airport, with the two aircraft catching fire after the collision. Initial information indicates that neither aircraft was carrying anyone other than its pilot, according to Kronen Zeitung.

Both pilots died in the accident.

The exact circumstances of the crash are not yet clear.

One aircraft was towing a glider

According to the Krems volunteer fire brigade, the aircraft involved were two ultralight planes. One of them had been towing a glider when the collision occurred.

The glider had already detached from the towing aircraft shortly before the accident. The pilot of the aircraft then turned, after which the two ultralight planes collided.

The glider itself was not involved in the crash.

Police and emergency services are investigating the circumstances surrounding the fatal collision.

World.title: Orbán’s secret EU campaign revealed: How Hungary took its message to Europe – and how much we paid for it
World.content:
A newly obtained media plan reveals that Viktor Orbán’s government paid more than HUF 313 million for a campaign placing the Hungarian prime minister’s seven-point criticism of the European Union in newspapers across Europe in 2021.

Hungarian taxpayers paid more than HUF 313 million for a government advertising campaign that promoted then-Prime Minister Viktor Orbán’s criticism of the European Union in foreign newspapers, newly obtained documents reveal.

The campaign, launched in the summer of 2021, was considerably broader than previously known. While two full-page s – one in a Danish newspaper and another in Spain – attracted attention at the time, documents obtained by investigative outlet Átlátszó show that Orbán’s message was ultimately published in 18 foreign newspapers.

The campaign came at a particularly tense moment in Hungary’s relationship with the EU, following a series of disputes over the Hungarian government’s policies and its increasingly confrontational stance towards Brussels.

A HUF 313 million campaign against the “European empire”

The , titled On the Future of the European Union – Hungary’s Proposals, presented seven points under Orbán’s signature. Its opening message declared: “We say no to a European empire!”

According to the media plans obtained from the Prime Minister’s Cabinet Office, the government paid a total of HUF 313 million gross for the campaign. The net advertising cost was HUF 213.4 million. On top of this came a 15 per cent agency fee of HUF 32 million paid to New Land Media, the company responsible for organising the campaign, followed by VAT.

The documents indicate that the government initially targeted even more publications. In total, 25 newspapers appear to have been approached, although seven ultimately did not publish the . One of them, Bulgaria’s 24 Chasa, reportedly could not run it because of technical reasons. The campaign therefore went far beyond the two s that became publicly known at the time.

Why was Orbán’s message published in 2021?

The timing was important. In March 2021, Fidesz left the European People’s Party group in the European Parliament after changes to the group’s rules opened the way for an entire delegation to be expelled.

Three months later, Hungary’s parliament adopted the government’s so-called child protection law, which drew widespread criticism over its restrictions concerning LGBTQ-related content. The legislation was promulgated on 23 June.

Just days later, EU leaders gathered for a summit in Brussels, where the Hungarian government faced strong criticism over the law. Dutch Prime Minister Mark Rutte had already taken an exceptionally hard line before the summit, saying that, in his view, Hungary had no place in the EU.

At the summit itself, leaders from 17 member states signed a declaration condemning the Hungarian legislation as a “blatant form of discrimination”.

The first s featuring Orbán’s response appeared in foreign newspapers the following day, on 26 June. Over the next two weeks, readers of a further 16 publications encountered the Hungarian prime minister’s seven-point message.

What did Orbán’s seven points say?

The  presented a very Eurosceptic vision of the European Union. Orbán argued that Brussels was building a “superstate” without democratic authorisation and called for rejecting what he described as a European empire.

He also said European integration should be regarded as a means rather than an end in itself, arguing against the principle of an “ever closer union” being included in the EU treaties.

Another point called for decisions to be made by elected leaders rather than international NGOs, while accusing the EU of outsourcing the rule of law. The Hungarian prime minister also linked the future of European integration to economic success, arguing that the EU would have no future if member states could not become more successful together than separately.

Other points focused on migration and pandemics, strengthening national parliaments and restoring public confidence in European democracy. The final proposal was particularly notable: Serbia should be admitted to the European Union.

Several major European newspapers refused the 

Not every newspaper approached by the Hungarian government agreed to publish the campaign. The editor-in-chief of The Times of Malta said the newspaper did not want to accept money from a government that restricted press freedom, human rights and the rule of law. Publishing the , he argued, could have turned the newspaper into a tool of a policy running counter to press freedom.

Belgium’s De Standaard similarly rejected the  and instead published a full-page rainbow-coloured response. La Libre Belgique reportedly argued that Orbán’s  did not reflect the truth, while De Morgen rejected it because the message was incompatible with the values represented by the newspaper.

Sweden’s Dagens Nyheter offered Orbán an interview instead, but received no response. Meanwhile, The Irish Times argued that the Hungarian government was attempting to use money to bypass the editorial process and place its own message directly before readers.

A campaign designed to reach beyond Orbán’s allies

The newspapers that did publish the s were not exclusively sympathetic to the Hungarian government. According to the documents, roughly half of the publications that carried the campaign were critical of Orbán’s government to some degree, while the other half were more favourable towards it.

The selection also suggests that the government was seeking a broad international audience rather than simply targeting publications in countries considered political allies. The campaign included conservative and right-wing newspapers, but also mainstream titles such as France’s Le Figaro and Sweden’s Dagens Industri.

World.title: Romania’s leading Banca Transilvania posts 26.8% higher net profit in first half of 2026
World.content:
In the first six months of the year, Romania’s leading bank, Banca Transilvania (BVB: TLV), recorded a net profit of RON 2.5 billion, 26.8% above the level recorded in the same period last year, according to a press release.

The BT Group's assets reached RON 233.3 billion as of June 30, 2026, up 4% from the end of last year and 12.1% compared with the same period of the previous year. Loans and net leasing receivables granted to customers reached RON 115.7 billion, up 8.4% from the end of 2025 and 14.8% compared with the first half of last year. At the same time, the gross loans-to-deposits ratio increased to 68.5%, 3.8% above the level at the end of last year.

“Despite the challenging economic environment, we managed to grow the bank's customer base and operational activity, which is reflected in our results,” said Ömer Tetik, general manager of Banca Transilvania.

Within the Group, Banca Transilvania's own net profit reached RON 2.1 billion in the first half of the year, up 20.7% compared with the same period last year. Net profit in the second quarter was 25.6% higher compared with the first quarter of the year. The evolution was supported by commercial performance and the acceleration of activity in the second quarter.

The bank's assets increased to RON 217.8 billion, 3.5% above the level at the end of 2025 and 11.3% compared with June 30, 2025. Customer deposits reached RON 172.4 billion, up 2.1% from the end of last year and 8.8% compared with the same period of the previous year.

The gross loan portfolio granted to customers reached RON 113.7 billion, up 7.6% from the end of 2025 and 11.7% compared with June 30, 2025. The quality of the loan portfolio remained at a very good level, with the non-performing loan ratio according to the EBA definition falling to 2.41%, 0.24 percentage points below the level recorded in the same period last year.

The gross loans-to-deposits ratio reached 65.9%, an evolution that reflects the transformation of attracted resources into financing for individuals and companies.

BT also reported a strong capital position, with a solvency ratio of 21.96%, which includes the interim net profit for the first half of 2026. Return on equity remained at a solid level of 21.98%. At the same time, basic earnings per share (EPS) stood at RON 1.9389 for the first half of the year, up 24.2% from the value recorded in the same period of 2025.

Net interest income at the individual level reached RON 3.3 billion, up 4.6% from the first half of 2025. Net fee and commission income increased by 13.5% compared with the same period last year, amid an increase in transaction volumes. Net trading income was 4.9% above the level recorded in the first half of 2025, supported mainly by foreign exchange activity and the performance of financial assets held for trading.

Operating income increased to RON 5.3 billion, up 15.9% compared with the same period last year and 6.2% compared with the first quarter of 2026, as a result of increased commercial activity. The bank's operating expenses were influenced by investments in development and the integration into Banca Transilvania of the technology company Code Crafters, which was part of the BT Group. Compared with the first half of 2025, operating expenses increased by 12.9%, while compared with the first quarter of this year, they decreased by 8.9% in the second quarter of the year.

Operational efficiency remained at a competitive level, with a cost-to-income ratio of 44.6%, or 38.3% excluding the impact of the turnover tax. The figures show the bank's ability to support growth through an efficient and scalable business model.

BT provided companies with financing of RON 17.6 billion, RON 5.1 billion above the level recorded in the same period last year, while it provided RON 7 billion in financing to individuals, of which 31% were real estate/mortgage loans and 67% loans for current needs. The Large Corporate segment was the main driver of growth in financing granted to companies, contributing more than 80% (RON 4.2 billion) to the increase in lending compared with H1 2025, particularly through financing investment projects and working capital needs.

The outstanding balance of gross loans granted to companies increased by 10.1% compared with the end of 2025 and by 14.8% compared with June 30, 2025.

The number of transactions carried out by all customers through all the bank's channels was more than 17% higher than in the first half of last year.

World.title: Bucharest Exchange-listed Electro-Alfa reports 8.4% higher net profit in H1 2026
World.content:
Electro-Alfa International (BVB: EAI), a leading Romanian manufacturer of electrical equipment and provider of EPC and IT services, listed on the Bucharest Stock Exchange, reported consolidated total revenues of RON 364.3 million in the first half of 2026, up 18.1% compared to the same period of 2025. EBITDA remained resilient at RON 37.2 million, while net profit increased by 8.4% to RON 27.9 million.

According to the company, the results recorded in the first half of 2026 were supported by continued demand for low- and medium-voltage electrical equipment, the execution of energy and infrastructure projects, and strong international activity.

Export sales represented approximately 33% of total sales during the period, supported by deliveries of own-manufactured electrical equipment to customers in the United States and deliveries to Ukraine through international tender-based projects.

“During the first half of the year, we expanded into energy storage and railway infrastructure, strengthened our engineering capabilities and continued to develop our manufacturing capacity. These are deliberate steps to broaden the markets we address and increase the scale and complexity of the projects we deliver,” said Gheorghe Ciubotaru, Chairman of the Board of Directors of Electro-Alfa International.

In the first half of the year, cash generation from operating activities improved significantly. The group recorded net cash flow from operating activities of RON 30 million, compared to a negative net cash flow of RON 5.6 million in the corresponding period of 2025. The improvement was mainly driven by the collection of trade receivables, alongside solid operating profitability.

As of 30 June 2026, Electro-Alfa International’s total assets reached RON 1.15 billion, while total equity increased to RON 761.4 million, compared to RON 210.2 million at the end of 2025. The group held RON 107.7 million in cash and cash equivalents and RON 430.5 million in short-term bank deposits. At the same time, bank borrowings decreased to RON 54.8 million as of 30 June 2026.

The Manufacturing segment remained the main contributor to the group’s revenues and profitability. The segment generated external revenues of RON 206.8 million in H1 2026, up 18.5% compared to RON 174.4 million in H1 2025. Operating profit increased to RON 17.7 million from RON 14.5 million in the corresponding period of the previous year.

The EPC Services segment generated external revenues of RON 153.6 million in H1 2026, up 15.3% compared to RON 133.2 million in H1 2025. Operating profit amounted to RON 13.6 million, compared to RON 17.6 million in the prior-year period, corresponding to an operating margin of 8.8%. This performance reflects the revenue mix and cost structure associated with projects executed across contracting activities, green energy and international tenders.

The IT Services segment, operated through Alfa Factory Software, continued to expand its software development activities, generating external revenues of RON 0.6 million in H1 2026, compared to RON 0.2 million in H1 2025.

During H1 2026, Electro-Alfa International also added two new reportable segments: BESS and Railway Infrastructure. The BESS segment was added following the acquisition of Solar Technologies Consulting in April 2026, which holds a ready-to-build battery energy storage project with an installed capacity of 51.44 MW, located in Șelimbăr, Sibiu County.

The Railway Infrastructure segment was added following the completion of the acquisition of a 51% stake in SPIACT Craiova, expanding Electro-Alfa International’s technical expertise into railway signalling, control systems and specialized infrastructure works. The acquisition of SPIACT Craiova was completed in June 2026, so its contribution to H1 results was limited. The segment generated external revenues of RON 2 million and operating profit of RON 0.1 million.

Following the end of the reporting period, on 1 July 2026, Electro-Alfa International and SGB-SMIT Group inaugurated a new factory in Botoșani, SGB-Electroalfa.

Electro-Alfa completed an IPO in February 2026, through which it raised net proceeds of RON 544.3 million to support its medium-term growth strategy. The company currently has a market capitalization of over RON 3 billion (EUR 584 million).

World.title: Romania’s president congratulates Ukraine on Independence Day as European leaders gather in Kyiv
World.content:
Romanian president Nicușor Dan sent a message of congratulations to Ukraine on Monday, August 24, to mark the neighboring country’s Independence Day.

The official highlighted the “extraordinary courage and heroic resilience of the Ukrainian people in defence of our shared values and freedom.” He also promised that “Romania will continue to stand by Ukraine, steadfast in upholding the country’s independence, sovereignty and territorial integrity.”

“Ukraine can count on our multidimensional assistance. Romania also remains fully committed to supporting Ukraine's EU accession process and its post-conflict reconstruction. At the same time, NATO's continued engagement with Ukraine remains essential to the long-term stability and security of the entire Euro-Atlantic area,” Dan concluded the message posted on X.

The president’s partner, Mirabela Grădinaru, also traveled to Kyiv on an official visit to represent him as Ukraine marked its Independence Day. Romania's First Lady was invited to the Ukrainian capital by Olena Zelenska, the wife of Volodymyr Zelensky. During the same meeting, Mirabela Grădinaru received an invitation from Maia Sandu to visit Chișinău.

Dan also participated via videoconference in a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing, the alliance of states that back Ukraine in the war against Russia.

Meanwhile, Moldovan president Maia Sandu, the new British PM, Andy Burnham, and the leaders of Denmark, Norway, Finland, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania traveled to Kyiv. During the visit, Maia Sandu will participate in events dedicated to the 35th anniversary of Ukraine's independence.

In a post on her Facebook page, Maia Sandu said that she was in the Ukrainian capital to express her solidarity with the Ukrainian people, who have been defending themselves against Russian aggression for four and a half years. “For four and a half years, Ukrainians have been defending their country, and through their courage they are defending peace across the continent. Moldova is living in peace also thanks to this courage,” the president wrote.

Sandu announced that she would award Volodymyr Zelensky the Order of the Republic on the same occasion. According to the head of state, the distinction is being awarded “for his exceptional contribution to defending peace and freedom on the European continent” and as a sign of gratitude from the citizens of the Republic of Moldova for the courage of the Ukrainian people.

The new head of the British government, Andy Burnham, also arrived in Kyiv to mark Ukraine’s independence and struggle against Russia. He thanked all partners, emphasizing that their support “is part of Ukraine's strength.” During his visit to Kyiv, Burnham will participate in events organized on the occasion of Independence Day and will co-chair the first meeting of the “Coalition of the Willing,” to discuss how the United Kingdom can continue to support Ukraine.

A day earlier, the leaders of Denmark, Norway, Finland, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania arrived in Kyiv for a meeting of the Group of Eight Nordic and Baltic countries.
