The group includes private lenders Kapital Bank and PASHA Bank. Banks linked to the family control a significant share of Azerbaijan’s banking-sector assets — more than 40%, according to some estimates. SOCAR: Azerbaijan’s state oil company is also entering Uzbekistan’s retail fuel market and plans to establish a network of filling stations there. At the same time, the company plans to cooperate with BP and Uzbekneftegaz on the Ustyurt field. SOCAR has also faced questions over transparency in the past, including in connection with the Azerbaijani Laundromat scandal.

Azerbaijan’s state oil company is also entering Uzbekistan’s retail fuel market and plans to establish a network of filling stations there. At the same time, the company plans to cooperate with BP and Uzbekneftegaz on the Ustyurt field. SOCAR has also faced questions over transparency in the past, including in connection with the Azerbaijani Laundromat scandal. Other projects: Other businesses entering the Uzbek market include the Matanat-A gypsum plant, Landau STEAM schools, the Sur gold and silver processing plant, Gold Fresh Fruits orchards, the Baku City residential complex and other projects. Some are being implemented as public-private partnerships.

Statements by the two presidents

President Ilham Aliyev said in a statement to the press that relations between the two countries were built “on a very solid foundation, both spiritually and materially”. He said the range of projects under discussion in energy, transport, investment, tourism, mining, automotive manufacturing, agriculture, processing and banking gave the cooperation an “unprecedented character”.

Aliyev said that on every visit he was struck by the rapid development of Tashkent and Uzbekistan as a whole. He said increasing bilateral trade to $1bn was “no longer a dream of the distant future, but a target that can be achieved within a few years”. He also highlighted Mirziyoyev’s particular role in attracting investment to Karabakh and invited him to make a state visit to Azerbaijan at a time convenient to him.

Shavkat Mirziyoyev described Aliyev’s visit as a “historic event”, saying the “Treaty on Eternal Friendship” was evidence of this and that the provisions on strategic partnership and alliance were being backed up by concrete action. In his remarks, he highlighted a threefold increase in bilateral trade over the past five years, the goal of raising it to $1bn, the joint development of the Middle Corridor, and the idea of creating a separate Azerbaijani-Uzbek corridor across the Caspian Sea with a single operator.

Mirziyoyev also said the two countries spoke “with one voice” on the international stage. He described Azerbaijan’s full participation in the consultative meetings of Central Asian heads of state as a historic step and praised Aliyev’s policy of restoring Azerbaijan’s territorial integrity, as well as the meeting in Washington and the declaration signed there.

Hikmet Hajiyev, a representative of the Azerbaijani presidential administration, said before and during the visit that relations between the two countries had reached a new level: moving from strategic partnership to alliance and then to “eternal friendship”. He said this was the first such step in the history of Azerbaijani diplomacy. According to Hajiyev, the “eternal friendship” that had already existed de facto between the two peoples had now been formally enshrined at the political level as well.

World.title: “When the state serves an oligarch, villages and cities empty out.” Video podcast “Protests in Georgia”
World.content:
Video podcast “Protests in Georgia”

The traditional pro-European “Saturday march” in Tbilisi on August 22 was dedicated to Georgian citizens who have left the country in search of work and better opportunities.

Participants said the growing emigration is driven by the policies of the ruling Georgian Dream party, which they say have pushed the country away from the European integration path enshrined in the Constitution.

Many blame the party’s founder and honorary chairman, oligarch Bidzina Ivanishvili, personally.

“Villages and cities are emptying out when the state serves Ivanishvili” — this was the central message of the march, reflected in the slogans and statements by speakers.

Organisers announced that throughout September, the traditional “Saturday marches” will be held in support of Georgian emigrants.

For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. The results of the parliamentary elections held in autumn 2024 are still not recognised by part of Georgian society. Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms. For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years. To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

News in Georgia

World.title: Armenia’s new parliament: balance of power, tools of government and opposition’s dead end
World.content:
Balance of power in Armenia’s new parliament

The parliamentary election results in Armenia have confirmed the continuity of the country’s political system while exposing deep structural contradictions. Political competition has shifted decisively towards intense polarisation. The National Assembly risks turning into little more than a platform for mutual accusations resembling a television talk show, rather than the country’s highest legislative body.

Political analyst Alexander Iskandaryan’s assessment

Continuity of the system, limits of influence and a fragmented opposition

“The new National Assembly has retained the key feature of its predecessor. The Constitution allows the ruling Civil Contract party to make almost any decision on its own, except on issues that require a constitutional majority. The two opposition factions — former president Robert Kocharyan’s Armenia Alliance and businessman Samvel Karapetyan’s Strong Armenia — have access to the media and the parliamentary platform, and can openly express their views and criticise the government. However, they have no real leverage over current policy.

The opposition forces have undergone a reshuffle. In the eighth National Assembly, Kocharyan’s faction held the largest number of seats. In the new parliament, however, it is the smaller of the two opposition factions. They are also unlikely to build a stable coalition or an “umbrella” structure. Because of their different origins and the lack of a practical basis for cooperation, even if they unite, they will not secure 50% of the seats needed to take the initiative. A long-term alliance is impossible. In 35 years of the Third Republic, the opposition has never managed to produce a successful example of unity. The minority is therefore left with little more than keeping the protest movement alive.”

Legitimacy, voters and the government’s narratives

“The ruling party has significant external legitimacy. This includes recognition of the election results by the US, EU, Turkey and Azerbaijan, as well as Russia’s refusal to withhold recognition from Nikol Pashinyan. The ruling force also relies on support from the bureaucracy. In fact, bureaucratic legitimacy has grown stronger. Civil servants clearly understand their ties to the political leadership and recognise the risks that a change of elites could bring.

At the same time, the government’s social legitimacy remains low. Kocharyan won 10% despite his high negative rating, while Karapetyan’s party, hastily assembled over six months with its leader under arrest, won a quarter of the vote despite high turnout. This is a serious signal of the level of public dissatisfaction.

Realising that its support will not grow, the government abandoned any real ideology. Political strategists pragmatically discarded the “high-minded Yerevan intelligentsia”, which would not have voted for the government anyway and would not have gone to the polls. Instead, they focused on their target audience: residents of small towns and villages with lower levels of education, young people and older generations.

To maintain control, the government uses several narratives:

“Peace versus war” — portraying opponents as the “party of war” and frightening voters with the prospect that an opposition victory would lead to a new war in September.

“Democrats versus oligarchs” — selectively labelling businesses. Wealthy entrepreneurs who support the government are simply called “businessmen”, while any affluent opponents are automatically branded “oligarchs”.

“Europe versus Russia” — systematically linking the entire opposition to Moscow. Karapetyan is portrayed this way because he came from Russia, Gagik Tsarukyan because of his ties to Belarus, and Kocharyan as Putin’s personal friend.

Accusing voters of supporting the opposition solely for money. This new level of polarisation has emerged in official statements by the authorities.”

The government’s geopolitical narrative and the opposition’s dead end

“The government’s anti-Russian discourse found fertile ground. These sentiments had been developing for years, and the events of 2020 and 2023 — the war in Karabakh, followed by the exodus of the entire Armenian population from Nagorno-Karabakh — only strengthened them.

At the same time, people across the post-Soviet space have traditionally associated the word “European” with quality and development: European healthcare, European education, European cars and so on. The government has effectively exploited this perception. Direct public support for Pashinyan from senior US officials, up to and including the US president, also played an important role.

The opposition has found itself in a strategic dead end. It cannot openly say “we are pro-Russian” or “we are not pro-Russian”. Unable to reject the geopolitical trend that enjoys broad public support, opposition parties have had to adapt and repeat that they are “also in favour of cooperation with Europe, but for a more carefully calibrated policy”.

Personal attacks instead of alternative programmes

“Instead of substantive work, the opposition is sliding into negative rhetoric and personal attacks: who is corrupt, who got their wife a job, who owns which flat and who once “didn’t even have a washing machine”. Armenian society knows perfectly well how the bureaucratic hierarchy works, so such “exposés” do not work. All these scandals only play into the government’s hands, allowing it to say: “Look who we have to work with in parliament.”

A constructive alternative would be to develop concrete programmes in different areas — healthcare, pensions, the economy, the army and so on. Even if the ruling majority rejects, say, 15 such professional programmes in a row, a systematic effort to offer solutions will eventually resonate with society. For now, trolling has replaced politics.”

Real state priorities: security, energy and meritocracy

“While parliament is busy trolling, the country’s key problems remain unresolved. One of them is security.

It is wrong to call the situation with Azerbaijan peace. You can see what real peace looks like on the border with Georgia, for example: people can cross freely using an ID card, while there are no transport corridors, European observers, military guards or concrete walls, even though 30% of the border remains undelimited. With Baku, however, there is only a state of “no war”. That is far from peace. At the same time, Azerbaijan is rapidly expanding its military capabilities in every sphere, including its air force.

Armenia needs to make foreign policy decisions and find ways to overcome the energy crisis.

Relations with all four neighbours — Russia, Turkey, Azerbaijan and Iran — are in crisis. Meanwhile, the Armenian-American TRIPP “Trump Route” project — a transit route through Armenia — remains little more than a political narrative. At the same time, launching new facilities, such as an AI data centre in Hrazdan, could create an acute electricity shortage that talk of American small modular nuclear reactors alone cannot solve.

In the Armenian city of Hrazdan, Firebird AI’s artificial intelligence factory has begun operations. The facility is the largest AI data centre in the region. The first phase of the project, worth more than $500 million, uses advanced NVIDIA accelerators and server equipment from leading global manufacturers. Some experts believe the factory’s launch could put additional pressure on the country’s energy system. (firebird.ai)

The state needs a competent administration to overcome these challenges.

The country needs to embrace meritocracy, appointing people based on competence rather than loyalty.

Finally, the country’s leadership needs to reconsider its attitude towards citizens.

Nikol Pashinyan is the prime minister of all Armenians, not just the voters of Civil Contract. The claim that people could only have voted against the government in exchange for money is false and toxic. The government now faces a vast array of real problems. Its first task is to recognise the scale of those challenges and start addressing them.

Balance of power in Armenia’s new parliament

World.title: Anea the raccoon’s favourite activity at Tbilisi Zoo – video
World.content:
Anea the raccoon at Tbilisi Zoo

Raccoons love water. You can often see them swimming, wetting their fur or carefully washing their paws. Anea, a resident of Tbilisi Zoo, is no exception.

On hot days, Anea particularly enjoys dipping her paws in water and having a cool shower. So her keepers set up an improvised shower in her enclosure, which, as you can see in the video below, delighted her.

There is a metal container in her enclosure for drinking water, but who says she cannot take a bath in it too? Despite its small size, Anea fits perfectly inside, happily splashes around in the water and uses it to escape the summer heat. After noticing the raccoon’s love of bathing, her keepers have already ordered a bigger “bath”.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status.



The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo.



We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

Anea the raccoon at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Opinion: ‘Moscow’s main fear is that Armenia will choose European Union’
World.content:
Opinion on Russia’s demand for a referendum in Armenia

In recent days, Russia‘s demand for Armenia to hold a referendum on whether the country should remain in the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) or choose the European Union has increasingly been seen as a threat. Experts from the “Armenian Council” think tank made the assessment in an article.

Russia has long demanded such a referendum, including at the highest level. But there are now threats to initiate proceedings concerning Armenia’s membership of the EAEU. Decisions within the bloc require consensus, and Yerevan has the right to veto them.

“Russia’s main phobia is that the situation will deteriorate over time, leading the Armenian people to choose the European Union,” the authors argue.

They stress that this is not only Russia’s “main phobia”, but also its “main misconception”. The analysts believe that even the “economic pressure and blackmail” that Russia began applying to Armenia in May, during the pre-election period, have not changed Armenian public opinion. They cite the results of the parliamentary election on 7 June as evidence: Armenia’s ruling party won, rather than pro-Russian forces.

Ahead of Armenia’s parliamentary election, Russia imposed restrictions on imports of Armenian agricultural products. It also banned imports of flowers, Jermuk mineral water, certain alcoholic drinks and fish products. The authorities justified the measures by citing failures to meet required quality standards. However, Armenian experts and officials viewed the issue in the context of the election campaign. They therefore expected the pressure to end after the election. But that did not happen. Moreover, Russia introduced new restrictions after the election. At the same time, in early June, four EAEU member states called on Armenian authorities to hold a referendum as soon as possible on choosing between the Eurasian bloc and the EU. Yerevan responded that there were currently no grounds for such a vote because Armenia’s European integration process had not yet reached the stage at which citizens could make a choice. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has repeatedly said that Armenia should first obtain EU candidate status or, at the very least, put the issue on the agenda. However, Moscow continues to insist. Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin said the EAEU expects Armenia to hold a referendum by December. Otherwise, the bloc’s leaders would “take this fact into account when determining appropriate further joint steps”. He said a report on the possible consequences of suspending the EAEU Treaty in relation to Armenia would be discussed at the December meeting of the Supreme Eurasian Economic Council.

Armenia’s prime minister spoke about a referendum on EU membership

“No one in Armenia has ever talked about holding a referendum on EAEU membership or an alternative in the form of the EU.

On 9 January 2025, when the Armenian government discussed and approved a bill to launch the EU accession process, Prime Minister Pashinyan said:

“Armenia can begin the process of joining the EU only if a certain number of referendum participants vote ‘yes’ in accordance with the procedure established by the Constitution.”

Senior Armenian officials later repeated this point on various occasions.

The key point is that Armenia will hold a referendum on joining the European Union, not on whether to remain in or leave the EAEU.

This fundamental difference significantly changes the forecasts for the expected outcome. However, if Armenia votes to join the EU, it will inevitably leave the EAEU at some stage of the subsequent process.”

Russia is pushing for a referendum on a different question

“Armenia’s willingness to hold a referendum on EU membership is fundamentally different from what Moscow wants to impose.

Russia is clearly manipulating the situation by demanding a referendum on the EAEU now, when Armenia is at least a decade away from joining the EU.

We need to understand the real reason for this urgency.

The Kremlin understands that if EU membership becomes a genuine possibility, no rational society could vote against it.

Therefore, to keep Armenia in the EAEU and have a chance of stopping its move towards the EU, a referendum must take place as soon as possible, while the prospect of EU membership remains unclear and uncertain.”

Moscow is trying to “beat” Europe by exploiting Armenian businesses’ dependence

“The EAEU mechanisms currently work in favour of Armenian businesses, creating influence and dependence.

At the same time, Armenia is steadily diversifying its economy, reducing that influence and dependence.

The question of whether to remain in the EAEU directly affects many companies with specific interests in Russia. By contrast, EU membership remains a more abstract issue for them for now.

Moscow does not expect to “beat” Europe in economic competition over the next few years or even decades and offer Armenia more attractive conditions. It therefore believes it still has an opportunity to influence the situation now. That is why it is in such a hurry.”

Opinion on Russia’s demand for a referendum in Armenia

World.title: Victorian premier plans to make $2b saving on Suburban Rail Loop
World.content:
Victorian Premier Ben Carroll will announce $2 billion in savings on the first leg of the Suburban Rail Loop (SRL), half of which is yet to be identified.

The SRL East, connecting Cheltenham to Box Hill, a project championed by former premiers Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan, was budgeted at up to $34.5 billion.

But the government will on Tuesday announce about $1 billion worth of "unnecessary additions to the project's scope" will be cut, making the total estimated investment $33.3 billion.

A further $1 billion saving will be identified in an independent technical review, which the government hopes will make the project closer to $32.3 billion.

Until then, further contracts will not be awarded. The Victorian government — which has already signed more than $14 billion worth of contracts — was shortly due to ink contracts to construct the six stations.

The multi-billion-dollar project is designed to create trans-suburban public transport across Melbourne. (Supplied: Infrastructure Victoria)

'Unnecessary' extras to be scrapped

The "unnecessary" extras that will no longer go ahead include underground station interchanges at Box Hill and Glen Waverley. The government will also find "alternative ways to deliver sufficient parking in Glen Waverley".

Clayton will only have one station entrance, rather than two, and Burwood and Cheltenham will lose "complex pedestrian bridges".

The SRL community projects fund — grants for local groups surrounding the planned stations — will come to an end after this round and some future precinct works will be scaled back, the government said.

The Suburban Rail Loop Authority will also be absorbed by the Victorian Infrastructure Delivery Authority to reduce duplication.

"I respect your money," Mr Carroll said in a statement.

" The SRL will be built on time. Today's changes mean it will be built under budget. "

Tunnelling will still begin next month, making the task for Opposition Leader Jess Wilson more challenging if elected in November. She has promised to pause and review the project.

"We don't have the visibility that the premier has," Ms Wilson told radio station 3AW on Monday.

"I say to the premier, why don't we make all of the contracts public so all Victorians can understand what they've been signed up to? And if we have that visibility then we can make that informed decision."

An artist's impression of a future train platform at one of the stations on Melbourne's Suburban Train Loop. (Supplied: Victorian Government)

The government has not yet explained whether cutting these extras will impact the cost-benefit ratio, an analysis to determine whether the benefits to the community outweigh the costs.

Mr Carroll had fuelled speculation he could review contracts and redirect funding to other priorities, such as his preferred project Airport Rail Link, when he took over as leader last month.

"There are other projects that are so much more needed and urgent, and I want to make sure Victorians know I'm governing for every corner of this state," he told 774 Melbourne Radio on Monday.

The state has been under pressure to explain how the $34.5 billion price tag had not grown in line with inflation, given cost blowouts on other taxpayer-funded construction sites.

Victoria is counting on one-third of the budget to be funded by the federal government, which has so far committed $6 billion. The state government hopes another one-third of the cost will be recovered through taxes and charges, known as value capture.

Mr Carroll's cabinet reshuffle also abolished the transport infrastructure and Suburban Rail Loop portfolios.

World.title: 'Life sentence of grief' for Irma Palasics's family after cold case killing
World.content:
A "life sentence of grief" is how the grandson of Canberra woman Irma Palasics has described the effect of her death, during a violent home invasion in 1999.

John Mikita and his family have delivered victim impact statements to the ACT Supreme Court, as it prepares to sentence two Melbourne men over the crime.

"It was not simply the loss of my grandmother," Mr Mikita said.

" It was the destruction of our family, the theft of our future. "

Irma Palasics's grandson John Mikita told the court her death destroyed his family and stole their future. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

Mr Mikita said he also mourned the loss of his grandfather, who was forever changed by the events, and died a few years later.

His mother Elizabeth told of how she has struggled to deal with the trauma and the impact on her family.

"This will continue to torture me beyond the grave," Elizabeth Mikita said.

The two men, Steve Fabriczy and Joseph Vekony, now in their 70s, were found guilty of manslaughter by an ACT Supreme Court jury earlier this year.

They were only identified after a lucky DNA match by police, which linked Fabriczy to the crime scene.

One of Canberra's longest-running cold cases

Both Irma and Gregor Palasics were gagged, bound and beaten during the 1999 home invasion. (Supplied)

The case haunted Canberra for more than two decades.

Irma Palasics and her husband Gregor had been bashed, bound and gagged in their home, as they settled in for the evening.

The thieves ransacked the house, stealing $30,000 from a hidden compartment in the kitchen and fleeing, leaving Irma dead and Gregor injured.

Police drew a blank, and after several years the case turned cold.

But Mr Mikita and his mother Elizabeth made sure nobody forgot, running a campaign with posters, asking 'Who Killed Irma Palasics'.

John and Elizabeth Mikita ran a campaign to identify those responsible for the death of Irma Palasics for years. (ABC News)

They thought someone local must know something.

Inside the Irma Palasics killing Twenty-four years after the killing of a Canberra grandmother, a coffee cup discarded on an east coast road trip leads to the arrest and convictions of her killers.

Police had always kept secret the fact they had two DNA samples from the couple's fridge, one on a milk bottle and one on a water bottle.

It was not linked to Fabriczy until 2019.

But that was not enough to convict him.

Police drew Fabriczy into a fictitious crime syndicate, which eventually led to admissions about being at the scene and the identification of his accomplice.

His lawyer Skye Jerome told the court his later conversations with police were of assistance.

"The information provided by Mr Fabriczy was helpful," Ms Jerome said.

" We ask the court to recognise this with a reduction in sentence. "

She said her client had offered to plead guilty to charges including manslaughter at one point, but the deal fell through.

In 2019 police matched DNA from a milk bottle in the Palasics's fridge to Steve Fabriczy. He was arrested at his Melbourne home in 2023. (Supplied)

Ms Jerome also said Fabriczy had shown the potential to rehabilitate, saying he had spent a significant period "crime free".

But prosecutors reminded the court that Fabriczy had been arrested after working for what he thought was a criminal group.

Prosecutor Trent Hickey said his cooperation was "to help himself".

Fabriczy first identified Vekony as his accomplice before his arrest, and later in interviews with police.

Vekony's DNA was later linked to the scene from more than 20 years before.

During the trial he had been too ill to attend court some days, and watched on from Canberra's jail, hearing the verdict from hospital.

The court heard he has liver cancer, and his days are likely numbered.

Along with the manslaughter charge, Joseph Vekony was also found guilty of an earlier burglary at the Palasics's home in 1998. (Supplied: ACT Policing)

His lawyer Travis Jackson provided the court with material from a doctor about his life expectancy, leading Justice David Mossop to observe "It's fluid, but on any analysis it's short".

Mr Jackson admitted Vekony had shown no remorse and made no acceptance of guilt.

The jury found him guilty not just of manslaughter and other charges from the 1999 burglary, but also of assaulting Mrs Palasics during a burglary at her former home in Red Hill in 1998.

That burglary followed a 1997 robbery of more than $100,000 when the Palasics were out, although nobody has ever been charged with the crime.

Joseph Vekony was also found guilty of assaulting Irma Palasics the year before her death during a burglary at her Red Hill home, pictured. (ABC News: Supplied)

Prosecutor Trent Hickey told the court that in 1999 the pair had gone in with a plan, carrying cable ties, duct tape and a weapon.

"The Palasics were specifically targeted," Mr Hickey said.

He said the sensor lights were disabled, and the pair would have clearly known the couple were home, and that they were in their 70s at the time, while Fabriczy and Vekony were only in their 40s.

Mr Hickey said Mrs Palasics had been subjected to a degrading death, with tape wrapped around her face and neck, leaving her no way to breathe.

"She had no hope of rescuing herself," he said.

Prosecutor Trent Hickey told the court Irma and Gregor Palasics were deliberately targeted. (ABC News: Supplied)

Mr Hickey told the court manslaughter ranged from a "joke gone wrong" to "just short of murder".

He suggested the case fell into the worst category, and deserved the maximum sentence.

But the defence lawyers argued that might not be fair, given the absence of evidence about who carried out the specific actions.

"There is limited evidence about who did what to who," Skye Jerome told the court as she argued that there was also no evidence that serious harm had been intended.

But prosecutor Morgan Howe countered, saying that made no difference.

"That inability to prove who did what does not detract from this falling into the worse case category," Mr Howe said.

World.title: England drop fast bowler Carse after nightclub incident
World.content:
England fast bowler Brydon Carse has been dropped from the squad for the second Test against Pakistan following an investigation into an incident at a club in Derby, the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) says.

"Following a referral from the ECB, the Cricket Regulator has confirmed that they will investigate events on Saturday night in Derby," the ECB said in a statement.

Bazball's complex legacy Brendon McCullum deliberately set out to make England's men's Test team a less complicated team to play cricket for. After four years of Bazball's highs and lows, it leaves a very complicated legacy.

"Brydon Carse will no longer be available for selection for the second men's Test while this investigation is ongoing and the full facts are obtained."

Carse, who did not play in the opening test victory at Headingley, will be replaced by Sonny Baker.

Videos circulated on social media appearing to show the 31-year-old Durham bowler in handcuffs being spoken to by police officers outside a venue.

According to reports, Carse was not arrested, and no charges were brought.

BBC reported that Derbyshire Police confirmed a man in his 30s was arrested, but then de-arrested shortly afterwards.

"A man in his 30s was arrested on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly in Derby city centre on Saturday night, 22 August," a police statement said, according to the BBC.

"However, the man was de-arrested shortly afterwards, having agreed to leave the area."

It has been a busy summer for England's Cricket Regulator, the body set up to investigate matters where there is an allegation of a breach of the ECB's code of conduct.

In June it concluded an investigation into former test captain Ben Stokes and fast bowler Gus Atkinson after a nightclub incident following the first test against New Zealand.

Both were left out of the second test before the Regulator ruled that there was insufficient evidence to establish that any regulatory breach occurred.

The latest investigation comes less than a week after England's returning test captain Joe Root spoke of the players being "really good role models and human beings" following a series of incidents and accusations of a drinking culture.

Controversy has followed England in recent times, with off-field issues during last winter's tours, including Harry Brook being fined £30,000 ($57,200) following an altercation in Wellington, as well as reports of drinking during a mid-Ashes series trip to Noosa.

Stokes eventually announced his retirement from international cricket while Brendon McCullum was sacked as Test coach, with Root confirming that the team had done away with the curfews under new coach Stephen Fleming.

Reuters

World.title: Manu's talks with PNG PM helped lock in Chiefs deal
World.content:
Joey Manu has revealed how a conversation with Papua New Guinea's prime minister helped convince him to return to the NRL and join the Chiefs in 2028.

The two-time premiership winner will be 31 by the time the two-year deal starts, and will arrive with the ability to play fullback, centre or even five-eighth in the club's first year.

Manu toured PNG last month and met with Prime Minister James Marape while there, before signing the deal from France on Sunday.

Manu unveiled as PNG signing The PNG Chiefs confirm Joey Manu will join them, ending the former Roosters star's dream of playing for the All Blacks.

"Talking to the prime minister and how passionate he was about making it not just a PNG team, but a Pacific team and trying to get the Pacific nations behind this team, I think it's going to be special," Manu said.

"I'm a really proud Cook Island and Māori man, and I know my family's real proud back in Tokoroa in New Zealand and also in the Cook Islands too.

"It's a big decision to make, but bringing that positive impact to PNG but also young Pacific Island kids (is big).

"There's so much talent in the Pacific Islands, and rugby league is taking over the islands, so it's really cool to have a Pacific team."

Manu's signing means he follows Jarome Luai, Alex Johnston, Connor Watson, Brian To'o, Zac Lomax and English Test prop Matty Lees as Chiefs signings.

The PNG outfit will officially be able to hit the open market in November, with all eyes on whether Nathan Cleary or Sam Walker will still be available at that point.

Canberra second-rower Hudson Young also shapes as a potential target, given he is yet to agree to terms for an extension at the Raiders.

"Just joining the Chiefs is pretty special in the first year," Manu said.

"With how it can affect the country, that's why I wanted to go there.

"It's got a lot of positives about how passionate the country is, and what we can do for the country and how we can make a positive impact on people's lives."

Manu left the Sydney Roosters for rugby union at the end of 2024, initially to Japan's Toyota Verblitz before moving to Racing 92 in France.

His current deal expires next May, meaning it is possible he could sign for an NRL club for the second half of next season before joining PNG.

"I still keep a close eye on a few games and I get to watch a few games when I can," Manu said.

"You miss certain things when you're watching. I'm just grateful that I get to come back and play.

"I really enjoy playing rugby league, so I'm excited.

"Rugby league is a special game for myself, and to come back and play in the NRL is very special."

AAP

World.title: AI-generated music to be banned from ARIA charts
World.content:
Songs created mostly or entirely by artificial intelligence will be excluded from Australia's official music charts from this Friday, under new rules set down by the recording industry.

However, AI-assisted recordings can still chart if they are substantially human made.

The Australian Recording Industry Association (ARIA), which runs the charts of the most popular music in Australia, has updated its Charts Code of Practice to put it in line with principles put out by the global recording industry.

The updated code excludes music that has used generative AI unless it is "substantially human-made" and "raises no stream or chart manipulation concerns".

The new code lets ARIA remove ineligible recordings, alter chart positions and revoke chart awards. Artists and representatives can contest exclusions.

The change will apply to the charts released on Friday.

Songs created mostly or entirely by AI will be excluded from the ARIA charts from Friday. (Supplied: ARIA)

ARIA chief executive Annabelle Herd said while artists were already using AI tools, music generated wholly by services built on artists' recordings was a different matter altogether.

"This gives everyone who releases music in Australia a clear rule to work to," she said.

" We call on all parties who have a role in deciding the music played and promoted to Australian audiences, particularly radio, to support human artistry and implement similar changes across their own codes. "

AI-generated music storming up the charts

The decision follows scrutiny of Queensland DJ and producer Josh Fawaz's cover of Madonna's Like a Prayer, which became the most-played song on Australian radio and reached number four on two ARIA charts in July.

The track attracted criticism from music figures who believed generative AI had been used.

Fawaz said he used AI "as a tool" and later updated the track listing on Spotify to say the vocals and drums were AI-generated.

ARIA's move draws from the principles published in July by the global body representing the recorded music industry, which said more than 20 official chart programs were adopting rules intended to distinguish human-created recordings from wholly AI-generated material.

An ARIA spokesperson told the ABC that the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI) rules would likely disqualify music with lead vocals or key instrumentals are AI generated, suggesting Fawaz's song may not qualify under the new rules.

IFPI said its concerns included AI models trained on artists' music without authorisation from rights holders.

Loading...

Spotify has taken a different transparency measure when it comes to AI music.

It has pledged to badge AI personas and exclude them from recommendations by default, however that badge applies to just the identity behind an artist profile, not whether AI was used to make a particular recording.

ARIA's move comes amid a wider dispute between creative industries and AI companies, many of which have built their technology using copyrighted material without artists' permission.

The federal government is working on new rules for AI and data centres that would include "strong copyright protections for Australian creators".

World.title: Data centres to use nearly as much power as every NSW and Victorian home by 2036
World.content:
The rush of data centres coming to Australia will consume almost as much power from the electricity grid in a decade as all households in New South Wales and Victoria do today, the latest energy market forecast has found.

The Australian Energy Market Operator considered the expected energy demands of 225 known projects at various stages of development that want to hook up to the national electricity market, saying even with high uncertainty over how many proceed, it now expects a surge in power demand far larger than its estimates even a year ago.

There are 165 data centres already in operation across the national electricity market, which covers all states and territories except Western Australia and the Northern Territory.

Those data centres are consuming about 3 per cent of electricity supplied to the grid, but in just ten years AEMO expects energy-hungry data centres to consume 13 per cent of power demand — even after accounting for the high cancellation rate of projects in the pipeline.

That amounts to 34TWh (terawatt-hours) of electricity from the grid by 2036, almost as much as the 38TWh consumed by every home in NSW and Victoria today.

Just a year ago, AEMO forecast that data centres would not consume that much power until some time after 2050, and even under its "accelerated transition" forecast, estimated data centres would consume about 24TWh by mid-2035.

While the outlook is uncertain, particularly after 2030, AEMO has documented a data centre rush over the past 12 months, with the number of known data centres in development more than doubling since last year from 97 to 225.

There are more than double the number of data centres in development compared to a year ago. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

The vast majority of that data centre growth is expected in NSW and Victoria, with South Australia the next-largest in the national electricity market.

Rules to require data centres to bring renewables with them

The federal government has expressed its concern that the data centre rush, which promises as much as $150 billion in new investment to Australia, would also strain the grid and increase power prices without intervention.

At a Business Council dinner this evening, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will tell business leaders that AI's success depends on ensuring it does not drive up energy bills.

"Australia is in a strong position to attract investment in data centres, but maintaining social licence will be essential," Mr Albanese will say.

"That means ensuring energy bills do not rise, water security is maintained, and locations are appropriate."

The Albanese government expects to settle new rules at a national cabinet meeting on Wednesday that would require data centres to guarantee new renewables supply to cover their energy use, to counteract the forecasted surge in electricity demand.

Albanese to override Queensland on data centres Queensland's rejection of rules tying data centre construction to new renewables projects means the federal government will be forced to legislate to override the state.

Data centres would have to strike power purchase agreements with new renewables projects — which would also enable those projects to secure financing, a roadblock currently holding up several renewables projects in the development pipeline that have been unable to prove customer demand when trying to get a loan.

The Coalition has criticised that approach, saying the federal government is tying an enormous economic opportunity to the renewables transition, which could weaken investment in Australia.

The Queensland government has also opposed the proposal for a renewables guarantee, meaning the federal government will have to legislate "guarantee of origin" laws to override Queensland's refusal to tie data centres to renewables.

Those rules are proposed to apply when data centres seek to connect to the grid.

Wednesday's agreement will also ask states and territories to minimise community impacts, avoiding major developments in "inappropriate locations" near homes, schools and prime land that could be used for housing.

Data centres will also have to use more efficient technologies to minimise water use and meet their own water infrastructure costs.

Alongside the renewables and water requirements, Mr Albanese has said the legislation to be introduced next year will set conditions for AI on copyright, security, safety, and skills development, developed under a single framework within the prime minister's department.

"We must establish conditions to attract investment in frontier AI training, ensuring AI is developed safely, securely, and in ways that respect copyright and provide control and payment to the creative sector," Mr Albanese said.

"Getting this right can ensure Australia is the infrastructure partner for our region, aided by our status as a Five Eyes Partner. It will advance our national sovereignty."

While the government will hope to legislate that quickly so rules are in place in all states and territories, the Greens have indicated they will not simply wave through data centre laws.

"Of course data centres should be using more renewables — but sky-high energy and water usage is just one part of why people are growing increasingly worried about the massive roll-out of AI data centres across our communities," Greens leader Larissa Water said.

"We don't need to roll out the red carpet for tech bros. The government should put a pause on data centres until we get the rules right."

AEMO said the grid's reliability was not yet under threat, but warned that it depended on new supply being delivered "on time" to cover retiring coal facilities and growing electricity demand.

World.title: 500 diphtheria cases recorded as experts warn actual numbers likely higher
World.content:
There have been almost 540 cases of diphtheria across the country so far this year, as experts caution a drop in testing could mean actual numbers of a disease once considered eliminated are much higher.

Federal and state governments continue to work to mitigate the largest outbreak of diphtheria since records began in 1991, with 538 cases recorded primarily in the Northern Territory and Western Australia, as well as in South Australia and Queensland.

That is more than 17 times the previous peak in 2022, when 31 cases were recorded.

The latest report from the Australian Centre for Disease Control (CDC) notes cases peaked between late May and early June this year, and have since declined across affected jurisdictions.

The CDC told the ABC that in the last fortnight 26 cases of diphtheria were reported, compared to almost 80 at the height of the outbreak.

Diphtheria is spreading in Australia and so is misinformation Falsehoods about diphtheria are spreading online as a worsening outbreak of the disease affects Indigenous communities.

However, Megan Campbell, a public health physician and medical adviser at the National Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Organisation (NACCHO), said while the lower case numbers were encouraging, testing rates had not been consistently high across affected areas.

"We're just a little bit cautious about how we interpret that data when we're hearing that testing is quite low in some parts of Australia," Dr Campbell said.

"So we do worry with that drop in numbers that part of that may be due to a lack of testing in some areas."

What is diphtheria?

Diphtheria is a highly contagious and dangerous bacterial infection that can affect the nose, throat, airways or the skin.

It is treated with antibiotics, and vaccination is considered the primary line of defence against the disease.

Diphtheria spreads through respiratory droplets from coughing or sneezing, or direct contact with infected wounds.

Most of the cases this year have spread through skin lesions, with the vast majority among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in outer regional and remote areas.

Diphtheria is a serious infection that can block airways and damage the heart and nerves. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

Professor of epidemiology at Adelaide University, Adrian Esterman, said while the type of diphtheria which mainly affected the skin was generally milder, that could mean it sometimes went undetected or could be mistaken for something else.

"Unfortunately Aboriginal children and adults are prone to skin lesions, especially in crowded housing."

He said if people had scabies or insect bites, that could increase the risk of diphtheria spreading.

Dr Campbell urged people in affected regions to remain vigilant and proactive in being tested.

"We still really want people to be coming in early for testing if they've got skin infections or skin sores or a sore throat," she said.

"Serious illness can occur from diphtheria, and the hospitalisation rate for this outbreak has been around 20 per cent … we really do want people to keep thinking about diphtheria and keep talking to their health professionals and coming in to get their vaccination."

How did this outbreak occur?

Once a leading cause of childhood deaths and historically known as the "strangling angel", diphtheria has been considered largely eliminated in Australia since the 1950s, on the back of routine vaccination use.

Governments and public health experts have attributed this outbreak to a complex cluster of factors, such as waning immunity and housing conditions.

The CDC report said a high proportion of people with diphtheria in 2026 had received at least three valid vaccine doses.

However, CDC epidemiologist Stephanie Williams said vaccine immunity wanes over time and urged people to stay up to date with vaccines and boosters.

"Whilst those antibody levels generally do decline over time, they are still providing some protection [and] when we look at the cases in this outbreak, we have seen mostly mild disease," Dr Williams said.

Public health alert was issued one month after NT diphtheria cases surged Leaked Northern Territory Health data reveals diphtheria case numbers surged in the territory a month before a public health alert was issued.

Experts note the outbreak has disproportionately affected people in lower socio-economic areas, where poor housing conditions and crowding have meant the disease has spread easily.

"What I'm talking about is overcrowded housing, housing that's not been designed or maintained for large families and where there's inadequate health hardware in the home," Dr Campbell said.

"So that's making sure there's enough space, enough beds and bedding, enough towels, consistent water, soap and so on so that people can maintain a healthy living situation."

Can diphtheria be eliminated again?

As the outbreak peaked in May, the federal government announced a multi-million-dollar package to build a surge workforce to administer booster vaccinations and treatments, as well as to procure additional vaccines and antibiotics.

A health department spokesperson said that package now totalled $13 million.

Are your vaccines up to date? Some vaccines need to be updated regularly, especially if you are travelling. Here's what you need to know to ensure you stay protected.

Professor Esterman said he believes Australia can stamp out diphtheria once again but only if meaningful improvements to Aboriginal housing are made.

"We can vaccinate until the cows come home, but it won't help unless they do something about housing and sanitation," he said.

Dr Campbell agreed improving living conditions needed to be a priority.

She said while there were "proactive partnerships" between governments and the community-controlled health sector to respond to the outbreak, more investment was needed in environmental health programs.

A Health Department spokesperson said the government's $13 million package was supporting affected jurisdictions to respond to the outbreak, and included $3 million for NACCHO to deliver community liaison and on-the-ground health supports.

A CDC spokesperson said the public health response was focusing on identifying and treating cases, tracing contacts and providing vaccination and treatment.

"Maintaining strong immunisation uptake remains the best way to prevent severe cases of diphtheria," they said.

"We encourage people in affected areas to continue to follow advice from their local public health authorities and Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Services."

World.title: What does bird flu do to humans and does it have pandemic potential?
World.content:
The detection of a deadly strain of bird flu in seals in Australia may have you wondering about the risk to humans.

Although H5N1 has previously spread to mammals elsewhere in the world, the chance of people catching it is considered low by Australia's Centre for Disease Control (CDC).

Since a dominant new clade, H5N1 2.3.4.4b, emerged in Europe six years ago, there have been just 141 reported cases of H5N1 globally, including 24 deaths.

CDC director-general Zoe Wainer said bird flu rarely transmitted from animals to people and spreading between people was also very rare.

While the current risk of being infected is low, with no human cases in Australia, scientists are studying the potential of the virus to mutate and cause a human pandemic in the future.

Raina MacIntyre, the head of the biosecurity program at the Kirby Institute, said flu viruses mutated rapidly and the H5N1 strain had already changed a lot since it emerged.

A long-nosed fur seal was the first mammal to die from H5N1 bird flu in Australia. (iNaturalist: Greg Smith/Long-nosed fur seal/CC BY-NC 4.0)

That's because the virus has been hopping around a lot of different species beyond birds.

"There's much greater opportunities for mixing between humans and infected birds or animals," Professor MacIntyre said.

So how can you catch H5N1, what are the symptoms and how can you help protect yourself if it takes hold in Australia?

How do humans get bird flu from animals?

So far, most infections have come from close contact with farm animals.

Seventy-one of the H5N1 cases in humans in the past six years have been in the US and mostly among poultry and dairy farm workers.

Only a handful of people in the US have been infected from contact with wild animals or unknown sources.

Professor MacIntyre said there were a couple of ways people could get bird flu from poultry.

"The virus can be transmitted from infected poultry by direct contact or aerosolisation of any poultry components including faeces, respiratory secretions, and contaminated dust in coops, as well," she said.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (US CDC) warns human infection may happen when someone touches the virus and then touches their eyes, nose or mouth.

Dairy cows became a surprise carrier of H5N1 in the US with more than 1,000 herds experiencing outbreaks as of June. (Reuters: Loren Elliott)

Raw milk from infected dairy cows is also thought to be a key transmission risk if workers come into contact with contaminated milk and touch their face or it splashes their eyes.

Veterinary epidemiologist Jason Lombard, from Colorado State University, said how exactly the virus moved from cow-to-cow or people was still unknown.

"Milk, which has the highest concentration of the virus, is believed to be a key component of disease transmission but studies evaluating transmission of disease during milking has not been able to replicate disease transmission," he said.

" Other routes of exposure, including aerosol exposure has been documented but none of the possible modes of transmission has risen to the top as the most likely route. "

Human-to-human transmission of bird flu viruses is rare.

But Professor MacIntyre said there was a report from Indonesia of this happening with a different clade of H5N1 in 2006.

"This occurred in Sumatra in a remote area, where a family cluster of eight cases occurred," she said.

"It was possibly because of the remote location that it died out."

Can you get bird flu from eggs or milk?

There have been no reported cases in the world of humans getting infected with H5N1 from consuming eggs or milk.

Australian CDC advice said it was safe to eat properly handled and cooked meat or eggs.

According to the US CDC, it could be possible to get infected by eating uncooked or undercooked poultry and eggs.

But the watchdog also noted pasteurisation killed bacteria and viruses, including bird flu, in milk.

Although there aren't any examples of people getting bird flu from consuming eggs or milk, there is some evidence animals can be infected.

ViroEpiVet veterinary virologist and epidemiologist Robyn Hall said raw milk consumed by cats appeared to give them the virus.

"What we've seen in the US, where a lot of cats on dairies were dying, is often the virus goes to the brain in cats and there's a very high mortality in that species," she said.

Chickens usually die quickly after being infected with H5N1. (Reuters: Luc Gnago)

What are the symptoms of bird flu in people?

Professor MacIntyre said many people in the US infected with bird flu had conjunctivitis (eye inflammation).

The Australian Centre for Disease Control highlighted several other symptoms, which usually start between one and 10 days of being infected, to watch out for:

fever

coughing

sore throat

runny nose

muscle aches and pains

headache

fatigue

nausea and vomiting

Diarrhoea is also a less common but potential symptom.

Some people who are infected with bird flu could also be asymptomatic and show no obvious signs of infection.

How deadly is bird flu in humans?

Professor MacIntyre said the fatality rate of the 2.3.4.4b clade was much lower than other H5N1 clades in the past.

Out of the 71 cases of H5N1 in the US there has been one death. A second US bird flu death in November was from a different strain, H5N5.

Most of the human cases in the US contracted from poultry and dairy herds have been from two different types of H5N1 2.3.4.4b known as D1.1 and B3.13.

The type of bird flu detected in Australia is known as B3.2 and entered Australia via Antarctic islands.

Are there treatments if you got bird flu?

The US CDC recommends people are treated with an antiviral drug, like baloxavir and oseltamivir, as soon as possible if they show flu symptoms after being exposed to infected birds or animals.

Antivirals are thought to work best within the first two days of symptoms and can reduce some complications from flu.

A study published in Nature Communications earlier this year found mice infected with H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b didn't die when given a dose of baloxavir.

The researchers recommended baloxavir be considered in pandemic planning as a potential frontline therapeutic approach to treatment of humans.

Professor Wainer said Australia had access to antivirals and pandemic influenza vaccines through the National Medical Stockpile as part of preparedness planning.

What should you do about bird flu?

There are a few ways you can keep yourself safe while authorities continue to investigate.

The CDC recommends:

Washing your hands thoroughly before and immediately after handling any bird even if they are healthy

Staying away from sick or dead birds and their surroundings, droppings, body fluids, feathers and eggs

Not allowing pets to touch or eat sick and dead birds

Thoroughly cooking meat and eggs before eating

There is currently no bird flu vaccine for the general public, but Professor MacIntyre urged people to stay up to date with their seasonal flu jab.

That's because it could reduce the chance of someone getting human and bird flus at the same time.

Could bird flu turn into a human pandemic?

The virus would need to mutate further for this bird flu outbreak to turn into a pandemic.

Professor MacIntyre said there were certain mutations in the different types of H5N1 that researchers were looking out for associated with adaptation to mammals.

A particular mutation linked with mammal-to-mammal spread in the US is not present in the strain we know has arrived on Australian shores so far.

Loading...

The strain detected in Australia, the B3.2 genotype, is most closely related to an outbreak on Heard Island and McDonald Islands where thousands of birds and mammals, like southern elephant seals, were killed.

But this genotype, according to a pre-print study on bioRxiv, has several mutations that increased disease severity or aided virus replication in mammals.

Loading Instagram content

Professor Wainer said the risk of a pandemic could increase if someone got both bird flu and seasonal human flu at the same time.

"The viruses could exchange genetic material and this may create a new strain that more easily infects humans," she said.

This is when you could get a pandemic, according to Professor MacIntyre.

"A flu pandemic, if it starts, will start quite suddenly and could start anywhere in the world," she said.

"It's not necessarily going to start in Australia."

Professor Wainer said there were currently no human cases of bird flu in Australia.

"Public health authorities are identifying and monitoring any individuals who may have had close contact with infected birds," she said.

If you find a sick or dead bird take photos or video, if possible, and report it to the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline on 1800 675 888.

World.title: US warns countries to end all financial dealings with Iran or face punishment
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaMiddle East at war US warns countries to end all financial dealings with Iran or face punishment Michael Koziol Updated August 25, 2026 — 5:33am ,first published 4:36am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: The US is issuing deadlines to countries to stop all financial dealings with Iran as part of a new “Operation Economic Outcast” aimed at isolating the Islamic regime in Tehran from the rest of the world. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said President Donald Trump was calling his global counterparts with specific demands regarding their commercial interactions with Iran. If they fail to comply, their institutions face exclusion from the US financial system. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the launch of “Operation Economic Outcast” against Iran. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson “Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone,” Bessent said at a news conference in Washington on Monday (US time). “It is no longer acceptable to operate in the grey spaces of this conflict … Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system. The clock just started ticking.”



In a speech that was heavy on threatening rhetoric, Bessent likened the announcement to an economic “D-Day” – the start of the allied invasion of Nazi-controlled Europe during World War II. But he provided few specifics, and did not unveil any immediate secondary sanctions against other countries or banks. He said it was likely that a major financial institution would be hit with sanctions by the end of the week. The move comes just weeks before Chinese President Xi Jinping is due to meet Donald Trump at the White House. Getty Asked why the US was not imposing secondary sanctions straight away, Bessent said: “We are giving everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behaviour. Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” The US has so far resisted targeting Chinese banks and intermediaries, which process the bulk of Iranian oil sales. Trump has a high-stakes meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House in September.



Bessent suggested Chinese banks would not be immune from sanctions, but said the US preferred to engage in “quiet diplomacy” with other countries. “If they facilitate transactions and are part of the ecosystem that turns Iranian oil into money – into repression – they will be targeted,” he said. Motorcyclists in Tehran pass a billboard depicting Donald Trump with the words: “Great Victory! Strait of Hormuz.” AP Photo/Vahid Salemi Several new measures were announced on Monday, including sanctions against nearly 60 Iran-linked entities, individuals and vessels. That included a procurement scheme for Iran’s ballistic missile development and nuclear research, a malicious cyber group and a network of brokers and vessels transporting Iranian oil, Treasury said.



And the US expanded its list of sectoral sanctions against Iran. Anyone operating in the fields of digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping was now liable to be sanctioned. Related Article Iran sanctions Trump announces ‘economic D-Day’ of Iran sanctions, moving war to new phase Bessent said that every branch of Iran’s Bank Melli – the largest regime-controlled commercial bank – must be “shuttered and dark”. The move signals a transition in the war against Iran from primarily a military conflict to an economic battle where the US will try to use the weight of its financial system to cut Tehran off from all revenue. Friday marks the six-month anniversary of the war, which Trump initially said would last four to six weeks. Although fighting has subsided for most of that time, a peace deal to end the conflict has proved elusive.



Trump pulled back from a threatened military offensive against Iran’s energy infrastructure and bridges, but reinstated a naval blockade on all Iranian ports in July. Meanwhile, the US is trying to establish safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz for the rest of the world’s ships. Shortly before Bessent’s speech, Iranian parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who signed the now-expired memorandum of understanding with the US, said no one was buying America’s “bombast”. “The United States is not in an economic position to further restrict its relations with other countries. Iran’s trading partners, both in the media and through messages sent to us, have made it clear that they don’t take these statements into account anywhere,” Ghalibaf said on X. American analysts drew attention to the gulf between the Trump administration’s rhetoric and the fact that Bessent had not yet announced any significant secondary sanctions.



Aaron David Miller, a former State Department negotiator and Middle East expert, said time would tell if the administration would actually cut off China, Turkey, India, Pakistan and others from the US financial system, initiating a trade war. “This really doesn’t seem to be D-Day,” he said. “This is D-Day plus however many days the administration is going to give all these countries … It’s hard for me to believe, on the eve of Xi’s visit here, that that’s the way they’re going.” Miller said Iran’s enablers were unlikely to comply with US sanctions. And “the Iranians are not going to sit around like some potted plant and just suffer this”, he added. “They’re going to strike back.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: These suburbs may never be the same as Melbourne’s population soars to 10 million
World.content:
Maribyrnong Mayor Mohamed Semra at the derelict Forges site which is earmarked for redevelopment.

We asked planners what Melbourne would look like if it went up or out by 2101. Explore the interactive.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Melbourne Assembly brings together the people, ideas and conversations shaping the future of our city. See all stories .

Sunshine, Dandenong, Broadmeadows and Footscray would see the most significant change in housing density as Melbourne faces “crunch time” finding places to live for its burgeoning population. Projections of what Melbourne could look like in 2101 if urban sprawl is contained show the number of dwellings increasing by almost 2 million, and the city’s west, as far out as Melton, copping the brunt of that change. The suburban centre with the largest increase in dwelling numbers would be Box Hill, rising from 6826 today to 24,427. It is followed by Footscray with 20,117 and Sunshine with 11,689 dwellings. However, if you look at residences per hectare – the true identifier of housing density – Sunshine is pushed to No.1. The impact of not adding this density and allowing sprawl to continue as it has been, would see Melbourne swallow up small rural communities like Toolern Vale, in the outer north-west, and Pearcedale near Tooradin in the south-east. The population and housing projections from Johnny Barnard, founder of the National Forecasting Program at demographic consultancy Informed Decisions (.id), and commissioned by The Age, show where Melbourne will have to build up, or grow out, to fit more than 10 million people.



The data looks at two growth scenarios: a “business as usual” approach where the city continues to sprawl outwards, or a “containment” model where growth occurs within the city’s current official boundary. Developer pressure is mounting for the opening up of Melbourne’s metropolitan frontier, the urban growth boundary, as the size and shape of the city looms as an election issue in November. “We’re at crunch time,” says Barnard, a demographer who has tracked the development of Australian cities for 30 years. “There will be pressure from the property industry to extend the boundary within the next 10 years and probably pressure on whoever forms government after the November election.” In 2002, the state government established the urban growth boundary, as a hard limit on housing expansion which extends around Pakenham, Cranbourne, Lilydale, Epping, Wallan, Melton and Werribee. Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny has promised to resist developer pressure and maintain the urban edge, committing instead to putting 70 per cent of growth in established suburbs, including a network of activity centres, and just 30 per cent in greenfield areas. The Coalition supports more fringe housing but has not declared a position on the boundary.



Either way, Melbourne’s rate of growth – which is higher than that of most developed countries – poses challenges for all levels of government and the city’s residents. If we settle for business as usual, our city’s footprint will swell by almost one third, from 2464 to 3436 square kilometres, gobbling up ever more farmland and green space. If we consolidate, we’ll need to squeeze an extra half a million homes into existing neighbourhoods. Shaping the city is a key topic of The Age and the University of Melbourne’s forum Melbourne Assembly, a three-day event in October bringing together some of the world’s brightest minds in city planning, innovation, education, arts and sport to discuss ideas for the city’s future. On Wednesday, we will explore what a megacity Melbourne – similar to New York City or Istanbul – would look like, and the potential for decentralisation alternatives. A sprawling Melbourne Melton mayor Lara Carli knows only too well what outward growth looks like.



Some 200 new residents arrive every week in this once-tiny country town on the city’s north-western edge, now part of Australia’s fastest growing region, Melbourne’s west. Only last week, the state government opened up yet another suburb, Melton East, earmarked for 12,000 homes and seven schools. But the arrival of new residents has not been matched by the trains, roads and other infrastructure and services that politicians seem to picture when they crow about Melbourne’s liveability. Melton Mayor Lara Carli at Mt Atkinson Estate in Truganina. Joe Armao A high priority is the long-awaited electrification of the Melton line and additional train stations at Thornhill Park and Mount Atkinson (Truganina), a yet-to-be delivered government promise from 2018. The further the city spreads, the wider the gap between where people live and public transport, jobs, major sporting and cultural activities. More than 80 per cent of residents leave Melton every day to go to work. Most drive because public transport is not close or frequent enough. Locals jokingly refer to the freeways in the area as car parks.



“If growth continues in outer metropolitan areas like Melton, infrastructure and services must be delivered alongside that growth, not years later, so communities remain connected, liveable and prosperous for generations to come,” Carli says. Development in cow paddocks is always easier than building in established neighbourhoods – the land is cheaper, construction formulaic and less complex, and cows can’t object. Related Series

City life Melbourne Assembly Melbourne has gobbled up swaths of native grasslands and prime farmland and, especially to the south-east, once bountiful market gardens. Under the “business as usual” growth scenario, the current population in the Kurunjang and Toolern Vale area, within wider Melton, would explode eleven-fold to 130,000 – 88.4 per cent more than would be the case if the boundary remained firm. In the north, the population of already fast-growing Greenvale would triple to 86,225 – 35 per cent greater than if the city were contained. In the south-east, the city would spread to Garfield, past Pakenham. At Pearcedale near Tooradin, the current population of just over 8000 would swell to 61,000 – 83 per cent more than if the city were contained.

World.title: ASX set to edge up, Wall Street weighed down by tech stocks
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to edge up, Wall Street weighed down by tech stocks Stan Choe August 25, 2026 — 5:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks are drifting ahead of a week packed with potentially market-moving events. The areas of the bond market that the US Treasury Department is trying to calm down, meanwhile, eased a bit. The S&P 500 slipped 0.3 per cent and pulled a bit further from its all-time high set earlier this month. The Dow Jones was up 59 points, or 0.1 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite was 0.6 per cent lower. Most stocks rose, but tech giant Nvidia weighed on the market. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to edge higher, with futures at 4.56am AEST pointing to a rise of 10 points, or 0.1 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.5 per cent on Monday. The Australian dollar was trading at US71.47¢. Reporting season continues, with Coles and Woodside Energy among companies set to release results today. Tech stocks led the way downward on Wall Street following big swings through the summer on worries that the frenzy around artificial-intelligence technology sent prices too high and that the huge demand for AI chips won’t be sustainable if they don’t produce enough profits.



Chip giant Nvidia has been a tremendous winner of the AI boom and become Wall Street’s largest and most influential stock because of it. It will deliver its latest quarterly earnings report on Wednesday, which could dictate the next big move for AI-related stocks. Nvidia sank 2.3 per cent and was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500, where the majority of stocks rose. Drops of 6 per cent for Micron Technology and 2 per cent for Broadcom also helped drag the index lower. Related Article Opinion

Big four accountants KPMG’s sackings are just the start of the fallout for the firm Elizabeth Knight Business columnist The other big factor moving stocks recently has been the bond market, where longer-term Treasury yields climbed through the summer on worries about high inflation, huge government debts and other factors. High yields make it more expensive for everyone to borrow, not just the government, and have already been pushing up mortgage rates and hurting the housing industry. The US Treasury Department announced a surprise move last week to increase the size of planned buybacks of Treasurys, which could help contain the rise in yields for 10- and 30-year Treasurys. But analysts warned the move may have only a limited effect because of how small the size of the buybacks are and how they do not fix the fundamental problems of too-high debt for the US government and expensive oil prices because of the war with Iran.



On Monday, the yield of the 10-year Treasury eased to 4.70 per cent from 4.74 per cent late Friday and is back below where it was late Tuesday, before the US Treasury Department made its surprise announcement. Helping to bring yields down on Monday was a drop in oil prices. Brent crude fell 2.3 per cent to $90.55 per barrel. Last month it zigzagged between $72 and $102 as hopes rose and fell that the United States and Iran could reach a deal that would allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again. That was even though the United States announced new sanctions on Iran, which helped drag the value of Iran’s currency to a record low. Despite Monday’s easing of yields, analysts warn the US government’s attempts to influence the bond market could ultimately mean higher pressure on inflation. Inflation already is higher than nearly everyone would like and has been for years. That raises the pressure on the Federal Reserve to raise the federal funds rate, which affects very short-term overnight loans. When the Fed raises that rate, it could help keep a lid on inflation by trying to slow the overall economy and undercutting prices for stocks and other investments.



The Fed’s new chairman, Kevin Warsh, is set to deliver a speech on Friday at an economic symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming. The mountain setting has been the backdrop for major Fed policy announcements in the past, but investors are unsure of what they may get from Warsh this time around. Warsh has insisted that he wants to give financial markets fewer clues about what the Fed will do with interest rates, hoping that markets react more to incoming data about the economy and inflation than to what the Fed is signalling. Related Article Medicine Big pharma’s next $10 billion gamble: Ozempic for your brain But with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announcing his move last week, Warsh now holds the ball, according to economists at Bank of America. Expectations are high among investors for Warsh to talk about inflation and how the Fed could potentially react, and a failure to deliver could lead to bond yields jumping, they said. In stock markets abroad, indexes dipped around much of the world. South Korea’s Kospi fell 3.1 per cent, and Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 1.9 per cent for two of the biggest moves.



Seoul has been home to some of the world’s sharpest swings this summer because it is dominated by two tech titans benefiting from the AI boom, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.
