World.title: The daily choices that actually matter for longevity
World.content:
LifestyleHealth & wellnessAgeing The daily choices that actually matter for longevity Zora Benhamou August 25, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

People often assume that because I’m a gerontologist – a specialist in the science of ageing – I’m trying to live to 120, yet my ambitions are much simpler. I want to be the 80-something woman still travelling, lifting her own suitcase into the overhead locker, opening jars without help and living independently for as long as possible. That’s what healthy ageing looks like to me. When my mother died from breast cancer at 57, I was only 23. Until then, I’d always been interested in health, but mostly from the perspective of looking good. After losing her, it suddenly wasn’t about fitting into a bikini, but understanding why we age and what I could do to protect my future. Your future 80-year-old self is being created by the choices you make today Getty Images This eventually led me to study the science of ageing. What I love about it is that it doesn’t just look at biology. We study the whole picture: our psychology, our relationships, our environment and the experiences we’ve had throughout life. The biggest thing I’ve learnt is that ageing isn’t just about what happens after 60; your future 80-year-old self is being created by the choices you make today. Here’s what really works – and what not to bother with.



You don’t have to lift the heaviest weights One message I hear all the time is that we have to start lifting heavy weights. Don’t get me wrong, I absolutely believe muscle is one of our most important longevity organs. I even call it our “metabolic Spanx” because muscle protects us in so many different ways as we age. But I think we’ve become obsessed with the idea that heavier is always better. If you’ve never lifted weights before, you have painful joints, osteoarthritis or you’re nervous about injuring yourself, being told to deadlift can be enough to put you off exercising altogether. The goal isn’t just to have muscle that looks good, but to have strength so you can carry your shopping, lift your suitcase, get up the stairs and stay independent. Related Article Ageing The eight ‘good’ activities to avoid if you want to age well Older adults I work with rarely tell me they want six-pack abs; they say they don’t want to become a burden on their children. Consistency matters more than chasing the heaviest weight in the gym. My own routine isn’t extreme. Twice a week I do progressive strength training with a personal trainer, who gradually increases the weight until those last few reps feel almost impossible – but never at the expense of good form. I hire a personal trainer because I want somebody watching my form and, as I’ve grown older, I’m keen to ward off injury. But I don’t think everyone has to train that way to build muscle.



Twice a week I also do a high-intensity interval training (HIIT) class with lighter weights, and over the course of the week I make sure I’m ticking off strength, cardio, balance, mobility and flexibility too. Recovery is just as important, so my easier days might be yin yoga, walking or an easy bike ride. The strength-building technique I swear by I wish more people knew about blood-flow-restriction training. You wear specialised bands around your upper arms or thighs, which partially restrict blood flow, while you exercise with much lighter weights than usual. The research is exciting because it shows you can stimulate muscle growth without putting the same stress through your joints. It completely changed the way I exercised when I was diagnosed with hip osteoarthritis in my late 40s, eventually needing both hips replaced at 54. Towards the end everything hurt and I could hardly move, let alone do my favourite workouts. A little movement, I realised, was still far better than none. Using blood flow restriction bands meant I could keep doing gentle leg lifts and tiny squats within a pain-free range of movement. By the time I went in for surgery, I’d slightly increased my muscle percentage despite hardly being able to train properly.



A little movement is far better than none. iStock My father-in-law, who is nearly 90, is a fan. I was never going to persuade him into the gym, but he’ll happily put the bands on while he’s pottering around the house. There is science behind them too. Muscle strength increased in older adults who wore them while walking slowly. I use them myself most days. I see them not as a replacement for physical exercise in fit people, but as a great add-on to those of us who want to lift lighter but get results without risk of injury. They should be used properly, with guidance, and they’re not suitable for everyone. But for older adults, people recovering from surgery or anyone who struggles with heavy lifting, I think they’re one of the most exciting developments I’ve seen. Worry more about falls than wrinkles People think about ageing faces, but I think about falling. Around 90 per cent of osteoporotic (fragility) fractures happen because of falls, and the statistics after a hip fracture are frightening. If you can improve your balance, agility and reaction times, you’re giving yourself a much better chance of avoiding the fall in the first place.



That doesn’t mean everyone needs complicated exercises. Sometimes it’s simply standing on one leg while holding on to the kitchen counter, practising heel-to-toe walking or doing exercises that gently challenge your stability. You don’t need to give up your favourite foods People are constantly asking me if they should cut out gluten, dairy or carbs. Unless you’ve got a medical reason, i.e. you’re coeliac, I don’t believe we should be terrified of food. And for most people gluten is never an issue (though people always think it bloats them.) Personally, I follow what most people would recognise as a Mediterranean-style diet, but I lived in Hong Kong for years and still cook lots of Asian food. I don’t think there’s one perfect way to eat. What matters is variety, eating plenty of whole foods and enjoying your meals. I follow an 80/20 approach. Most of the time I eat well. If I fancy something less nutritious, I eat it. In Portugal and Spain, where I live with my husband, I see all these beautiful summer cocktails and try to tempt myself, but I’ve never really enjoyed alcohol, so I rarely drink. But that’s because I don’t like the taste – not because I think one glass of wine is going to ruin my longevity.



I tape my mouth shut to sleep This one always makes people laugh. I do use mouth tape most nights, as does my husband as he snores – and yes, I admit sometimes I do, too. When I started using mouth tape at night five years ago, I noticed I slept better, and many of the people I work with reported the same thing. Some found it reduced snoring too. I trained as a breathwork instructor and became fascinated by how many of us breathe through our mouths instead of our noses. You don’t have to tape your whole mouth closed, some products are just a small strip in the middle. It’s about encouraging your body to breathe through your nose instead. Training yourself during sleep means that during exercise you recover faster and build better endurance. It’s hard at first but becomes easier over time. Get comfortable doing uncomfortable things One thing I’ve noticed about people who age exceptionally well is that they don’t stop challenging themselves. They keep learning, moving, doing things that feel a little uncomfortable. Whether that’s trying a new hobby or walking into a room full of strangers.



I am learning Portuguese and practise daily, even if it’s only for 10 or 15 minutes. Portuguese is my seventh language that I can hold a simple conversation in, but I’m still learning. You don’t need to travel or live in a foreign country. There are many free apps and programs out there to learn a language. Learning a language lights up multiple areas of the brain, and I think that’s just as important as training your muscles. Relationships are your longevity superpower Editor's pick Sunday Life Wendy Euler had a baby at 46 and moved countries at 57. Now 58, she’s entered the ‘power decades’ The single biggest predictor of healthy ageing isn’t protein or supplements, it’s relationships. One of the most influential studies in ageing – the Harvard Study of Adult Development – has followed people for decades and has found that strong, supportive relationships predict healthy ageing better than almost anything else. I’ve been with my husband for more than 30 years and every year we jokingly ask each other: “Are we signing up for another year?” We laugh, but it’s important. A good relationship reduces stress. A toxic one does exactly the opposite. And if a marriage is making you unhappy, midlife may be the time to get out.



I always tell people to protect their relationships just as much as they protect their muscles. One of the biggest lessons I’ve learnt from studying ageing is that the people around us shape our health more than we realise. I often say you’re the average of the five people you spend the most time with. If they’re positive, active and curious, you’re much more likely to be the same. If they’re heavy drinkers or constantly negative, that rubs off too. As we get older, we naturally become more selective about who we spend time with. I want to be around people who lift me up, not drain my energy. And finally… Will doing all of this make me live longer? None of us knows how long we will live, but for me, it’s about living better. I know that every decision I make today – whether it’s building muscle, sleeping well or nurturing my relationships – is shaping the woman I’ll become decades from now. I’m not trying to become the oldest person in the room, but be a woman in her 80s who is still curious, still travelling and living life to the full. The Telegraph

World.title: The everyday foods a leading gut expert always adds to her supermarket basket
World.content:
Professor Felice Jacka takes us shopping and shares the best foods you can eat for a healthy gut – along with the foods she thinks should be banned.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Professor Felice Jacka beams as we hit the rolled oat section of Woolworths. “Here it is, the gut health epicentre of the supermarket,” she declares. The world-recognised director of the Food and Mood Centre at Deakin University says whole grains such as oats, barley and rye are the best foods you can eat for a healthy gut. She yanks a packet of unstabilised (raw, untreated) oats off the shelf. “These are the least processed; that’s what you want. I put yoghurt on mine for breakfast, maybe honey, and berries. Delicious.” We begin our three-hour fact-finding tour of Woolies Bellarine Village, in Geelong, with a chat near the trolley bay about why we should care about our gut. ‘Eat lots of plants, avoid ultra-processed food, seek out whole grains, legumes and especially eat fermented food.’ Professor Felice Jacka, gut expert The digestive system is increasingly viewed as the body’s health control centre. Around 70 per cent of our immune cells live in the gut, giving it a massive impact on our physical health. Jacka’s landmark research shows that our gut bacteria – collectively known as the microbiome – also act as a crucial bridge between the food we eat and how our brain functions. The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up



Improving our diet can therefore help alleviate clinical depression and other mental disorders, alongside protecting against conditions like cardiovascular disease and cancer. Professor Jacka recommends we more fermented food, such as kimchi, for better gut health. Getty Images “The food we eat is critical to our microbiome and the molecules it produces. These impact our gene expression, metabolic health, stress response system, and particularly our immune system. They affect virtually every aspect of our physical health, as well as mental and brain health,” she says. While the exact science is complicated, what we need to do for a healthy gut is super simple, Jacka says. “Eat lots of different types of plants, avoid ultra-processed food, seek out whole grains and legumes, and especially eat fermented food.” We cover a lot of ground between the leek display at the supermarket’s entrance and the freezer cabinet containing her favourite Mr Chen’s vegetable gyoza at the end: from the fact that “the industrialised food system is the leading cause of illness and death globally”, to her view that two-minute noodles “should be banned”. This is what Professor Jacka, recent recipient of a UNESCO award for her nutrition and brain health research, puts in her supermarket basket. Along with a few things she never would.



Professor Felice Jacka stocks up on healthy snacks. Eddie Jim Snacks We start our gut-boosting tour of the supermarket in the health food section. Aware that these shelves can be crammed with junk food masquerading as nourishment, I am surprised when she pulls out numerous snacky treats. Her crucial rule of thumb is to avoid any products with emulsifiers. These are often listed on nutrition labels as stabilisers, thickeners, Xanthan gum or guar gum. “I never buy anything with emulsifiers in them,” she says. “They are bad for the mucus lining of the gut and therefore disruptive to gut health.” Gravitating towards products with whole grains and nuts, her preferred snacks are: Smooshed Dark Cacao Protein Balls, Wallaby Original Bites (made with nuts, seeds and grains), Munchme nut and seed clusters, Orgran Quinoa and Buckwheat Crispibread crackers and Ceres Organic Brown Rice Cakes. A glimpse into Professor Jacka’s shopping basket, loaded with vegetables and snacks. Eddie Jim



Vegetables We wheel our way into the veg section. All types of plants are a boon to gut health because they are loaded with fibre and polyphenols, excellent sources of “food” for gut bacteria. But Jacka hones in on three main types: Cruciferous vegetables: Broccoli, broccolini and cabbage contain fibres and compounds that strengthen the gut lining, reduce inflammation, and protect against cancer. Having had breast cancer twice, she always includes these in her diet.

Broccoli, broccolini and cabbage contain fibres and compounds that strengthen the gut lining, reduce inflammation, and protect against cancer. Having had breast cancer twice, she always includes these in her diet. Leafy greens: Spinach, lettuce and silverbeet contain a sugar (sulfoquinovose) that fuels good microbes, and are rich in magnesium and other health-essential compounds such as polyphenols.

Spinach, lettuce and silverbeet contain a sugar (sulfoquinovose) that fuels good microbes, and are rich in magnesium and other health-essential compounds such as polyphenols. Alliums: Garlic, onions, and leeks are packed with fructans, a prebiotic fibre that ferments in the gut and feeds good bacteria while keeping “bad” bacteria from taking over. “Some people struggle with alliums, but the emerging evidence suggests that improving the function of your microbiome can help with digestion of these forms of fibre,” she says. Related Recipe collection 40 interesting ways to eat your (leafy) greens Yoghurt Anyone serious about gut health should eat at least one type of fermented food every day, and yoghurt is a good place to start, says Jacka.



She recommends full-fat Greek yoghurt, after scanning the label to check that it contains live cultures. Yoghurt is made by fermenting milk with cultures of beneficial bacteria. These live bacteria, known as probiotics, help balance the gut microbiome and make it easier for us to absorb nutrients. Why Greek? Because Greek yoghurt usually contains fewer carbs and sugar than regular yoghurt because of the way it is processed. Stay away from the added sugars in flavoured yoghurts, Jacka says, and add your own toppings such as berries (“I love frozen, organic berries”). Not many people realise tempeh is a fermented food and Dr Jacka eats it regularly. Eddie Jim Kefir, kombucha and other fermented foods Sponsored by the letter “k”, the roll call of fermented foods containing precious probiotics (live bacteria) includes kimchi, kefir and kombucha, along with sauerkraut, sourdough, tempeh and miso. If yoghurt is an entry-level fermented food, kefir – a thinner, drinkable version – is the next step up because it contains a much more diverse array of bacteria. While yoghurt typically contains two to six bacterial strains, kefir offers anywhere from 30 to 50.

World.title: How Blak sisterhood transformed this playwright’s motherhood journey
World.content:
CultureTheatreStage shows How Blak sisterhood transformed this playwright’s motherhood journey Nicole Elphick August 25, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Playwright Jorjia Gillis feels like she’s about to give birth to two babies this year – the child she’s currently six months pregnant with and the world premiere of her new play Mum Club for Griffin Theatre Company. The comedy stars Stephanie Somerville as Sadie, a Martu woman and new mum who has moved from Western Australia to Sydney. Sadie has no community and is dealing with the aftermath of a traumatic birth, so joins an exclusive inner-west mums’ club that turns out to be heavy on the maternal judgement. Mum Club playwright Jorjia Gillis. Steven Siewert “What I wanted to show as somebody who’d been through it [and] was not shying away from those lonely, tough, raw moments,” Gillis says. “Struggling with breastfeeding, mastitis, feeling ostracised. And also that thing where the mum club, I think everyone had the best intentions, but it felt at times like you were going back to high school.” The play draws heavily on Gillis’s own experiences after giving birth to her first child, a daughter, in 2020, in which she felt the burden of isolation.



“Literally the week after I had her, we had the COVID lockdown, so I was separated from my family, my community. I didn’t know anything about postnatal PTSD or anxiety and had a lot of stuff going on from the birth, so I joined a mum club, which was very heightened because of the COVID world,” Gillis recalls. “I had a lot of funny stories from all these adventures that I tried to go on to meet people, but I just really struggled. I had always thought, ‘oh, maybe I’ll write this, but it’s just so personal’.” Mum Club playwright Jorjia Gillis with castmembers Ruby Teys, Alex Malone, Stephanie Somerville and Zarif. Steven Siewert When Gillis, a recipient of the prestigious Balnaves Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Fellowship at Belvoir in 2020, applied for the 2024 Griffin Studio artist development program she had been planning to pitch a dark psychological thriller. However when it came time for the meeting she found herself spilling forth a completely different concept. “I had no intention of pitching this,” says Gillis. “I thought no one cares about mums on stage, who’s going to watch this? And in the interview they asked me, ‘What are you most excited about?’ and it just came out. After the interview, I went to my family and I was like, ‘Oh well, stuffed that up.’



“Then [Griffin] was like we love it. It started as a one-woman show and I very quickly realised there are so many amazing characters that I wanted to showcase, we need a proper comedic ensemble for this.” Jorjia Gillis was isolated by COVID but found support from other First Nations mums. Steven Siewert The rehearsals for Mum Club have looked a little unusual with lessons on how to swaddle and education on placentas, a necessity given that no one in the cast of five is a mother. The show also took the family-friendly step of programming two babes-in-arms sessions for the play (both of which are sold out). As a Budawang/Yuin woman herself, Gillis’ play examines the experience of Blak motherhood and draws on the real-life support she received from other Indigenous mums. Sadie finds solace in a connection with a character she meets outside of her mothers’ club at the Aboriginal Medical Service in Redfern. “She’s based on four women who really shaped my motherhood experience, who were all Aboriginal. They provided reassurance and went above and beyond to be there for me and my daughter, so it was really important to highlight that. I wanted to show the craziness, the competitiveness and the funniness of a mum club world, but also that difference of how Blak motherhood works.”



Despite having been in the works since she started writing it in 2024, Mum Club arrives on stage at a particularly timely juncture, with mothers’ groups gone rotten having come into the spotlight earlier this year when High School Musical actor Ashley French (formerly Ashley Tisdale) wrote a viral article entitled “Breaking Up With My Toxic Mom Group” for The Cut. In it she detailed feeling excluded from her allegedly celeb-filled mothers’ club. “I can’t remember what draft I was on, but I was like, see, this is what I’m talking about!” says Gillis of the essay. “One of the girls in the play went on a full-blown deep dive and then got up in front of everyone during the first week of rehearsals. She’d researched Mandy Moore’s page, Hilary Duff’s, from all the perspectives, and then gave her take on it. So I think it is in the zeitgeist.” While Mum Club is billed as a “takedown of modern parenting culture”, Gillis says what she’d most like to see change is the impossible expectations and criticism levelled at mothers. “That real pressure that especially new mothers feel, just give them a break. You get so many random people on the street commenting you should be holding your baby like this, they’re crying, they’re cold, they’re this, they’re that. Let’s let a lot of this stuff go. We should be celebrating mums.” Griffin Theatre Company’s Mum Club is at Belvoir St Theatre from August 22 to September 20.

World.title: The six-year learning gap dividing WA students
World.content:
Exclusive NationalWANAPLAN The six-year learning gap dividing WA students Holly Thompson August 25, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

West Australian students who come from advantaged backgrounds could be more than six years ahead of their peers when it comes to learning outcomes, new research suggests. For the first time, researchers have developed a methodology to convert NAPLAN scores into equivalent years of learning to paint a clearer picture of the gap between students from different socioeconomic groups, instead of comparing students by achievement bands or results. Student reading levels across NAPLAN testing. Advantaged students were considered to have parents who had obtained a bachelors degree or higher, while disadvantaged students were those with parents who did not complete school. Parents’ level of education is often used as a proxy for a students’ socioeconomic background in combination with other variables, according to Andres Molina, a senior research fellow at the Centre for International Research on Education Systems.



Molina led the new research, which compiled 17 years’ worth of NAPLAN data to look at how inequalities and gaps in student learning outcomes were behaving over time. “There’s large and persistent learning gaps between advantaged and disadvantaged students,” he said. “Those gaps have been growing over time, and these widening gaps are mostly due to disadvantaged students faring worse over time compared to the average Australian, and that these inequalities are a feature of schooling in all Australian states and territories, including Western Australia.” Molina pulled the figures, released by the Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority, from the reading section of NAPLAN testing between 2023 and 2026 for WA students. He then translated that data into years of learning. Year 3 students from disadvantaged backgrounds were more than two years behind their peers from advantaged backgrounds in 2026’s results.



By year 9, that gap had widened to six years and eight months. “The gaps grow as students progress through school, so the gaps are low in year three, and they tend to increase as students move in their school journey,” Molina said. “There’s theories about why that happens. One is that disadvantage compounds over time, and students who have difficulties mastering certain subjects and skills have a harder time achieving more sophisticated or advanced skills that come later on. “It could also be that there is a greater concentration of disadvantage in secondary schools. A lot of parents make choices and move schools between primary and secondary based on the privilege or the opportunities that those schools will give for further education. “That creates a strong, uneven distribution of students, and that produces a double disadvantage.”



It’s not all bad news Related Article NAPLAN WA’s NAPLAN results for 2026 reveal ‘clearly concerning’ trend Students in general across WA perform at a slightly lower level than the rest of Australia when compared to students of a similar background, according to Molina, but in the past five to six years that situation has changed for disadvantaged students. “They are performing slightly better than the rest of their peers, resulting in actually lower gaps than the ones observed for Australia,” he said. To improve the situation further, Molina said it was important to acknowledge there was an uneven distribution of students, and to examine the policies behind it.



“That ties to funding, to competition between schools for students, the selective entry schools, all those mechanisms help create a divided school system,” he said. “If a school is not the preferred choice of parents, their enrolments reduce, they have high teacher turnover, and they face more difficult conditions. “But changing this takes time and we need to help those schools that are suffering from this situation currently.” Molina said he was an advocate of “full-service schools”, which would mean they operate to provide wraparound services across many other areas that have not been the traditional work of the schools. “So we’re talking about health, wellbeing, food, all sorts of services that help remove the barriers to learning that disadvantaged students face so that these students can come to school ready to learn,” he said.



“We need national and state frameworks, which are supported with long-lasting funding because as soon as the funding is not there, these initiatives die.”

World.title: I don’t want a hotel that’s a ‘home away from home’. I want the opposite
World.content:
InspirationTravel tips Opinion I don’t want a hotel that’s a ‘home away from home’. I want the opposite Lee Tulloch Travel columnist August 25, 2026 — 5:00am

August 25, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Staying a night in a hotel room is transactional. The hotel provides the service, and we pay for it. Which is why small irritations, such as night lights that won’t switch off, incomprehensible shower mechanisms, misbehaving iPads, and housekeepers that don’t turn up, become major annoyances, even to the point of ruining a stay. Claridges in Mayfair, London. Hotel stays are an opportunity to spoil yourself. We guests have played our part in the deal by choosing the hotel and paying the tariff. In return, we expect safety and convenience, at the very least. “Guest” sometimes feels like a stretch, especially if you strike a Fawlty Towers-like situation, or when hotel management seems indifferent to your complaints. But I don’t want to gripe about hotels. I want to give them some love. Because when hotels do things well, they are marvellous.



One of my favourite things in the world is to have a big, comfortable hotel room all to myself, preferably with a fabulous view and a deep bath, and to know there is someone a telephone call away who will handle my luggage and bring me things I need. 



It’s a spoil, even if you’re just in transit. Give me doormen, concierges, porters, housekeepers and room service waiters. Chocolates on the pillow. Fresh flowers. Towel art. Trolleys with breakfast eggs under silver domes. I love the whole performance of it. The more theatrical the better, as long as it’s not a farce. It’s so much more than an Airbnb or short-term rental. Of course, there are circumstances, such as longer stays or family travels, when renting an apartment makes more sense and is more economical than a hotel room. But as a solo traveller, I don’t love staggering around in the dark in unfamiliar streets looking for the right key lock. I like a reception desk. The upkeep of historical hotels is costly, and this is reflected in the tariff. Alamy I’ve stayed in many of the world’s storied hotels, the ones that make the “world’s best” list year after year. And they are truly wonderful, especially those that have been in the hands of the same family or owners for decades. They have thought about what guests need across generations. And they’ve respected their history and invited guests to be part of the story too. Many of these, it is true, are expensive stays. The upkeep of historical hotels is costly, and this is reflected in the tariff. These days, the wealthy who tend to gravitate towards them demand more luxuries than ever. (Frankly, I like my historic hotels a little shabby.)



But if you think of value rather than price, the memory of a night in a plush hotel can be worth more than the room rate. That’s why honeymooners and people celebrating anniversaries splurge on them. If there wasn’t something inherently magical about the experience, no one would bother. Still, a hotel doesn’t have to be expensive to be good. I remember checking into a cheap airport hotel at Haneda, Tokyo, for an overnight layover and falling totally in love with the room. It was minuscule, but it had more amenities than some luxury hotels I’ve stayed in. Pyjamas. Robes. Toothbrush. Eye mask. Face creams. Coffee machine. I couldn’t get over how thoughtful the details were and how inventive they had been in providing everything I needed in such a tiny space, in simple Japanese style. Related Article Opinion

Travel tips Ten basic things even five-star hotels can’t get right Ben Groundwater Travel writer When you arrive in Fiji and the staff have spent time decorating your bed with flowers spelling your name, it’s the same thing. It’s called hospitality. A lot of effort has gone into welcoming and pleasing the guest. It doesn’t matter if a hotel has one or five stars, golden key concierges or a charming guy in a tropical shirt doing the check in, the great hotel experience is not just about a room. It’s about the world the hotel creates and the key you’re given that lets you in.

World.title: US warns countries to end all financial dealings with Iran or face punishment
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaMiddle East at war US warns countries to end all financial dealings with Iran or face punishment Michael Koziol Updated August 25, 2026 — 5:33am ,first published 4:36am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: The US is issuing deadlines to countries to stop all financial dealings with Iran as part of a new “Operation Economic Outcast” aimed at isolating the Islamic regime in Tehran from the rest of the world. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said President Donald Trump was calling his global counterparts with specific demands regarding their commercial interactions with Iran. If they fail to comply, their institutions face exclusion from the US financial system. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced the launch of “Operation Economic Outcast” against Iran. AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson “Our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone,” Bessent said at a news conference in Washington on Monday (US time). “It is no longer acceptable to operate in the grey spaces of this conflict … Any entity that facilitates money laundering on behalf of Iran will be removed from the US dollar system. The clock just started ticking.”



In a speech that was heavy on threatening rhetoric, Bessent likened the announcement to an economic “D-Day” – the start of the allied invasion of Nazi-controlled Europe during World War II. But he provided few specifics, and did not unveil any immediate secondary sanctions against other countries or banks. He said it was likely that a major financial institution would be hit with sanctions by the end of the week. The move comes just weeks before Chinese President Xi Jinping is due to meet Donald Trump at the White House. Getty Asked why the US was not imposing secondary sanctions straight away, Bessent said: “We are giving everyone the opportunity to remedy bad behaviour. Why would I want to blow up the global financial system?” The US has so far resisted targeting Chinese banks and intermediaries, which process the bulk of Iranian oil sales. Trump has a high-stakes meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House in September.



Bessent suggested Chinese banks would not be immune from sanctions, but said the US preferred to engage in “quiet diplomacy” with other countries. “If they facilitate transactions and are part of the ecosystem that turns Iranian oil into money – into repression – they will be targeted,” he said. Motorcyclists in Tehran pass a billboard depicting Donald Trump with the words: “Great Victory! Strait of Hormuz.” AP Photo/Vahid Salemi Several new measures were announced on Monday, including sanctions against nearly 60 Iran-linked entities, individuals and vessels. That included a procurement scheme for Iran’s ballistic missile development and nuclear research, a malicious cyber group and a network of brokers and vessels transporting Iranian oil, Treasury said.



And the US expanded its list of sectoral sanctions against Iran. Anyone operating in the fields of digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping was now liable to be sanctioned. Related Article Iran sanctions Trump announces ‘economic D-Day’ of Iran sanctions, moving war to new phase Bessent said that every branch of Iran’s Bank Melli – the largest regime-controlled commercial bank – must be “shuttered and dark”. The move signals a transition in the war against Iran from primarily a military conflict to an economic battle where the US will try to use the weight of its financial system to cut Tehran off from all revenue. Friday marks the six-month anniversary of the war, which Trump initially said would last four to six weeks. Although fighting has subsided for most of that time, a peace deal to end the conflict has proved elusive.



Trump pulled back from a threatened military offensive against Iran’s energy infrastructure and bridges, but reinstated a naval blockade on all Iranian ports in July. Meanwhile, the US is trying to establish safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz for the rest of the world’s ships. Shortly before Bessent’s speech, Iranian parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who signed the now-expired memorandum of understanding with the US, said no one was buying America’s “bombast”. “The United States is not in an economic position to further restrict its relations with other countries. Iran’s trading partners, both in the media and through messages sent to us, have made it clear that they don’t take these statements into account anywhere,” Ghalibaf said on X. American analysts drew attention to the gulf between the Trump administration’s rhetoric and the fact that Bessent had not yet announced any significant secondary sanctions.



Aaron David Miller, a former State Department negotiator and Middle East expert, said time would tell if the administration would actually cut off China, Turkey, India, Pakistan and others from the US financial system, initiating a trade war. “This really doesn’t seem to be D-Day,” he said. “This is D-Day plus however many days the administration is going to give all these countries … It’s hard for me to believe, on the eve of Xi’s visit here, that that’s the way they’re going.” Miller said Iran’s enablers were unlikely to comply with US sanctions. And “the Iranians are not going to sit around like some potted plant and just suffer this”, he added. “They’re going to strike back.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: These suburbs may never be the same as Melbourne’s population soars to 10 million
World.content:
Maribyrnong Mayor Mohamed Semra at the derelict Forges site which is earmarked for redevelopment.

We asked planners what Melbourne would look like if it went up or out by 2101. Explore the interactive.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Melbourne Assembly brings together the people, ideas and conversations shaping the future of our city. See all stories .

Sunshine, Dandenong, Broadmeadows and Footscray would see the most significant change in housing density as Melbourne faces “crunch time” finding places to live for its burgeoning population. Projections of what Melbourne could look like in 2101 if urban sprawl is contained show the number of dwellings increasing by almost 2 million, and the city’s west, as far out as Melton, copping the brunt of that change. The suburban centre with the largest increase in dwelling numbers would be Box Hill, rising from 6826 today to 24,427. It is followed by Footscray with 20,117 and Sunshine with 11,689 dwellings. However, if you look at residences per hectare – the true identifier of housing density – Sunshine is pushed to No.1. The impact of not adding this density and allowing sprawl to continue as it has been, would see Melbourne swallow up small rural communities like Toolern Vale, in the outer north-west, and Pearcedale near Tooradin in the south-east. The population and housing projections from Johnny Barnard, founder of the National Forecasting Program at demographic consultancy Informed Decisions (.id), and commissioned by The Age, show where Melbourne will have to build up, or grow out, to fit more than 10 million people.



The data looks at two growth scenarios: a “business as usual” approach where the city continues to sprawl outwards, or a “containment” model where growth occurs within the city’s current official boundary. Developer pressure is mounting for the opening up of Melbourne’s metropolitan frontier, the urban growth boundary, as the size and shape of the city looms as an election issue in November. “We’re at crunch time,” says Barnard, a demographer who has tracked the development of Australian cities for 30 years. “There will be pressure from the property industry to extend the boundary within the next 10 years and probably pressure on whoever forms government after the November election.” In 2002, the state government established the urban growth boundary, as a hard limit on housing expansion which extends around Pakenham, Cranbourne, Lilydale, Epping, Wallan, Melton and Werribee. Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny has promised to resist developer pressure and maintain the urban edge, committing instead to putting 70 per cent of growth in established suburbs, including a network of activity centres, and just 30 per cent in greenfield areas. The Coalition supports more fringe housing but has not declared a position on the boundary.



Either way, Melbourne’s rate of growth – which is higher than that of most developed countries – poses challenges for all levels of government and the city’s residents. If we settle for business as usual, our city’s footprint will swell by almost one third, from 2464 to 3436 square kilometres, gobbling up ever more farmland and green space. If we consolidate, we’ll need to squeeze an extra half a million homes into existing neighbourhoods. Shaping the city is a key topic of The Age and the University of Melbourne’s forum Melbourne Assembly, a three-day event in October bringing together some of the world’s brightest minds in city planning, innovation, education, arts and sport to discuss ideas for the city’s future. On Wednesday, we will explore what a megacity Melbourne – similar to New York City or Istanbul – would look like, and the potential for decentralisation alternatives. A sprawling Melbourne Melton mayor Lara Carli knows only too well what outward growth looks like.



Some 200 new residents arrive every week in this once-tiny country town on the city’s north-western edge, now part of Australia’s fastest growing region, Melbourne’s west. Only last week, the state government opened up yet another suburb, Melton East, earmarked for 12,000 homes and seven schools. But the arrival of new residents has not been matched by the trains, roads and other infrastructure and services that politicians seem to picture when they crow about Melbourne’s liveability. Melton Mayor Lara Carli at Mt Atkinson Estate in Truganina. Joe Armao A high priority is the long-awaited electrification of the Melton line and additional train stations at Thornhill Park and Mount Atkinson (Truganina), a yet-to-be delivered government promise from 2018. The further the city spreads, the wider the gap between where people live and public transport, jobs, major sporting and cultural activities. More than 80 per cent of residents leave Melton every day to go to work. Most drive because public transport is not close or frequent enough. Locals jokingly refer to the freeways in the area as car parks.



“If growth continues in outer metropolitan areas like Melton, infrastructure and services must be delivered alongside that growth, not years later, so communities remain connected, liveable and prosperous for generations to come,” Carli says. Development in cow paddocks is always easier than building in established neighbourhoods – the land is cheaper, construction formulaic and less complex, and cows can’t object. Related Series

City life Melbourne Assembly Melbourne has gobbled up swaths of native grasslands and prime farmland and, especially to the south-east, once bountiful market gardens. Under the “business as usual” growth scenario, the current population in the Kurunjang and Toolern Vale area, within wider Melton, would explode eleven-fold to 130,000 – 88.4 per cent more than would be the case if the boundary remained firm. In the north, the population of already fast-growing Greenvale would triple to 86,225 – 35 per cent greater than if the city were contained. In the south-east, the city would spread to Garfield, past Pakenham. At Pearcedale near Tooradin, the current population of just over 8000 would swell to 61,000 – 83 per cent more than if the city were contained.

World.title: ASX set to edge up, Wall Street weighed down by tech stocks
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to edge up, Wall Street weighed down by tech stocks Stan Choe August 25, 2026 — 5:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US stocks are drifting ahead of a week packed with potentially market-moving events. The areas of the bond market that the US Treasury Department is trying to calm down, meanwhile, eased a bit. The S&P 500 slipped 0.3 per cent and pulled a bit further from its all-time high set earlier this month. The Dow Jones was up 59 points, or 0.1 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite was 0.6 per cent lower. Most stocks rose, but tech giant Nvidia weighed on the market. Bloomberg The Australian sharemarket is set to edge higher, with futures at 4.56am AEST pointing to a rise of 10 points, or 0.1 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.5 per cent on Monday. The Australian dollar was trading at US71.47¢. Reporting season continues, with Coles and Woodside Energy among companies set to release results today. Tech stocks led the way downward on Wall Street following big swings through the summer on worries that the frenzy around artificial-intelligence technology sent prices too high and that the huge demand for AI chips won’t be sustainable if they don’t produce enough profits.



Chip giant Nvidia has been a tremendous winner of the AI boom and become Wall Street’s largest and most influential stock because of it. It will deliver its latest quarterly earnings report on Wednesday, which could dictate the next big move for AI-related stocks. Nvidia sank 2.3 per cent and was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500, where the majority of stocks rose. Drops of 6 per cent for Micron Technology and 2 per cent for Broadcom also helped drag the index lower. Related Article Opinion

Big four accountants KPMG’s sackings are just the start of the fallout for the firm Elizabeth Knight Business columnist The other big factor moving stocks recently has been the bond market, where longer-term Treasury yields climbed through the summer on worries about high inflation, huge government debts and other factors. High yields make it more expensive for everyone to borrow, not just the government, and have already been pushing up mortgage rates and hurting the housing industry. The US Treasury Department announced a surprise move last week to increase the size of planned buybacks of Treasurys, which could help contain the rise in yields for 10- and 30-year Treasurys. But analysts warned the move may have only a limited effect because of how small the size of the buybacks are and how they do not fix the fundamental problems of too-high debt for the US government and expensive oil prices because of the war with Iran.



On Monday, the yield of the 10-year Treasury eased to 4.70 per cent from 4.74 per cent late Friday and is back below where it was late Tuesday, before the US Treasury Department made its surprise announcement. Helping to bring yields down on Monday was a drop in oil prices. Brent crude fell 2.3 per cent to $90.55 per barrel. Last month it zigzagged between $72 and $102 as hopes rose and fell that the United States and Iran could reach a deal that would allow oil tankers to freely exit the Persian Gulf again. That was even though the United States announced new sanctions on Iran, which helped drag the value of Iran’s currency to a record low. Despite Monday’s easing of yields, analysts warn the US government’s attempts to influence the bond market could ultimately mean higher pressure on inflation. Inflation already is higher than nearly everyone would like and has been for years. That raises the pressure on the Federal Reserve to raise the federal funds rate, which affects very short-term overnight loans. When the Fed raises that rate, it could help keep a lid on inflation by trying to slow the overall economy and undercutting prices for stocks and other investments.



The Fed’s new chairman, Kevin Warsh, is set to deliver a speech on Friday at an economic symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming. The mountain setting has been the backdrop for major Fed policy announcements in the past, but investors are unsure of what they may get from Warsh this time around. Warsh has insisted that he wants to give financial markets fewer clues about what the Fed will do with interest rates, hoping that markets react more to incoming data about the economy and inflation than to what the Fed is signalling. Related Article Medicine Big pharma’s next $10 billion gamble: Ozempic for your brain But with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announcing his move last week, Warsh now holds the ball, according to economists at Bank of America. Expectations are high among investors for Warsh to talk about inflation and how the Fed could potentially react, and a failure to deliver could lead to bond yields jumping, they said. In stock markets abroad, indexes dipped around much of the world. South Korea’s Kospi fell 3.1 per cent, and Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dropped 1.9 per cent for two of the biggest moves.



Seoul has been home to some of the world’s sharpest swings this summer because it is dominated by two tech titans benefiting from the AI boom, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: The daily choices that actually matter for longevity
World.content:
LifestyleHealth & wellnessAgeing The daily choices that actually matter for longevity Zora Benhamou August 25, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

People often assume that because I’m a gerontologist – a specialist in the science of ageing – I’m trying to live to 120, yet my ambitions are much simpler. I want to be the 80-something woman still travelling, lifting her own suitcase into the overhead locker, opening jars without help and living independently for as long as possible. That’s what healthy ageing looks like to me. When my mother died from breast cancer at 57, I was only 23. Until then, I’d always been interested in health, but mostly from the perspective of looking good. After losing her, it suddenly wasn’t about fitting into a bikini, but understanding why we age and what I could do to protect my future. Your future 80-year-old self is being created by the choices you make today Getty Images This eventually led me to study the science of ageing. What I love about it is that it doesn’t just look at biology. We study the whole picture: our psychology, our relationships, our environment and the experiences we’ve had throughout life. The biggest thing I’ve learnt is that ageing isn’t just about what happens after 60; your future 80-year-old self is being created by the choices you make today. Here’s what really works – and what not to bother with.



You don’t have to lift the heaviest weights One message I hear all the time is that we have to start lifting heavy weights. Don’t get me wrong, I absolutely believe muscle is one of our most important longevity organs. I even call it our “metabolic Spanx” because muscle protects us in so many different ways as we age. But I think we’ve become obsessed with the idea that heavier is always better. If you’ve never lifted weights before, you have painful joints, osteoarthritis or you’re nervous about injuring yourself, being told to deadlift can be enough to put you off exercising altogether. The goal isn’t just to have muscle that looks good, but to have strength so you can carry your shopping, lift your suitcase, get up the stairs and stay independent. Related Article Ageing The eight ‘good’ activities to avoid if you want to age well Older adults I work with rarely tell me they want six-pack abs; they say they don’t want to become a burden on their children. Consistency matters more than chasing the heaviest weight in the gym. My own routine isn’t extreme. Twice a week I do progressive strength training with a personal trainer, who gradually increases the weight until those last few reps feel almost impossible – but never at the expense of good form. I hire a personal trainer because I want somebody watching my form and, as I’ve grown older, I’m keen to ward off injury. But I don’t think everyone has to train that way to build muscle.



Twice a week I also do a high-intensity interval training (HIIT) class with lighter weights, and over the course of the week I make sure I’m ticking off strength, cardio, balance, mobility and flexibility too. Recovery is just as important, so my easier days might be yin yoga, walking or an easy bike ride. The strength-building technique I swear by I wish more people knew about blood-flow-restriction training. You wear specialised bands around your upper arms or thighs, which partially restrict blood flow, while you exercise with much lighter weights than usual. The research is exciting because it shows you can stimulate muscle growth without putting the same stress through your joints. It completely changed the way I exercised when I was diagnosed with hip osteoarthritis in my late 40s, eventually needing both hips replaced at 54. Towards the end everything hurt and I could hardly move, let alone do my favourite workouts. A little movement, I realised, was still far better than none. Using blood flow restriction bands meant I could keep doing gentle leg lifts and tiny squats within a pain-free range of movement. By the time I went in for surgery, I’d slightly increased my muscle percentage despite hardly being able to train properly.



A little movement is far better than none. iStock My father-in-law, who is nearly 90, is a fan. I was never going to persuade him into the gym, but he’ll happily put the bands on while he’s pottering around the house. There is science behind them too. Muscle strength increased in older adults who wore them while walking slowly. I use them myself most days. I see them not as a replacement for physical exercise in fit people, but as a great add-on to those of us who want to lift lighter but get results without risk of injury. They should be used properly, with guidance, and they’re not suitable for everyone. But for older adults, people recovering from surgery or anyone who struggles with heavy lifting, I think they’re one of the most exciting developments I’ve seen. Worry more about falls than wrinkles People think about ageing faces, but I think about falling. Around 90 per cent of osteoporotic (fragility) fractures happen because of falls, and the statistics after a hip fracture are frightening. If you can improve your balance, agility and reaction times, you’re giving yourself a much better chance of avoiding the fall in the first place.



That doesn’t mean everyone needs complicated exercises. Sometimes it’s simply standing on one leg while holding on to the kitchen counter, practising heel-to-toe walking or doing exercises that gently challenge your stability. You don’t need to give up your favourite foods People are constantly asking me if they should cut out gluten, dairy or carbs. Unless you’ve got a medical reason, i.e. you’re coeliac, I don’t believe we should be terrified of food. And for most people gluten is never an issue (though people always think it bloats them.) Personally, I follow what most people would recognise as a Mediterranean-style diet, but I lived in Hong Kong for years and still cook lots of Asian food. I don’t think there’s one perfect way to eat. What matters is variety, eating plenty of whole foods and enjoying your meals. I follow an 80/20 approach. Most of the time I eat well. If I fancy something less nutritious, I eat it. In Portugal and Spain, where I live with my husband, I see all these beautiful summer cocktails and try to tempt myself, but I’ve never really enjoyed alcohol, so I rarely drink. But that’s because I don’t like the taste – not because I think one glass of wine is going to ruin my longevity.



I tape my mouth shut to sleep This one always makes people laugh. I do use mouth tape most nights, as does my husband as he snores – and yes, I admit sometimes I do, too. When I started using mouth tape at night five years ago, I noticed I slept better, and many of the people I work with reported the same thing. Some found it reduced snoring too. I trained as a breathwork instructor and became fascinated by how many of us breathe through our mouths instead of our noses. You don’t have to tape your whole mouth closed, some products are just a small strip in the middle. It’s about encouraging your body to breathe through your nose instead. Training yourself during sleep means that during exercise you recover faster and build better endurance. It’s hard at first but becomes easier over time. Get comfortable doing uncomfortable things One thing I’ve noticed about people who age exceptionally well is that they don’t stop challenging themselves. They keep learning, moving, doing things that feel a little uncomfortable. Whether that’s trying a new hobby or walking into a room full of strangers.



I am learning Portuguese and practise daily, even if it’s only for 10 or 15 minutes. Portuguese is my seventh language that I can hold a simple conversation in, but I’m still learning. You don’t need to travel or live in a foreign country. There are many free apps and programs out there to learn a language. Learning a language lights up multiple areas of the brain, and I think that’s just as important as training your muscles. Relationships are your longevity superpower Editor's pick Sunday Life Wendy Euler had a baby at 46 and moved countries at 57. Now 58, she’s entered the ‘power decades’ The single biggest predictor of healthy ageing isn’t protein or supplements, it’s relationships. One of the most influential studies in ageing – the Harvard Study of Adult Development – has followed people for decades and has found that strong, supportive relationships predict healthy ageing better than almost anything else. I’ve been with my husband for more than 30 years and every year we jokingly ask each other: “Are we signing up for another year?” We laugh, but it’s important. A good relationship reduces stress. A toxic one does exactly the opposite. And if a marriage is making you unhappy, midlife may be the time to get out.



I always tell people to protect their relationships just as much as they protect their muscles. One of the biggest lessons I’ve learnt from studying ageing is that the people around us shape our health more than we realise. I often say you’re the average of the five people you spend the most time with. If they’re positive, active and curious, you’re much more likely to be the same. If they’re heavy drinkers or constantly negative, that rubs off too. As we get older, we naturally become more selective about who we spend time with. I want to be around people who lift me up, not drain my energy. And finally… Will doing all of this make me live longer? None of us knows how long we will live, but for me, it’s about living better. I know that every decision I make today – whether it’s building muscle, sleeping well or nurturing my relationships – is shaping the woman I’ll become decades from now. I’m not trying to become the oldest person in the room, but be a woman in her 80s who is still curious, still travelling and living life to the full. The Telegraph
