World.title: The everyday foods a leading gut expert always adds to her supermarket basket
World.content:
Professor Felice Jacka takes us shopping and shares the best foods you can eat for a healthy gut – along with the foods she thinks should be banned.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Professor Felice Jacka beams as we hit the rolled oat section of Woolworths. “Here it is, the gut health epicentre of the supermarket,” she declares. The world-recognised director of the Food and Mood Centre at Deakin University says whole grains such as oats, barley and rye are the best foods you can eat for a healthy gut. She yanks a packet of unstabilised (raw, untreated) oats off the shelf. “These are the least processed; that’s what you want. I put yoghurt on mine for breakfast, maybe honey, and berries. Delicious.” We begin our three-hour fact-finding tour of Woolies Bellarine Village, in Geelong, with a chat near the trolley bay about why we should care about our gut. ‘Eat lots of plants, avoid ultra-processed food, seek out whole grains, legumes and especially eat fermented food.’ Professor Felice Jacka, gut expert The digestive system is increasingly viewed as the body’s health control centre. Around 70 per cent of our immune cells live in the gut, giving it a massive impact on our physical health. Jacka’s landmark research shows that our gut bacteria – collectively known as the microbiome – also act as a crucial bridge between the food we eat and how our brain functions. The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up



Improving our diet can therefore help alleviate clinical depression and other mental disorders, alongside protecting against conditions like cardiovascular disease and cancer. Professor Jacka recommends we more fermented food, such as kimchi, for better gut health. Getty Images “The food we eat is critical to our microbiome and the molecules it produces. These impact our gene expression, metabolic health, stress response system, and particularly our immune system. They affect virtually every aspect of our physical health, as well as mental and brain health,” she says. While the exact science is complicated, what we need to do for a healthy gut is super simple, Jacka says. “Eat lots of different types of plants, avoid ultra-processed food, seek out whole grains and legumes, and especially eat fermented food.” We cover a lot of ground between the leek display at the supermarket’s entrance and the freezer cabinet containing her favourite Mr Chen’s vegetable gyoza at the end: from the fact that “the industrialised food system is the leading cause of illness and death globally”, to her view that two-minute noodles “should be banned”. This is what Professor Jacka, recent recipient of a UNESCO award for her nutrition and brain health research, puts in her supermarket basket. Along with a few things she never would.



Professor Felice Jacka stocks up on healthy snacks. Eddie Jim Snacks We start our gut-boosting tour of the supermarket in the health food section. Aware that these shelves can be crammed with junk food masquerading as nourishment, I am surprised when she pulls out numerous snacky treats. Her crucial rule of thumb is to avoid any products with emulsifiers. These are often listed on nutrition labels as stabilisers, thickeners, Xanthan gum or guar gum. “I never buy anything with emulsifiers in them,” she says. “They are bad for the mucus lining of the gut and therefore disruptive to gut health.” Gravitating towards products with whole grains and nuts, her preferred snacks are: Smooshed Dark Cacao Protein Balls, Wallaby Original Bites (made with nuts, seeds and grains), Munchme nut and seed clusters, Orgran Quinoa and Buckwheat Crispibread crackers and Ceres Organic Brown Rice Cakes. A glimpse into Professor Jacka’s shopping basket, loaded with vegetables and snacks. Eddie Jim



Vegetables We wheel our way into the veg section. All types of plants are a boon to gut health because they are loaded with fibre and polyphenols, excellent sources of “food” for gut bacteria. But Jacka hones in on three main types: Cruciferous vegetables: Broccoli, broccolini and cabbage contain fibres and compounds that strengthen the gut lining, reduce inflammation, and protect against cancer. Having had breast cancer twice, she always includes these in her diet.

Broccoli, broccolini and cabbage contain fibres and compounds that strengthen the gut lining, reduce inflammation, and protect against cancer. Having had breast cancer twice, she always includes these in her diet. Leafy greens: Spinach, lettuce and silverbeet contain a sugar (sulfoquinovose) that fuels good microbes, and are rich in magnesium and other health-essential compounds such as polyphenols.

Spinach, lettuce and silverbeet contain a sugar (sulfoquinovose) that fuels good microbes, and are rich in magnesium and other health-essential compounds such as polyphenols. Alliums: Garlic, onions, and leeks are packed with fructans, a prebiotic fibre that ferments in the gut and feeds good bacteria while keeping “bad” bacteria from taking over. “Some people struggle with alliums, but the emerging evidence suggests that improving the function of your microbiome can help with digestion of these forms of fibre,” she says. Related Recipe collection 40 interesting ways to eat your (leafy) greens Yoghurt Anyone serious about gut health should eat at least one type of fermented food every day, and yoghurt is a good place to start, says Jacka.



She recommends full-fat Greek yoghurt, after scanning the label to check that it contains live cultures. Yoghurt is made by fermenting milk with cultures of beneficial bacteria. These live bacteria, known as probiotics, help balance the gut microbiome and make it easier for us to absorb nutrients. Why Greek? Because Greek yoghurt usually contains fewer carbs and sugar than regular yoghurt because of the way it is processed. Stay away from the added sugars in flavoured yoghurts, Jacka says, and add your own toppings such as berries (“I love frozen, organic berries”). Not many people realise tempeh is a fermented food and Dr Jacka eats it regularly. Eddie Jim Kefir, kombucha and other fermented foods Sponsored by the letter “k”, the roll call of fermented foods containing precious probiotics (live bacteria) includes kimchi, kefir and kombucha, along with sauerkraut, sourdough, tempeh and miso. If yoghurt is an entry-level fermented food, kefir – a thinner, drinkable version – is the next step up because it contains a much more diverse array of bacteria. While yoghurt typically contains two to six bacterial strains, kefir offers anywhere from 30 to 50.

World.title: How Blak sisterhood transformed this playwright’s motherhood journey
World.content:
CultureTheatreStage shows How Blak sisterhood transformed this playwright’s motherhood journey Nicole Elphick August 25, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Playwright Jorjia Gillis feels like she’s about to give birth to two babies this year – the child she’s currently six months pregnant with and the world premiere of her new play Mum Club for Griffin Theatre Company. The comedy stars Stephanie Somerville as Sadie, a Martu woman and new mum who has moved from Western Australia to Sydney. Sadie has no community and is dealing with the aftermath of a traumatic birth, so joins an exclusive inner-west mums’ club that turns out to be heavy on the maternal judgement. Mum Club playwright Jorjia Gillis. Steven Siewert “What I wanted to show as somebody who’d been through it [and] was not shying away from those lonely, tough, raw moments,” Gillis says. “Struggling with breastfeeding, mastitis, feeling ostracised. And also that thing where the mum club, I think everyone had the best intentions, but it felt at times like you were going back to high school.” The play draws heavily on Gillis’s own experiences after giving birth to her first child, a daughter, in 2020, in which she felt the burden of isolation.



“Literally the week after I had her, we had the COVID lockdown, so I was separated from my family, my community. I didn’t know anything about postnatal PTSD or anxiety and had a lot of stuff going on from the birth, so I joined a mum club, which was very heightened because of the COVID world,” Gillis recalls. “I had a lot of funny stories from all these adventures that I tried to go on to meet people, but I just really struggled. I had always thought, ‘oh, maybe I’ll write this, but it’s just so personal’.” Mum Club playwright Jorjia Gillis with castmembers Ruby Teys, Alex Malone, Stephanie Somerville and Zarif. Steven Siewert When Gillis, a recipient of the prestigious Balnaves Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Fellowship at Belvoir in 2020, applied for the 2024 Griffin Studio artist development program she had been planning to pitch a dark psychological thriller. However when it came time for the meeting she found herself spilling forth a completely different concept. “I had no intention of pitching this,” says Gillis. “I thought no one cares about mums on stage, who’s going to watch this? And in the interview they asked me, ‘What are you most excited about?’ and it just came out. After the interview, I went to my family and I was like, ‘Oh well, stuffed that up.’



“Then [Griffin] was like we love it. It started as a one-woman show and I very quickly realised there are so many amazing characters that I wanted to showcase, we need a proper comedic ensemble for this.” Jorjia Gillis was isolated by COVID but found support from other First Nations mums. Steven Siewert The rehearsals for Mum Club have looked a little unusual with lessons on how to swaddle and education on placentas, a necessity given that no one in the cast of five is a mother. The show also took the family-friendly step of programming two babes-in-arms sessions for the play (both of which are sold out). As a Budawang/Yuin woman herself, Gillis’ play examines the experience of Blak motherhood and draws on the real-life support she received from other Indigenous mums. Sadie finds solace in a connection with a character she meets outside of her mothers’ club at the Aboriginal Medical Service in Redfern. “She’s based on four women who really shaped my motherhood experience, who were all Aboriginal. They provided reassurance and went above and beyond to be there for me and my daughter, so it was really important to highlight that. I wanted to show the craziness, the competitiveness and the funniness of a mum club world, but also that difference of how Blak motherhood works.”



Despite having been in the works since she started writing it in 2024, Mum Club arrives on stage at a particularly timely juncture, with mothers’ groups gone rotten having come into the spotlight earlier this year when High School Musical actor Ashley French (formerly Ashley Tisdale) wrote a viral article entitled “Breaking Up With My Toxic Mom Group” for The Cut. In it she detailed feeling excluded from her allegedly celeb-filled mothers’ club. “I can’t remember what draft I was on, but I was like, see, this is what I’m talking about!” says Gillis of the essay. “One of the girls in the play went on a full-blown deep dive and then got up in front of everyone during the first week of rehearsals. She’d researched Mandy Moore’s page, Hilary Duff’s, from all the perspectives, and then gave her take on it. So I think it is in the zeitgeist.” While Mum Club is billed as a “takedown of modern parenting culture”, Gillis says what she’d most like to see change is the impossible expectations and criticism levelled at mothers. “That real pressure that especially new mothers feel, just give them a break. You get so many random people on the street commenting you should be holding your baby like this, they’re crying, they’re cold, they’re this, they’re that. Let’s let a lot of this stuff go. We should be celebrating mums.” Griffin Theatre Company’s Mum Club is at Belvoir St Theatre from August 22 to September 20.

World.title: The six-year learning gap dividing WA students
World.content:
Exclusive NationalWANAPLAN The six-year learning gap dividing WA students Holly Thompson August 25, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

West Australian students who come from advantaged backgrounds could be more than six years ahead of their peers when it comes to learning outcomes, new research suggests. For the first time, researchers have developed a methodology to convert NAPLAN scores into equivalent years of learning to paint a clearer picture of the gap between students from different socioeconomic groups, instead of comparing students by achievement bands or results. Student reading levels across NAPLAN testing. Advantaged students were considered to have parents who had obtained a bachelors degree or higher, while disadvantaged students were those with parents who did not complete school. Parents’ level of education is often used as a proxy for a students’ socioeconomic background in combination with other variables, according to Andres Molina, a senior research fellow at the Centre for International Research on Education Systems.



Molina led the new research, which compiled 17 years’ worth of NAPLAN data to look at how inequalities and gaps in student learning outcomes were behaving over time. “There’s large and persistent learning gaps between advantaged and disadvantaged students,” he said. “Those gaps have been growing over time, and these widening gaps are mostly due to disadvantaged students faring worse over time compared to the average Australian, and that these inequalities are a feature of schooling in all Australian states and territories, including Western Australia.” Molina pulled the figures, released by the Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority, from the reading section of NAPLAN testing between 2023 and 2026 for WA students. He then translated that data into years of learning. Year 3 students from disadvantaged backgrounds were more than two years behind their peers from advantaged backgrounds in 2026’s results.



By year 9, that gap had widened to six years and eight months. “The gaps grow as students progress through school, so the gaps are low in year three, and they tend to increase as students move in their school journey,” Molina said. “There’s theories about why that happens. One is that disadvantage compounds over time, and students who have difficulties mastering certain subjects and skills have a harder time achieving more sophisticated or advanced skills that come later on. “It could also be that there is a greater concentration of disadvantage in secondary schools. A lot of parents make choices and move schools between primary and secondary based on the privilege or the opportunities that those schools will give for further education. “That creates a strong, uneven distribution of students, and that produces a double disadvantage.”



It’s not all bad news Related Article NAPLAN WA’s NAPLAN results for 2026 reveal ‘clearly concerning’ trend Students in general across WA perform at a slightly lower level than the rest of Australia when compared to students of a similar background, according to Molina, but in the past five to six years that situation has changed for disadvantaged students. “They are performing slightly better than the rest of their peers, resulting in actually lower gaps than the ones observed for Australia,” he said. To improve the situation further, Molina said it was important to acknowledge there was an uneven distribution of students, and to examine the policies behind it.



“That ties to funding, to competition between schools for students, the selective entry schools, all those mechanisms help create a divided school system,” he said. “If a school is not the preferred choice of parents, their enrolments reduce, they have high teacher turnover, and they face more difficult conditions. “But changing this takes time and we need to help those schools that are suffering from this situation currently.” Molina said he was an advocate of “full-service schools”, which would mean they operate to provide wraparound services across many other areas that have not been the traditional work of the schools. “So we’re talking about health, wellbeing, food, all sorts of services that help remove the barriers to learning that disadvantaged students face so that these students can come to school ready to learn,” he said.



“We need national and state frameworks, which are supported with long-lasting funding because as soon as the funding is not there, these initiatives die.”

World.title: I don’t want a hotel that’s a ‘home away from home’. I want the opposite
World.content:
InspirationTravel tips Opinion I don’t want a hotel that’s a ‘home away from home’. I want the opposite Lee Tulloch Travel columnist August 25, 2026 — 5:00am

August 25, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Staying a night in a hotel room is transactional. The hotel provides the service, and we pay for it. Which is why small irritations, such as night lights that won’t switch off, incomprehensible shower mechanisms, misbehaving iPads, and housekeepers that don’t turn up, become major annoyances, even to the point of ruining a stay. Claridges in Mayfair, London. Hotel stays are an opportunity to spoil yourself. We guests have played our part in the deal by choosing the hotel and paying the tariff. In return, we expect safety and convenience, at the very least. “Guest” sometimes feels like a stretch, especially if you strike a Fawlty Towers-like situation, or when hotel management seems indifferent to your complaints. But I don’t want to gripe about hotels. I want to give them some love. Because when hotels do things well, they are marvellous.



One of my favourite things in the world is to have a big, comfortable hotel room all to myself, preferably with a fabulous view and a deep bath, and to know there is someone a telephone call away who will handle my luggage and bring me things I need. 



It’s a spoil, even if you’re just in transit. Give me doormen, concierges, porters, housekeepers and room service waiters. Chocolates on the pillow. Fresh flowers. Towel art. Trolleys with breakfast eggs under silver domes. I love the whole performance of it. The more theatrical the better, as long as it’s not a farce. It’s so much more than an Airbnb or short-term rental. Of course, there are circumstances, such as longer stays or family travels, when renting an apartment makes more sense and is more economical than a hotel room. But as a solo traveller, I don’t love staggering around in the dark in unfamiliar streets looking for the right key lock. I like a reception desk. The upkeep of historical hotels is costly, and this is reflected in the tariff. Alamy I’ve stayed in many of the world’s storied hotels, the ones that make the “world’s best” list year after year. And they are truly wonderful, especially those that have been in the hands of the same family or owners for decades. They have thought about what guests need across generations. And they’ve respected their history and invited guests to be part of the story too. Many of these, it is true, are expensive stays. The upkeep of historical hotels is costly, and this is reflected in the tariff. These days, the wealthy who tend to gravitate towards them demand more luxuries than ever. (Frankly, I like my historic hotels a little shabby.)



But if you think of value rather than price, the memory of a night in a plush hotel can be worth more than the room rate. That’s why honeymooners and people celebrating anniversaries splurge on them. If there wasn’t something inherently magical about the experience, no one would bother. Still, a hotel doesn’t have to be expensive to be good. I remember checking into a cheap airport hotel at Haneda, Tokyo, for an overnight layover and falling totally in love with the room. It was minuscule, but it had more amenities than some luxury hotels I’ve stayed in. Pyjamas. Robes. Toothbrush. Eye mask. Face creams. Coffee machine. I couldn’t get over how thoughtful the details were and how inventive they had been in providing everything I needed in such a tiny space, in simple Japanese style. Related Article Opinion

Travel tips Ten basic things even five-star hotels can’t get right Ben Groundwater Travel writer When you arrive in Fiji and the staff have spent time decorating your bed with flowers spelling your name, it’s the same thing. It’s called hospitality. A lot of effort has gone into welcoming and pleasing the guest. It doesn’t matter if a hotel has one or five stars, golden key concierges or a charming guy in a tropical shirt doing the check in, the great hotel experience is not just about a room. It’s about the world the hotel creates and the key you’re given that lets you in.

World.title: Schools adopt NCEA alternative as number of unqualified school leavers soars
World.content:
Schools adopting NCEA alternative Morning Report Download MP3 3m

As the number of school leavers with no qualifications soars, some schools are adopting an alternative to NCEA for students who need it.

They are offering the New Zealand Certificate of Foundation Skills, a qualification originally provided by polytechnics and other tertiary institutes.

Teachers from the Aotearoa Foundation Skills and Pathways Association adapted the certificate for school use and the association last year won Education Ministry funding to help more schools take it on.

They told RNZ it could slash the 19 percent of teens leaving school with no qualifications by providing an alternative for those who struggled with the regular school qualification.

Esther Williams from Pukekohe High School said like NCEA, the certificate was a 60-credit qualification at levels 1, 2 and 3.

It covered literacy and numeracy, but also skills like self-management, resilience, communication, and leadership.

Williams said the certificate offered an alternative for teens struggling to pass NCEA's literacy and numeracy tests.

"There's a group of students who either for cognitive reasons or high neurodiversity or maybe other reasons are unable to engage with the curriculum level that is required for those literacy and numeracy exams and they simply need more time to develop their literacy and numeracy skills," she said.

"We feel every student deserves a successful pathway through school. We want to keep these kids at school and allow them to finish school with a qualification and so that's why we've brought in these qualifications."

Students studying the certificate might also complete NCEA standards and some might achieve an NCEA qualification, but the foundation certificate itself set students up for tertiary study and employment.

Liz Carrick from Ashburton College said students who achieved the certificate were going into apprenticeships and even degree-level study.

"We have a class of 30 at level 2 and the motto in the classroom is nobody leaves without a job or a pathway into education," she said.

"So we don't have students leave with no qualification and we certainly don't have them leave to go and sit on a couch. We have them leave to go into really good jobs."

Carrick said students studying the certificate were more likely to turn up for class and more likely to stay in school.

"Attendance is improving remarkably, actually, across all the schools that we've been working with and that are working within the programme," she said.

"Anecdotally what we're finding is that the students that we are putting into this programme are now starting to gain confidence and so much so that rather than leave the day they turn 16, they're now wanting to come back to school at level 2 to do the level 2 qualification."

Some schools are adopting an alternative to NCEA for students who need it. 123RF

Williams said the certificate could put a huge dent in the number of students leaving school with no qualifications.

"If all schools offered this to even five pecent of their school, then that's five percent that are not going to be leaving without a qualification," she said.

"But in most schools it's about 10 percent of students that are in these programmes, the ones that are offering it, so literally we could be halving that number of students that are leaving school without a qualification in the first couple of years."

She said the certificate would become even more important when the government replaced NCEA with a less flexible qualification and even tougher literacy and numeracy settings from 2028.

Williams said the government expected its reforms would improve children's literacy and numeracy, but students now in Years 9-10 would not get the full benefit of those changes and some would struggle to get the new qualification.

Carrick said about 40 schools were at various stages of implementing the certificate.

Putting success within reach

At Taita College in Hutt Valley, Year 12 student Brooklyn said he was enjoying the school's New Zealand Certificate of Foundation Studies class.

"I really like this programme, it actually helps me," he told RNZ.

The keen sportsman (he's a sprinter and rugby player) said he would return to school for Year 13 and hoped to get an NCEA certificate as well as the foundation qualification.

Year 12 Taita College student Brooklyn says he'll return to school for Year 13. RNZ Pacific / Eleisha Foon

Nearby a teacher aide is encouraging a student to write a few more paragraphs for an assignment on leadership. Other students are working quietly.

Teacher Jenny Wooding said the class was taught parallel to NCEA but with more explicit teaching, pitched at the right level for its students.

"It means these guys get to share success because the goalposts are within reach to them. Which is so important because otherwise they'd be alienated from school because no matter how hard they tried NCEA would be just out of reach," she said.

Wooding said the class helped to ensure more teens stayed at school long enough to earn a qualification.

"We've kept them at school. These kids would be early leavers if they didn't have this stepping stone."

The class included neurodiverse students, refugees, and students who simply struggled with learning.

Wooding said the students also studied regular NCEA subjects and with the right support they experienced success.

World.title: National goes it alone on social media ban for under-16s
World.content:
National alone on social media ban for under-16s Morning Report Download MP3 3m

The prime minister and education minister's announcement the government has introduced a bill to ban social media for under-16s has caused two of the three parties in government to distance themselves from it, while it also appears to have caught Labour on the hop.

National is progressing its efforts to ban under-16 year olds from social media platforms, but so far is going it alone, unable to gather the support of its coalition partners, and Labour holding its support until it gets some more answers.

The bill puts the pressure on social media companies to take "reasonable steps" to check users are of-age, and includes the establishment of an online safety regulator and penalty regime.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon with students at the government announcement of a plan to ban social media for under 16 year olds. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

The bill was introduced to Parliament on Monday as a government bill, and announced through a government press release, even though New Zealand First and ACT confirmed they had invoked the agree to disagree provision.

With 11 sitting days to go, the prime minister admitted the bill would not get its first reading before the election.

"We've got a lot of important bills to get out the door, but then we'll pick this up on the other side of the election. But I think now this is the right thing to do," Christopher Luxon said on Monday.

Minister Stanford on proposed social media ban Morning Report Download MP3 8m

With New Zealand First and ACT long making it clear they opposed a ban, and without Labour's guaranteed support, it meant Erica Stanford brought the bill to Cabinet for sign-off knowing that National did not currently have the numbers to progress it past first reading.

It leaft Labour free to push out its decision on the bill until after November, or for New Zealand First and ACT to fight against it should there be another round of coalition negotiations.

Labour, which had released a list of 79 questions it wanted answered, was likely to discuss the bill further at Tuesday's caucus meeting, with leader Chris Hipkins open to coming to a position before the election.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Hipkins said his party would continue to engage with National on the bill "in good faith", even though the prime minister's admission the bill would not get its day in Parliament any time soon came as a surprise.

"We were working on the basis that we thought they were asking us to support it before the election. It's clear, I now understand from the press conference, not from any communication with them on it, that they don't intend to progress it," Hipkins said.

National's coalition partners were even more unimpressed with the way the bill was announced, with New Zealand First leader Winston Peters going through great pains to stress it was a National bill, not a government bill.

"Here we are having to tell a coalition partner how MMP works, and this is not how it works on this occasion. You've got two parties that aren't agreeing," he said.

ACT leader David Seymour. RNZ / Nathan McKinnon

Deputy PM David Seymour on proposed social media ban First Up Download MP3 6m

David Seymour, meanwhile, said it was National's right to "go it alone" and put the bill out before the election, and wished the party luck, but he did not believe it was a serious solution.

"I think people can judge for themselves, one party pushing through what is really an election campaign policy for themselves, at exactly the time the government needs to stick together," he said.

Seymour acknowledged on First Up that social media caused serious harm to young people.

But he said proposals such as fining social media company 10 percent of its global revenue didn't make sense.

"If you take Meta, which is Facebook and Instagram, their global revenue is $200 billion. That means that the New Zealand government would be demanding $20 billion. That's about $33 billion," he said.

"Now, if they were going to pay us that for some breach, that would be fantastic, that would put the New Zealand government way back out of deficit and into surplus for a few years, which would be great.

"But I don't think anyone seriously thinks that they would pay many times more than they've ever made doing business in New Zealand."

Seymour said France and Australia have had little success with their approach.

He said change would need to be driven by larger markers and larger governments, like what was happening in several American states.

New Zealand will benefit from the social media industry changing, but we're not actually in a position to force that, Seymour sad.

"If the New Zealand government was going to do something, I think it would be far more effective if it was to put a restriction on selling and supplying smartphones, that is something small enough to fit in a pocket, touchscreen, internet access, camera, restrict under-16s from having those.

"Let them have dumb phones so they can still keep in touch with their parents and so on. But that would be something the New Zealand government can practically enforce. It's something it could physically do within its own territory."

Luxon said it was "perfectly reasonable" that parties formed their own view of the bill, but insisted the bill was "not a political thing".

"It's actually a Kiwi thing, and that's what this is really about, and that's what we really want the other parties to think about too."

Stanford rejected an allegation from Peters that New Zealand First had only been made aware National wanted to introduce the bill on Friday, and had first seen the Cabinet paper over the weekend.

"The bill has been circulated for a number of weeks. It's been with all parties. In fact, I offered New Zealand First a full briefing with my officials, which they accepted, so they certainly have had the Cabinet papers for a really long time."

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Hipkins said it had been "difficult" to get information out of the minister, but he did not want the matter to become a political football.

"My comments here are relatively moderate. I'm a little frustrated, but they're moderate because I do want to find a way forward."

Luxon and Stanford were also keen to put politics aside, with Stanford saying Labour would get a response to its questions shortly.

"It was quite a long, detailed list. Nothing particularly insurmountable. They're just actually intelligent questions, but nothing of serious concern," she said.

"We're happy to engage with any political party on this, because it's about the kids, not about political parties per se," Luxon added.

Despite the political back-and-forth, the policy is popular with the public, even amongst supporters of parties that oppose it.

A RNZ-Reid Research poll from June 2025 had 57.8 percent of respondents say they supported a ban, with 31.6 percent opposed.

National supporters overwhelmingly agreed with a ban - 75.1 percent - while even ACT and New Zealand First supporters were also in favour.

Those invited to the announcement included students, principals, and members of the B416 campaign group, which has lobbied the government extensively for a ban.

Whangaparāoa College principal Steve McCracken, who is also chair of the Secondary Principals' Council, said there had been some success in Australia of children disengaging with social media, which he said was a good sign.

"This is a step towards trying to help our young people actually just reconnect with each other, and become better citizens overall."

Whangaparāoa College principal Steve McCracken. Supplied / Whangaparāoa College

A government fact sheet released alongside the announcement said around three in 10 children in Australia no longer had social media accounts.

The prime minister said the government was trying to make it the new normal.

"I came through an era in schooling where actually you didn't have to have a bike helmet in primary and intermediate school, and then eventually at intermediate school it became a law, or became normal, that actually everyone wears their bike helmet, and then it became abnormal when you didn't have a bike helmet on, and it's no different here."

Dr Maneesh Deva, a paediatrician but also an adviser for the B416 group, said he welcomed any action to protect children against big tech.

Paediatrician Dr Maneesh Deva is an adviser for the B416 group. Supplied / B416

"We've moved from a play-based generation to a phone-based generation. What we're seeing is really high rates of anxiety, self-harm presentations, sleep disturbance, and attention problems," he said.

"I think the kids describe it well when they say that, what are you seeing on social media? They call it brain rot. And I think they've pretty much got it right."

Not everyone in attendance was convinced.

"I don't think it's going to work. I strongly believe that people are going to find ways around it," said Naenae College student Josiah Scott.

"I think a ban is quite a privileged stance. People that can't interact, like marginalised communities, a big part of their ability to interact with each other. Disabled people who can't get out of the house as easily as most people, people who can't afford to do extra activities, aren't going to be able to connect with these people anymore," said student Lily Sang.

She said a better step would be to fund 'third spaces' better, and give teenagers a place to go and build connection.

"If you're going to take away one form of connection, you need to be able to build up spaces and make them more accessible for people."

But Queen Margaret College (QMC) student Biju Kim said she often found herself scrolling instead of studying.

Fellow QMC student Ana Bareta agreed, saying while social media could bring good things like connection, she also found herself scrolling without realising how long she had been scrolling for.

"I could have been doing study, I could have been outside, I could have been hanging out with my friends. But no, I've just been scrolling, or just on social media."

Attendees received a short heads up, with Stanford's office confirming to RNZ they were invited to an "update to the work being done to reduce online harm" late last week.

RNZ has approached TikTok and Meta. Meta declined to comment.

Stanford had pre-emptively dismissed any opposition the ban was likely to get.

"I've met with some of the tech companies, and they make all the same excuses that you would expect them to make: 'oh, but we're trying, oh, but there's worse things out there'. At which point, I say, 'what? Worse than learning how to self-harm on your platform?'.

World.title: Pensioners' growing tax bill
World.content:
People who are over the age of entitlement to NZ Super are contributing 15 percent of all personal taxes, data shows, but economists say even as that amount grows, it won't help balance the books.

Data released under the Official Information Act showed there were 268,800 working superannuitants in the most recent tax year for which data was available, and 632,300 non-working.

The working group paid $6.6 billion in tax on all income and $1.56b in tax on NZ Super.

The non-working group paid $4.24b in tax on all income and $2.6b on tax on NZ Super.

Across non-working and working superannuitants, they paid $9.84b in income tax in the 2024/2025 tax year. Of that, $4.166b was tax paid on super.

Inland Revenue said the "working" group in 2024/2025 received $772 million more in net superannuation than they paid in income tax on their other earnings, to a net transfer of an average $2872 per person.

For the non-working group, the figure was a net transfer of $19,018 per person on average.

At the other end of the scale, 14 and 15-year-olds paid $9.9m in tax in the 2024/25 year, and $7.3m in progress data for the most recent tax year.

Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold said the amount of tax paid by older taxpayers was likely to continue to grow as more people stayed in the workforce longer.

He said Stats NZ population projections were that the percentage of people aged 65 would rise from 16.5 percent in 2024 to closer to 19 percent in 2031 and just over 20 percent in 2036.

Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold. Supplied / LinkedIn

"There's more of them so, in principle, you've got the potential there for there to be more taxpayers. The other thing is that there has been a rising employment rate and participation rate of over 65s in the workforce.

"Since 2016, the proportion of the employment rate, so that's the proportion of over 65s that are in employment, has risen from 23 percent to around just under 27 percent ... that's a reasonably significant increase in the proportion of older New Zealanders that are actually working, presumably because perhaps the labour market's getting a bit easier for them relative to before. Maybe they need to work for longer. Maybe they just want to work for longer as well."

He said, because New Zealand did not reduce a person's NZ Super entitlement if they were still working, there was not the disincentive to keep working that might be there in other countries.

He said while young people's employment had dropped in recent years, that was likely to reflect the economic environment and would change again as it improved. Older people working were more of a structural shift, he said.

Shamubeel Eaqub, principal economist at the New Zealand Institute of Economic Research Supplied

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub said some older people were working because they wanted to but others had little choice.

But he said the net effect was still that over 65s consumed more in public services than they contributed in taxes.

Treasury work showed children and people aged over 65 generally received more in government support than they paid in tax, while working age people paid more than they received.

That would continue even as the number of working older people increased. "The sheer volume of people in those older and especially oldest age groups balloons the costs.

"Rising older people's participation in work and thus increased tax contributions via income tax and also GST - because they are likely to spend more - helps improve the revenue side of the ledger. Just not enough to fix the fiscal math - which still doesn't work."

Eckhold agreed. "The reality is that even though there'll be more people working over 65, there will be a limit to when you can work to. And healthcare costs are rising … we're getting better treatments, more expensive treatments, people have higher expectations about what they can do now. So that all costs money."

World.title: RNZ-Reid Research poll: Did National make the wrong call keeping Luxon?
World.content:
National's decision to stick with Christopher Luxon appears at odds with the wider public, with more voters saying the caucus got it wrong than right.

The latest RNZ-Reid Research poll gauged voters' views on National's emergency caucus meeting two weeks ago, where a majority of MPs opted to keep Luxon as leader, foiling a bid to replace him.

Asked whether that was the right call, 45.4 percent of respondents said no, compared with 36.8 percent who said yes.

Another 17.8 percent were unsure.

National supporters were the most likely to support Luxon, with 78 percent endorsing his continued leadership, against just 11.5 percent who disagreed.

ACT voters were less emphatic - with 54.2 percent in support of the decision to keep Luxon and 28.7 percent opposed.

In contrast, New Zealand First voters leant against Luxon staying on, with 52.4 percent saying National MPs made the wrong decision, compared with 31.6 percent who backed them.

Labour and Green supporters were much more likely to say National got it wrong, with 64.6 percent and 69.8 percent respectively registering their disapproval.

The poll also asked those who wanted Luxon gone who they would have picked to take over from a selection of names discussed during the recent leadership turmoil.

Erica Stanford was the most popular name, at 16.6 percent, narrowly ahead of Chris Bishop on 15.2 percent.

Nicola Willis was third on 9 percent, followed by Chris Penk on 7.6 percent.

But the largest share by far went to 'none of the above', selected by 39.6 percent.

A further 13.3 percent said they did not know.

Following the failed leadership coup, Luxon sacked Chris Penk from Cabinet, declaring that the rogue MP had acted alone in challenging the prime ministership.

But sources within and close to the party connected Stanford to the failed bid.

In the aftermath, Stanford denied any involvement, but prior to the meeting, she stayed silent when repeatedly asked by reporters if she had confidence in Luxon.

Bishop and Willis were also believed to be positioning themselves if the party leadership was vacated.

Both declared loyalty to Luxon before and after the caucus meeting.

World.title: Man due in court following two assaults including alleged stabbing
World.content:
A 38-year-old man is due to appear in the Hastings District Court after two assaults in Flaxmere.

In the first incident on Monday morning, a person was taken to hospital after an assault on Kirkwood road.

They are in a critical condition.

A short time later, police were made aware of a second assault in the Flaxmere area where another person suffered stab wounds.

They were not seriously injured.

World.title: Could Bitcoin collapse?
World.content:
Could cryptocurrencies actually collapse?

Actor Ben McKenzie has released a documentary calling cryptocurrencies stupid, four years after telling the US senate that they were the "largest Ponzi scheme in history".

While McKenzie is vocal about his wish to take down cryptocurrency, even local supporters say it's possible that at least some of them could see their value go to zero. But which, and why?

Cryptocurrencies are a decentralised form of digital currency that can be used for transactions between individuals, but are most commonly held as an investment asset. It is even possible to invest in cryptocurrency via KiwiSaver, such as through Koura's bitcoin fund.

Bitcoin is the best known currency but there are a large number in circulation including Ethereum and Ripple.

Bitcoin's price has fallen from a peak of more than NZ$210,000 late last year to NZ$128,489.

Bitcoin's price has fallen from a peak of more than NZ$210,000 late last year to NZ$128,489. Jonathan Raa / NurPhoto via AFP

Ethereum has dropped from about NZ$7500 this time last year to $4000.

The values can move a lot because they are not backed by any government, and the price is set by supply and demand factors rather than any specific use case.

Rupert Carlyon, founder of Koura, said there was a scenario where Bitcoin values could fall to zero.

"Do I think that's likely? No, I think that there is too much behind it now. And I think that Bitcoin has become a little bit of the gold standard and the piece that sits in behind the whole industry. Would I be entirely surprised if one of those second-tier layers fell to zero? No, not, whether it be Ethereum, Alana, Avalanche, Ripple.

"Will there be one of those that ends up as the winner or maybe two of them as the winner and a few of the others turn into the Alta Vista of the search game? Yes. But Bitcoin kind of just seems to stand out on its own and be the bellwether of where it's at.

"And it's got so much institutional backing now, it's hard to see it going anywhere else."

Some commentators have suggested the recent fall in value is because people who would have previously invested in cryptocurrencies have withdrawn money to move to AI stocks.

University of Auckland professor Alex Sims said if enough holders sold and switched their investments, that had the highest chance of sending the value of cryptocurrencies to zero.

"I'm not sure that will actually occur, reasonably switched on crypto holders will be wary of the AI bubble. Plus, there is a lot of institutional holding of crypto. But if some of those large institutional investors do decide to sell as well, then crypto has a chance of going to zero."

Carlyon said the situation was complicated. "For a long time, crypto kind of stood out on its own as a high-risk investment play.

"Investors have got a range of things. They've got the AI stuff… personally I disagree with the hypothesis that tech is speculation, but that's a different point. You've got these chip makers that are growing at 50 percent, 100 percent a year…. Assets that are showing absolutely phenomenal, abnormal returns. You've also got Polymarket and what is happening in the betting markets where online gambling and online betting is getting bigger and bigger every day.

"There are other things that are looking for that retail investor's desire for cash… personally I think it's oversimplifying it, though. There are clearly other demands there and there hasn't been a massive story for Bitcoin over the last six to 12 months."

The currencies can be very volatile. Bitcoin was worth less than NZ$30,000 in late 2022.

"The low level of liquidity means that a slight change in the narrative makes very strong changes in where we're at. The narrative has changed because we've got increased action out of the White House, but also the whole debasement of the US dollar with Treasury Secretary Besson talking about how the US government twill start buying bonds, basically moving us back into a money printing world in order to keep interest rates low," Carlyon said.

He said some people might have switched their attention to stablecoins, which could have affected demand for bitcoin. Stablecoins are designed to have steady value by being linked to an asset like the US or NZ dollar.

"If you think about it, a lot of people are using Bitcoin as a way to hold value, as a way to kind of avoid the banking system … you can now do that with stablecoins. That is probably one of the things just rattling around in the back of my mind going, actually, will stablecoins supplant Bitcoin?

"Stablecoins are never going to be the protection against inflation… But if you just want to hold value somewhere that's outside of the banking system that you can access and move around freely, stablecoins give you all of that."

Sims said the death of bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies had been proclaimed "many, many times".

She said another scenario that could send values to zero would be if there was a breakthrough in quantum computing that meant private keys were compromised and bitcoin could be stolen.

"As I've said many times over the years, if quantum computing does advance rapidly so that it defeats encryption, before post quantum encryption is put in place, then cryptocurrencies are the least of our worries. Why? Likely that the water, power, money in your bank accounts, supply chains etc and most other things will go offline as they all involve the use of encryption. "

"There could be fatal flaws or code vulnerabilities in different blockchains. The issue with this is that it would be individual blockchains, and there are thousands of them. It would have to be a flaw in Bitcoin or Ethereum to really have an impact, the occasional blockchain/crypto going down doesn't mean anything."

She said anything that was not tangible had a risk of going to zero.

"Which is why gold and silver have increased in price over the past year or so, as they are hard assets. Also, of course, because of the risk of intangible assets going to zero, that's why diversification is sensible. "

World.title: Neonatal nurse on why infant mental health matters
World.content:
Dressed in colourful scrubs and yellow Crocs, neonatal nurse practitioner Fiona Dineen is a pop of colour against the stark white hospital walls.

Wellington Hospital's Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) can be a scary place for families, awash with bright lights, beeps, monitors and feeding tubes.

But nowadays, infant mental health is treated as equally important to physical symptoms, meaning parents are tasked with playing a big role in hospital-based care.

Dineen has been caring for sick newborns for nearly three decades, two of those in Wellington.

A baby in Wellington Hospital's NICU. Supplied / Health NZ

She was 2025's Neonatal Nurses College of Aotearoa Quality and Innovation Award winner, for leading work to ensure babies in NICU were cared for not just physically, but emotionally and relationally too.

She told RNZ that, although "infant mental health" might conjure images of a baby lying on a therapist's couch, the first thousand days of their lives were crucial for their brain development.

"Within the neonatal unit, some of our babies can be here for up to six months and very seldom sometimes a year," she said, when RNZ visited the unit one Friday morning in August.

"So we have this opportunity of supporting babies with their brain growth, their emotional status, their connections, their attachments with their parents. And that's what infant mental health is."

That hadn't always been a priority, she said.

"Thirty years ago, parents weren't allowed into the neonatal units. They had viewing platforms where they would come and look at their baby through a window and they weren't allowed to have hands-on touching with their babies."

Paediatric nurse Fiona Dineen in front of Wellington Hospital. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

But these days, parents formed an integral part of the care team.

"Yes, you need the technology," said Dineen. "Yes, you need the medicine. But with the parents being the main caregivers to their babies and teaching them how to do that, it makes the trajectory even more complete and babies get discharged a lot quicker when we have parents more active."

Alex and Zach Thompson from Wairarapa were new parents to twins, Isabella and Leo.

"So we're mostly here all day," said Alex. "The only time I really leave is to eat food. I spend most of the day with them, sometimes cuddling one or the other, and sometimes we do double cuddles, which is nice."

She said it wasn't how she had pictured starting life as a parent. She had spent the first few days in hospital herself, and now they were staying in the Ronald McDonald House across the road from the hospital.

"It's still hard," Alex said. "Having that different routine because you do expect to just go home with your baby and start life as a family, but we've had to do it slightly differently."

Wellington Hospital's Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU). Supplied / Health NZ

One-on-one time with the babies was important, and it was clear the babies thought so too.

"They realise that it's been a certain amount of time since we last had a cuddle and they either get fidgety or grumpy - and you can tell."

And their personalities were already shining through.

"Leo is definitely a mama's boy," she said. "He's quite soft, you know, he is really just a sweetie. Whereas Isabella, she's tiny but she's fierce and she'll tell you how it is even if she can't talk yet."

Jaydene Latu has a baby girl, Shekinah.

She was born at 23 weeks, the length of her mother's forearm, weighing 335 grams - the nappies she wore when she arrived would fit in the palm of your hand.

Her birth 10 weeks ago had been touch-and-go.

World.title: Water, sewage and solar top new survey of infrastructure priorities
World.content:
Water supply, sewage, solar and flood protection have topped the list of infrastructure priorities for Kiwis, according to global research company Ipsos.

The company conducts global research on attitudes towards infrastructure investment and has released its latest two yearly findings on how New Zealand shapes up.

It showed that water and sewage had emerged as the top investment concern for Kiwis, with 47 percent ranking it the most important.

That's followed by solar energy infrastructure on 40 percent and flood protection at 39 percent.

Ipsos country manager Carin Hercock said the results were a shift from the survey two years ago, when housing supply was the number one infrastructure concern for Kiwis.

However, Hercock said housing supply was now back at number six.

"We have definitely seen a shift towards more resilient types of infrastructure. Water supply and sewage is sitting at number one at 47 percent, but solar energy has jumped up to number two and they were number six just two years ago," Hercock said.

Hercock said the change could be a good message ahead of the election, with New Zealanders' priorities moving towards more sustainable things.

In general, more Kiwis were dissatisfied than satisfied with infrastructure in New Zealand.

The Ipsos survey found that 41 percent were dissatisfied with national infrastructure, compared with 31 percent that were satisfied.

The global average for satisfaction with infrastructure was 38 percent.

"We did see, our satisfaction with infrastructure was quite high prior to Cyclone Gabrielle and then it dropped significantly after that event and I think it potentially showed we could be really vulnerable to infrastructure during national disasters, and we haven't really recovered since that time, although it has improved statistically significantly in the last two years," Hercock said.

Over two-thirds, or 69 percent, of Kiwis felt the country was not doing enough to meet its infrastructure needs, while only 21 percent believed New Zealand had a good record of delivering national infrastructure projects.

When it came to paying more for infrastructure, just 41 percent supported higher taxes or consumer costs, with Kiwis generally most likely to favour a combination of public and private funding models.

World.title: Swan's assistant takes-over as Essendon coach
World.content:
Mark McVeigh, a former Essendon player and Sydney assistant coach, will take over as Essendon's senior coach after what the club said was an "extensive" and "deliberate" selection process.

McVeigh, 45, won the role ahead of Bombers great and ex-coach James Hird, as well as Jaymie Graham and Murray Davis.

Essendon confirmed the announcement on Monday afternoon, a day after the stricken club's narrow loss to Port Adelaide.

McVeigh would take over "effective immediately", the club said in a statement.

The official announcement came following a day of speculation and a message of congratulations from former teammate and Bomber's legend, James Hird.

"I put my heart and soul into the effort, but obviously fell short and that's the way it goes," Hird said on Nine yesterday night.

James Hird (L) and Dean Solomon (C) speak with Mark McVeigh (R). (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

Brad Scott was sacked on May 25, with Dean Solomon taking over as interim coach for the rest of the season.

Solomon rounded out the Bomber's worst season in club history with a 10-point defeat to Port Adelaide on Sunday.

McVeigh commits to building Essendon's 'next great era'

The search for a new coach has involved a tumultuous selection process, with opinion sharply divided on whether Hird should win another tenure in the role.

Club president Andrew Welsh, who played at Essendon alongside McVeigh and Hird, said the appointment was a unanimous board decision.

"Mark was clearly the best candidate for what this role demands," Welsh said on the club website.

"We are building the next successful era for Essendon, with a view to playing finals, winning finals and competing for premierships.

"We weighed every candidate against what this role actually demands, and Mark was the clear stand-out."

Hird congratulates McVeigh A 'very disappointed' James Hird congratulates former teammate Mark McVeigh, as the Bombers prepare to unveil their new coach.

McVeigh played 232 games for Essendon and returns to the club on a three-year contract after nearly 14 years away, which also included working as an assistant coach at the Greater Western Sydney Giants.

He also acted as caretaker coach at the Giants in 2022.

"We're not looking backwards, we're building the next great era of this football club," McVeigh said.

"That's not built on promises. It's built on our standards, our actions and the work we put in every single day."

AAP/ABC

World.title: Matildas star receives rousing welcome in return after mother's death
World.content:
Matildas midfielder Kyra Cooney-Cross has played her first match in more than five months after taking time away from football to spend time with her mother before her death.

Cooney-Cross was sent on in the 63rd minute as Arsenal recorded a 1-0 pre-season win over Paris FC in Borehamwood.

The 67-time international recorded her first minutes since the 2026 AFC Women's Asian Cup final in March, when she started in the Matildas' 1-0 loss to Japan in Sydney.

Cooney-Cross announced on January 8 via Instagram that her mother Jessica Cooney was diagnosed with terminal Stage 4 bile duct cancer. She died on July 10.

Arsenal manager Renee Slegers confirmed on March 28 Cooney-Cross was granted indefinite compassionate leave and would remain in Australia after the Asian Cup to be with her mother.

"You're my biggest inspiration and the person I aspire to be," Cooney-Cross wrote on social media after her mother's death.

"Mum, my favourite part is knowing that I'm a little piece of you."

The 24-year-old returned to Arsenal's pre-season training on August 17, with the Gunners' Women's Super League campaign set to begin on Sunday evening against former Socceroo Dario Vidosic's Brighton & Hove Albion.

Cooney-Cross received a rousing ovation at Meadow Park as she was substituted on alongside compatriot Steph Catley.

Loading Instagram content

The former A-League Women's star with Melbourne Victory and Western Sydney Wanderers was involved in the build up to Canadian attacker Olivia Smith's 91st minute winner.

Arsenal's final pre-season match is against Charlton Athletic on August 26.

The Addicks signed Australian trio Emily van Egmond, who marked a national record 170 international appearances during the AFC Women's Asian Cup, alongside fellow Matildas midfielder Leah Davidson and youth international Grace Johnston, following the club's promotion from the Women's Super League 2 in May.

Meanwhile, goalkeeper Jada Whyman is returning to A-League club Sydney FC after a stint in Sweden.

Whyman is yet to play for the Matildas but has been selected in multiple national squads.

World.title: England bowler Brydon Carse under investigation over nightclub video
World.content:
England bowler Brydon Carse is being investigated over an incident in Derby on Saturday night, according to the England and Wales ​Cricket Board (ECB).

Videos circulating on social media appear to show the Durham bowler in handcuffs being led away from a club by police officers.

"We are aware of an incident which is reported to have taken place in Derby last night and we are currently investigating," an ECB spokesperson said.

"We ​will provide a ‌further update when possible."

Carse is part ‌of England's squad for the second Test against Pakistan starting next ⁠week at Lord's.

He was not on England duty at ‌the time of the alleged ​incident after being an ‌unused member of the squad for the first Test, which England won comfortably at Headingley.

Bazball's complex legacy Brendon McCullum deliberately set out to make England's men's Test team a less complicated team to play cricket for. After four years of Bazball's highs and lows, it leaves a very complicated legacy.

The investigation comes five days after England's returning Test captain Joe Root spoke of the players being "really good role models and ​human ‌beings" after a series of incidents and accusations of a drinking culture.

Controversy has followed England around in recent times with off-field ⁠issues during last winter's tours, including ‌Harry Brook being fined £30,000 ($57,200) after ‌an altercation with a bouncer in Wellington as well as reports of drinking ‌during a mid-Ashes trip to Noosa.

This summer Ben Stokes broke a team curfew along with Gus Atkinson, with the pair ‌dropped ​from the second Test ⁠against New Zealand at the Oval.

Former Test captain Stokes eventually announced his retirement from international cricket while Brendon McCullum was sacked as Test coach, with Root confirming that the team had done away with the curfews under new coach Stephen Fleming.

The ECB would not confirm whether Carse was still ⁠in the squad for the second test against Pakistan. Reuters has contacted Carse's county side Durham ‌to request comment ‌from the player.

In 2024, South Africa-born Carse was suspended ​from cricket for three months for historic betting offences.

World.title: 'I'm a has-been': Injury ends Broncos captain Adam Reynolds's career
World.content:
Brisbane Broncos captain Adam Reynolds will end his NRL career sidelined by injury after failing a fitness test ahead of Thursday's game against the Melbourne Storm.

The Broncos have two games left, but the Storm clash marks their final home game of the year.

Reynolds had hoped to overcome a calf injury to play on Thursday and bid farewell to the stadium he has called home since 2022.

"I trained today, obviously thought I'd be a chance to play one last home game and then hand it over to the rest of the boys to finish off the season," he told Triple M.

"But it's not to be. … I'm officially a has-been."

Initially struggling with nerve issues in his left calf, Reynolds then suffered a strain in his right calf.

Reynolds said he "felt pretty good" during the training session, but the call was made for him to not play.

"I had some conversations with Madge [coach Michael Maguire] and the medical staff and they were quite concerned with the limited training I've done in the past couple of weeks," he in a club statement.

Reynolds has endured a number of lower-body injuries over his career and has not played since suffering a concussion in round 22 against the Knights.

"You wanna play the game forever but that's not reality," the 36-year-old said.

"The reality is you get old and you get brittle and at the end of the day you can't keep competing forever. I knew this day was coming, I knew in the back of my mind that I had to say goodbye at some stage and unfortunately it's today."

Reynolds confirmed 2026 would be his last year in the league before the season started.

The diminutive halfback played 323 NRL games over 15 seasons and is the league's second-highest point-scorer with 2,598 points.

He leaves the game as a two-time premiership winner — in 2014 with South Sydney and 2025 with Brisbane — and a State of Origin player.

"I've had a great career," he said.

"I'm extremely fortunate I get to carry some great memories moving forward."

World.title: Zak Butters informs Port Adelaide he will depart club
World.content:
Port Adelaide's three-time best and fairest winner Zak Butters has requested to leave the club via free agency and return home to Victoria.

The 25-year-old dual All-Australian's future has dominated headlines all season with reports of offers of up to $18 million over eight years from Richmond, Geelong, Collingwood and the Western Bulldogs.

"I've made a decision to head home. It's obviously been one that I've wrestled with for a while now," he said.

"It's been a tough decision and one that I haven't taken lightly.

"Although I've loved my time in Adelaide … I'm probably at a stage in my life where I'd like to get back around some family and friends and enjoy some more time with them.

"There are so many special memories I'll take with me and hold with me forever … I'll be forever in debt to the football club for drafting a skinny club from Darley."

Butters said he would "always be a Port Adelaide person" and would "always value this club and what it's done for me".

"The supporters have been everything, they've always got around since day one of being drafted, even this year they've been awesome and showed nothing but love and support," he said.

"I feel like I've always tried to repay them in the right way and play football in the right way."

Zak Butters is a dual all-Australian. (Supplied: Port Adelaide Football Club)

In a club statement, the Power said they would now work to facilitate his request whilst securing the best outcome for the club.

"Port Adelaide has been informed by Zak Butters and his management that he intends to exercise his rights as a restricted free agent and explore a return home to Victoria," the statement said.

"Zak has been an outstanding servant to the football club since debuting in 2019.

"He is a three-time John Cahill Medallist and dual All-Australian and we thank him for everything he has given to Port Adelaide."

ABC Sport reported Zak Butters had informed some teammates in June of his decision to move to Victoria; a story that was denied by the club at the time.

Butters played 17 games this season before a syndesmosis injury in Round 18 prematurely ended his campaign, with coach Josh Carr admitting the star midfielder was likely departing after their 10-point win over Essendon on the weekend.

Port Adelaide has been adamant all season they would match any bid on Butters and force a trade to try maximise their draft capital.

Speaking to ABC Sport in May, chief executive Matthew Richardson said the club would focus on their best interests.

"There will be offers that we can match and we will match. It does give the club a fair bit of control in what happens," he said.

World.title: Ex-NBA player who says he identifies as woman ejected from WNBA game
World.content:
Former NBA centre Enes Kanter Freedom has been ejected from an Indiana-Chicago WNBA game after Sky guard Natasha Cloud yelled and pointed in his direction late in the third quarter.

Freedom was sitting along the baseline on Sunday night (Monday AEST). He had on a black shirt that read "WOMAN noun. adult human female".

The Fever called for a timeout after Cloud scored with 1:22 left in the third. Cloud then went to confront Kanter, who held his arms out and took one step on the court. Security and a handful of Sky players stepped in between the two before the dispute escalated.

Freedom was then escorted from the court area. He displayed his shirt as he walked toward the lobby. He had a conversation with a group of police officers before departing Wintrust Arena.

Sky coach Tyler Marsh said the team had rallied around Cloud.

"Tash didn't wanna feel like she was a distraction and I told her she wasn't," he said.

"I told her that we all embrace her as someone that protects our team and protects people that need to be protected. Tash is always going to stand on that, and we stand for Tash."

Freedom and Royce White, another former NBA player, declared themselves eligible for the WNBA draft this month, saying they identified as women.

The argument that's hijacking the WNBA Sophie Cunningham insists she wants to protect the sanctity of women's sport, but her comments have opened her league up to an unprecedented attack.

"I'm transgender. I'm a woman … I identify as sometimes identifying as a woman for purposes of … professional basketball," White previously said.

"I think I'd be unstoppable."

Freedom said he and his team had reviewed the WNBA's eligibility criteria and its approach to self-identification and inclusion, and argued that if declaring an identity were sufficient, then he met the requirements to compete.

The confrontation came in a game that Indiana star Sophie Cunningham was playing in. Cunningham previously voiced support for barring transgender girls and women from girls' and women's sports in an extensive ESPN profile.

"I got a lot of negative feedback about me hating trans," Cunningham said.

"And I'm like, 'I never once said that.' I think that I am here to extend love.

"But I also think with that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men."

Protesters from both sides of the argument have gathered outside a number of WNBA games, with fans at the Sky-Fever game calling out Kanter as he entered the arena.

Sophie Cunningham (left) has been at the centre of the controversy, highlighted by Enes Kanter's (right) stunt. (Getty Images: Michael Reaves)

One was heard telling the former NBA centre to get his "bitch ass out of Chicago", while another said "I'm not touching him I'm just saying f*** you, bitch".

"Knowing that rallies are happening on both sides shows the platform that the W has and the stunts for attention are just continuing to try and ride the wave that we have,” New York Liberty star Breanna Stewart said.

"I want Liberty fans and even Indy fans that are going to come here tonight to be able to have this arena be a safe space."

There has never been a transgender woman player in the WNBA.

Commissioner Cathy Engelbert last week denounced people she said were trying to "sow divisiveness" over the issue.

Engelbert's comments in a pre-game gathering before a Fever-Wings game in Dallas were her first public remarks since the league called out what it said were bad faith efforts to use the debate to "demean or marginalise others".

"People are trying to use the league to sow divisiveness," Engelbert said.

"We're being the centre of political football for people who have never watched the WNBA, never have written about the WNBA or reported on the WNBA."

The league's collective bargaining agreement states that "only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA", but it does not include any more specific language about gender identity or sex assigned at birth.

Engelbert sent a memo this month to team presidents and general managers saying the league would discuss the subject of transgender women in women's basketball.

"There's always going to be haters out there and we denounce it," Engelbert said last week.

"But that's what happens when you have made it as a legitimate sports media and entertainment product."

World.title: AFL boss says suspended Swans will not be invited to Brownlow ceremony
World.content:
AFL boss Andrew Dillon has spoken to the media about the Sydney Swans scandal, saying "the actions of a few don't define the actions of the entire industry".

Dillon was at the launch of the men's AFL finals series and the first-ever wildcard round but was mainly asked about the AFL's handling of the Sydney Swans scandal, as well as details on allegations of drug use by the players.

Players Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon have been stood down by the Sydney Swans for breaching the club's standards on drinking and staying out late after last Sunday's win over Essendon in Melbourne.

Police from Victoria's sexual crimes squad are separately investigating a report of sexual assault, which the ABC understands centres on a player allegedly touching a woman without her consent.

A police investigation is still underway, but no charges have been laid or arrests made.

Dillon and the AFL released a statement on Tuesday evening, the day after the story emerged, but today marked the first time Dillon or any of the league's higher-ups had fronted the media on the matter.

Chief executive Dillon said it was fair to say the scandal had "overshadowed" the start of the finals, but that he hoped football could bring people together, as evidenced by the emotional scenes after the Swans' men's and women's double header at the SCG on Sunday.

Swans fans descend on SCG amid club scandal Sydney Swans fans react to an emotional week, where a scandal continues to engulf the club, as they prepare to watch a historic double header at the SCG.

"The actions of a few do not take away from the thousands of people involved in football at all different levels who do great things all the time," he said.

"But what we do know is that we can do things better and we will continue to do that and we will continue to learn to be better.

"I think the actions of a few don't define the actions of the entire industry."

Dillon said the five suspended players would not be invited to the Brownlow Medal ceremony, held on the Monday before the grand final, but remained eligible for the award.

Dillon said the league would not conduct its own enquiries into the incident until after the police investigation was finished.

On Saturday, police provided an update about the investigation being undertaken by detectives from the Sexual Crimes Squad.

"The exact circumstances of the matter are still being established, and a number of people have been spoken to," the statement read.

"As the investigation remains active and ongoing, we will not be commenting further, including providing information on the specific circumstances of the matter, movements of detectives and any statements or interviews taken."

In a statement, the Sydney Swans said the club "supports the action taken by Victoria Police in releasing today's statement regarding the investigation".

The club's statement also addressed comments relating to other men, beyond the five players identified by the club, being present in the hotel room at the centre of the allegations.

"The Sydney Swans categorically confirms that no member of staff is involved in the investigation. This includes being in the hotel room central to the police investigation," it read.

"The club reiterates that no player has been interviewed by police at this stage."

Live Moment Look back at how ABC readers and other Australians responded to this live moment. That's the end of the press conference 'It is a privilege to play AFL': Dillon Dillon is asked a follow up whether the five named players relating to the scandal have been held accountable. "There's been accountability for those players," he says. "It is a privilege to play AFL and with that comes responsibilities." AFL has reviewed illicit drugs policy Dillon is asked whether the alleged drug use that has created part of the story around the Swans scandal has prompted a rethink over the league's illicit drugs policy. "We've just undergone an extensive review of the illicit drugs policy," Dillon says. "That will be taking effect from this off season. "There's accountability for the players and there will continue to be." Show more

World.title: Runner smashes half-marathon record, heads straight to the football
World.content:
Yomif Kejelcha has smashed the half-marathon world record, running a staggering 56 minutes and 51 seconds at the Media Maratón Ciudad de Buenos Aires in Argentina on Sunday.

The Ethiopian shaved 29 seconds off the previous mark of 57:20, which had been set by Uganda's Jacob Kiplimo in Lisbon in March.

Kejelcha's time and that of the record he just beat are still subject to ratification by World Athletics.

The Media Maratón Ciudad de Buenos Aires is a World Athletics Label road race and took place under favourable conditions of 6 degrees Celsius and with a slight breeze.

As ever, the super shoe gets plenty of post-race love from Yomif Kejelcha. (Instagram: @maratondebuenosaires)

Tadese Worku (59:20) and Bereket Nega (1:00:20) of Ethiopia completed the podium.

"I'm over the moon," Kejelcha told World Athletics.

"I'm super happy and right now I don't feel any tiredness. The travel from Ethiopia was too long and I was tired the first days here, but later I felt better and today I was full of beans.

"I had planned to run conservatively over the early stages, but I felt good and decided to give it my all.

"This time is unbelievable. I can't describe it with words.

"I now hope to try the Argentinian meat, which has a very good reputation, and this afternoon I have been invited to watch the River Plate-Vélez football match. I'm very grateful."

At the historic Estadio Monumental, Kejelcha showed off his new record on a new River Plate shirt, although would have been disappointed as Vélez Sarsfield came from 2-0 down to draw 2-2 in their Argentine Primera División clash.

Clearly Los Millonarios don't share Kejelcha's stamina.

Yomif Kejelcha showed off his record on a new River Plate kit at at the Estadio Monumental. (Instagram: @maratondebuenosaires)

Kejelcha's time allowed him to reclaim the record, which he previously held with a 57:30 in Valencia in October 2024.

The time is slower than that recorded by Kiplimo in Barcelona last year, when he ran what he described as "the perfect race" to stop the clock in 56:42.

But World Athletics did not ratify that time because race conditions did not comply with their regulations.

Kejelcha ran the race at an average pace of 2 minutes and 42 seconds per kilometre — which would give you a 5km parkrun time of 13 minutes and 28 seconds.

However, as was the case when he became the second man to run an official race marathon in less than two hours in London last year, he negative split the race, running the second half faster than the first.
